The user wants to learn "HFT" (or, if blank, you choose the most valuable concept to teach next based on their progress and this project's code). This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

import argparse
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Tuple

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yfinance as yf
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
import joblib

"""Paper trading backtest using yfinance and Gradient Boosting.

Summary
- Downloads daily OHLCV data with yfinance for a list of tickers.
- Builds simple technical features per ticker (returns, moving averages, RSI).
- Splits each ticker's history into train/test by time, trains one model,
  and produces out-of-sample predictions on the test segment for every ticker.
- Forms a daily long-only portfolio by picking the top-N predicted names and
  rolls the equity curve forward net of a simple trade cost.

Usage
- Example: python paper_trading_sim.py --tickers AAPL,MSFT,NVDA --start 2019-01-01 --out_csv equity.csv
- All data fetching is via yfinance (Option 1), so no separate data step required.
"""


def _rsi(series: pd.Series, window: int = 14) -> pd.Series:
    """Compute a simple RSI indicator.

    Args:
        series: Price series (e.g., close).
        window: RSI lookback window.

    Returns:
        RSI values in [0, 100] as a Series.
    """
    delta = series.diff()
    gain = (delta.clip(lower=0)).rolling(window).mean()
    loss = (-delta.clip(upper=0)).rolling(window).mean()
    rs = gain / (loss.replace(0, np.nan))
    rsi = 100 - (100 / (1 + rs))
    return rsi


def build_features(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Create per-ticker features and 1-day-ahead return target.

    Features: close price, 1d return, 5/10d MAs, MA gap, 10d volatility,
    and RSI(14). The target is next-day return (fwd_ret_1d).

    Args:
        df: Ticker-level OHLCV DataFrame from yfinance with column 'Close'.

    Returns:
        Feature frame indexed by date with column 'fwd_ret_1d' as target.
    """
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
    out["close"] = df["Close"]
    out["ret_1d"] = out["close"].pct_change()
    out["ma_5"] = out["close"].rolling(5).mean()
    out["ma_10"] = out["close"].rolling(10).mean()
    out["ma_gap"] = (out["ma_5"] / out["ma_10"]) - 1
    out["vol_10"] = out["ret_1d"].rolling(10).std()
    out["rsi_14"] = _rsi(out["close"], 14) / 100.0
    out["fwd_ret_1d"] = out["ret_1d"].shift(-1)
    return out.dropna()


def chunk(lst: List[str], n: int) -> List[List[str]]:
    """Split a list into batches of size n (last may be smaller)."""
    return [lst[i : i + n] for i in range(0, len(lst), n)]

-- =============================================================================
-- @file    market_maker.vhd
-- @brief   Fixed-point market-making spread engine
-- @detail  Given a live bid price and ask price, computes the mid-price and
--          derives a buy quote and a sell quote separated by a configurable
--          spread.  Arithmetic uses Q16.16 fixed-point (signed 32-bit integers
--          where the lower 16 bits represent the fractional part).
--
--          Formula:
--            mid_price  = (bid_price_in + ask_price_in) / 2
--            buy_price  = mid_price - spread_in / 2
--            sell_price = mid_price + spread_in / 2
--
--          Pipeline: 1 clock cycle latency.
--          valid_in asserted for exactly one cycle triggers one output cycle.
--
-- @author  HFT Practice Project
-- @version 1.0
--
-- @note    Q16.16 encoding:
--            real_value = integer_signal / 65536
--            e.g. $100.50  ->  100.50 * 65536 = 6_586_368  (0x0064_8000)
--                 spread $0.01 ->  0.01 * 65536 =       655  (0x0000_028F)
--
-- @note    Synthesizable with Vivado 2022.1+; targets Artix-7 / Kintex-7 /
--          UltraScale+ devices.  No floating-point DSP required.
-- =============================================================================

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

-- =============================================================================
-- Entity
-- =============================================================================
entity market_maker is
    port (
        -- Clock / reset
        clk          : in  std_logic;                     -- Rising-edge clock
        rst_n        : in  std_logic;                     -- Active-low sync reset

        -- Input prices (Q16.16 fixed-point, signed 32-bit)
        bid_price_in : in  signed(31 downto 0);           -- Best bid price
        ask_price_in : in  signed(31 downto 0);           -- Best ask price
        spread_in    : in  signed(31 downto 0);           -- Desired order spread

        -- Input handshake
        valid_in     : in  std_logic;                     -- Input data valid

        -- Output quotes (Q16.16 fixed-point, signed 32-bit)
        buy_price_out  : out signed(31 downto 0);         -- Computed buy  quote
        sell_price_out : out signed(31 downto 0);         -- Computed sell quote

        -- Output handshake
        order_valid_out : out std_logic                   -- Output data valid
    );
end entity market_maker;

-- =============================================================================
-- Architecture
-- =============================================================================
architecture rtl of market_maker is

    -- Internal registered pipeline signals
    signal mid_price   : signed(31 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal half_spread : signed(31 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal buy_price_r : signed(31 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal sell_price_r: signed(31 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal valid_r     : std_logic            := '0';

    -- Wider accumulator to avoid overflow during (bid + ask) addition
    signal bid_plus_ask : signed(32 downto 0) := (others => '0');

begin

    -- =========================================================================
    -- Registered 1-cycle pipeline
    -- All arithmetic is performed combinatorially then registered on the
    -- rising edge, giving a clean single-cycle latency with no glitching.
    -- =========================================================================
    pipeline_reg : process(clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            if rst_n = '0' then
                mid_price    <= (others => '0');
                half_spread  <= (others => '0');
                buy_price_r  <= (others => '0');
                sell_price_r <= (others => '0');
                valid_r      <= '0';
            else
                valid_r <= valid_in;

                if valid_in = '1' then
                    -- Extend by one bit to hold the carry from addition, then
                    -- arithmetic right-shift by 1 to divide by 2.
                    bid_plus_ask <= resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33);
                    mid_price    <= resize(
                                        shift_right(
                                            resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33),
                                            1),
                                        32);

                    -- half_spread = spread_in / 2  (arithmetic right shift)
                    half_spread  <= shift_right(spread_in, 1);

                    -- buy  quote = mid - half_spread
                    -- sell quote = mid + half_spread
                    buy_price_r  <= shift_right(
                                        resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33),
                                        1)(31 downto 0)
                                    - shift_right(spread_in, 1);

                    sell_price_r <= shift_right(
                                        resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33),
                                        1)(31 downto 0)
                                    + shift_right(spread_in, 1);
                end if;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process pipeline_reg;

    -- Drive output ports from registered values
    buy_price_out   <= buy_price_r;
    sell_price_out  <= sell_price_r;
    order_valid_out <= valid_r;

end architecture rtl;

import os
from typing import List

import pandas as pd


def rh_login():
    try:
        import robin_stocks.robinhood as r
    except Exception as e:
        raise SystemExit("Please pip install robin_stocks to use this script") from e

    user = os.getenv("RH_USERNAME")
    pwd = os.getenv("RH_PASSWORD")
    mfa = os.getenv("RH_MFA")
    if not user or not pwd:
        raise SystemExit("Set RH_USERNAME and RH_PASSWORD in your environment")
    r.login(username=user, password=pwd, mfa_code=mfa)
    return r


def fetch_last_price(r, symbol: str) -> float:
    try:
        q = r.get_latest_price(symbol, includeExtendedHours=False)
        if q and q[0]:
            return float(q[0])
    except Exception:
        pass
    return float("nan")


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Submit Robinhood orders from an allocation CSV")
    p.add_argument("--alloc_csv", required=True, help="CSV with columns: ticker, weight, dollars, shares (optional)")
    p.add_argument("--side", default="buy", choices=["buy", "sell"], help="Order side")
    p.add_argument("--time_in_force", default="gfd", help="Time in force (gfd, gtc, etc.)")
    p.add_argument("--dry_run", action="store_true", help="Print orders instead of submitting")
    p.add_argument("--min_dollars", type=float, default=50.0, help="Skip tiny orders below this size")
    args = p.parse_args()

    df = pd.read_csv(args.alloc_csv)
    if "ticker" not in df.columns or "dollars" not in df.columns:
        raise SystemExit("alloc_csv must include 'ticker' and 'dollars' columns")

    orders = []
    r = None if args.dry_run else rh_login()

    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        sym = str(row["ticker"]).strip().upper()
        dollars = float(row["dollars"]) if not pd.isna(row["dollars"]) else 0.0
        if dollars < args.min_dollars:
            continue
        shares = None
        if "shares" in df.columns and not pd.isna(row["shares"]):
            shares = float(row["shares"])
        else:
            px = fetch_last_price(r, sym) if r else float("nan")
            if not (px and math.isfinite(px) and px > 0):
                continue
            shares = math.floor(dollars / px)
        if shares <= 0:
            continue

        orders.append((sym, args.side, shares))

## Key Concepts

**Limit Order Book (LOB):**
A limit order book is the core mechanism of modern electronic markets, containing two lists of pending orders: buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks). The highest bid and lowest ask define the best bid and ask, and their difference is the bid-ask spread.

**Order Types:**
A limit order is passive—it rests in the book at a chosen price until matched. A market order is aggressive—it executes immediately against the best available prices.

Market makers face several risks: inventory risk (holding large unbalanced positions), adverse selection risk (trading against informed agents), and execution risk (orders not being filled).

input.content:
Lesson 0001 Quiz: 0 / 5

Basic HFT Concepts

Why this matters for HFT_practice: the repo is named "HFT" but most of its Python is daily-frequency portfolio rebalancing. The actual HFT muscle lives in fpga/market_maker.vhd and the C++ ONNX path in gradient_boosting/. To grow either side, you need the vocabulary that professional HFT systems are built on.

1. What HFT actually is

High-Frequency Trading (HFT) is a style of automated trading distinguished by three things, in order of importance:

  1. Latency — measured in microseconds (µs) or nanoseconds (ns), not seconds.
  2. High order rates — thousands to millions of messages per second per strategy.
  3. Short holding periods — positions opened and closed inside a day, often within seconds.

The "high frequency" refers to the rate of orders, not the rate of profitable trades. A typical HFT firm sends far more order cancels than fills.

The vocabulary HFT is built on

TermWhat it means
BidThe highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.
Ask (Offer)The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.
Spreadask − bid. The cost of crossing the book.
Mid-price(bid + ask) / 2. A common "fair value" reference.
Limit Order Book (LOB)The full list of resting buy/sell orders at every price level.
Limit order"I will buy at X or lower." Rests in the book. Passive.
Market order"Fill me now at the best price." Crosses the spread. Aggressive.
TickA single market data update (a trade, a quote change, a cancel).
Tick-to-tradeTime from receiving a market tick to your order leaving your NIC.
Market makerStrategy that posts both a bid and an ask, earning the spread.
ColocationRenting rack space inside the exchange's building to cut wire latency.
The single most important sentence in HFT: a market maker quotes both sides of the book and tries to capture the spread on round-trips. Everything in fpga/market_maker.vhd is in service of that.

Latency scale (memorize this)

SystemTypical tick-to-trade
Python script over the internet (you, today)~50–500 milliseconds
Tuned CPU C++ in colocation~500 ns – 5 µs
FPGA in colocation (top firms)~100–300 ns tick-to-trade

Source: industry summaries for 2025 cite FPGA tick-to-trade in the 100–500 ns range, vs. 500–1000 µs for CPU systems. That's a ~1000× gap, which is exactly why market_maker.vhd exists in this repo even though the Python is daily-frequency.

2. A minimal market-maker, in plain Python

Forget FPGAs for a moment. Here is the logic a market maker runs every time a new tick arrives. Read every comment. 

# minimal_market_maker.py — illustrative; not for real trading

def quote(bid: float, ask: float, my_spread: float):
    # 1. "Fair value" reference: midpoint of the current book.
    mid = (bid + ask) / 2

    # 2. We want to sit INSIDE the current spread to be at the top of the queue.
    #    Our buy quote sits below mid, our sell quote sits above mid,
    #    separated by `my_spread` (the edge we want to earn).
    my_bid = mid - my_spread / 2
    my_ask = mid + my_spread / 2

    # 3. If we get filled on BOTH sides we pocket roughly `my_spread` per share,
    #    minus exchange fees and minus inventory risk.
    return my_bid, my_ask

# Example: book shows bid=100.00, ask=100.04. We want a 2-cent edge.
buy, sell = quote(100.00, 100.04, my_spread=0.02)
# buy  = 100.01   (better than current bid → top of queue on buy side)
# sell = 100.03   (better than current ask → top of queue on sell side)

That's it. The math is trivial. The hard part of HFT is doing this arithmetic, plus risk checks, plus order submission, in under a microsecond, on every tick, on every symbol, every day.

3. In this project

Now look at the same logic, in VHDL, running on an FPGA.

fpga/market_maker.vhd (lines 93–117, condensed) 
if valid_in = '1' then
    -- (bid + ask) / 2  → mid price.  resize(_, 33) avoids overflow.
    bid_plus_ask <= resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33);
    mid_price    <= resize(
                        shift_right(
                            resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33),
                            1),
                        32);

    -- spread / 2  → half-spread.  Arithmetic right shift = divide by 2.
    half_spread  <= shift_right(spread_in, 1);

    -- buy quote  = mid − half_spread
    -- sell quote = mid + half_spread
    buy_price_r  <= ... - shift_right(spread_in, 1);
    sell_price_r <= ... + shift_right(spread_in, 1);
end if;

Map it back to the Python:

Python you just read

mid = (bid + ask) / 2

my_bid = mid - my_spread/2

my_ask = mid + my_spread/2

VHDL doing the same thing

bid_plus_ask + resize → /2 via shift_right(_, 1)

buy_price_r <= mid - half_spread

sell_price_r <= mid + half_spread

Two things to notice:

  • Q16.16 fixed-point. The header says real_value = integer_signal / 65536. Why not floating point? Because float DSP blocks burn cycles and silicon. Integer + shift is one cycle. In HFT, every cycle is a position in the order queue.
  • 1 clock-cycle latency (line 14 of the header). On a 250 MHz clock, that's 4 ns. Compare to the Python interpreter doing the same arithmetic: ~hundreds of ns just for the function call overhead.

Meanwhile in the Python world, paper_trading_sim.py trains a GradientBoostingRegressor on daily OHLCV bars from yfinance, ranks tomorrow's expected returns, and rebalances once per day. That's not HFT — it's quantitative daily allocation. The C++ ONNX path in gradient_boosting/main.cpp is the bridge: same model, but loaded into a low-latency runtime so it could sit next to the FPGA logic one day.

Repo honesty: calling this project "HFT_practice" is aspirational. The Python is daily/quant; the FPGA + C++ are the genuine HFT building blocks. Knowing which is which will save you from misnaming things in interviews and PRs.

4. Often confused with

HFT vs. Algorithmic Trading

All HFT is algorithmic, but not all algorithmic trading is HFT. Algo trading just means "decisions made by code." HFT additionally demands microsecond-grade latency. Your paper_trading_sim.py is algorithmic; it is not HFT.

HFT vs. Day Trading

A day trader holds for minutes-to-hours and clicks a mouse. HFT holds for milliseconds-to-seconds and never touches a mouse. Both close positions intraday — that's where the confusion comes from.

Market Making vs. Stat-Arb

Market making posts both sides and earns the spread; it is directionally neutral and worries about inventory. Stat-arb takes a directional view (long X, short Y) based on a statistical signal. Your model in predict_next.py is closer to stat-arb / momentum than to market making.

Limit Order vs. Market Order

A limit order says "this price or better, otherwise wait" — it rests in the book, costs no spread, may never fill. A market order says "fill now" — it pays the spread, always fills (if liquidity exists). Market makers post limits; takers send markets.

Latency vs. Throughput

Latency = time for one message to traverse the pipeline. Throughput = messages per second the pipeline can handle. HFT firms care about both, but the marketing number quoted in headlines is almost always latency.

FPGA vs. CPU

A CPU runs general code and pays for it with branch prediction, caches, and OS jitter. An FPGA is a sea of logic gates that you wire into a fixed pipeline at synthesis time — no OS, no cache misses, no instruction fetch. Deterministic latency in nanoseconds is the prize.

5. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Answer order is shuffled on every page load. Read each option before clicking.

Q1. What is the bid-ask spread?

  • The difference between the lowest ask and the highest bid in the order book.
  • The midpoint between the bid and the ask.
  • The fee an exchange charges per filled order.
  • How much the price moves while your order is in flight.

Q2. A market maker's core source of profit is…

  • Predicting price direction and holding for hours.
  • Posting both a bid and an ask and capturing the spread when both sides fill.
  • Exchange rebates alone, independent of price action.
  • Trading against informed flow whenever possible.

Q3. Why is market_maker.vhd written in VHDL with Q16.16 fixed-point arithmetic instead of Python with floats?

  • VHDL is more concise than Python for this kind of math.
  • Floating-point is too imprecise for stock prices.
  • An FPGA computing fixed-point math in one clock cycle is ~1000× faster and more deterministic than a Python interpreter.
  • Because floating-point is unable to represent risk constraints.

Q4. Which of these statements about paper_trading_sim.py is most accurate?

  • It is true HFT because it processes ticks in microseconds.
  • It is algorithmic daily-frequency trading, not HFT, because it rebalances once per day on yfinance daily bars.
  • It is HFT because the backtest runs quickly.
  • It is manual trading because a user runs the script from a CLI.

Q5. You see bid=100.00, ask=100.04, spread_in=0.02 handed to market_maker.vhd. What buy/sell quotes does the module emit?

  • buy = 100.00, sell = 100.04
  • buy = 100.01, sell = 100.03
  • buy = 99.99, sell = 100.01
  • buy = 99.98, sell = 100.06

6. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. A teammate says "let's run paper_trading_sim.py on a colocated server to make it HFT." What do you say?

Colocation only helps if your bottleneck is wire latency. This script's bottleneck is that it makes one decision per day from yfinance bars. Colocation cuts microseconds off network hops; it does nothing for a strategy whose decision cadence is 24 hours. To make it "HFT," you'd need to replace the data feed, the model loop, and the execution path — essentially everything except the ticker list.

S2. Why does market_maker.vhd have a valid_in input even though arithmetic could run every cycle?

Because not every clock cycle has a fresh price tick. valid_in is a handshake: "this cycle's bid_price_in / ask_price_in are meaningful — go compute." Downstream consumers watch order_valid_out to know when the buy/sell quotes are real outputs versus stale registers. This is the universal pattern for pipelined hardware: every meaningful datum carries a valid bit.

S3. Why might a market maker prefer to cancel a quote rather than let it fill?

Because a fill that happens right before the mid-price moves against you is called adverse selection — the other side knew something you didn't. If your tick-to-trade is too slow to update quotes when the market shifts, you become a systematic loser to faster participants. That's why HFT firms cancel far more orders than they execute, and why nanoseconds of cancel latency are existential.

Next lesson idea: The Limit Order Book in depth — price-time priority, queue position, and what "top of book" actually means. That builds directly on this one and unlocks reading the next layer of HFT papers.

Meanwhile in the Python world, paper_trading_sim.py trains a GradientBoostingRegressor on daily OHLCV bars from yfinance, ranks tomorrow's expected returns, and rebalances once per day. That's not HFT — it's quantitative daily allocation. The C++ ONNX path in gradient_boosting/main.cpp is the bridge: same model, but loaded into a low-latency runtime so it could sit next to the FPGA logic one day.

Repo honesty: calling this project "HFT_practice" is aspirational. The Python is daily/quant; the FPGA + C++ are the genuine HFT building blocks. Knowing which is which will save you from misnaming things in interviews and PRs.

4. Often confused with

HFT vs. Algorithmic Trading

All HFT is algorithmic, but not all algorithmic trading is HFT. Algo trading just means "decisions made by code." HFT additionally demands microsecond-grade latency. Your paper_trading_sim.py is algorithmic; it is not HFT.

HFT vs. Day Trading

A day trader holds for minutes-to-hours and clicks a mouse. HFT holds for milliseconds-to-seconds and never touches a mouse. Both close positions intraday — that's where the confusion comes from.

Market Making vs. Stat-Arb

Market making posts both sides and earns the spread; it is directionally neutral and worries about inventory. Stat-arb takes a directional view (long X, short Y) based on a statistical signal. Your model in predict_next.py is closer to stat-arb / momentum than to market making.

Limit Order vs. Market Order

A limit order says "this price or better, otherwise wait" — it rests in the book, costs no spread, may never fill. A market order says "fill now" — it pays the spread, always fills (if liquidity exists). Market makers post limits; takers send markets.

Latency vs. Throughput

Latency = time for one message to traverse the pipeline. Throughput = messages per second the pipeline can handle. HFT firms care about both, but the marketing number quoted in headlines is almost always latency.

FPGA vs. CPU

A CPU runs general code and pays for it with branch prediction, caches, and OS jitter. An FPGA is a sea of logic gates that you wire into a fixed pipeline at synthesis time — no OS, no cache misses, no instruction fetch. Deterministic latency in nanoseconds is the prize.

5. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Answer order is shuffled on every page load. Read each option before clicking.

Q1. What is the bid-ask spread?

  • The difference between the lowest ask and the highest bid in the order book.
  • The midpoint between the bid and the ask.
  • The fee an exchange charges per filled order.
  • How much the price moves while your order is in flight.

Q2. A market maker's core source of profit is…

  • Predicting price direction and holding for hours.
  • Posting both a bid and an ask and capturing the spread when both sides fill.
  • Exchange rebates alone, independent of price action.
  • Trading against informed flow whenever possible.

Q3. Why is market_maker.vhd written in VHDL with Q16.16 fixed-point arithmetic instead of Python with floats?

  • VHDL is more concise than Python for this kind of math.
  • Floating-point is too imprecise for stock prices.
  • An FPGA computing fixed-point math in one clock cycle is ~1000× faster and more deterministic than a Python interpreter.
  • Because floating-point is unable to represent risk constraints.

Q4. Which of these statements about paper_trading_sim.py is most accurate?

  • It is true HFT because it processes ticks in microseconds.
  • It is algorithmic daily-frequency trading, not HFT, because it rebalances once per day on yfinance daily bars.
  • It is HFT because the backtest runs quickly.
  • It is manual trading because a user runs the script from a CLI.

Q5. You see bid=100.00, ask=100.04, spread_in=0.02 handed to market_maker.vhd. What buy/sell quotes does the module emit?

  • buy = 100.00, sell = 100.04
  • buy = 100.01, sell = 100.03
  • buy = 99.99, sell = 100.01
  • buy = 99.98, sell = 100.06

6. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. A teammate says "let's run paper_trading_sim.py on a colocated server to make it HFT." What do you say?

Colocation only helps if your bottleneck is wire latency. This script's bottleneck is that it makes one decision per day from yfinance bars. Colocation cuts microseconds off network hops; it does nothing for a strategy whose decision cadence is 24 hours. To make it "HFT," you'd need to replace the data feed, the model loop, and the execution path — essentially everything except the ticker list.

S2. Why does market_maker.vhd have a valid_in input even though arithmetic could run every cycle?

Because not every clock cycle has a fresh price tick. valid_in is a handshake: "this cycle's bid_price_in / ask_price_in are meaningful — go compute." Downstream consumers watch order_valid_out to know when the buy/sell quotes are real outputs versus stale registers. This is the universal pattern for pipelined hardware: every meaningful datum carries a valid bit.

S3. Why might a market maker prefer to cancel a quote rather than let it fill?

Because a fill that happens right before the mid-price moves against you is called adverse selection — the other side knew something you didn't. If your tick-to-trade is too slow to update quotes when the market shifts, you become a systematic loser to faster participants. That's why HFT firms cancel far more orders than they execute, and why nanoseconds of cancel latency are existential.

# Glossary — HFT_practice

Terms the learner has been introduced to. A term is promoted from *introduced* to
*understood* only after they've answered a question about it correctly or used it
correctly themselves.

Status legend: `intro` = covered in a lesson · `solid` = demonstrably grasped.

---

### Algorithmic trading — `intro`
Any trading where decisions are made by code rather than a human. A superset of HFT.

### Ask (offer) — `intro`
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.

### Adverse selection — `intro`
The risk that the counterparty who hit your quote knew more than you did about
where the price was about to go. The reason market makers cancel orders aggressively.

### Bid — `intro`
The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.

### Colocation — `intro`
Renting rack space inside the exchange's data center so your trading server is
physically next to the matching engine, minimizing wire latency.

### FPGA — `intro`
Field-Programmable Gate Array. Reconfigurable hardware wired into a fixed
pipeline at synthesis time. Used in HFT for deterministic nanosecond-scale latency.
Example in this repo: `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### HFT (High-Frequency Trading) — `intro`
Automated trading defined by microsecond-to-nanosecond latency, very high order
rates, and short (often sub-second) holding periods.

### Limit order — `intro`
"Buy/sell at price X or better." Rests passively in the book until matched or
cancelled. The order type market makers post.

### Limit Order Book (LOB) — `intro`
The full list of resting buy and sell orders at every price level on a venue.
The core data structure of modern electronic markets.

### Market maker — `intro`
A strategy that simultaneously posts both a bid and an ask, earning the spread
when both sides fill. `fpga/market_maker.vhd` is a hardware example.

### Market order — `intro`
"Fill me now at the best available price." Crosses the spread and pays for
immediacy. The order type takers send.

### Mid-price — `intro`
`(bid + ask) / 2`. A common reference for "fair value" between the two sides of
the book. Computed explicitly in `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### Q16.16 fixed-point — `intro`
A 32-bit signed integer encoding where the lower 16 bits represent the
fractional part: `real_value = integer_signal / 65536`. Used in
`fpga/market_maker.vhd` so all arithmetic stays in one-cycle integer ops.

### Spread — `intro`
`ask − bid`. The cost of crossing the book; the prize a market maker tries to
capture on round-trips.

### Tick — `intro`
A single market data update — a trade, a quote change, a cancel. The unit of
input to an HFT pipeline.

### Tick-to-trade latency — `intro`
The time between receiving a market data tick and your responding order leaving
your NIC. The headline latency number in HFT (top firms: ~100–500 ns on FPGA).

2	-- @file    linear_regression_predictor.vhd
3	-- @brief   Fixed-point linear regression price-change predictor
4	-- @detail  Implements the same model as sample_with_linear_regression.cpp.
5	--          Weights are hardcoded and scaled by 1000 to avoid fractional
6	--          arithmetic (integer-only DSP path):
7	--
8	--            W0       = 0.05  ->  50
9	--            W[0]     = 0.30  ->  300   (feature 0: current price)
10	--            W[1]    = -0.10  -> -100   (feature 1: order-book imbalance)
11	--            W[2]     = 0.20  ->  200   (feature 2: volatility)
12	--
13	--          Prediction (×1000) = 50 + 300*f0 + (-100)*f1 + 200*f2
14	--
15	--          Signal thresholds (matching C++ SPREAD = 0.01 -> 10 at ×1000 scale):
16	--            prediction_scaled > +10  -> BUY  (signal_out = "01")
17	--            prediction_scaled < -10  -> SELL (signal_out = "10")
18	--            otherwise                -> HOLD (signal_out = "00")
19	--
20	--          Pipeline: 2 stages
21	--            Stage 1 (multiply): compute weighted products in parallel
22	--            Stage 2 (accumulate + threshold): sum products, compare
23	--
24	-- @author  HFT Practice Project
25	-- @version 1.0
26	--
27	-- @note    Feature inputs are assumed to be integer-scaled by 1000 on the
28	--          Python side before being passed in (e.g. price $100.50 -> 100500).
29	--          The output prediction_out is also in the ×1000 domain.
30	--
31	-- @note    Synthesizable with Vivado 2022.1+; no floating-point required.
32	-- =============================================================================
33	
34	library ieee;
35	use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
36	use ieee.numeric_std.all;
37	
38	-- =============================================================================
39	-- Entity
40	-- =============================================================================
41	entity linear_regression_predictor is
42	    port (
43	        -- Clock / reset
44	        clk       : in  std_logic;          -- Rising-edge clock
45	        rst_n     : in  std_logic;          -- Active-low synchronous reset
46	
47	        -- Input features (integer, scaled ×1000)
48	        feature_0 : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- Current price        (×1000)
49	        feature_1 : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- Order-book imbalance (×1000)
50	        feature_2 : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- Volatility           (×1000)
51	
52	        -- Input handshake
53	        valid_in  : in  std_logic;
54	
55	        -- Output prediction (scaled ×1000×1000 = ×10^6 before dividing by 1000)
56	        prediction_out : out signed(63 downto 0);  -- Raw accumulator value
57	
58	        -- Output handshake
59	        valid_out  : out std_logic;
60	
61	        -- Trading signal
62	        -- "00" = Hold, "01" = Buy, "10" = Sell, "11" = reserved
63	        signal_out : out std_logic_vector(1 downto 0)
64	    );
65	end entity linear_regression_predictor;
66	
67	-- =============================================================================
68	-- Architecture
69	-- =============================================================================
70	architecture rtl of linear_regression_predictor is
71	
72	    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
73	    -- Hardcoded model weights (scaled ×1000 to keep everything integer)

76	    constant W_F0 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 300, 32);   --  0.30 ×1000
77	    constant W_F1 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(-100, 32);   -- -0.10 ×1000

81	    -- Original C++ threshold: 0.01 → 0.01 × 1000 (weight) × 1000 (feature) = 10,000
82	    constant THRESHOLD_POS : signed(63 downto 0) := to_signed( 10_000, 64);
83	    constant THRESHOLD_NEG : signed(63 downto 0) := to_signed(-10_000, 64);
84	
85	    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------

89	    signal prod_f0  : signed(63 downto 0) := (others => '0');
90	    signal prod_f1  : signed(63 downto 0) := (others => '0');
91	    signal prod_f2  : signed(63 downto 0) := (others => '0');
92	    signal valid_s1 : std_logic           := '0';
93

96	    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
97	    signal accumulator : signed(63 downto 0)     := (others => '0');

111	                prod_f0  <= (others => '0');
112	                prod_f1  <= (others => '0');
113	                prod_f2  <= (others => '0');
114	                valid_s1 <= '0';
115	            else
116	                valid_s1 <= valid_in;
117	                if valid_in = '1' then
118	                    prod_f0 <= W_F0 * feature_0;   -- 32×32 -> 64-bit signed
119	                    prod_f1 <= W_F1 * feature_1;
120	                    prod_f2 <= W_F2 * feature_2;
121	                end if;
122	            end if;
123	        end if;
124	    end process stage1_multiply;

128	    -- =========================================================================

141	                    -- promoted to the same ×10^6 scale as the products.
142	                    -- W0_scaled = W0 × 1000 = 50 × 1000 = 50,000
143	                    acc := prod_f0 + prod_f1 + prod_f2
144	                           + resize(W0 * to_signed(1000, 32), 64);

155	                    end if;
156	                end if;
157	            end if;
158	        end if;
159	    end process stage2_accumulate;

-- =============================================================================
-- @file    linear_regression_predictor.vhd
-- @brief   Fixed-point linear regression price-change predictor
-- @detail  Implements the same model as sample_with_linear_regression.cpp.
--          Weights are hardcoded and scaled by 1000 to avoid fractional
--          arithmetic (integer-only DSP path):
--
--            W0       = 0.05  ->  50
--            W[0]     = 0.30  ->  300   (feature 0: current price)
--            W[1]    = -0.10  -> -100   (feature 1: order-book imbalance)
--            W[2]     = 0.20  ->  200   (feature 2: volatility)
--
--          Prediction (×1000) = 50 + 300*f0 + (-100)*f1 + 200*f2
--
--          Signal thresholds (matching C++ SPREAD = 0.01 -> 10 at ×1000 scale):
--            prediction_scaled > +10  -> BUY  (signal_out = "01")
--            prediction_scaled < -10  -> SELL (signal_out = "10")
--            otherwise                -> HOLD (signal_out = "00")
--
--          Pipeline: 2 stages
--            Stage 1 (multiply): compute weighted products in parallel
--            Stage 2 (accumulate + threshold): sum products, compare
--
-- @author  HFT Practice Project
-- @version 1.0
--
-- @note    Feature inputs are assumed to be integer-scaled by 1000 on the
--          Python side before being passed in (e.g. price $100.50 -> 100500).
--          The output prediction_out is also in the ×1000 domain.
--
-- @note    Synthesizable with Vivado 2022.1+; no floating-point required.
-- =============================================================================

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

-- =============================================================================
-- Entity
-- =============================================================================
entity linear_regression_predictor is
    port (
        -- Clock / reset
        clk       : in  std_logic;          -- Rising-edge clock
        rst_n     : in  std_logic;          -- Active-low synchronous reset

        -- Input features (integer, scaled ×1000)
        feature_0 : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- Current price        (×1000)
        feature_1 : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- Order-book imbalance (×1000)
        feature_2 : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- Volatility           (×1000)

        -- Input handshake
        valid_in  : in  std_logic;

        -- Output prediction (scaled ×1000×1000 = ×10^6 before dividing by 1000)
        prediction_out : out signed(63 downto 0);  -- Raw accumulator value

        -- Output handshake
        valid_out  : out std_logic;

        -- Trading signal
        -- "00" = Hold, "01" = Buy, "10" = Sell, "11" = reserved
        signal_out : out std_logic_vector(1 downto 0)
    );
end entity linear_regression_predictor;

-- =============================================================================
-- Architecture
-- =============================================================================
architecture rtl of linear_regression_predictor is

    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    -- Hardcoded model weights (scaled ×1000 to keep everything integer)
    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    constant W0   : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(  50, 32);   --  0.05 ×1000
    constant W_F0 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 300, 32);   --  0.30 ×1000
    constant W_F1 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(-100, 32);   -- -0.10 ×1000
    constant W_F2 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 200, 32);   --  0.20 ×1000

    -- Decision thresholds (in units of weight_scale × feature_scale = ×10^6)
    -- Original C++ threshold: 0.01 → 0.01 × 1000 (weight) × 1000 (feature) = 10,000
    constant THRESHOLD_POS : signed(63 downto 0) := to_signed( 10_000, 64);
    constant THRESHOLD_NEG : signed(63 downto 0) := to_signed(-10_000, 64);

    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    -- Stage-1 pipeline registers: products
    -- product width = 32 + 32 = 64 bits (no overflow)
    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    signal prod_f0  : signed(63 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal prod_f1  : signed(63 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal prod_f2  : signed(63 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal valid_s1 : std_logic           := '0';

    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    -- Stage-2 pipeline registers: accumulation and decision
    -- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    signal accumulator : signed(63 downto 0)     := (others => '0');
    signal signal_r    : std_logic_vector(1 downto 0) := "00";
    signal valid_s2    : std_logic               := '0';

begin

    -- =========================================================================
    -- Stage 1 — Multiply features by their respective weights in parallel
    -- Registered at end of stage.
    -- =========================================================================
    stage1_multiply : process(clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            if rst_n = '0' then
                prod_f0  <= (others => '0');
                prod_f1  <= (others => '0');
                prod_f2  <= (others => '0');
                valid_s1 <= '0';
            else
                valid_s1 <= valid_in;
                if valid_in = '1' then
                    prod_f0 <= W_F0 * feature_0;   -- 32×32 -> 64-bit signed
                    prod_f1 <= W_F1 * feature_1;
                    prod_f2 <= W_F2 * feature_2;
                end if;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process stage1_multiply;

    -- =========================================================================
    -- Stage 2 — Accumulate products + intercept, then threshold comparison
    -- =========================================================================
    stage2_accumulate : process(clk)
        variable acc : signed(63 downto 0);
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            if rst_n = '0' then
                accumulator <= (others => '0');
                signal_r    <= "00";
                valid_s2    <= '0';
            else
                valid_s2 <= valid_s1;
                if valid_s1 = '1' then
                    -- Sum: W0 (intercept, already at ×1000) needs to be
                    -- promoted to the same ×10^6 scale as the products.
                    -- W0_scaled = W0 × 1000 = 50 × 1000 = 50,000
                    acc := prod_f0 + prod_f1 + prod_f2
                           + resize(W0 * to_signed(1000, 32), 64);

                    accumulator <= acc;

                    -- Threshold comparison → trading signal
                    if acc > THRESHOLD_POS then
                        signal_r <= "01";   -- BUY
                    elsif acc < THRESHOLD_NEG then
                        signal_r <= "10";   -- SELL
                    else
                        signal_r <= "00";   -- HOLD
                    end if;
                end if;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process stage2_accumulate;

    -- Drive outputs
    prediction_out <= accumulator;
    signal_out     <= signal_r;
    valid_out      <= valid_s2;

end architecture rtl;

# FPGA / VHDL Integration for HFT Practice

## Why FPGAs for HFT?

Modern high-frequency trading firms routinely achieve **sub-microsecond** (even nanosecond) round-trip latencies using FPGAs. The advantages over CPU-based execution are:

| Concern | CPU / Python | FPGA |
|---|---|---|
| Latency | ~1–100 µs | ~100–500 ns |
| Jitter | High (OS scheduler) | Near-zero (deterministic) |
| Parallelism | Sequential core execution | True parallel data paths |
| Power | ~65–250 W | ~5–25 W (Artix-7) |
| Reconfigurability | Any time | Seconds (bitstream reload) |

An FPGA implements your trading logic directly in configurable logic cells — there is no operating system, no cache miss penalty, and no branch misprediction. The same bid/ask spread computation that takes 1 µs in Python runs in 4 ns on a 250 MHz FPGA fabric.

---

## Directory Structure

```
fpga/
├── README.md                        ← this file
├── hls_synthesis.tcl                ← Vivado HLS automation script
├── market_maker.vhd                 ← Core market-making spread engine
├── linear_regression_predictor.vhd  ← Fixed-point LR prediction + signal
└── moving_average_trader.vhd        ← Windowed moving-average strategy
```

### `market_maker.vhd`
Maps directly to `sample_algorithm.cpp` (`MarketMaker::placeOrders`).
Given a live bid and ask, it computes:
```
mid_price  = (bid + ask) / 2
buy_price  = mid_price  - spread / 2
sell_price = mid_price  + spread / 2
```
All arithmetic uses **Q16.16 fixed-point** (signed 32-bit, 16 fractional bits) to avoid floating-point DSP overhead.

### `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`
Maps to `sample_with_linear_regression.cpp`.
Hardcoded weights matching the C++ constants:
- Intercept W0 = 0.05 → 50 (×1000 integer scaling)
- W[0] = 0.30 → 300
- W[1] = −0.10 → −100
- W[2] = 0.20 → 200

A two-stage pipeline computes the dot product in one cycle and the threshold comparison in the next, outputting a 2-bit signal: `00`=Hold, `01`=Buy, `10`=Sell.

### `moving_average_trader.vhd`
Implements a configurable-length (generic `WINDOW`, default 20) simple moving average. A shift register stores the last N prices; the average is computed incrementally. Buy/sell signals are generated by comparing the current price against the moving average ± spread.

### `hls_synthesis.tcl`
Vivado HLS Tcl script that automates project creation, design-file addition, constraint setup, synthesis, and IP-core export for the Zynq UltraScale+ target.

---

## Synthesizing with Vivado HLS

### Prerequisites
- Xilinx Vivado Design Suite (2022.1 or later) with HLS licence  
  Download: https://www.xilinx.com/support/download.html
- Target hardware (see below)

### One-command synthesis
```bash
vivado_hls -f fpga/hls_synthesis.tcl
```
The script will:
1. Create `./hft_hls_project/`
2. Add all three `.vhd` source files
3. Target **xczu7ev-ffvc1156-2-e** (Zynq UltraScale+) at 250 MHz (4 ns clock)
4. Run C/RTL synthesis
5. Export an IP-XACT core to `./hft_hls_project/solution1/impl/ip/`

### Manual flow (Vivado GUI)
1. Open Vivado → Create Project → RTL Project
2. Add sources: `fpga/*.vhd`
3. Set part: `xczu7ev-ffvc1156-2-e` (or your board)
4. Run Synthesis → Implementation → Generate Bitstream

---

## Supported Hardware

| Board / Device | Family | Part Number | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basys 3 | Artix-7 | xc7a35tcpg236-1 | Entry-level, good for simulation |
| Nexys A7 | Artix-7 | xc7a100tcsg324-1 | More LUTs, BRAM |
| KC705 | Kintex-7 | xc7k325tffg900-2 | Mid-range production target |
| Alveo U250 | UltraScale+ | xcu250-figd2104-2L-e | Data-centre HFT, 100 GbE |
| ZCU102 (default) | Zynq US+ | xczu9eg-ffvb1156-2-e | Embedded PS + PL |

Artix-7 boards are sufficient for learning. Production HFT firms use Kintex-7 UltraScale or Alveo cards connected directly to a 10/100 GbE switch with kernel-bypass networking.

---

## Alternative Open-Source Toolchains

If you do not have a Vivado licence:

| Tool | Language | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **LegUp HLS** (UofT) | C → Verilog | Academic, free for research |
| **Bambu HLS** (Polimi) | C/C++ → VHDL/Verilog | Active open-source project |
| **VHDLwhiz** | VHDL | Online simulator, good for learning |
| **GHDL** | VHDL simulation | Free, fast, CLI-based |
| **Yosys + nextpnr** | Synthesis | Open source; targets iCE40/ECP5, not Xilinx |
| **SymbiFlow / F4PGA** | Synthesis | Experimental Xilinx open-source flow |

For simulation only (no hardware required):
```bash
# Install GHDL
brew install ghdl           # macOS
apt-get install ghdl        # Debian/Ubuntu

# Simulate market_maker.vhd (add a testbench first)
ghdl -a fpga/market_maker.vhd
ghdl -e market_maker
ghdl -r market_maker --vcd=market_maker.vcd --stop-time=1us

# View waveforms
gtkwave market_maker.vcd
```

---

## How the Python / C++ Code Maps to VHDL

```
Python / C++ concept           → VHDL construct
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
double / float                 → signed(31 downto 0) Q16.16
std::vector<double> weights    → constant array of integers
for loop over features         → unrolled multiply-accumulate
if/else branch                 → concurrent signal assignment
function call                  → process + registered pipeline
```

Fixed-point Q16.16 encoding:
```
real_value = integer_value / 65536
e.g. price $100.50 → 100.50 × 65536 = 6,586,368  (0x0064_8000)
     spread $0.01  → 0.01 × 65536  = 655.36 ≈ 655 (0x0000_028F)
```

---

## ML Model Inference on FPGA

Gradient boosting trees (the primary model in this project) are challenging to implement directly in RTL because:
- Trees branch on float comparisons → deep multiplexer trees
- Ensemble of 100+ trees → very large LUT usage
- Training happens in Python — weights must be extracted and re-encoded

**Recommended approach for ML on FPGA:**

1. **FINN** (Xilinx Research) — neural network inference, quantization-aware  
   https://github.com/Xilinx/finn

2. **hls4ml** — converts sklearn / Keras / PyTorch models to HLS C++ (then to RTL)  
   ```bash
   pip install hls4ml
   python -c "
   import hls4ml, joblib
   model = joblib.load('models/first_model.joblib')
   cfg = hls4ml.utils.config_from_sklearn_model(model, granularity='model')
   hls_model = hls4ml.converters.convert_from_sklearn(model, cfg)
   hls_model.compile()
   "
   ```

3. **ONNX → Vitis AI** — the project already exports ONNX models  
   (`gradient_boosting/model_to_onnx.py`) — Vitis AI can consume these directly.

For the linear regression predictor the weights are small enough to hard-code directly in VHDL (as done in `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`).

---

## Simulation with ModelSim / GHDL

### ModelSim (included with Vivado)
```tcl
vlib work
vcom -2008 fpga/market_maker.vhd
vsim market_maker
add wave -r /*
run 1us
```

### GHDL (open-source)
```bash
# Analyse, elaborate, and run (requires a testbench entity)
ghdl -a --std=08 fpga/market_maker.vhd fpga/tb_market_maker.vhd
ghdl -e --std=08 tb_market_maker
ghdl -r --std=08 tb_market_maker --vcd=tb_market_maker.vcd
gtkwave tb_market_maker.vcd &
```

---

## Future Roadmap

| Milestone | Description |
|---|---|
| PCIe DMA interface | Connect FPGA to host CPU via PCIe; use XDMA IP core for low-latency order injection |
| 10 GbE UDP stack | Implement raw UDP TX on SFP+ port; target <500 ns from signal to wire |
| FIX protocol parser | Hardware FIX 4.4/FAST decoder feeding directly into the order engine |
| Order book aggregator | Hardware limit order book (price-level array) with O(1) best-bid/ask lookup |
| Risk engine | Real-time position limits checked in single clock cycle before order emission |
| ML inference pipeline | hls4ml-generated gradient boosting inference at 250 MHz |
| Co-location simulation | Loopback testbench modelling exchange matching engine latency |

input.content:
Lesson 0002 Quiz: 0 / 5

How FPGAs Are Used in HFT

Why this matters for HFT_practice: the fpga/ folder holds three working VHDL modules — market_maker.vhd, linear_regression_predictor.vhd, and moving_average_trader.vhd. To extend them honestly you need to understand what FPGAs do in HFT systems and, just as important, what they don't do.

1. Why an FPGA, and not a fast CPU?

A CPU is a general-purpose machine. It fetches instructions, predicts branches, fights cache misses, and obeys an operating system that can interrupt it at any moment. None of that is free, and the variability — the jitter — is what kills HFT strategies, even more than the average latency.

An FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array) is a sea of configurable logic blocks (LUTs), flip-flops, DSP slices, and routing fabric. You describe your trading logic in HDL (VHDL or Verilog), the tools synthesize that description into a wire-level circuit, and the chip becomes that circuit until you reload it. There is no instruction stream. There is no OS. There is a clock, and on every rising edge, every register in your design updates simultaneously.

The numbers that justify the complexity

PathTick-to-tradeJitterNotes
Python over the internet ~50–500 ms Massive (GIL, network) Where paper_trading_sim.py lives.
Tuned C++ with kernel bypass (DPDK / Solarflare OpenOnload) ~750–800 ns Low (~100 ns) 20–30% latency win vs vanilla TCP.
FPGA NIC (parsing in hardware → strategy on chip → packet out) ~100–500 ns Near-zero (deterministic) Where market_maker.vhd wants to live.

Sources: industry summaries on Solarflare OpenOnload latencies and FPGA tick-to-trade in 2025 (see chat).

What an FPGA actually buys you (4 things)

  1. Determinism. No OS scheduler, no cache, no branch predictor. The same input takes the same number of cycles every single time. Strategies are easier to certify against exchange latency floors.
  2. True parallelism. The 3-feature dot product in linear_regression_predictor.vhd computes all three multiplies in the same cycle. A CPU pipelines them serially.
  3. Wire-speed I/O. The NIC is the FPGA. Market data packets enter the PHY and are parsed inside the same chip that emits the order packet — no PCIe round-trip, no kernel hop.
  4. Low and predictable power. An Artix-7 fabric burns 5–25 W. A tuned Xeon burns hundreds. Power matters in colocation cabinets where thermal headroom is the real constraint.
What FPGAs don't buy you: developer velocity, complex branching logic, or floating-point ML. Every change requires a 10-minute-to-hours synthesis run. Decision trees are notoriously bad on FPGAs (the fpga/README.md notes this on lines 152–155). Big neural nets need HLS toolchains like hls4ml or FINN — not handwritten VHDL.

2. The universal HFT-FPGA pattern: registered pipelines + valid handshakes

Almost every HFT FPGA module — including all three in this repo — follows the same shape:

0Market data tick arrives at the PHY (e.g. parsed from a 10 GbE UDP packet by an on-chip decoder)~25 ns
▼
1Feature extraction stage — registered. Combinational arithmetic this cycle, latched at the next clock edge.4 ns @ 250 MHz
▼
2Decision stage — registered. Threshold compare, signal generation, risk check.4 ns
▼
3Order build + emit — registered. Pack a FIX/OUCH message, hand to MAC, out the SFP+.~50 ns

Two ideas to internalize:

(a) Registered pipeline

Each stage does some arithmetic between clock edges and latches the result at the next edge. More stages = lower clock period (faster clock, more throughput) but more cycles of latency. It's a knob, not a free win.

(b) The valid handshake

Every stage carries a valid_in bit alongside its data. The next stage only accepts and processes data when valid_in = '1'. After processing, it asserts valid_out = '1' for exactly one cycle so the next consumer knows the output is real. This is the universal solution to "what does this cycle's register actually mean?" 

-- The pattern, in any HFT VHDL module ever written:
process(clk)
begin
    if rising_edge(clk) then
        if rst_n = '0' then
            -- everything to zero on reset
            valid_out <= '0';
        else
            valid_out <= valid_in;   -- carry the valid bit forward
            if valid_in = '1' then
                -- ONLY compute when the input is real
                result_reg <= some_arithmetic(input_reg);
            end if;
        end if;
    end if;
end process;

3. The three modules in fpga/, read as one system

Imagine the data flow that doesn't exist yet in the repo but is implied by the modules:

market data → linear_regression_predictor  OR  moving_average_trader → trading signal → market_maker → quotes out

(a) linear_regression_predictor.vhd — a 2-stage dot product

fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd (lines 107–124, condensed) 
-- Stage 1: three multiplies, all running in parallel on the SAME cycle.
stage1_multiply : process(clk)
begin
    if rising_edge(clk) then
        if valid_in = '1' then
            prod_f0 <= W_F0 * feature_0;   -- 0.30 × price
            prod_f1 <= W_F1 * feature_1;   -- -0.10 × imbalance
            prod_f2 <= W_F2 * feature_2;   -- 0.20 × volatility
        end if;
    end if;
end process;

Three DSP slices, fired simultaneously, all done in one 4 ns cycle. A CPU would dispatch those multiplies sequentially through its FPU.

fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd (lines 139–155, condensed) 
-- Stage 2: sum the products, add the intercept, threshold to a 2-bit signal.
acc := prod_f0 + prod_f1 + prod_f2 + resize(W0 * to_signed(1000, 32), 64);

if acc > THRESHOLD_POS then
    signal_r <= "01";   -- BUY
elsif acc < THRESHOLD_NEG then
    signal_r <= "10";   -- SELL
else
    signal_r <= "00";   -- HOLD
end if;

Notice the integer scaling: weights are ×1000, features are ×1000, so the accumulator is at ×10⁶. That's how the comparator can be a pure integer compare with no floating-point cost. Total module latency: 2 cycles ≈ 8 ns.

(b) moving_average_trader.vhd — a O(1) sliding window

A naive moving average over a 20-sample window would need 20 adders in series. This module uses the classic incremental trick: add the newest sample, subtract the oldest. One adder, one subtractor, every cycle, regardless of window size.

fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd (lines 136–149, condensed) 
if warmed_up = '1' then
    -- Full window: subtract outgoing, add incoming. O(1) regardless of WINDOW.
    running_sum <= running_sum
                   + resize(price_in,         SUM_BITS)
                   - resize(price_reg(WINDOW-1), SUM_BITS);
else
    -- Warm-up: just accumulate the first WINDOW samples.
    running_sum <= running_sum + resize(price_in, SUM_BITS);
end if;

This is why HFT FPGA code looks so unfamiliar — every algorithm has to be re-expressed so it fits in a fixed-depth combinational chain that meets the clock period. A Python one-liner like df['close'].rolling(20).mean() hides hundreds of operations; on the FPGA each one of those operations is silicon you have to lay out.

(c) market_maker.vhd — quote generator (covered in Lesson 0001)

Reminder of how it fits: when the predictor emits a non-HOLD signal, the market maker block is what actually produces the buy_price_out and sell_price_out to send to the exchange. The predictor decides whether to quote; the market maker decides what the quote is. 1 clock-cycle latency (4 ns).

End-to-end latency budget for this project (theoretical)

StageLatencyStatus in repo
10 GbE UDP parse~25 nsNot built (README "Future Roadmap")
linear_regression_predictor (2 stages)~8 nsBuilt
market_maker (1 stage)~4 nsBuilt
Order encode + TX~50 nsNot built
Total tick-to-trade (estimated)~90 ns

Compare to the ~750–800 ns of a Solarflare-class CPU stack. The arithmetic kernels in this repo are already in the right ballpark for top-quartile HFT. The missing pieces are I/O, not math.

4. Often confused with

FPGA vs ASIC

An ASIC is silicon manufactured for one specific design — fastest possible, but tape-out costs millions and the design is frozen forever. An FPGA is generic silicon you reprogram in seconds via a new bitstream. HFT firms iterate strategies weekly; nobody tapes out an ASIC for that.

FPGA vs GPU

A GPU is massively parallel but its parallelism is SIMD across thousands of threads on the same instruction — great for training neural nets, wrong shape for "one tick → one quote." Latency from PCIe + driver alone exceeds what an FPGA's entire tick-to-trade budget allows.

VHDL vs Verilog

Two HDLs that compile to the same gates. VHDL is verbose, strongly typed, popular in defense/aerospace and this repo. Verilog (and SystemVerilog) is terser and more common at web-scale silicon firms. Religious choice; not technical.

HDL vs HLS

HDL (VHDL/Verilog) describes hardware register-by-register. HLS (High-Level Synthesis) takes annotated C++ and generates HDL for you. Faster to write; sometimes worse area/timing. hls_synthesis.tcl in this repo drives the HLS flow on the hand-written VHDL.

Combinational vs Sequential logic

Combinational logic produces outputs that depend only on current inputs — no clock involved. Sequential logic uses flip-flops driven by a clock, holding state between cycles. HFT pipelines are combinational between stages, sequential at each stage boundary.

Synthesis vs Place & Route

Synthesis turns VHDL into a netlist of generic gates. Place & Route (PAR) assigns each gate to physical LUTs on the chip and routes the wires. Timing closure (meeting the clock period) is won or lost at PAR — that's why HFT engineers stare at PAR reports for hours.

5. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. linear_regression_predictor.vhd uses two pipeline stages. If you ran a single tick through it, how long until you got the trading signal at 250 MHz?

  • ~4 ns (one cycle).
  • ~8 ns (two cycles).
  • ~100 ps.
  • ~750 ns.

Q2. Why does moving_average_trader.vhd maintain a running_sum and only add the new sample / subtract the oldest, instead of summing all 20 samples each cycle?

  • Because VHDL can't express a 20-input adder.
  • Because the incremental update is O(1) and meets the clock-period budget regardless of window size; a 20-deep adder tree might fail timing.
  • Because there isn't enough BRAM for the shift register.
  • Because floating-point adders have too much rounding error.

Q3. Your colleague wants to deploy a 100-tree GradientBoostingRegressor directly as hand-written VHDL on the FPGA. What's the best response?

  • "Sure, just use a bigger FPGA — Alveo U250 has plenty of LUTs."
  • "Yes, hand-written VHDL is always best for HFT."
  • "Hand-VHDL is great for the linear predictor, but 100-tree GBMs need an HLS toolchain like hls4ml or Vitis AI — the README documents exactly that."
  • "Move it to a GPU instead — they're better at ML inference."

Q4. What does the valid_in / valid_out handshake in these modules actually do?

  • It resets the module's internal state.
  • It marks which cycles carry real data versus stale register contents, propagating through every pipeline stage so consumers know when to act.
  • It's a checksum that verifies the input bits weren't corrupted.
  • It throttles the clock frequency of the module.

Q5. Which statement about FPGA-NIC HFT systems is most accurate?

  • Market data is parsed by the kernel, then DMA'd to the FPGA over PCIe for the strategy to run.
  • Packets enter the FPGA's own PHY, are parsed in-fabric, drive the strategy, and exit as orders on the same chip — PCIe is reserved for configuration and slow-path telemetry.
  • A modern FPGA NIC achieves sub-nanosecond tick-to-trade.
  • FPGAs run a tiny embedded Linux that processes ticks.

6. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. You change the constant W_F0 in linear_regression_predictor.vhd from 300 to 450. What do you have to do before the change runs on the board?

You have to re-synthesize and re-place-and-route the design, then load the new bitstream onto the FPGA. The constants are baked into the configuration of the LUTs and DSP slices at synthesis time — there is no "runtime variable" to write to. This is why HFT firms that want online-tunable parameters wire them as input ports driven by a register file on the PCIe side, not as constants.

S2. moving_average_trader.vhd has a warmed_up flag that only goes high after WINDOW samples have arrived. Why does valid_s2 in stage 2 use valid_s1 and warmed_s1?

Because the moving average is meaningless during warm-up — you'd be dividing a partial sum by 20 instead of by the (smaller) number of samples actually seen. Emitting valid_s2 = '0' until warm-up is complete tells any downstream consumer "ignore my outputs; they're not real yet." This is the same valid-handshake discipline as in the rest of the file, just guarded by the additional warm-up condition.

S3. The README's roadmap mentions "10 GbE UDP stack" and "Risk engine in one clock cycle." Why are those the next two priorities if you wanted real tick-to-trade?

Because the three modules in fpga/ only implement the arithmetic kernel. To call this end-to-end you need (a) a way to receive market data without going through the kernel, which is the 10 GbE UDP stack, and (b) a last-cycle gate that vetoes orders that would breach position or notional limits — a hardware risk engine. Without (b) a single bug in the predictor can blow up the firm before any human can react. Without (a) you've built a Ferrari engine with no wheels.

Next lesson idea: The Limit Order Book in depth — price-time priority, queue position, and what "top of book" actually means. That builds on why market_maker.vhd wants to quote inside the spread, not just at the existing best bid/ask.

    running_sum <= running_sum + resize(price_in, SUM_BITS);
end if;

This is why HFT FPGA code looks so unfamiliar — every algorithm has to be re-expressed so it fits in a fixed-depth combinational chain that meets the clock period. A Python one-liner like df['close'].rolling(20).mean() hides hundreds of operations; on the FPGA each one of those operations is silicon you have to lay out.

(c) market_maker.vhd — quote generator (covered in Lesson 0001)

Reminder of how it fits: when the predictor emits a non-HOLD signal, the market maker block is what actually produces the buy_price_out and sell_price_out to send to the exchange. The predictor decides whether to quote; the market maker decides what the quote is. 1 clock-cycle latency (4 ns).

End-to-end latency budget for this project (theoretical)

StageLatencyStatus in repo
10 GbE UDP parse~25 nsNot built (README "Future Roadmap")
linear_regression_predictor (2 stages)~8 nsBuilt
market_maker (1 stage)~4 nsBuilt
Order encode + TX~50 nsNot built
Total tick-to-trade (estimated)~90 ns

Compare to the ~750–800 ns of a Solarflare-class CPU stack. The arithmetic kernels in this repo are already in the right ballpark for top-quartile HFT. The missing pieces are I/O, not math.

4. Often confused with

FPGA vs ASIC

An ASIC is silicon manufactured for one specific design — fastest possible, but tape-out costs millions and the design is frozen forever. An FPGA is generic silicon you reprogram in seconds via a new bitstream. HFT firms iterate strategies weekly; nobody tapes out an ASIC for that.

FPGA vs GPU

A GPU is massively parallel but its parallelism is SIMD across thousands of threads on the same instruction — great for training neural nets, wrong shape for "one tick → one quote." Latency from PCIe + driver alone exceeds what an FPGA's entire tick-to-trade budget allows.

VHDL vs Verilog

Two HDLs that compile to the same gates. VHDL is verbose, strongly typed, popular in defense/aerospace and this repo. Verilog (and SystemVerilog) is terser and more common at web-scale silicon firms. Religious choice; not technical.

HDL vs HLS

HDL (VHDL/Verilog) describes hardware register-by-register. HLS (High-Level Synthesis) takes annotated C++ and generates HDL for you. Faster to write; sometimes worse area/timing. hls_synthesis.tcl in this repo drives the HLS flow on the hand-written VHDL.

Combinational vs Sequential logic

Combinational logic produces outputs that depend only on current inputs — no clock involved. Sequential logic uses flip-flops driven by a clock, holding state between cycles. HFT pipelines are combinational between stages, sequential at each stage boundary.

Synthesis vs Place & Route

Synthesis turns VHDL into a netlist of generic gates. Place & Route (PAR) assigns each gate to physical LUTs on the chip and routes the wires. Timing closure (meeting the clock period) is won or lost at PAR — that's why HFT engineers stare at PAR reports for hours.

5. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. linear_regression_predictor.vhd uses two pipeline stages. If you ran a single tick through it, how long until you got the trading signal at 250 MHz?

  • ~4 ns (one cycle).
  • ~8 ns (two cycles).
  • ~100 ps.
  • ~750 ns.

Q2. Why does moving_average_trader.vhd maintain a running_sum and only add the new sample / subtract the oldest, instead of summing all 20 samples each cycle?

  • Because VHDL can't express a 20-input adder.
  • Because the incremental update is O(1) and meets the clock-period budget regardless of window size; a 20-deep adder tree might fail timing.
  • Because there isn't enough BRAM for the shift register.
  • Because floating-point adders have too much rounding error.

Q3. Your colleague wants to deploy a 100-tree GradientBoostingRegressor directly as hand-written VHDL on the FPGA. What's the best response?

  • "Sure, just use a bigger FPGA — Alveo U250 has plenty of LUTs."
  • "Yes, hand-written VHDL is always best for HFT."
  • "Hand-VHDL is great for the linear predictor, but 100-tree GBMs need an HLS toolchain like hls4ml or Vitis AI — the README documents exactly that."
  • "Move it to a GPU instead — they're better at ML inference."

Q4. What does the valid_in / valid_out handshake in these modules actually do?

  • It resets the module's internal state.
  • It marks which cycles carry real data versus stale register contents, propagating through every pipeline stage so consumers know when to act.
  • It's a checksum that verifies the input bits weren't corrupted.
  • It throttles the clock frequency of the module.

Q5. Which statement about FPGA-NIC HFT systems is most accurate?

  • Market data is parsed by the kernel, then DMA'd to the FPGA over PCIe for the strategy to run.
  • Packets enter the FPGA's own PHY, are parsed in-fabric, drive the strategy, and exit as orders on the same chip — PCIe is reserved for configuration and slow-path telemetry.
  • A modern FPGA NIC achieves sub-nanosecond tick-to-trade.
  • FPGAs run a tiny embedded Linux that processes ticks.

6. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. You change the constant W_F0 in linear_regression_predictor.vhd from 300 to 450. What do you have to do before the change runs on the board?

You have to re-synthesize and re-place-and-route the design, then load the new bitstream onto the FPGA. The constants are baked into the configuration of the LUTs and DSP slices at synthesis time — there is no "runtime variable" to write to. This is why HFT firms that want online-tunable parameters wire them as input ports driven by a register file on the PCIe side, not as constants.

S2. moving_average_trader.vhd has a warmed_up flag that only goes high after WINDOW samples have arrived. Why does valid_s2 in stage 2 use valid_s1 and warmed_s1?

Because the moving average is meaningless during warm-up — you'd be dividing a partial sum by 20 instead of by the (smaller) number of samples actually seen. Emitting valid_s2 = '0' until warm-up is complete tells any downstream consumer "ignore my outputs; they're not real yet." This is the same valid-handshake discipline as in the rest of the file, just guarded by the additional warm-up condition.

S3. The README's roadmap mentions "10 GbE UDP stack" and "Risk engine in one clock cycle." Why are those the next two priorities if you wanted real tick-to-trade?

Because the three modules in fpga/ only implement the arithmetic kernel. To call this end-to-end you need (a) a way to receive market data without going through the kernel, which is the 10 GbE UDP stack, and (b) a last-cycle gate that vetoes orders that would breach position or notional limits — a hardware risk engine. Without (b) a single bug in the predictor can blow up the firm before any human can react. Without (a) you've built a Ferrari engine with no wheels.

Next lesson idea: The Limit Order Book in depth — price-time priority, queue position, and what "top of book" actually means. That builds on why market_maker.vhd wants to quote inside the spread, not just at the existing best bid/ask.
