### Tick-to-trade latency — `intro`
The time between receiving a market data tick and your responding order leaving
your NIC. The headline latency number in HFT (top firms: ~100–500 ns on FPGA).

---

## Added in Lesson 0002 (FPGAs in HFT)

### ASIC — `intro`
Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. Silicon manufactured for one design.
Fastest possible, but multi-million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen forever —
which is why HFT firms use FPGAs (reconfigurable) instead.

### Bitstream — `intro`
The binary file produced by synthesis + place-and-route. Loading it onto the
FPGA configures every LUT, flip-flop, and routing switch to realize your
design. Reloading is a seconds-long operation, not a recompile of a chip.

### Combinational logic — `intro`
Logic whose outputs depend only on current inputs — no clock involved. Inside
each pipeline stage in `fpga/*.vhd`, arithmetic between clock edges is
combinational.

### Determinism (FPGA sense) — `intro`
The property that the same input takes the same number of cycles every time.
The opposite of CPU jitter from OS scheduling, cache misses, branch prediction.
The single biggest reason HFT firms tolerate the pain of FPGA development.

### DSP slice — `intro`
A dedicated multiply-accumulate block inside the FPGA fabric. Each `*` in
VHDL (e.g. `W_F0 * feature_0` in `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`) typically
maps to one DSP slice.

### HDL — `intro`
Hardware Description Language. VHDL or Verilog. Describes hardware
register-by-register, not as an executing program.

### HLS — `intro`
High-Level Synthesis. Toolchain that takes annotated C/C++ and generates HDL
for you. Faster to write than hand-VHDL; sometimes worse timing or area.
`fpga/hls_synthesis.tcl` drives the HLS flow in this repo.

### Jitter — `intro`
Variability in latency from one event to the next. HFT cares about jitter as
much as average latency, because strategies are sized against the worst-case
not the median.

### Kernel bypass — `intro`
Networking techniques (DPDK, Solarflare OpenOnload, XDP) that route packets
from the NIC directly to userspace, skipping the Linux kernel network stack.
A 20–30% latency win for CPU-based HFT; obsolete on FPGA NICs where parsing
is on-chip already.

### LUT (Look-Up Table) — `intro`
The basic configurable unit of FPGA fabric. A small truth table that can be
programmed to compute any function of N inputs (typically N=6). LUT count is
the headline capacity metric of an FPGA part.

### Pipeline stage — `intro`
A combinational chunk of logic terminated by a register (flip-flop). More
stages = higher clock frequency but more cycles of latency. `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`
has 2 stages; `market_maker.vhd` has 1.

### Place-and-Route (PAR) — `intro`
The step after synthesis that assigns each gate in your netlist to a physical
LUT on the chip and routes the wires between them. Where timing closure is
won or lost.

### Sequential logic — `intro`
Logic that uses flip-flops driven by a clock to hold state between cycles.
Each pipeline stage boundary in the repo's VHDL is sequential.

### Synthesis — `intro`
The step that turns HDL source into a netlist of generic gates. Distinct from
Place-and-Route, which maps those gates onto the physical chip.

### Timing closure — `intro`
The act of making your design meet the target clock period at every register-
to-register path. The real bottleneck of FPGA HFT development — not the
arithmetic, not the algorithm, but proving the silicon can run that fast.

### Valid handshake — `intro`
The convention of carrying a `valid` bit alongside every datum through a
pipeline, so each stage knows which cycles contain real data. Used uniformly
in all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules.

### VHDL vs Verilog — `intro`
Two HDLs that compile to the same gates. VHDL: verbose, strongly typed, used
in this repo. Verilog/SystemVerilog: terser, more common at web-scale silicon
firms. The choice is cultural, not technical.

# Glossary — HFT_practice

Terms the learner has been introduced to. A term is promoted from *introduced* to
*understood* only after they've answered a question about it correctly or used it
correctly themselves.

Status legend: `intro` = covered in a lesson · `solid` = demonstrably grasped.

---

### Algorithmic trading — `intro`
Any trading where decisions are made by code rather than a human. A superset of HFT.

### Ask (offer) — `intro`
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.

### Adverse selection — `intro`
The risk that the counterparty who hit your quote knew more than you did about
where the price was about to go. The reason market makers cancel orders aggressively.

### Bid — `intro`
The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.

### Colocation — `intro`
Renting rack space inside the exchange's data center so your trading server is
physically next to the matching engine, minimizing wire latency.

### FPGA — `intro`
Field-Programmable Gate Array. Reconfigurable hardware wired into a fixed
pipeline at synthesis time. Used in HFT for deterministic nanosecond-scale latency.
Example in this repo: `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### HFT (High-Frequency Trading) — `intro`
Automated trading defined by microsecond-to-nanosecond latency, very high order
rates, and short (often sub-second) holding periods.

### Limit order — `intro`
"Buy/sell at price X or better." Rests passively in the book until matched or
cancelled. The order type market makers post.

### Limit Order Book (LOB) — `intro`
The full list of resting buy and sell orders at every price level on a venue.
The core data structure of modern electronic markets.

### Market maker — `intro`
A strategy that simultaneously posts both a bid and an ask, earning the spread
when both sides fill. `fpga/market_maker.vhd` is a hardware example.

### Market order — `intro`
"Fill me now at the best available price." Crosses the spread and pays for
immediacy. The order type takers send.

### Mid-price — `intro`
`(bid + ask) / 2`. A common reference for "fair value" between the two sides of
the book. Computed explicitly in `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### Q16.16 fixed-point — `intro`
A 32-bit signed integer encoding where the lower 16 bits represent the
fractional part: `real_value = integer_signal / 65536`. Used in
`fpga/market_maker.vhd` so all arithmetic stays in one-cycle integer ops.

### Spread — `intro`
`ask − bid`. The cost of crossing the book; the prize a market maker tries to
capture on round-trips.

### Tick — `intro`
A single market data update — a trade, a quote change, a cancel. The unit of
input to an HFT pipeline.

### Tick-to-trade latency — `intro`
The time between receiving a market data tick and your responding order leaving
your NIC. The headline latency number in HFT (top firms: ~100–500 ns on FPGA).

The time between receiving a market data tick and your responding order leaving
your NIC. The headline latency number in HFT (top firms: ~100–500 ns on FPGA).
+## Added in Lesson 0002 (FPGAs in HFT)
+### ASIC — `intro`
+Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. Silicon manufactured for one design.
+Fastest possible, but multi-million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen forever —
+which is why HFT firms use FPGAs (reconfigurable) instead.
+### Bitstream — `intro`
+The binary file produced by synthesis + place-and-route. Loading it onto the
+FPGA configures every LUT, flip-flop, and routing switch to realize your
+design. Reloading is a seconds-long operation, not a recompile of a chip.
+### Combinational logic — `intro`
+Logic whose outputs depend only on current inputs — no clock involved. Inside
+each pipeline stage in `fpga/*.vhd`, arithmetic between clock edges is
+combinational.
+### Determinism (FPGA sense) — `intro`
+The property that the same input takes the same number of cycles every time.
+The opposite of CPU jitter from OS scheduling, cache misses, branch prediction.
+The single biggest reason HFT firms tolerate the pain of FPGA development.
+### DSP slice — `intro`
+A dedicated multiply-accumulate block inside the FPGA fabric. Each `*` in
+VHDL (e.g. `W_F0 * feature_0` in `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`) typically
+maps to one DSP slice.
+### HDL — `intro`
+Hardware Description Language. VHDL or Verilog. Describes hardware
+register-by-register, not as an executing program.
+### HLS — `intro`
+High-Level Synthesis. Toolchain that takes annotated C/C++ and generates HDL
+for you. Faster to write than hand-VHDL; sometimes worse timing or area.
+`fpga/hls_synthesis.tcl` drives the HLS flow in this repo.
+### Jitter — `intro`
+Variability in latency from one event to the next. HFT cares about jitter as
+much as average latency, because strategies are sized against the worst-case
+not the median.
+### Kernel bypass — `intro`
+Networking techniques (DPDK, Solarflare OpenOnload, XDP) that route packets
+from the NIC directly to userspace, skipping the Linux kernel network stack.
+A 20–30% latency win for CPU-based HFT; obsolete on FPGA NICs where parsing
+is on-chip already.
+### LUT (Look-Up Table) — `intro`
+The basic configurable unit of FPGA fabric. A small truth table that can be
+programmed to compute any function of N inputs (typically N=6). LUT count is
+the headline capacity metric of an FPGA part.
+### Pipeline stage — `intro`
+A combinational chunk of logic terminated by a register (flip-flop). More
+stages = higher clock frequency but more cycles of latency. `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`
+has 2 stages; `market_maker.vhd` has 1.
+### Place-and-Route (PAR) — `intro`
+The step after synthesis that assigns each gate in your netlist to a physical
+LUT on the chip and routes the wires between them. Where timing closure is
+won or lost.
+### Sequential logic — `intro`
+Logic that uses flip-flops driven by a clock to hold state between cycles.
+Each pipeline stage boundary in the repo's VHDL is sequential.
+### Synthesis — `intro`
+The step that turns HDL source into a netlist of generic gates. Distinct from
+Place-and-Route, which maps those gates onto the physical chip.
+### Timing closure — `intro`
+The act of making your design meet the target clock period at every register-
+to-register path. The real bottleneck of FPGA HFT development — not the
+arithmetic, not the algorithm, but proving the silicon can run that fast.
+### Valid handshake — `intro`
+The convention of carrying a `valid` bit alongside every datum through a
+pipeline, so each stage knows which cycles contain real data. Used uniformly
+in all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules.
+### VHDL vs Verilog — `intro`
+Two HDLs that compile to the same gates. VHDL: verbose, strongly typed, used
+in this repo. Verilog/SystemVerilog: terser, more common at web-scale silicon
+firms. The choice is cultural, not technical.

    Args:

    cols = [
        c for c in feat.columns
        if c not in ignore and pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(feat[c])
    ]
    X = feat[cols].astype(float).values
    y = feat["fwd_ret_1d"].astype(float).values
    return X, y, cols


def align_panel(datas: dict) -> pd.DatetimeIndex:
    """Deprecated: previously returned the intersection of all dates.

    Keeping this for backward-compatibility, but most workflows should NOT
    intersect all tickers, as it collapses history to the youngest IPOs.
    """
    idx = None
    for df in datas.values():
        idx = df.index if idx is None else idx.union(df.index)
    return idx if idx is not None else pd.DatetimeIndex([])


def build_feature_panel(datas: dict) -> dict:
    """Build feature frames per ticker from raw OHLCV data."""
    return {t: build_features(df) for t, df in datas.items()}


def split_by_time(feat: pd.DataFrame, ratio: float) -> Tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Time-based split into train/test by a ratio of the index length."""
    n = len(feat)
    k = max(1, int(n * ratio))
    return feat.iloc[:k].copy(), feat.iloc[k:].copy()


def simulate(tickers: List[str], start: str, end: str, cfg: BacktestConfig) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Run the end-to-end backtest with yfinance data and GBM signals.

    Steps:
    - Fetch data, build features per ticker; do NOT force common intersection.
    - Split each ticker into train/test, stack, and train a single model.
    - Score the test set daily, pick top-N names, and update equity.

    Args:
        tickers: List of ticker symbols.
        start: Start date (YYYY-MM-DD).
        end: End date (YYYY-MM-DD) or None.
        cfg: Backtest configuration.

    Returns:
        DataFrame indexed by date with columns like 'equity' and 'n_picks'.
    """
    raw = fetch_history(tickers, start, end)
    feats = build_feature_panel(raw)
    # Do not force intersection; keep each ticker on its own timeline.
    feats = {t: f.copy() for t, f in feats.items() if not f.empty}
    if not feats:
        raise RuntimeError("No data fetched; check tickers or dates.")

    stacked = []
    for t, f in feats.items():
        f2 = f.copy()
        f2["ticker"] = t
        stacked.append(f2)
    panel = pd.concat(stacked).dropna()

    groups = panel.groupby("ticker")
    train_frames = []
    test_frames = []
    for t, g in groups:
        tr, te = split_by_time(g, cfg.train_ratio)
        train_frames.append(tr)
        test_frames.append(te)
    train_df = pd.concat(train_frames)
    test_df = pd.concat(test_frames)

    X_train, y_train, feat_cols = prepare_xy(train_df)
    model = train_model(X_train, y_train)

    preds = []
    for t, g in test_df.groupby("ticker"):
        X = g[feat_cols].values
        p = model.predict(X)
        tmp = pd.DataFrame({"pred": p, "fwd_ret_1d": g["fwd_ret_1d"].values}, index=g.index)
        tmp["ticker"] = t
        preds.append(tmp)
    pred_df = pd.concat(preds).sort_index()

    equity = cfg.initial_cash
    daily = []
    for dt, day_df in pred_df.groupby(level=0):
        day_sorted = day_df.sort_values("pred", ascending=False)
        picks = day_sorted.head(cfg.top_n)
        if picks.empty:
            daily.append({"date": dt, "equity": equity, "n_picks": 0})
            continue
        weight = 1.0 / len(picks)
        day_ret = float((picks["fwd_ret_1d"].mean()))
        traded_cost = (cfg.trade_cost_bps / 10000.0)
        equity *= (1 + weight * day_ret * len(picks))
        equity *= (1 - traded_cost)
        daily.append({"date": dt, "equity": equity, "n_picks": int(len(picks))})

    result = pd.DataFrame(daily).set_index("date")
    # Attach auxiliary objects to return alongside result for optional saving
    result._pred_df = pred_df  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    result._model = model      # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    result._feat_cols = feat_cols  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    return result


def metrics(equity: pd.Series) -> dict:
    """Compute simple performance metrics on an equity curve.

    Returns CAGR (approx), annualized volatility, Sharpe (mean/vol),
    and max drawdown of the cumulative return series.
    """
    ret = equity.pct_change().dropna()
    ann = 252
    cagr = (equity.iloc[-1] / equity.iloc[0]) ** (ann / max(1, len(ret))) - 1 if len(ret) else 0.0
    vol = ret.std() * math.sqrt(ann) if len(ret) else 0.0
    sharpe = (ret.mean() * ann) / vol if vol > 0 else 0.0
    cum = (1 + ret).cumprod()
    roll_max = cum.cummax()
    dd = (cum / roll_max - 1).min() if len(cum) else 0.0
    return {"CAGR": cagr, "Vol": vol, "Sharpe": sharpe, "MaxDD": dd}


def main() -> None:
    """CLI entrypoint for the paper trading backtest."""
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="AI-driven paper trading backtest (historical)")
    p.add_argument("--tickers", type=str, default="AAPL,MSFT,GOOG,AMZN,NVDA")
    p.add_argument("--start", type=str, default="2019-01-01")
    p.add_argument("--end", type=str, default=None)
    p.add_argument("--initial_cash", type=float, default=100000)
    p.add_argument("--top_n", type=int, default=5)
    p.add_argument("--trade_cost_bps", type=float, default=1.0)
    p.add_argument("--train_ratio", type=float, default=0.7)
    p.add_argument("--out_csv", type=str, default="paper_backtest_equity.csv")
    p.add_argument("--save_model", type=str, default=None, help="Path to save trained model (joblib).")
    p.add_argument("--save_preds", type=str, default=None, help="Path to save test set predictions CSV.")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
from typing import List, Dict, Tuple

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yfinance as yf
import joblib

from paper_trading_sim import build_features


def parse_tickers(arg_str: str, file_path: str | None) -> List[str]:
    """Parse tickers from comma list or a file (one per line)."""
    if file_path:
        with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            tickers = [ln.strip().upper() for ln in f if ln.strip() and not ln.startswith("#")]
            return tickers
    return [t.strip().upper() for t in arg_str.split(",") if t.strip()]


def fetch_latest_frames(tickers: List[str], period: str = "2y") -> Dict[str, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Fetch recent daily OHLCV for tickers using yfinance.

    Args:
        tickers: List of symbols.
        period: yfinance period string (e.g., "1y", "2y", "5y").

    Returns:
        Dict[ticker, DataFrame]
    """
    data: Dict[str, pd.DataFrame] = {}
    for t in tickers:
        df = yf.download(t, period=period, interval="1d", auto_adjust=True, progress=False)
        if isinstance(df, pd.DataFrame) and not df.empty:
            data[t] = df
    return data


def compute_returns(data: Dict[str, pd.DataFrame], lookback: int = 90) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Build aligned daily returns panel for covariance estimation.

    Args:
        data: Dict[ticker, OHLCV DataFrame] with 'Close'.
        lookback: Number of most recent rows to keep after alignment.

    Returns:
        DataFrame of aligned daily returns indexed by date, columns=tickers.
    """
    rets = []
    names = []
    for t, df in data.items():
        if "Close" not in df.columns:
            continue
        r = df["Close"].pct_change().dropna()
        if not r.empty:
            rets.append(r)
            names.append(t)
    if not rets:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    panel = pd.concat(rets, axis=1)
    panel.columns = names
    panel = panel.dropna(how="any")
    if lookback > 0 and len(panel) > lookback:
        panel = panel.iloc[-lookback:]
    return panel


def meanvar_long_only(mu: np.ndarray, Sigma: np.ndarray, max_w: float | None = 0.3) -> np.ndarray:
    """Compute simple long-only mean-variance weights with an optional cap.

    Uses w ∝ Σ^{-1} μ, projects negatives to 0, normalizes to sum 1, and
    enforces an optional per-asset cap via iterative capping + renormalization.
    """
    # Regularize for stability
    eps = 1e-6
    Sigma_reg = Sigma + eps * np.eye(Sigma.shape[0])
    w = np.linalg.pinv(Sigma_reg) @ mu
    w = np.maximum(w, 0.0)
    s = w.sum()
    if s <= 0:
        # Fallback: equal weight
        w = np.ones_like(w) / len(w)
    else:
        w = w / s
    if max_w is not None and max_w > 0:
        # Iteratively cap and renormalize remaining mass
        for _ in range(10):
            over = w > max_w
            if not np.any(over):
                break
            excess = float((w[over] - max_w).sum())
            w[over] = max_w
            under = ~over
            if np.any(under):
                add = excess
                denom = float(w[under].sum())
                if denom > 0:
                    w[under] = w[under] + add * (w[under] / denom)
                else:
                    # spread equally among uncapped
                    w[under] = w[under] + add / under.sum()
            # Re-normalize tiny drift
            w = np.maximum(w, 0)
            w = w / w.sum()
    return w


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Make next-day predictions and optional risk-aware allocations")
    p.add_argument("--model", required=True, help="Path to joblib bundle saved by paper_trading_sim (--save_model)")
    p.add_argument("--tickers", type=str, default="AAPL,MSFT,GOOG,AMZN,NVDA")
    p.add_argument("--tickers_file", type=str, default=None, help="Path to file with tickers (one per line)")
    p.add_argument("--period", type=str, default="2y", help="History length used to compute features")
    p.add_argument("--top_n", type=int, default=5)
    p.add_argument("--out_csv", type=str, default=None, help="Optional path to save predictions CSV")
    p.add_argument("--optimize", type=str, default="meanvar", choices=["none", "meanvar"], help="How to create portfolio weights")
    p.add_argument("--cov_lookback", type=int, default=90, help="Lookback days for covariance estimation")
    p.add_argument("--shrink", type=float, default=0.2, help="Shrinkage toward diagonal (0-1)")
    p.add_argument("--max_w", type=float, default=0.3, help="Max weight per asset for long-only portfolio")

input.content:
Lesson 0003 Quiz: 0 / 5

ML Algorithms Used in Trading

Why this matters for HFT_practice: three different learners are already in this repo. fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd uses linear regression. fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd uses a rule (technically not ML — and that matters). paper_trading_sim.py uses GradientBoostingRegressor — the project's flagship model. You should know what each one actually does and why each one lives where it does.

1. What does "ML for trading" actually mean in this repo?

Every supervised ML model is a function ŷ = f(x; θ) learned from (input, output) pairs. The art is choosing x, y, and the shape of f. This repo's choice:

VariableIn this projectWhere it's set
x (features) per-day, per-ticker: close, ret_1d, ma_5, ma_10, ma_gap, vol_10, rsi_14 build_features in paper_trading_sim.py
y (target) Next day's return, fwd_ret_1d = close.pct_change().shift(-1) same file, line 68
f (model) GradientBoostingRegressor from scikit-learn train_model, line 113
θ (parameters) The internal weights/tree structure learned from history Saved to models/*.joblib
The single most consequential design choice in the repo: predicting a continuous next-day return (regression), not a direction (up/down classification), not an absolute price. This is why the file is named GradientBoostingRegressor and not ...Classifier. The continuous predictions are then sorted, and the top-N become the portfolio.

The pipeline, from data to dollars

1
Raw data: daily OHLCV from yfinance for every ticker in the universe.
▼
2
Features: build_features turns prices into returns, moving averages, an MA gap, 10-day vol, RSI. 7 numbers per (ticker, date).
▼
3
Target: next day's return is shifted into the same row. Training pairs (x, y) ready.
▼
4
Model: a single GradientBoostingRegressor is fit on the stacked data from all tickers (one model, not one-per-ticker).
▼
5
Rank & allocate: for each day, predict next-day returns for every ticker, sort, take top_n, send to meanvar_long_only for risk-aware weights.

2. The three algorithms in this repo, side by side

Linear Regression — small, fast, FPGA-friendly

ŷ = w₀ + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₙxₙ

Just a weighted sum. Parametric (fixed number of parameters regardless of dataset size). Trained by closed-form least squares.

Lives in fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd and the C++ at gradient_boosting/sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp (despite the filename).

Moving Average Crossover — a rule, not ML

Buy when price < (MA − spread). Sell when price > (MA + spread).

Zero learned parameters. This is not machine learning — it's a hand-coded mean-reversion rule. Useful baseline to beat.

Lives in fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd.

Gradient Boosting Regressor — flagship

An ensemble of ~100 small decision trees, where each tree corrects the errors of the previous ones. Non-parametric: model size grows with the data and complexity of the signal.

Lives in paper_trading_sim.py:train_model.

Why three? They serve different masters

Linear: tiny LUT footprint → FPGA viable. Moving average: zero training data needed → instant baseline. Gradient boosting: best predictive power → wins on the Sharpe ratio, but too big for one chip cycle.

What each one can express

ModelCan captureCannot captureTraining data needed
Moving avg rule Mean reversion at one timescale Anything else None
Linear regression Monotonic, additive effects per feature Interactions, non-linearities Hundreds of rows
Gradient boosting Non-linear effects, feature interactions, thresholds Very long-range temporal dependencies (use RNN/transformer for that) Thousands to millions of rows

3. What GradientBoostingRegressor actually does

The name confuses people. Break it down:

  • "Regressor" = predicts a continuous number (next-day return), not a class.
  • "Gradient" = each new tree is trained to predict the gradient of the loss — i.e., the direction the current prediction needs to move. For squared-error loss, that's just the residual.
  • "Boosting" = combine many weak learners (shallow trees) sequentially, each one fixing what the previous ensemble got wrong.

Step by step, for the squared-error loss the regressor uses by default:

1
Initialize the ensemble prediction at the mean of y: F₀(x) = mean(y_train).
2
Compute residuals for every training row: rᵢ = yᵢ − F(xᵢ). These are how far off the current ensemble is on each row.
3
Fit a small tree to predict the residuals (depth typically 3–8). The tree carves the feature space into rectangles and predicts a constant residual in each rectangle.
4
Add the tree to the ensemble, scaled by a small learning rate (ν, e.g. 0.1): F_new(x) = F(x) + ν · tree(x).
5
Repeat from step 2 until you have n_estimators trees (default 100).

Final prediction: F(x) = mean(y) + ν · (tree₁(x) + tree₂(x) + … + tree₁₀₀(x)).

Why this works for trading returns: each individual tree is too weak to overfit, but the ensemble can compose hundreds of small, non-linear "this feature crosses that threshold AND that other feature is high" rules — exactly the kind of regime-specific signal that a single linear weight can't express.

Tiny, runnable example

from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
import numpy as np

# Toy: 200 days, 2 features (e.g., today's return and 10-day vol)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 2))
# True signal: positive when feature 0 > 0 AND feature 1 < 0 (an interaction)
y = (X[:, 0] > 0) * (X[:, 1] < 0) * 0.02 + rng.normal(0, 0.005, 200)

model = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1)
model.fit(X, y)

# Predict and inspect feature importances
print(model.predict(X[:5]))
print(model.feature_importances_)   # which feature contributes most to splits

Linear regression would miss the interaction signal in that toy entirely — it would only see "feature 0 has slight positive correlation" and shrug. Gradient boosting picks up the joint rule because depth-3 trees can split on both features at once.

4. In this project

paper_trading_sim.py (lines 48–69) 
def build_features(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
    out["close"]   = df["Close"]
    out["ret_1d"]  = out["close"].pct_change()
    out["ma_5"]    = out["close"].rolling(5).mean()
    out["ma_10"]   = out["close"].rolling(10).mean()
    out["ma_gap"]  = (out["ma_5"] / out["ma_10"]) - 1     # short-vs-long-MA
    out["vol_10"]  = out["ret_1d"].rolling(10).std()
    out["rsi_14"]  = _rsi(out["close"], 14) / 100.0      # normalized RSI
    out["fwd_ret_1d"] = out["ret_1d"].shift(-1)    # THE TARGET — note shift(-1)
    return out.dropna()

The .shift(-1) on the last line is doing the heavy semantic lifting: it puts tomorrow's return on today's row, so when you train, you're learning "given today's features → predict tomorrow's return." Get that direction wrong and you've built a look-ahead-biased model that looks great in backtests and loses money live.

paper_trading_sim.py (lines 113–125) 
def train_model(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> GradientBoostingRegressor:
    model = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=42)
    model.fit(X, y)
    return model

Notice what's not here: no hyperparameter tuning, no cross-validation, no regularization knobs explicitly set. sklearn's defaults are n_estimators=100, max_depth=3, learning_rate=0.1, loss="squared_error" — reasonable, conservative starting points for a learner this size. A real production pipeline would sweep these.

paper_trading_sim.py (lines 218–231) — what the prediction is used for 
for dt, day_df in pred_df.groupby(level=0):
    day_sorted = day_df.sort_values("pred", ascending=False)
    picks = day_sorted.head(cfg.top_n)        # <-- rank, take top-N
    weight = 1.0 / len(picks)
    day_ret = float((picks["fwd_ret_1d"].mean()))   # equal-weight realized return

Crucial insight: the model's predicted magnitude barely matters. What matters is its cross-sectional ranking — which tickers it ranks highest today. A model that systematically underestimates returns but still ranks them in the right order will beat a model with low MAE but a noisy ranking.

And on the FPGA: linear regression instead

fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd (lines 75–78) 
constant W0   : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(  50, 32);   --  0.05 ×1000 — intercept
constant W_F0 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 300, 32);   --  0.30 ×1000 — feature 0 weight
constant W_F1 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(-100, 32);   -- -0.10 ×1000 — feature 1 weight
constant W_F2 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 200, 32);   --  0.20 ×1000 — feature 2 weight

Four numbers. That's the entire model. This is what makes linear regression FPGA-viable: 4 constants → 3 multiplies + 3 adds → done in 2 clock cycles. The 100-tree gradient booster cannot collapse into that.

Repo honesty: the Python gradient boosting model is more accurate but can't run on the FPGA. The FPGA linear regression is fast but expresses only a tiny fraction of what the Python model learned. 1. What does "ML for trading" actually mean in this repo?

Every supervised ML model is a function ŷ = f(x; θ) learned from (input, output) pairs. The art is choosing x, y, and the shape of f. This repo's choice:

VariableIn this projectWhere it's set
x (features) per-day, per-ticker: close, ret_1d, ma_5, ma_10, ma_gap, vol_10, rsi_14 build_features in paper_trading_sim.py
y (target) Next day's return, fwd_ret_1d = close.pct_change().shift(-1) same file, line 68
f (model) GradientBoostingRegressor from scikit-learn train_model, line 113
θ (parameters) The internal weights/tree structure learned from history Saved to models/*.joblib
The single most consequential design choice in the repo: predicting a continuous next-day return (regression), not a direction (up/down classification), not an absolute price. This is why the file is named GradientBoostingRegressor and not ...Classifier. The continuous predictions are then sorted, and the top-N become the portfolio.

1
Raw data: daily OHLCV from yfinance for every ticker in the universe.
▼
2
Features: build_features turns prices into returns, moving averages, an MA gap, 10-day vol, RSI. 7 numbers per (ticker, date).
▼
3
Target: next day's return is shifted into the same row. Training pairs (x, y) ready.
▼
4
Model: a single GradientBoostingRegressor is fit on the stacked data from all tickers (one model, not one-per-ticker).
▼
5
Rank & allocate: for each day, predict next-day returns for every ticker, sort, take top_n, send to meanvar_long_only for risk-aware weights.

ŷ = w₀ + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + wₙxₙ

Just a weighted sum. Parametric (fixed number of parameters regardless of dataset size). Trained by closed-form least squares.

Lives in fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd and the C++ at gradient_boosting/sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp (despite the filename).

Buy when price < (MA − spread). Sell when price > (MA + spread).

Zero learned parameters. This is not machine learning — it's a hand-coded mean-reversion rule. Useful baseline to beat.

Lives in fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd.

ModelCan captureCannot captureTraining data needed

Step by step, for the squared-error loss the regressor uses by default:

1
Initialize the ensemble prediction at the mean of y: F₀(x) = mean(y_train).
2
Compute residuals for every training row: rᵢ = yᵢ − F(xᵢ). These are how far off the current ensemble is on each row.
3
Fit a small tree to predict the residuals (depth typically 3–8). The tree carves the feature space into rectangles and predicts a constant residual in each rectangle.
4
Add the tree to the ensemble, scaled by a small learning rate (ν, e.g. 0.1): F_new(x) = F(x) + ν · tree(x).

Repeat from step 2 until you have n_estimators trees (default 100).

Final prediction: F(x) = mean(y) + ν · (tree₁(x) + tree₂(x) + … + tree₁₀₀(x)).

from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor

# Toy: 200 days, 2 features (e.g., today's return and 10-day vol)

### VHDL vs Verilog — `intro`
Two HDLs that compile to the same gates. VHDL: verbose, strongly typed, used
in this repo. Verilog/SystemVerilog: terser, more common at web-scale silicon
firms. The choice is cultural, not technical.

---

## Added in Lesson 0003 (ML Algorithms in Trading)

### Boosting — `intro`
Sequentially combine many weak learners (typically shallow trees), each trained
to correct the errors of the previous ensemble. Contrast with bagging
(independent learners averaged together).

### Classification vs Regression — `intro`
**Classification** predicts a discrete label (up/down). **Regression** predicts
a continuous number. This repo uses regression because the downstream step
ranks tickers by predicted-return magnitude, which requires the number itself.

### Cross-sectional ranking — `intro`
At each date, rank all tickers by their predicted return and act on the top-N.
The model's predicted *magnitude* matters less than its *order*. The whole
selection step in `paper_trading_sim.py` (`sort_values("pred")`) depends on this.

### Ensemble — `intro`
A model made of many sub-models combined to produce one prediction.
`GradientBoostingRegressor`'s default is 100 trees combined additively with a
0.1 learning rate.

### Feature engineering — `intro`
Turning raw data into model inputs. In this repo: returns, moving averages,
MA gap, rolling vol, RSI — all computed in `build_features` from raw Close prices.

### Gradient Boosting — `intro`
A boosting method where each new weak learner is fit to the gradient of the
loss with respect to the current ensemble's predictions. For squared error,
the gradient is just the residual `y − F(x)`, so each tree learns the current
error pattern.

### GradientBoostingRegressor — `intro`
scikit-learn's class for gradient-boosted decision trees on a continuous target.
The flagship model in `paper_trading_sim.py:train_model`.

### Inference — `intro`
Applying a trained model to make predictions (`model.predict(X)`). The
latency-sensitive half of ML — what HFT cares about almost exclusively.

### Learning rate (ν) — `intro`
The scalar that scales each new tree's contribution before adding it to the
ensemble. Smaller = more conservative updates, more trees needed, better
generalization. Default 0.1 in sklearn.

### Linear Regression — `intro`
`ŷ = w₀ + Σ wᵢ xᵢ`. Closed-form least-squares fit. Parametric, additive, fast.
Used in `fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd` because four constants fit in
silicon trivially.

### Look-ahead bias — `intro`
The bug where a feature secretly contains information from the future relative
to the target. Backtests look great; live trading loses money. The
`.shift(-1)` discipline in `build_features` is what prevents this when done
correctly.

### Mean-variance optimization — `intro`
Markowitz's portfolio framework: choose weights `w` to balance expected return
`μᵀw` against risk `wᵀΣw`. Closed-form long-only solution `w ∝ Σ⁻¹μ` is
implemented in `predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only`. Not ML — it's optimization
on top of the ML output.

### Non-parametric model — `intro`
A model whose effective parameter count grows with the data. Gradient-boosted
trees are non-parametric in this sense. Contrast: linear regression's
parameter count is fixed at N+1 regardless of dataset size.

### Overfitting — `intro`
When a model fits noise in the training data and fails to generalize to new
data. In `GradientBoostingRegressor` it appears as training R² climbing while
test R² drops. Fixes: lower learning rate, shallower trees, more
regularization, early stopping.

### Parametric model — `intro`
A model with a fixed number of parameters regardless of dataset size. Linear
regression: N feature weights plus an intercept, done. Parametric models are
much easier to fit on an FPGA.

### Residual — `intro`
`y − F(x)` — what the current ensemble got wrong on a given row. Gradient
boosting fits each new tree to predict the residuals of the previous step.

### RSI (Relative Strength Index) — `intro`
A 0–100 momentum oscillator that rises when up-days dominate down-days within
the lookback window. Computed in `paper_trading_sim._rsi` with window=14 and
normalized to 0–1 in `build_features`.

### Supervised learning — `intro`
Learning a mapping from inputs `x` to known outputs `y`, using a dataset of
labeled examples. All three "ML" elements in this repo (linear regression and
gradient boosting) are supervised. The MA rule in VHDL is *not* supervised —
it isn't learned at all.

### Target — `intro`
The value the model is trained to predict. In this repo: `fwd_ret_1d`, the
next-day return, computed via `out["ret_1d"].shift(-1)`.

### Training vs Inference — `intro`
**Training** is the expensive offline step that produces parameters (`fit`).
**Inference** is the cheap online step that uses them (`predict`). HFT cares
about inference latency; training latency essentially doesn't matter.

# Glossary — HFT_practice

Terms the learner has been introduced to. A term is promoted from *introduced* to
*understood* only after they've answered a question about it correctly or used it
correctly themselves.

Status legend: `intro` = covered in a lesson · `solid` = demonstrably grasped.

---

### Algorithmic trading — `intro`
Any trading where decisions are made by code rather than a human. A superset of HFT.

### Ask (offer) — `intro`
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.

### Adverse selection — `intro`
The risk that the counterparty who hit your quote knew more than you did about
where the price was about to go. The reason market makers cancel orders aggressively.

### Bid — `intro`
The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.

### Colocation — `intro`
Renting rack space inside the exchange's data center so your trading server is
physically next to the matching engine, minimizing wire latency.

### FPGA — `intro`
Field-Programmable Gate Array. Reconfigurable hardware wired into a fixed
pipeline at synthesis time. Used in HFT for deterministic nanosecond-scale latency.
Example in this repo: `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### HFT (High-Frequency Trading) — `intro`
Automated trading defined by microsecond-to-nanosecond latency, very high order
rates, and short (often sub-second) holding periods.

### Limit order — `intro`
"Buy/sell at price X or better." Rests passively in the book until matched or
cancelled. The order type market makers post.

### Limit Order Book (LOB) — `intro`
The full list of resting buy and sell orders at every price level on a venue.
The core data structure of modern electronic markets.

### Market maker — `intro`
A strategy that simultaneously posts both a bid and an ask, earning the spread
when both sides fill. `fpga/market_maker.vhd` is a hardware example.

### Market order — `intro`
"Fill me now at the best available price." Crosses the spread and pays for
immediacy. The order type takers send.

### Mid-price — `intro`
`(bid + ask) / 2`. A common reference for "fair value" between the two sides of
the book. Computed explicitly in `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### Q16.16 fixed-point — `intro`
A 32-bit signed integer encoding where the lower 16 bits represent the
fractional part: `real_value = integer_signal / 65536`. Used in
`fpga/market_maker.vhd` so all arithmetic stays in one-cycle integer ops.

### Spread — `intro`
`ask − bid`. The cost of crossing the book; the prize a market maker tries to
capture on round-trips.

### Tick — `intro`
A single market data update — a trade, a quote change, a cancel. The unit of
input to an HFT pipeline.

### Tick-to-trade latency — `intro`
The time between receiving a market data tick and your responding order leaving
your NIC. The headline latency number in HFT (top firms: ~100–500 ns on FPGA).

---

## Added in Lesson 0002 (FPGAs in HFT)

### ASIC — `intro`
Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. Silicon manufactured for one design.
Fastest possible, but multi-million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen forever —
which is why HFT firms use FPGAs (reconfigurable) instead.

### Bitstream — `intro`
The binary file produced by synthesis + place-and-route. Loading it onto the
FPGA configures every LUT, flip-flop, and routing switch to realize your
design. Reloading is a seconds-long operation, not a recompile of a chip.

### Combinational logic — `intro`
Logic whose outputs depend only on current inputs — no clock involved. Inside
each pipeline stage in `fpga/*.vhd`, arithmetic between clock edges is
combinational.

### Determinism (FPGA sense) — `intro`
The property that the same input takes the same number of cycles every time.
The opposite of CPU jitter from OS scheduling, cache misses, branch prediction.
The single biggest reason HFT firms tolerate the pain of FPGA development.

### DSP slice — `intro`
A dedicated multiply-accumulate block inside the FPGA fabric. Each `*` in
VHDL (e.g. `W_F0 * feature_0` in `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`) typically
maps to one DSP slice.

### HDL — `intro`
Hardware Description Language. VHDL or Verilog. Describes hardware
register-by-register, not as an executing program.

### HLS — `intro`
High-Level Synthesis. Toolchain that takes annotated C/C++ and generates HDL
for you. Faster to write than hand-VHDL; sometimes worse timing or area.
`fpga/hls_synthesis.tcl` drives the HLS flow in this repo.

### Jitter — `intro`
Variability in latency from one event to the next. HFT cares about jitter as
much as average latency, because strategies are sized against the worst-case
not the median.

### Kernel bypass — `intro`
Networking techniques (DPDK, Solarflare OpenOnload, XDP) that route packets
from the NIC directly to userspace, skipping the Linux kernel network stack.
A 20–30% latency win for CPU-based HFT; obsolete on FPGA NICs where parsing
is on-chip already.

### LUT (Look-Up Table) — `intro`
The basic configurable unit of FPGA fabric. A small truth table that can be
programmed to compute any function of N inputs (typically N=6). LUT count is
the headline capacity metric of an FPGA part.

### Pipeline stage — `intro`
A combinational chunk of logic terminated by a register (flip-flop). More
stages = higher clock frequency but more cycles of latency. `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`
has 2 stages; `market_maker.vhd` has 1.

### Place-and-Route (PAR) — `intro`
The step after synthesis that assigns each gate in your netlist to a physical
LUT on the chip and routes the wires between them. Where timing closure is
won or lost.

### Sequential logic — `intro`
Logic that uses flip-flops driven by a clock to hold state between cycles.
Each pipeline stage boundary in the repo's VHDL is sequential.

### Synthesis — `intro`
The step that turns HDL source into a netlist of generic gates. Distinct from
Place-and-Route, which maps those gates onto the physical chip.

### Timing closure — `intro`
The act of making your design meet the target clock period at every register-
to-register path. The real bottleneck of FPGA HFT development — not the
arithmetic, not the algorithm, but proving the silicon can run that fast.

### Valid handshake — `intro`
The convention of carrying a `valid` bit alongside every datum through a
pipeline, so each stage knows which cycles contain real data. Used uniformly
in all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules.

### VHDL vs Verilog — `intro`
Two HDLs that compile to the same gates. VHDL: verbose, strongly typed, used
in this repo. Verilog/SystemVerilog: terser, more common at web-scale silicon
firms. The choice is cultural, not technical.

+### Overfitting — `intro`
+When a model fits noise in the training data and fails to generalize to new
+data. In `GradientBoostingRegressor` it appears as training R² climbing while
+test R² drops. Fixes: lower learning rate, shallower trees, more
+regularization, early stopping.
+### Parametric model — `intro`
+A model with a fixed number of parameters regardless of dataset size. Linear
+regression: N feature weights plus an intercept, done. Parametric models are
+much easier to fit on an FPGA.
+### Residual — `intro`
+`y − F(x)` — what the current ensemble got wrong on a given row. Gradient
+boosting fits each new tree to predict the residuals of the previous step.
+### RSI (Relative Strength Index) — `intro`
+A 0–100 momentum oscillator that rises when up-days dominate down-days within
+the lookback window. Computed in `paper_trading_sim._rsi` with window=14 and
+normalized to 0–1 in `build_features`.
+### Supervised learning — `intro`
+Learning a mapping from inputs `x` to known outputs `y`, using a dataset of
+labeled examples. All three "ML" elements in this repo (linear regression and
+gradient boosting) are supervised. The MA rule in VHDL is *not* supervised —
+it isn't learned at all.
+### Target — `intro`
+The value the model is trained to predict. In this repo: `fwd_ret_1d`, the
+next-day return, computed via `out["ret_1d"].shift(-1)`.
+### Training vs Inference — `intro`
+**Training** is the expensive offline step that produces parameters (`fit`).
+**Inference** is the cheap online step that uses them (`predict`). HFT cares
+about inference latency; training latency essentially doesn't matter.

# =============================================================================
# Stage 1: Builder
# Install uv and sync all dependencies into an isolated virtual environment.
# =============================================================================
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder

ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1

# Install uv (fast Python package manager)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir uv

WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency manifests first so Docker layer-caches the venv
# on subsequent builds when only source code changes.
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./

# Sync all runtime deps into .venv.
# --no-install-project : skip installing the project itself at this stage
# Note: --frozen is intentionally omitted because the lockfile predates
# some deps (fastapi, uvicorn); uv resolves from pyproject.toml instead.
RUN uv sync --no-install-project

# =============================================================================
# Stage 2: Runtime
# Lean final image — only the venv and application source.
# =============================================================================
FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime

ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    # Activate the venv from the builder stage
    PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH" \
    # Use the non-interactive Agg backend so matplotlib never tries to open a display
    MPLBACKEND=Agg

# Create a non-root user for security
RUN groupadd --gid 1001 appuser && \
    useradd --uid 1001 --gid appuser --no-create-home --shell /bin/false appuser

WORKDIR /app

# Copy the fully-populated virtual environment from the builder
COPY --from=builder /app/.venv /app/.venv

# Copy application source (chowned to non-root user)
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .

# Declare volume mount points for large runtime-only data.
# These directories are bind-mounted at runtime — nothing is baked in.
VOLUME ["/app/data", "/app/models", "/app/results", "/app/news_files"]

# Drop to non-root user
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000

# Health check — uses Python's built-in urllib so no curl needed in slim image
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
    CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/'); exit(0)" \
    || exit 1

CMD ["/app/.venv/bin/uvicorn", "webapp.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

input.content:
Lesson 0004 Quiz: 0 / 5

Linux Internal Networking

Why this matters for HFT_practice: your docker-compose.yml quietly stands up a Linux network namespace with a virtual interface, a bridge, and an iptables NAT rule — every time you type docker compose up. And every HTTP request the FastAPI app handles traverses the Linux kernel network stack, which is the exact stack the fpga/README.md roadmap wants to bypass. Understanding both halves explains the difference between web-app latency (good enough at 1 ms) and HFT latency (catastrophic at 1 ms).

1. The Linux network stack, top to bottom

When uvicorn webapp.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 accepts a request, or when yf.download() in predict_next.py fetches a CSV, the data crosses a fixed set of layers in a fixed order. Knowing this map tells you where latency hides and what kernel bypass actually bypasses.

ApplicationYour Python (FastAPI, requests, yfinance). Calls socket(), send(), recv().your code
▼ syscall ▼
Socket layer (kernel)Validates the syscall, picks the right protocol, copies data from user memory into a kernel skb (socket buffer).~1–5 µs
▼
TCP / UDP (L4)Sequence numbers, retransmits, checksums, flow control. Adds an L4 header. This is the headline "TCP stack."~1–3 µs
▼
IP (L3)Routing table lookup, TTL, fragmentation. Adds an IP header. Picks which interface to send out.~1 µs
▼
Netfilter / iptablesFirewall and NAT rules. This is where Docker's ports: 8000:8000 rewrites destination addresses.~1–10 µs
▼
Qdisc / Traffic ControlQueueing discipline. Picks the next packet to hand to the driver.~1 µs
▼
NIC driver + DMADMA descriptor written; NIC fetches the packet from RAM and pushes it onto the wire.~1–5 µs
▼
Wire (PHY → switch → exchange)Physical layer. Latency dominated by distance and switch hops.100 ns – ms

Total round-trip through this stack on a busy Linux box: typically ~50–120 µs in the kernel alone, before the packet even reaches the wire. Recent research benchmarks ping at ~120 µs over the kernel stack and ~18 µs with busy-poll tuning. That's why HFT firms either go around this stack (kernel bypass) or replace it entirely (FPGA NICs).

2. Sockets, ports, and the three addresses you need to know

A socket is the kernel object that pairs an application process with a transport-layer endpoint. Identified by the 5-tuple (proto, src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port). Your uvicorn process owns one listening socket, and the kernel creates a fresh connected socket for every accepted TCP connection.

The bind address — meaning the port number alone is half the story

Bind addressListens onReachable fromWhen to use
127.0.0.1 Loopback interface only (lo) Same host (or same network namespace) Local-only dev, intra-container services.
0.0.0.0 Every interface on the host (or container) Anywhere routable to those IPs Servers exposed to other machines or to Docker's port mapping. This is what your Dockerfile uses.
192.168.x.y (specific) Just that one interface Anyone routable to that IP Multi-homed hosts where you want to expose a service on one network only.

The lo (loopback) interface — special and important

lo (with IP 127.0.0.1) is a virtual interface inside the kernel. Packets sent to it never touch a NIC, never see the wire, and skip the driver entirely. That's why python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/')" — the Dockerfile's HEALTHCHECK — is fast and reliable. The same loopback inside one container is a different loopback than the host's. They share an address (127.0.0.1) but live in different network namespaces.

3. Network namespaces — how Docker isolates networking

A network namespace is a kernel object that gives a group of processes their own private copy of the network stack: their own interfaces, their own routing table, their own iptables rules, their own lo. This is the Lego brick that makes containers possible.

When you run docker compose up on this repo, here's what happens:

  1. Docker creates a new network namespace for the hft_web container.
  2. It creates a veth pair — two virtual ethernet interfaces, like a network cable with both ends in software. One end (eth0) sits in the container's namespace; the other (vethXXXX) sits in the host's namespace.
  3. The host-side veth is plugged into a Linux bridge (docker0 by default, or a per-compose-project bridge).
  4. The bridge gets a private subnet (e.g. 172.18.0.0/16) and assigns the container an IP from it.
  5. ports: "8000:8000" installs an iptables DNAT rule (or starts docker-proxy) so that traffic hitting host:8000 gets rewritten to containerIP:8000.
  6. Egress from the container (e.g. yfinance fetching prices) hits an iptables MASQUERADE rule that rewrites the source to the host's IP — classic NAT.

This is why the inside and outside of a container disagree about networking:

Inside the container

  • eth0 with an IP like 172.18.0.2
  • Its own lo (127.0.0.1) — distinct from the host's
  • Default route → bridge IP → host
  • Sees 0.0.0.0:8000 as "all my interfaces"

On the host

  • docker0 (or per-project) bridge with the subnet
  • vethXXXX dangling off the bridge
  • iptables: DNAT rule forwards 0.0.0.0:8000 → 172.18.0.2:8000
  • Host's 127.0.0.1:8000 works only because of that NAT rule

A minimal mental experiment

# Run on the host while the container is up:
$ ip netns list                          # list namespaces (Docker hides these from the default location)
$ docker exec hft_web ip addr            # show the container's interfaces
$ ip addr show docker0                   # show the bridge on the host
$ sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n      # show the DNAT rules Docker installed
$ ss -tlnp | grep :8000                  # who's listening on port 8000 from the host's POV?

4. In this project

Dockerfile (line 64) 
CMD ["/app/.venv/bin/uvicorn", "webapp.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

--host 0.0.0.0 tells uvicorn to bind to every interface inside the container's namespace. If this were 127.0.0.1, only processes inside the same container could reach it — port forwarding from the host would fail because the DNAT target wouldn't have anything listening on its eth0 address. Common newbie mistake; harmless to fix.

docker-compose.yml (lines 23–24) 
ports:
  - "8000:8000"     # host_port:container_port

The host_port:container_port form is a directive to install a DNAT rule. Type "8000" alone (no colon) and Docker picks a random host port — useful for parallel test environments where you don't want port collisions.

Dockerfile (lines 60–62) + docker-compose.yml (lines 34–45) 
HEALTHCHECK ... CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/')"

Healthcheck runs inside the container, so localhost here means the container's own lo — same network namespace as uvicorn. This works because uvicorn bound to 0.0.0.0, which includes 127.0.0.1. If uvicorn had bound to a specific eth0 IP only, the loopback healthcheck would fail even though external HTTP would work. Yes, that is a fun debugging afternoon.

And outbound traffic — yfinance, Alpha Vantage, Robinhood

When news_fetch.py hits Alpha Vantage, or paper_trading_sim.py calls yf.download(), the packet path from inside the container is:

Python requests → kernel socket inside container ns → container eth0 → veth → host bridge (docker0) → iptables MASQUERADE rewrites source to host IP → host's real NIC → internet

This explains the .env.docker setup. The Docker container has its own resolv.conf for DNS, its own routing table, its own iptables rules. Credentials (ALPHAVANTAGE_API_KEY, RH_*) have to be injected via env vars because the container otherwise has no idea how to fetch them from your host's filesystem.

5. Why this all matters for the HFT roadmap

Look back at the latency table in §1. The Linux kernel network stack costs roughly 50–120 µs round-trip. fpga/README.md's roadmap is aiming for <500 ns tick-to-trade — three orders of magnitude smaller than the kernel's contribution alone. The only way to hit that budget is to refuse to use the kernel network stack at all. Three techniques, in increasing order of radicalness:

Busy polling (the cheap win)

Tell the kernel to spin-wait on the NIC's RX queue (SO_BUSY_POLL, napi_busy_read) instead of sleeping for an interrupt. Saves the scheduling latency. Recent benchmarks show ping latency dropping from ~120 µs to ~18 µs. Cheap, no new hardware, but still in the kernel.

Kernel bypass (DPDK, OpenOnload)

Map the NIC's DMA rings directly into userspace and skip the kernel for the hot path. Solarflare/AMD OpenOnload achieves ~750–800 ns wire-to-wire on commodity hardware (Lesson 0002). Trading firms use this on most non-FPGA paths.

FPGA NIC (the nuclear option)

The NIC is the FPGA. Packets enter the PHY and are parsed in-fabric by linear_regression_predictor.vhd-style logic; orders exit on the same chip. ~100–500 ns total. Skips the kernel, skips PCIe (for the hot path), skips userspace.

Where this repo lives today

The Python (webapp + scripts) uses the regular kernel stack. Fine — none of it is latency-critical. The FPGA modules are arithmetic ready for the nuclear option, but the network plumbing (10 GbE UDP parser, FIX decoder) is on the roadmap, not built.

Repo honesty: the only Python in this repo that talks to a real exchange is scripts/robinhood_executor.py, and it uses ordinary HTTPS over the kernel stack. That's correct for a retail brokerage — Robinhood's REST API is comfortably above microsecond latencies. The kernel-bypass conversation only becomes real if and when this repo gets a direct exchange feed.

6. Often confused with

localhost vs 0.0.0.0

localhost / 127.0.0.1 is an address — "I only listen on the loopback interface." 0.0.0.0 is a wildcard — "I listen on every interface in this namespace." They are not synonyms; binding to one and connecting to the other has different reachability consequences.

Port vs Socket

A port is a 16-bit number that distinguishes endpoints on a host. A socket is the kernel object that owns one end of a connection, identified by the full 5-tuple. One listening socket can spawn thousands of connected sockets, all bound to the same port.

Bridge vs Switch vs Router

A bridge (Docker's docker0) forwards Ethernet frames within one broadcast domain — L2. A switch is the hardware version of the same thing. A router moves packets between L3 networks and rewrites L3 addresses (NAT). Docker uses all three concepts at once.

NAT vs Port Forwarding

NAT (specifically MASQUERADE / SNAT) rewrites the source IP of outbound traffic so replies come back to the host. Port forwarding (DNAT) rewrites the destination of inbound traffic so it lands on a specific container. Docker installs both — and most "why can't I reach my container" questions are about one of them being missing.

Container network ns vs Host network

--network host in Docker puts the container in the host's namespace — no veth, no bridge, no NAT. Faster (no virtual hops) but breaks isolation. HFT-style apps sometimes use this; web apps generally shouldn't.

Kernel stack vs Kernel bypass

Kernel stack: data goes through socket(), read(), the TCP/IP code in the kernel. ~50–120 µs. Kernel bypass: DMA rings mapped to userspace; the application polls the NIC directly. ~1 µs. FPGAs go further still.

7. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. Your Dockerfile starts uvicorn with --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 by mistake, and your docker-compose.yml still has ports: "8000:8000". What happens when you hit http://localhost:8000 from your laptop?

  • Connection refused. uvicorn is only listening on the container's loopback; the DNAT rule sends traffic to the container's eth0 IP, which has nothing on port 8000.
  • It works fine — host loopback and container loopback are the same interface.
  • It works, but slowly, because of an IP collision between host and container 127.0.0.1.
  • The healthcheck would fail and Docker would mark the container unhealthy.

Q2. The Dockerfile's HEALTHCHECK uses urlopen('http://localhost:8000/') and it succeeds. What does localhost resolve to in that context?

  • The host machine's loopback (127.0.0.1 on your laptop).
  • The container's own loopback interface (127.0.0.1 inside its private network namespace).
  • The docker0 bridge's IP.
  • The host's public IP, via DNS resolution.

Q3. Why does fpga/README.md's roadmap want a "10 GbE UDP stack" implemented directly on the FPGA instead of reusing the Linux kernel's UDP stack?

  • Because Linux doesn't support raw UDP sockets without root.
  • The Linux kernel UDP stack adds ~50–120 µs of latency per round-trip; the FPGA's entire tick-to-trade budget is ~100–500 ns, so any kernel involvement blows the budget by ~100×.
  • Because the kernel's UDP implementation drops too many packets to be reliable.
  • Because exchange traffic is encrypted and the kernel can't decrypt it fast enough.

Q4. You change docker-compose.yml from ports: "8000:8000" to network_mode: host. What's the most important consequence?

  • The container becomes just a process on the host with no isolation at all.
  • The container shares the host's network namespace — no veth, no bridge, no NAT rule. uvicorn binds directly to the host's interfaces. Lower latency, no isolation, no port-collision protection.
  • The application becomes slower because the host's network stack is busier.
  • Port 8000 becomes available to other applications because Docker stops claiming it.

Q5. Inside the container, news_fetch.py calls Alpha Vantage. By the time the packet reaches Alpha Vantage's servers, what is its source IP?

  • The container's internal IP (e.g. 172.18.0.2).
  • The docker0 bridge's IP.
  • The host's public-facing IP (via iptables MASQUERADE on egress, then any further NAT done by your router or cloud provider).
  • 127.0.0.1, because the container's loopback handles outbound traffic.

8. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. A teammate adds a Redis cache to docker-compose.yml and is confused that webapp.main can't reach it via redis://127.0.0.1:6379. How do you explain the fix?

Each service in docker-compose.yml gets its own network namespace. Inside the web container, 127.0.0.1 is its own loopback — Redis isn't there. Docker Compose, however, sets up DNS so each service is reachable by its compose-name on the project's bridge. The fix is redis://redis:6379: the hostname redis resolves to the Redis container's eth0 IP on the shared bridge network. This is why "localhost doesn't work between containers" is one of the most common Docker confusions.

S2. You suspect news_fetch.py is being rate-limited because the entire container's egress shares one source IP at Alpha Vantage's gateway. What single Docker change would prove or disprove this?

The cleanest test is to run two separate containers concurrently and watch whether the rate limit is per-container or per-source-IP. By default they both NAT through the same host IP, so the rate limiter would treat them as one client. To prove the rate limit is per-source-IP rather than per-API-key, you'd need to put the second container behind a different host IP — easiest via a second host or a second cloud egress address. A configuration-only test on one host can't fully disentangle it, but a quick proxy through a different VPC interface usually does.

S3. You enable SO_BUSY_POLL on the FastAPI socket. Why might overall system throughput go down even though per-request latency goes down?

Busy polling burns a CPU core spinning instead of sleeping. The kernel can't let that core run other work — your gradient boosting training thread, your news-fetcher, your background equity curve renderer — so total throughput drops. This is the universal latency-vs-throughput tradeoff and the reason HFT firms dedicate specific cores to busy-polling and isolate them from the scheduler (isolcpus, nohz_full). For a web app where p99 latency is fine in the millisecond range, busy polling is strictly a loss.

Next lesson candidates: (a) Walk-forward backtesting and look-ahead bias grounded in walkforward_sim.py, or (b) Mean-variance portfolio optimization grounded in predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only. Both were teed up by Lesson 0003.

Tell the kernel to spin-wait on the NIC's RX queue (SO_BUSY_POLL, napi_busy_read) instead of sleeping for an interrupt. Saves the scheduling latency. Recent benchmarks show ping latency dropping from ~120 µs to ~18 µs. Cheap, no new hardware, but still in the kernel.

Kernel bypass (DPDK, OpenOnload)

Map the NIC's DMA rings directly into userspace and skip the kernel for the hot path. Solarflare/AMD OpenOnload achieves ~750–800 ns wire-to-wire on commodity hardware (Lesson 0002). Trading firms use this on most non-FPGA paths.

FPGA NIC (the nuclear option)

The NIC is the FPGA. Packets enter the PHY and are parsed in-fabric by linear_regression_predictor.vhd-style logic; orders exit on the same chip. ~100–500 ns total. Skips the kernel, skips PCIe (for the hot path), skips userspace.

Where this repo lives today

The Python (webapp + scripts) uses the regular kernel stack. Fine — none of it is latency-critical. The FPGA modules are arithmetic ready for the nuclear option, but the network plumbing (10 GbE UDP parser, FIX decoder) is on the roadmap, not built.

Repo honesty: the only Python in this repo that talks to a real exchange is scripts/robinhood_executor.py, and it uses ordinary HTTPS over the kernel stack. That's correct for a retail brokerage — Robinhood's REST API is comfortably above microsecond latencies. The kernel-bypass conversation only becomes real if and when this repo gets a direct exchange feed.

6. Often confused with

localhost vs 0.0.0.0

localhost / 127.0.0.1 is an address — "I only listen on the loopback interface." 0.0.0.0 is a wildcard — "I listen on every interface in this namespace." They are not synonyms; binding to one and connecting to the other has different reachability consequences.

Port vs Socket

A port is a 16-bit number that distinguishes endpoints on a host. A socket is the kernel object that owns one end of a connection, identified by the full 5-tuple. One listening socket can spawn thousands of connected sockets, all bound to the same port.

Bridge vs Switch vs Router

A bridge (Docker's docker0) forwards Ethernet frames within one broadcast domain — L2. A switch is the hardware version of the same thing. A router moves packets between L3 networks and rewrites L3 addresses (NAT). Docker uses all three concepts at once.

NAT vs Port Forwarding

NAT (specifically MASQUERADE / SNAT) rewrites the source IP of outbound traffic so replies come back to the host. Port forwarding (DNAT) rewrites the destination of inbound traffic so it lands on a specific container. Docker installs both — and most "why can't I reach my container" questions are about one of them being missing.

Container network ns vs Host network

--network host in Docker puts the container in the host's namespace — no veth, no bridge, no NAT. Faster (no virtual hops) but breaks isolation. HFT-style apps sometimes use this; web apps generally shouldn't.

Kernel stack vs Kernel bypass

Kernel stack: data goes through socket(), read(), the TCP/IP code in the kernel. ~50–120 µs. Kernel bypass: DMA rings mapped to userspace; the application polls the NIC directly. ~1 µs. FPGAs go further still.

7. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. Your Dockerfile starts uvicorn with --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 by mistake, and your docker-compose.yml still has ports: "8000:8000". What happens when you hit http://localhost:8000 from your laptop?

  • Connection refused. uvicorn is only listening on the container's loopback; the DNAT rule sends traffic to the container's eth0 IP, which has nothing on port 8000.
  • It works fine — host loopback and container loopback are the same interface.
  • It works, but slowly, because of an IP collision between host and container 127.0.0.1.
  • The healthcheck would fail and Docker would mark the container unhealthy.

Q2. The Dockerfile's HEALTHCHECK uses urlopen('http://localhost:8000/') and it succeeds. What does localhost resolve to in that context?

  • The host machine's loopback (127.0.0.1 on your laptop).
  • The container's own loopback interface (127.0.0.1 inside its private network namespace).
  • The docker0 bridge's IP.
  • The host's public IP, via DNS resolution.

Q3. Why does fpga/README.md's roadmap want a "10 GbE UDP stack" implemented directly on the FPGA instead of reusing the Linux kernel's UDP stack?

  • Because Linux doesn't support raw UDP sockets without root.
  • The Linux kernel UDP stack adds ~50–120 µs of latency per round-trip; the FPGA's entire tick-to-trade budget is ~100–500 ns, so any kernel involvement blows the budget by ~100×.
  • Because the kernel's UDP implementation drops too many packets to be reliable.
  • Because exchange traffic is encrypted and the kernel can't decrypt it fast enough.

Q4. You change docker-compose.yml from ports: "8000:8000" to network_mode: host. What's the most important consequence?

  • The container becomes just a process on the host with no isolation at all.
  • The container shares the host's network namespace — no veth, no bridge, no NAT rule. uvicorn binds directly to the host's interfaces. Lower latency, no isolation, no port-collision protection.
  • The application becomes slower because the host's network stack is busier.
  • Port 8000 becomes available to other applications because Docker stops claiming it.

Q5. Inside the container, news_fetch.py calls Alpha Vantage. By the time the packet reaches Alpha Vantage's servers, what is its source IP?

  • The container's internal IP (e.g. 172.18.0.2).
  • The docker0 bridge's IP.
  • The host's public-facing IP (via iptables MASQUERADE on egress, then any further NAT done by your router or cloud provider).
  • 127.0.0.1, because the container's loopback handles outbound traffic.

8. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. A teammate adds a Redis cache to docker-compose.yml and is confused that webapp.main can't reach it via redis://127.0.0.1:6379. How do you explain the fix?

Each service in docker-compose.yml gets its own network namespace. Inside the web container, 127.0.0.1 is its own loopback — Redis isn't there. Docker Compose, however, sets up DNS so each service is reachable by its compose-name on the project's bridge. The fix is redis://redis:6379: the hostname redis resolves to the Redis container's eth0 IP on the shared bridge network. This is why "localhost doesn't work between containers" is one of the most common Docker confusions.

S2. You suspect news_fetch.py is being rate-limited because the entire container's egress shares one source IP at Alpha Vantage's gateway. What single Docker change would prove or disprove this?

The cleanest test is to run two separate containers concurrently and watch whether the rate limit is per-container or per-source-IP. By default they both NAT through the same host IP, so the rate limiter would treat them as one client. To prove the rate limit is per-source-IP rather than per-API-key, you'd need to put the second container behind a different host IP — easiest via a second host or a second cloud egress address. A configuration-only test on one host can't fully disentangle it, but a quick proxy through a different VPC interface usually does.

S3. You enable SO_BUSY_POLL on the FastAPI socket. Why might overall system throughput go down even though per-request latency goes down?

Busy polling burns a CPU core spinning instead of sleeping. The kernel can't let that core run other work — your gradient boosting training thread, your news-fetcher, your background equity curve renderer — so total throughput drops. This is the universal latency-vs-throughput tradeoff and the reason HFT firms dedicate specific cores to busy-polling and isolate them from the scheduler (isolcpus, nohz_full). For a web app where p99 latency is fine in the millisecond range, busy polling is strictly a loss.

Next lesson candidates: (a) Walk-forward backtesting and look-ahead bias grounded in walkforward_sim.py, or (b) Mean-variance portfolio optimization grounded in predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only. Both were teed up by Lesson 0003.

### Training vs Inference — `intro`
**Training** is the expensive offline step that produces parameters (`fit`).
**Inference** is the cheap online step that uses them (`predict`). HFT cares
about inference latency; training latency essentially doesn't matter.

---

## Added in Lesson 0004 (Linux Internal Networking)

### 0.0.0.0 (wildcard bind) — `intro`
A wildcard address meaning "listen on every interface in this network
namespace." Used in this repo's `Dockerfile`. Distinct from `127.0.0.1`,
which means "loopback only."

### Bridge (Linux bridge) — `intro`
A software L2 switch in the kernel. Docker creates one (`docker0` by default,
or a per-project bridge for `docker-compose`) and plugs every container's
veth into it so they can talk to each other and to the outside.

### Busy polling — `intro`
Kernel networking option (`SO_BUSY_POLL`) that spins a CPU on the NIC's RX
queue instead of sleeping for an interrupt. Trades a CPU core for ~100 µs
of latency reduction. Useful for HFT-adjacent workloads, wasteful for web apps.

### DNAT (Destination NAT) — `intro`
iptables rule that rewrites the destination IP/port of inbound packets. Docker
installs DNAT rules to implement `ports: "HOST:CONTAINER"` mappings.

### DPDK — `intro`
Data Plane Development Kit. Userspace networking framework that maps the NIC's
DMA rings directly into application memory, bypassing the kernel stack. Common
in HFT and high-perf network appliances.

### eth0 (container) — `intro`
The conventional name of a container's primary virtual ethernet interface.
One end of a veth pair; the other end sits on the host bridge.

### iptables / Netfilter — `intro`
The Linux kernel's packet-filtering and NAT framework. Docker programs it to
implement port forwarding (DNAT) and outbound source rewriting (MASQUERADE).

### Kernel bypass — `solid` (promoted from intro in Lesson 0002)
Skipping the kernel network stack to cut tick-to-trade latency. DPDK,
OpenOnload, XDP are CPU-side; FPGA NICs go further by doing parsing in
hardware.

Six contrasts, 5 quiz questions, 3 scenarios (Redis-can't-be-reached, API rate-limit-per-source-IP, busy-poll throughput tradeoff).

## Honest framing in the lesson

The Python web app uses the regular kernel network stack, and that's fine — Robinhood's REST API is comfortably above microsecond timescales.
