This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

**Chronos (Amazon):** Chronos builds on T5, a text-to-text transformer originally developed for natural language tasks, contains 200 million parameters and was pre-trained on over 100 diverse time series datasets. It applies tokenization via scaling and quantization, allowing transformer-based encoder-decoder architectures to perform zero-shot probabilistic forecasting across various benchmarks.

## Application to Finance and Trading

Time-series foundation models promise to replace one-dataset-per-model pipelines with pretrained models that transfer in zero-/few-shot settings. Native TSFMs show more consistent zero-shot transfer on public forecasting suites, with TimesFM and Chronos outperforming LLM-for-TS on term-structure and volatility tasks.

Additionally, Kronos, introduced in a 2025 arXiv paper by researchers from Tsinghua University, is a family of decoder-only foundation models pre-trained specifically on financial K-line data with a pre-training corpus spanning over 12 billion K-line records across 45 global exchanges, multiple asset classes, and diverse timeframes.

1. A trading prediction model lives on five axes

A "model" in trading isn't just "GBM" or "LSTM." Two engineers can both say "gradient boosting" and have built completely different systems. The thing that actually differs is these five choices:

1. Target — what number (or class) you train to predict.
2. Horizon — over what future window the target is measured.
3. Pooling — one model across all assets, or one per asset.
4. Output shape — point estimate, distribution, or action.
5. Adaptivity — train once forever, or rolling retrain.

Where this repo sits:

AxisThis repo's choiceWhere it's set
TargetNext-day return magnitude (a continuous number)build_features → fwd_ret_1d
Horizon1 trading day.shift(-1) in build_features
PoolingCross-sectional — one model on stacked rows from all tickerssimulate in paper_trading_sim.py
Output shapePoint estimate (no uncertainty, no quantiles)GradientBoostingRegressor.predict
AdaptivityEither: one-shot train (paper_trading_sim) or rolling retrain (walkforward_sim with --rolling_retrain)walkforward_sim.py:184–207
The mental shift: "What model should I use?" is the wrong opening question. "What target, on what horizon, pooled how, expressed how, refreshed how often?" — answer those, and the algorithm choice (GBM, linear, neural) follows almost mechanically.

2. Axis 1 — What you predict

The single most consequential modeling choice. The same dataset can support several different prediction problems, each with different math, different evaluation, and different downstream use.

TargetTypeWhy pick itUsed in this repo?
Return direction (up/down) Binary classification You only care about side of the bet. No — would lose magnitude info needed for ranking.
Return magnitude (a number) Regression You need to rank N tickers and size positions. Yes. fwd_ret_1d.
Volatility (next-day or next-week) Regression (positive) Sizing positions, pricing options, risk overlays. Not directly, but vol_10 shows up as a feature.

Optimal action (buy/hold/sell amount) Reinforcement learning End-to-end optimization including execution. No. Out of scope.

What about horizon?

Horizon and target are tangled. "Next return" means nothing without a horizon. The repo's daily horizon shapes everything: yfinance OHLCV is daily, features are daily, target is 1-day-ahead, retraining (when enabled) is monthly. Move to a 5-second horizon and you'd need tick data, microsecond features, and a completely different infrastructure (see Lessons 0001–0002).

3. Axis 3 — Cross-sectional pooling, the non-obvious decision

The repo trains one GradientBoostingRegressor on stacked rows from every ticker. This is a meaningful choice, and many beginners would default to the other approach without realizing they've picked.

Per-asset models (one per ticker)

Train AAPL's model only on AAPL data, MSFT's only on MSFT data, etc. Captures asset-specific quirks; suffers from small training sets; completely fails on a ticker with no history (IPOs, additions to the index).

Cross-sectional pooled (this repo)

paper_trading_sim.py:simulate (lines 198–216) 
stacked = []
for t, f in feats.items():
    f2 = f.copy()
    f2["ticker"] = t                   # label the ticker on each row
    stacked.append(f2)
panel = pd.concat(stacked).dropna()  # one big tall DataFrame

# ... time-split each ticker ...

X_train, y_train, feat_cols = prepare_xy(train_df)
model = train_model(X_train, y_train)    # single model, all tickers' rows

Notice prepare_xy explicitly drops the ticker column from the feature matrix. The model never learns "AAPL behaves differently than MSFT" — it learns a universal mapping from technical features to return. That's the cross-sectional assumption baked in.

When pooling breaks: if a small-cap biotech behaves nothing like a mega-cap tech name, a pooled model averages across the difference and gets both wrong. Real production setups often pool within sector or market-cap bucket. The repo doesn't bucket at all — keep that limit in mind.

4. Axis-blind tour: the model families you'll see in trading literature

Linear / factor models

Fama-French, BARRA, Arbitrage Pricing Theory. Weights on a small set of risk factors (size, value, momentum). Still dominant in mid-frequency. FPGA-friendly. In repo: the predictor in linear_regression_predictor.vhd is the simplest case.

Tree ensembles

Time-series foundation models (2024–2025 wave)

For tabular daily-frequency equity prediction — exactly what this repo does — a well-tuned gradient booster beats almost everything. Neural sequence models and foundation models win on text-like or richly-sequential inputs, not on a few daily-bar features. The repo's choice of GBM is defensible, even with all the sexier options on the table.

5. In this project — the adaptivity axis

Of the five axes, the one Lesson 0003 didn't touch is adaptivity. The repo actually has both modes wired up — fair to know they exist.

Mode A: train-once (the simple backtest)

paper_trading_sim.py:simulate (overview) 
# 1. Take 70% of the timeline as training (default --train_ratio=0.7).
# 2. Fit ONE model on that block.
# 3. Use it unchanged for the entire 30% test block.
model = train_model(X_train, y_train)
preds = model.predict(X_test)

Simple to reason about, but the model never sees the regime shift between 2019 and 2024. A pre-COVID model "predicting" 2020 is, charitably, optimistic.

Mode B: rolling retrain

walkforward_sim.py (lines 184–235, condensed) 
if rolling_retrain and _should_retrain(last_train_dt, dt):
    # Re-fit the model using all rows up to (but not including) `dt`
    # Frequency: --retrain_freq {daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly}
    # Window:    --train_window_days N  (e.g. 756 = ~3y)
    model = refit_model(history_up_to(dt))
    last_train_dt = dt

Every retrain bin (default monthly), the model is refit on the most recent --train_window_days of past data only. Each prediction uses information that was actually available at the time — the textbook walk-forward discipline that prevents look-ahead bias.

Mode C (bolted on): a regime model as risk overlay

walkforward_sim.py (lines 300–317) 
# GaussianMixture as a stress/regime classifier on recent returns
gm = GaussianMixture(n_components=hmm_states, random_state=42)
gm.fit(returns_window)
probs = gm.predict_proba(returns_window)

if probs[-1, stress_comp] >= hmm_prob:
    gm_hit = True          # "today looks like the high-vol component"

stress = bool(high_vol or deep_dd or cusum_hit or gm_hit)
# If stress, scale portfolio weights down toward cash (--risk_scale)

Two things to notice:

  • The GMM doesn't predict returns. It predicts which of K hidden regimes today belongs to. The regime then gates the return-prediction model's output — a classic "decoupled signal + decoupled risk" architecture.
  • Four independent stress detectors are OR-ed together: vol filter, drawdown filter, CUSUM change-point test, and the GMM regime probability. This is ensembling at the regime level, not the prediction level.
Repo honesty: the regime overlay is impressive scaffolding, but none of the saved model bundles in models/ were trained with the full risk overlay turned on. The headline ~27% annualized number comes from the base GBM. Treat the HMM/CUSUM/etc. as available knobs rather than proven contributors until you ablate them yourself.

6. Often confused with

Predicting a return vs predicting a price

Always predict returns, not prices. Prices are non-stationary (a $200 AAPL is not comparable to a $100 AAPL), have wildly different scales across tickers, and are dominated by their long-run drift. Returns are stationary-enough, comparable, and zero-mean.

Cross-sectional vs time-series prediction

Cross-sectional = "given many assets on day T, rank them." Time-series = "given one asset, forecast its next value." The repo's GBM is cross-sectional in spirit (top-N over all tickers each day); a per-ticker LSTM would be time-series.

Forecasting vs filtering

Forecasting: estimate a future value (next return). Filtering: estimate a present hidden state from past observations (HMM regime "is today calm or stressed?"). The GMM overlay is filtering, not forecasting.

Point estimate vs distributional forecast

A point estimate says "expected return = 0.4%." A distributional forecast says "expected = 0.4%, std = 1.8%, 95% interval [−2.6%, 3.4%]." Risk-aware sizing wants the latter; the repo works around having only point estimates by computing covariance separately in predict_next.py.

Walk-forward retrain vs online learning

Walk-forward retrain: stop, refit on a window, resume. Online learning: model updates after every observation (incremental SGD, Bayesian update). The repo's rolling_retrain is the former — periodic batch refit, not true online.

Both numbers will be reported by any honest backtest. In-sample R² is always optimistic — it's the score on the rows the model has already seen. Out-of-sample R² is the only one anyone should trust. Look for "test_preds" in this repo's --save_preds output.

7. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. paper_trading_sim.py trains one GradientBoostingRegressor on the stacked dataset from all tickers, dropping the ticker column from the features. What is the implicit assumption?

  • That yfinance can't return per-ticker data, only stacked panels.
  • That the relationship between technical features and next-day return is roughly universal across tickers — i.e. it doesn't depend on which company you're looking at.
  • That including the ticker column would cause overfitting on a categorical variable.
  • That the model will learn its own ticker embedding from the numeric features.

Q2. What does the GaussianMixture block in walkforward_sim.py actually predict?

  • The next day's return magnitude.
  • The probability that the most recent day belongs to a 'high-vol' / 'stress' latent component, used to gate portfolio exposure.
  • The same thing as the GradientBoostingRegressor — it's an ensemble alternative.
  • Tomorrow's volatility level as a forecast.

Q3. You decide to add a target that predicts "will the stock move more than 5% tomorrow?" as a binary 0/1. What's the most accurate description of what you've just changed?

  • You've changed the adaptivity axis — the model will now retrain more often.
  • You've changed the target axis from continuous regression to binary classification, which cascades into a different loss function and a different downstream allocation step.
  • You've changed the pooling axis from cross-sectional to per-asset.
  • You've changed the output-shape axis from point to distributional.

Q4. Why does build_features in paper_trading_sim.py use pct_change (returns) rather than the raw close price as the target?

  • Because returns are smaller numbers, so the model converges faster.
  • Because daily returns are normally distributed, but prices aren't.
  • Because prices are non-stationary and not comparable across tickers; returns are roughly stationary and comparable, which the cross-sectional pooling assumption requires.
  • Because GradientBoostingRegressor rejects targets with non-zero mean.

Q5. A colleague proposes replacing the GBM with a time-series foundation model (TimesFM or Chronos) for daily next-day prediction. Best response?

  • "Great — these models are pretrained on billions of points, so they'll outperform our tiny dataset.
  • "Won't work — those models can't run on consumer hardware.
  • "Worth a side experiment but not a replacement — on tabular daily-bar features with cross-sectional ranking, well-tuned GBM is still hard to beat per recent finance benchmarks of TSFMs.
  • "Impossible — our pipeline is tabular, and these models only accept text.

8. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. You add a small-cap biotech to your tickers.txt alongside the existing large-cap tech names. The backtest's Sharpe drops noticeably. What's the most likely modeling-level cause?

The pooled model is now averaging across two regimes — small-cap biotech and large-cap tech — that have genuinely different relationships between technical features and next-day return (biotech is event-driven; tech is momentum-driven). The cross-sectional assumption breaks. Fixes: bucket the universe by sector or market cap and train one model per bucket, or add categorical/sector features back into the input. The repo doesn't bucket today — this is a real, fixable gap.

S2. You want to add a confidence interval to each prediction so predict_next.py can size positions smaller when the model is uncertain. What axis are you changing, and what's a clean way to do it without abandoning the current GBM?

That's the output-shape axis — moving from point estimate to distributional forecast. Option (a) is the simplest principled choice and lives within the existing toolchain.

S3. walkforward_sim.py with --rolling_retrain --retrain_freq monthly beats the train-once mode of paper_trading_sim.py on 2020–2024 by a wide margin. Why isn't rolling retrain just always the right choice?

Two reasons. First, compute: every retrain costs a full GBM fit; monthly is fine, daily is expensive. The default --train_window_days 756 (~3 years) and monthly retrain is a defensible bias-variance compromise — but it's a compromise, not a free win. Always-train-on-everything (no rolling window) drifts; always-retrain-on-the- last-month chases noise. The sweet spot is asset- and regime-dependent.

  • "Great — these models are pretrained on billions of points, so they'll outperform our tiny dataset.
  • "Won't work — those models can't run on consumer hardware.
  • "Worth a side experiment but not a replacement — on tabular daily-bar features with cross-sectional ranking, well-tuned GBM is still hard to beat per recent finance benchmarks of TSFMs.
  • "Impossible — our pipeline is tabular, and these models only accept text.

8. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. You add a small-cap biotech to your tickers.txt alongside the existing large-cap tech names. The backtest's Sharpe drops noticeably. What's the most likely modeling-level cause?

The pooled model is now averaging across two regimes — small-cap biotech and large-cap tech — that have genuinely different relationships between technical features and next-day return (biotech is event-driven; tech is momentum-driven). The cross-sectional assumption breaks. Fixes: bucket the universe by sector or market cap and train one model per bucket, or add categorical/sector features back into the input. The repo doesn't bucket today — this is a real, fixable gap.

S2. You want to add a confidence interval to each prediction so predict_next.py can size positions smaller when the model is uncertain. What axis are you changing, and what's a clean way to do it without abandoning the current GBM?

That's the output-shape axis — moving from point estimate to distributional forecast. Clean ways: (a) train two GBMs with quantile loss at the 10th and 90th percentiles to bracket the prediction (sklearn supports loss='quantile' via the HistGradientBoostingRegressor); (b) compute residual standard deviation on a held-out validation slice and use that as a constant uncertainty; (c) bootstrap-ensemble many GBMs and use the empirical spread. Option (a) is the simplest principled choice and lives within the existing toolchain.

S3. walkforward_sim.py with --rolling_retrain --retrain_freq monthly beats the train-once mode of paper_trading_sim.py on 2020–2024 by a wide margin. Why isn't rolling retrain just always the right choice?

Two reasons. First, compute: every retrain costs a full GBM fit; monthly is fine, daily is expensive. Second, and more important, statistical noise: a too-frequent retrain on a too-short window will overfit the most recent market microstructure and whiplash. The default --train_window_days 756 (~3 years) and monthly retrain is a defensible bias-variance compromise — but it's a compromise, not a free win. Always-train-on-everything (no rolling window) drifts; always-retrain-on-the- last-month chases noise. The sweet spot is asset- and regime-dependent.

Next lesson candidates: (a) Walk-forward backtesting + look-ahead bias formalized against walkforward_sim.py internals, or (b) Mean-variance portfolio optimization grounded in predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only. Lesson 0005's scenarios poked at both.

### veth pair — `intro`
A pair of virtual ethernet interfaces in the kernel, connected back-to-back.
Packets out one end appear at the other. Docker uses veth pairs to bridge a
container's network namespace to the host bridge.

---

## Added in Lesson 0005 (Prediction Models in Trading)

### Adaptivity (model) — `intro`
Whether a model is trained once (`paper_trading_sim.py`) or refit periodically
on rolling windows (`walkforward_sim.py --rolling_retrain`). One of the five
axes that define a trading prediction model.

### Cross-sectional model — `intro`
A model that ranks N assets against each other at the same point in time.
This repo's GBM is cross-sectional: every day it scores all tickers and picks
the top-N. Contrast with time-series, which forecasts one asset's future from
its own past.

### Cross-sectional pooling — `intro`
Training one model on rows from many assets stacked together, assuming the
feature→target relationship is roughly universal. The repo does this; sector
or market-cap bucketing is the production refinement.

### CUSUM (cumulative sum) — `intro`
A change-point detection statistic. Triggers when the cumulative deviation of
a series from its mean exceeds a threshold. Used in `walkforward_sim.py` as
one of four stress detectors that gate exposure.

### Distributional forecast — `intro`
A prediction that includes uncertainty — quantiles, mean+variance, or a full
distribution. Lets downstream sizing be risk-aware. This repo currently
emits only point estimates.

### Filtering (vs forecasting) — `intro`
Estimating a *present* hidden state from past observations (HMM/GMM regime
detection). Distinct from forecasting, which estimates a *future* value. The
repo's `GaussianMixture` overlay is filtering, not forecasting.

### Foundation model (time-series) — `intro`
Large pretrained model (TimesFM, Chronos, Kronos, Moirai) trained on billions
of time-series points, used for zero-/few-shot forecasting. On tabular daily
equity features, GBM still beats them for cross-sectional ranking — for now.

### Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) — `intro`
A probabilistic clustering model that fits K Gaussian components to a dataset.
Used in `walkforward_sim.py` to estimate the probability that today's returns
belong to a "high-vol" regime, then to scale exposure down accordingly.

### Hidden Markov Model (HMM) — `intro`
A state-space model where an unobserved discrete state evolves over time and
emits observations. Common as a regime model in finance. The repo's GMM is a
simpler cousin (no transition matrix — just clustering).

### Horizon (forecast horizon) — `intro`
The future window over which the target is measured. This repo: 1 trading
day. Choose tick-level and you need a completely different infrastructure.

### Output shape — `intro`
The form of a model's prediction: point estimate, distribution, or action.
One of the five axes; the repo emits point estimates only.

### Per-asset model — `intro`
One model per ticker, trained on that ticker's data only. Opposite of
cross-sectional pooling. Captures asset-specific quirks but starves on
data and fails for new tickers.

### Pooling (model pooling) — `intro`
The choice between training one shared model across assets vs one per asset.
One of the five axes; this repo pools across all tickers.

### Regime model — `intro`
Any model whose primary output is the identification of a hidden market state
(calm/stress, bull/bear). Used to switch strategies or scale exposure, not to
predict returns directly. `walkforward_sim.py:GaussianMixture` is the
project's regime model.

### Reinforcement learning (in trading) — `intro`
Learning an action policy directly from a reward signal (P&L). Promising for
execution and market-making but notoriously hard to train on financial data.
Not used in this repo.

### Rolling retrain — `intro`
Periodically refitting a model on a fixed-length window of the most recent
past data only. `walkforward_sim.py --rolling_retrain --retrain_freq monthly
--train_window_days 756` is the repo's default flavor.

### Stationarity — `intro`
A property of a time series whose statistical moments don't drift over time.
Returns are roughly stationary; prices are not. Pooling across tickers
requires features and targets that are at least approximately stationary —
this is why the repo predicts returns, not prices.

### Target axis — `intro`
The choice of what the model predicts: direction (binary), magnitude
(regression), volatility, jump probability, regime, or action (RL). The
single most consequential design decision in a trading model.

### TimesFM / Chronos / Kronos — `intro`
Time-series foundation models from the 2024–2025 wave (Google, Amazon,
Tsinghua respectively). Pretrained transformers for general forecasting.
Strong zero-shot on benchmarks; not yet a slam-dunk on tabular cross-sectional
equity alpha.

Lesson 0005 written. Open it with:

```
xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/0005-prediction-models-in-trading.html
```

## What you've got

- **`docs/learning/lessons/0005-prediction-models-in-trading.html`** — frames a trading prediction model as a choice along **five axes** (target, horizon, pooling, output shape, adaptivity), then drills into the two axes Lesson 0003 didn't cover: **cross-sectional pooling** (your repo's one-model-on-stacked-rows design and its limit on biotech-vs-tech) and **adaptivity** (the rolling retrain + GMM regime overlay in `walkforward_sim.py`). Quick tour of six model families with honest opinions (GBM still wins on tabular daily alpha; TimesFM/Chronos/Kronos are promising but not proven for this task). 5 quiz questions, 3 scenarios.
- **`docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`** — lesson 0005 logged.
- **`docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md`** — 20 new terms added: cross-sectional model, pooling, output shape, target axis, adaptivity, distributional forecast, filtering vs forecasting, GMM, HMM, CUSUM, regime model, foundation models (TimesFM/Chronos/Kronos), stationarity, rolling retrain, etc.

## Honest framing in the lesson

The repo's headline ~27% annualized number is the **base GBM**, not the full stack with HMM/CUSUM/rolling-retrain overlays turned on. Those overlays exist as available knobs — treat their contribution as unproven until you ablate them yourself. This matters because it stops you from over-attributing performance to the regime stack.

## Knowledge check — answer in chat

1. The repo trains one GBM on stacked rows from all tickers, with the ticker column dropped before `fit`. State the implicit assumption in one sentence, and name one concrete portfolio change that would most stress-test it.
2. The `GaussianMixture` overlay in `walkforward_sim.py` is *not* a prediction model in the same sense as the GBM. What kind of model is it (one word), and how does its output get used downstream?
3. You move from predicting next-day **return magnitude** to predicting **next-day volatility**. Which of the five axes did you change, and name one downstream piece of the pipeline (in `predict_next.py` or `paper_trading_sim.py`) that would now break or need rewriting.

Take a swing — then we pick Lesson 0006 (the queue points at walk-forward backtesting or mean-variance, whichever lands harder).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import math
import pandas as pd


def compute_metrics(eq: pd.Series) -> dict:
    eq = eq.dropna()
    if len(eq) < 2:
        return {"error": "Not enough data"}

    initial, final = float(eq.iloc[0]), float(eq.iloc[-1])
    total_return = final / initial - 1.0

    ret = eq.pct_change().dropna()
    n = len(ret)
    ann = 252.0

    cagr = (final / initial) ** (ann / max(1.0, n)) - 1.0
    vol = float(ret.std()) * math.sqrt(ann) if n else 0.0
    apr_simple = float(ret.mean()) * ann if n else 0.0
    sharpe = (float(ret.mean()) * ann) / vol if vol > 0 else 0.0

    cum = (1.0 + ret).cumprod()
    roll_max = cum.cummax()
    maxdd = float((cum / roll_max - 1.0).min()) if len(cum) else 0.0

    years = n / ann

    return {
        "Initial": initial,
        "Final": final,
        "TotalReturn": total_return,
        "Years(approx)": years,
        "CAGR": cagr,
        "APR_simple": apr_simple,
        "Vol": vol,
        "Sharpe": sharpe,
        "MaxDD": maxdd,
    }


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Compute portfolio performance metrics from an equity CSV")
    p.add_argument("--equity_csv", type=str, default="walkforward_equity.csv", help="Path to equity CSV (date index, column 'equity')")
    args = p.parse_args()

    df = pd.read_csv(args.equity_csv, index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
    if "equity" not in df.columns:
        raise SystemExit("CSV must contain an 'equity' column")

    m = compute_metrics(df["equity"])        
    for k, v in m.items():
        if isinstance(v, float):
            if k in ("TotalReturn", "CAGR", "APR_simple", "Vol", "Sharpe", "MaxDD"):
                # Print returns/vol as percents except Sharpe
                if k == "Sharpe":
                    print(f"{k}: {v:.2f}")
                else:
                    print(f"{k}: {v:.2%}")
            else:
                print(f"{k}: {v:.4f}")
        else:
            print(f"{k}: {v}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Lesson 0006 Quiz: 0 / 5

Statistics Math in Trading

Why this matters for HFT_practice: analyze_equity.py is 40 lines that compute every headline number you'll ever quote for a strategy — CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, annualized vol. Each line encodes a statistical idea you need to defend. This lesson walks the math behind those lines so you can interpret the numbers honestly and write the next ones yourself.

1. Returns: simple vs log, and why both exist

Every metric in this lesson starts with returns, not prices. (Recall Lesson 0005: returns are roughly stationary; prices aren't.) Two standard definitions:

rtsimple = (Pt − Pt−1) / Pt−1 = Pt/Pt−1 − 1 Simple return — what pct_change() computes
rtlog = ln(Pt / Pt−1) Log return — additive across time, used in academic papers and risk math

The two properties that make each useful:

Simple returnLog return
Compounds via∏(1 + r)   (product)∑ r   (sum)
Aggregates across assets linearly?Yes (portfolio return = Σ wᵢ rᵢ)No
Aggregates across time linearly?NoYes (multi-day log return = sum of daily log returns)
Symmetric around 0?No (−50% / +100% ≠ same magnitude)Yes

Both columns are right, in different contexts. This repo uses simple returns throughout (pct_change() everywhere) because the main operation is portfolio aggregation: "how did my equally-weighted top-N do today?" Portfolio math is cleaner with simple returns.

The one identity that ties them together: (1 + rsimple) = exp(rlog). For small returns (|r| < 5%) they are numerically nearly identical. They diverge fast for crypto-sized moves; equities are usually fine.

2. Volatility, the Sharpe ratio, and the annualization factor

Volatility in finance just means "standard deviation of returns." By itself, that number is daily — small and unhelpful for comparison across horizons. So we always annualize:

σann = σdaily × √252 252 ≈ number of US trading days per year

Why √252 and not 252?

If daily returns are independent with mean μ and variance σ², then over N days the sum has mean Nμ and variance Nσ². Means add; variances add. Annualized volatility is the standard deviation of the annual return, so you take the square root of the summed variance: √(252·σ²) = σ·√252. This is the central limit theorem doing its job.

The assumption of independence is wrong in detail (returns have autocorrelation, volatility clusters), but √T scaling is the universal first-pass convention and every reported "annualized vol" uses it.

The Sharpe ratio

A unit-free measure of return per unit of risk. The textbook version uses excess return over a risk-free rate; this repo uses the simpler "raw" version (assumes risk-free = 0):

Sharpe = (mean daily return × 252) / σann Equivalent to: mean daily / σdaily × √252

A Sharpe of 1.0 means "per unit of annual standard deviation, you earn one unit of annual mean." Industry rough guide: <0.5 mediocre, 1.0 solid, 2.0 excellent, 3.0+ raise eyebrows (or fees). HFT strategies routinely exceed Sharpe 5 because their bets are many and small.

Tiny worked example

import numpy as np
import math

# 252 daily returns, mean 0.05% per day, std 1% per day
ret = np.random.normal(0.0005, 0.01, 252)

mean_daily  = ret.mean()
std_daily   = ret.std()
mean_ann    = mean_daily * 252            # ~12.6%   — means scale linearly
vol_ann     = std_daily  * math.sqrt(252)  # ~15.9%   — std scales by sqrt(T)
sharpe      = mean_ann / vol_ann               # ~0.79

3. Drawdown and CAGR

Maximum drawdown — the worst the curve ever felt

Drawdown at time t is the percentage drop from the running peak so far:

DDt = equityt / maxs≤t(equitys) − 1 Always ≤ 0. The minimum over the whole period is the "max drawdown."

In code this is two lines: a running cumulative max, then a ratio: 

cum      = (1 + ret).cumprod()       # 1 + cumulative growth path
roll_max = cum.cummax()                # running peak so far
maxdd    = (cum / roll_max - 1).min()   # worst drop from peak

Why care: Sharpe says nothing about shape. Two strategies can have identical Sharpe and very different max drawdowns. Drawdown is the number investors actually pull capital over.

CAGR — geometric annual growth, the honest version of "average return"

Two ways to summarize "what return did I earn per year on average":

APRsimple = mean(daily return) × 252 Arithmetic — ignores compounding
CAGR = (final / initial)252/N − 1 Geometric — what actually compounded to that final value

They are not the same number. CAGR < APRsimple by an amount that grows with volatility (this is the volatility drag: CAGR ≈ μ − σ²/2 in log terms). A strategy with daily returns alternating +10% / −10% has APR ≈ 0 but CAGR ≈ −1.005% per period — because two such days compound to 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, not 1.00. Real money cares about CAGR.

4. Covariance matrix and the CUSUM statistic

Covariance — when assets move together

Variance generalizes to covariance when you have multiple assets:

Σij = E[(ri − μi)(rj − μj)] Σii = variance of asset i. Σij = how i and j co-move.

For a portfolio with weight vector w:

portfolio variance = wT Σ w

That single equation is why correlations matter: two highly-correlated assets in a portfolio don't diversify you, no matter how good each one is individually. The mean-variance optimizer (Lesson 0007's target) lives or dies on a stable estimate of Σ. The repo estimates it as the sample covariance of recent daily returns over a --cov_lookback window (default 90 days).

CUSUM — detecting a regime break

The cumulative sum (CUSUM) test detects when a time series has drifted away from its mean — i.e. when something structurally changed. Two running sums track upward and downward drift:

S+t = max(0, S+t−1 + (rt − μ) − k)
S−t = min(0, S−t−1 + (rt − μ) + k) k is a "slack" parameter, typically a multiple of σ. Trigger when |S| crosses a threshold.

The repo uses CUSUM as one of four stress detectors in walkforward_sim.py, with k = cusum_threshold × σ where cusum_threshold defaults to 3. The intuition: small noise should leave both running sums near zero; a sustained drift in either direction pushes one of them past the threshold and signals a regime change.

5. In this project

Time to read the actual code. Every formula above lives in roughly 20 lines of analyze_equity.py.

analyze_equity.py:compute_metrics (lines 7–40) 
def compute_metrics(eq: pd.Series) -> dict:
    eq = eq.dropna()
    initial, final = float(eq.iloc[0]), float(eq.iloc[-1])
    total_return = final / initial - 1.0          # cumulative return over the period

    ret = eq.pct_change().dropna()                # §1 — simple daily returns
    n   = len(ret)
    ann = 252.0                                  # §2 — trading days per year

    cagr       = (final / initial) ** (ann / max(1.0, n)) - 1.0   # §3 — geometric
    vol        = float(ret.std()) * math.sqrt(ann) if n else 0.0  # §2 — sigma × sqrt(252)
    apr_simple = float(ret.mean()) * ann if n else 0.0           # §3 — arithmetic
    sharpe     = (float(ret.mean()) * ann) / vol if vol > 0 else 0.0 # §2

    cum      = (1.0 + ret).cumprod()                # §3 — growth curve
    roll_max = cum.cummax()                          # §3 — running peak
    maxdd    = float((cum / roll_max - 1.0).min())  # §3 — worst peak-to-trough

    years = n / ann                                  # useful for sanity checks
    return {
        "Initial": initial, "Final": final,
        "TotalReturn": total_return, "Years(approx)": years,
        "CAGR": cagr, "APR_simple": apr_simple,
        "Vol": vol, "Sharpe": sharpe, "MaxDD": maxdd,
    }

Things to notice from reading the real code:

  • Both CAGR and APR_simple are returned. The CLI in main() prints both. Good practice — comparing them tells you how much volatility drag the strategy carries.
  • Sharpe is built without a risk-free rate. That's the convention this repo follows but in formal reporting you should subtract a benchmark (e.g. T-bill yield) from ret.mean() first.
  • roll_max = cum.cummax() uses pandas' running maximum — efficient and idiomatic. Don't roll your own; it's a one-line pattern worth remembering.
paper_trading_sim.py:metrics (almost identical) 
cagr = (equity.iloc[-1] / equity.iloc[0]) ** (ann / max(1, len(ret))) - 1
vol  = ret.std() * math.sqrt(ann) if len(ret) else 0.0
sharpe = (ret.mean() * ann) / vol if vol > 0 else 0.0

Same formulas, separate file. A small consolidation opportunity (DRY) — but nothing is mathematically inconsistent between the two. If you change the annualization convention you have to remember to change both places.

And the covariance / CUSUM math

predict_next.py (covariance for mean-variance) 
Sigma_emp = ret_panel.cov().to_numpy()       # sample covariance matrix
Sigma     = (1 - shrink) * Sigma_emp + shrink * np.diag(np.diag(Sigma_emp))
                                              # shrinkage toward the diagonal
w = meanvar_long_only(mu, Sigma, max_w=max_w)
walkforward_sim.py (CUSUM, condensed) 
sigma = market_ret.std()
k     = cusum_threshold * sigma                # slack = 3σ by default
# pos/neg running sums updated on each new return; cusum_hit when either crosses k
cusum_hit = (pos > 0) or (neg < 0)
Repo-specific gotcha: analyze_equity.py uses pandas.Series.std() which defaults to ddof=1 (sample std with Bessel's correction, divides by n−1). NumPy's np.std() defaults to ddof=0. Different libraries, different defaults, same name — a classic 1% bug when porting code between pandas and NumPy.

6. Often confused with

CAGR vs APR (arithmetic mean × 252)

Why this matters for HFT_practice: analyze_equity.py is 40 lines that compute every headline number you'll ever quote for a strategy — CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, annualized vol. Each line encodes a statistical idea you need to defend. This lesson walks the math behind those lines so you can interpret the numbers honestly and write the next ones yourself.

1. Returns: simple vs log, and why both exist

Every metric in this lesson starts with returns, not prices. (Recall Lesson 0005: returns are roughly stationary; prices aren't.) Two standard definitions:

rtsimple = (Pt − Pt−1) / Pt−1 = Pt/Pt−1 − 1 Simple return — what pct_change() computes
rtlog = ln(Pt / Pt−1) Log return — additive across time, used in academic papers and risk math

The two properties that make each useful:

Simple returnLog return
Compounds via∏(1 + r)   (product)∑ r   (sum)
Aggregates across assets linearly?Yes (portfolio return = Σ wᵢ rᵢ)No
Aggregates across time linearly?NoYes (multi-day log return = sum of daily log returns)
Symmetric around 0?No (−50% / +100% ≠ same magnitude)Yes

Both columns are right, in different contexts. This repo uses simple returns throughout (pct_change() everywhere) because the main operation is portfolio aggregation: "how did my equally-weighted top-N do today?" Portfolio math is cleaner with simple returns.

The one identity that ties them together: (1 + rsimple) = exp(rlog). For small returns (|r| < 5%) they are numerically nearly identical. They diverge fast for crypto-sized moves; equities are usually fine.

2. Volatility, the Sharpe ratio, and the annualization factor

Volatility in finance just means "standard deviation of returns." By itself, that number is daily — small and unhelpful for comparison across horizons. So we always annualize:

σann = σdaily × √252 252 ≈ number of US trading days per year

Why √252 and not 252?

If daily returns are independent with mean μ and variance σ², then over N days the sum has mean Nμ and variance Nσ². Means add; variances add. Annualized volatility is the standard deviation of the annual return, so you take the square root of the summed variance: √(252·σ²) = σ·√252. This is the central limit theorem doing its job.

The assumption of independence is wrong in detail (returns have autocorrelation, volatility clusters), but √T scaling is the universal first-pass convention and every reported "annualized vol" uses it.

The Sharpe ratio

A unit-free measure of return per unit of risk. The textbook version uses excess return over a risk-free rate; this repo uses the simpler "raw" version (assumes risk-free = 0):

Sharpe = (mean daily return × 252) / σann Equivalent to: mean daily / σdaily × √252

A Sharpe of 1.0 means "per unit of annual standard deviation, you earn one unit of annual mean." Industry rough guide: <0.5 mediocre, 1.0 solid, 2.0 excellent, 3.0+ raise eyebrows (or fees). HFT strategies routinely exceed Sharpe 5 because their bets are many and small.

Tiny worked example

import numpy as np
import math

# 252 daily returns, mean 0.05% per day, std 1% per day
ret = np.random.normal(0.0005, 0.01, 252)

mean_daily  = ret.mean()
std_daily   = ret.std()
mean_ann    = mean_daily * 252            # ~12.6%   — means scale linearly
vol_ann     = std_daily  * math.sqrt(252)  # ~15.9%   — std scales by sqrt(T)
sharpe      = mean_ann / vol_ann               # ~0.79

3. Drawdown and CAGR

Maximum drawdown — the worst the curve ever felt

Drawdown at time t is the percentage drop from the running peak so far:

DDt = equityt / maxs≤t(equitys) − 1 Always ≤ 0. The minimum over the whole period is the "max drawdown."

In code this is two lines: a running cumulative max, then a ratio: 

cum      = (1 + ret).cumprod()       # 1 + cumulative growth path
roll_max = cum.cummax()                # running peak so far
maxdd    = (cum / roll_max - 1).min()   # worst drop from peak

Why care: Sharpe says nothing about shape. Two strategies can have identical Sharpe and very different max drawdowns. Drawdown is the number investors actually pull capital over.

CAGR — geometric annual growth, the honest version of "average return"

Two ways to summarize "what return did I earn per year on average":

APRsimple = mean(daily return) × 252 Arithmetic — ignores compounding
CAGR = (final / initial)252/N − 1 Geometric — what actually compounded to that final value

They are not the same number. CAGR < APRsimple by an amount that grows with volatility (this is the volatility drag: CAGR ≈ μ − σ²/2 in log terms). A strategy with daily returns alternating +10% / −10% has APR ≈ 0 but CAGR ≈ −1.005% per period — because two such days compound to 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, not 1.00. Real money cares about CAGR.

4. Covariance matrix and the CUSUM statistic

Covariance — when assets move together

Variance generalizes to covariance when you have multiple assets:

Σij = E[(ri − μi)(rj − μj)] Σii = variance of asset i. Σij = how i and j co-move.

For a portfolio with weight vector w:

portfolio variance = wT Σ w

That single equation is why correlations matter: two highly-correlated assets in a portfolio don't diversify you, no matter how good each one is individually. The mean-variance optimizer (Lesson 0007's target) lives or dies on a stable estimate of Σ. The repo estimates it as the sample covariance of recent daily returns over a --cov_lookback window (default 90 days).

CUSUM — detecting a regime break

The cumulative sum (CUSUM) test detects when a time series has drifted away from its mean — i.e. when something structurally changed. Two running sums track upward and downward drift:

S+t = max(0, S+t−1 + (rt − μ) − k)
S−t = min(0, S−t−1 + (rt − μ) + k) k is a "slack" parameter, typically a multiple of σ. Trigger when |S| crosses a threshold.

The repo uses CUSUM as one of four stress detectors in walkforward_sim.py, with k = cusum_threshold × σ where cusum_threshold defaults to 3. The intuition: small noise should leave both running sums near zero; a sustained drift in either direction pushes one of them past the threshold and signals a regime change.

Time to read the actual code. Every formula above lives in roughly 20 lines of analyze_equity.py.

def compute_metrics(eq: pd.Series) -> dict:
    eq = eq.dropna()
    initial, final = float(eq.iloc[0]), float(eq.iloc[-1])
    total_return = final / initial - 1.0          # cumulative return over the period

    ret = eq.pct_change().dropna()                # §1 — simple daily returns
    n   = len(ret)
    ann = 252.0                                  # §2 — trading days per year

    cagr       = (final / initial) ** (ann / max(1.0, n)) - 1.0   # §3 — geometric
    vol        = float(ret.std()) * math.sqrt(ann) if n else 0.0  # §2 — sigma × sqrt(252)
    apr_simple = float(ret.mean()) * ann if n else 0.0           # §3 — arithmetic
    sharpe     = (float(ret.mean()) * ann) / vol if vol > 0 else 0.0 # §2

    cum      = (1.0 + ret).cumprod()                # §3 — growth curve
    roll_max = cum.cummax()                          # §3 — running peak
    maxdd    = float((cum / roll_max - 1.0).min())  # §3 — worst peak-to-trough

    years = n / ann                                  # useful for sanity checks
    return {

        "CAGR": cagr, "APR_simple": apr_simple,
        "Vol": vol, "Sharpe": sharpe, "MaxDD": maxdd,

## Suggested next lessons (in order)

1. **Walk-forward backtesting and look-ahead bias** — formalize the temporal discipline that lesson 0003 hinted at. Ground in `walkforward_sim.py` rolling retrain logic, contrast with `paper_trading_sim.py`'s single-split backtest. Concepts: leakage, survivorship bias, in-sample vs out-of-sample R².
2. **Mean-variance portfolio optimization** — what `predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only` actually does, why `w ∝ Σ⁻¹μ` is the canonical answer, what shrinkage (`--shrink`) buys, and why the per-name cap (`--max_w`) is non-negotiable in practice.
3. **The Limit Order Book in depth** — price-time priority, queue position, what "top of book" means. Ground in `fpga/market_maker.vhd` quoting logic.
4. **Adverse selection and inventory risk** — the two things that kill market makers. Illustrated against `market_maker.vhd`'s blind quote logic (no inventory tracking — a real gap). Motivates the README "Risk engine" roadmap item.
5. **From model to silicon** — the ONNX bridge in `gradient_boosting/main.cpp` plus the hls4ml / Vitis AI path mentioned in `fpga/README.md`. Why HFT firms compile models, what stays in CPU.
6. **Synthesis, place-and-route, and timing closure** — what actually happens when you run `vivado_hls -f fpga/hls_synthesis.tcl`, and why "meeting timing" is the real bottleneck in FPGA HFT development.
7. **Kernel-bypass networking deep dive** — follow-up to Lesson 0004: how DPDK / OpenOnload actually work, busy-polling tradeoffs, and what an FPGA UDP/FIX parser would replace.

## Notes for future-me (the teacher)

- This repo is named "HFT_practice" but its Python is daily-frequency. Don't perpetuate the misnomer — be clear about which files are genuinely HFT-style (the VHDL + C++ ONNX path) and which are quant rebalancing.

### TimesFM / Chronos / Kronos — `intro`
Time-series foundation models from the 2024–2025 wave (Google, Amazon,
Tsinghua respectively). Pretrained transformers for general forecasting.
Strong zero-shot on benchmarks; not yet a slam-dunk on tabular cross-sectional
equity alpha.

---

## Added in Lesson 0006 (Statistics Math in Trading)

### Annualization factor — `intro`
Convention for converting per-period statistics to per-year. For US equities,
252 trading days. Means scale by ×252; standard deviations scale by ×√252
(because variances add across independent periods).

### Bessel's correction (ddof=1) — `intro`
Dividing by (n−1) instead of n when computing sample variance/std, to get an
unbiased estimator. pandas defaults to `ddof=1`; NumPy defaults to `ddof=0`.
Cross-library default mismatches are a real bug source.

### CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate) — `intro`
Geometric annual return: `(final / initial)^(252/N) − 1`. The actual
compounded growth rate. Always ≤ arithmetic APR; gap is volatility drag.
Computed in `analyze_equity.py:compute_metrics`.

### Correlation — `intro`
Standardized covariance: `cov(i,j) / (σᵢ σⱼ)`. Unit-free, bounded in [−1, 1].
Use for comparing relationships across assets; covariance for portfolio
variance formulas.

### Covariance matrix (Σ) — `intro`
Symmetric matrix whose entry (i,j) is the covariance of asset i and asset j
returns. Diagonal entries are variances. The repo estimates Σ from the recent
`--cov_lookback` days in `predict_next.py:compute_returns`.

### CUSUM (cumulative sum) test — `intro`
Change-point statistic that tracks deviations from the mean. Two running sums
(positive and negative drift) update each period with a slack term k. The
repo uses `k = cusum_threshold * σ` (default 3σ) as one of four stress
detectors in `walkforward_sim.py`.

### Drawdown — `intro`
Percentage drop from the running peak so far:
`DD_t = equity_t / max_{s≤t}(equity_s) − 1`. Always ≤ 0.

### Log return — `intro`
`ln(P_t / P_{t-1})`. Sums across time linearly; symmetric around zero. Used in
academic risk math. Numerically ≈ simple return for small moves.

### Maximum drawdown (MaxDD) — `intro`
The minimum of the drawdown series over the full period — the worst
peak-to-trough loss the equity curve ever felt. Investors emotionally trade on
this number more than on Sharpe.

### Sharpe ratio — `intro`
Risk-adjusted return: `(mean_return × 252) / (std_return × √252)`. Unit-free.
This repo's version assumes risk-free rate = 0. >1 solid, >2 excellent, >3
raises eyebrows.

### Shrinkage (covariance) — `intro`
Mixing the sample covariance matrix with a more stable target (typically the
diagonal): `Σ_shrunk = (1−λ) Σ_sample + λ diag(Σ_sample)`. Trades a little
bias for much less estimation noise; vital when Σ is going to be inverted.
Lives in `predict_next.py` via `--shrink`.

### Simple return — `intro`
`(P_t − P_{t-1}) / P_{t-1}`. Computed by pandas `.pct_change()`. Aggregates
linearly across *assets* in a portfolio: `r_p = Σ wᵢ rᵢ`. This repo's
default everywhere.

### Sortino ratio — `intro`
Like Sharpe but divides by downside standard deviation only (negative returns
counted, positive ignored). Kinder to positively skewed strategies. Not
computed in this repo.

### Standard deviation (σ) — `intro`
Square root of variance. Same units as the underlying. In finance: "volatility."

### Variance — `intro`
`E[(r − μ)²]`. Units: returns². Adds linearly across independent periods,
which is why annual std = daily std × √252.

### Volatility drag — `intro`
The gap between arithmetic and geometric mean return, approximately σ²/2 in
log terms. A high-vol strategy with the same mean as a low-vol one will
compound *more slowly*. The reason `analyze_equity.py` returns both
`APR_simple` and `CAGR`.

This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	import argparse
3	from typing import List
4	
5	import numpy as np
6	import pandas as pd
7	from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
8	
9	
10	def load_news(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
11	    df = pd.read_csv(path)
12	    # Expect columns: time_published (YYYYMMDDTHHMM or YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS), ticker, sentiment, relevance
13	    if "time_published" not in df.columns:
14	        raise SystemExit("CSV must have time_published column")
15	    # Normalize ticker column if present
16	    if "ticker" in df.columns:
17	        df["ticker"] = df["ticker"].astype(str).str.strip().str.upper()
18	    # Parse timestamp as UTC, try multiple formats
19	    ts = pd.to_datetime(df["time_published"], format="%Y%m%dT%H%M", utc=True, errors="coerce")
20	    if ts.isna().any():
21	        ts2 = pd.to_datetime(df["time_published"], format="%Y%m%dT%H%M%S", utc=True, errors="coerce")
22	        ts = ts.fillna(ts2)
23	    if ts.isna().any():
24	        ts3 = pd.to_datetime(df["time_published"], utc=True, errors="coerce")
25	        ts = ts.fillna(ts3)
26	    df["ts_utc"] = ts
27	    # Drop rows without valid timestamp or ticker
28	    df = df.dropna(subset=["ts_utc"]) 
29	    if "ticker" in df.columns:
30	        df = df.dropna(subset=["ticker"]) 
31	    # Coerce numeric fields
32	    for c in ("sentiment", "relevance"):
33	        if c in df.columns:
34	            df[c] = pd.to_numeric(df[c], errors="coerce")
35	    return df
36	
37	
38	def session_date_usa(ts_utc: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
39	    # Map UTC timestamp to US/Eastern calendar date (session date proxy)
40	    # This bins after-hours news into the same calendar date; good for next-day prediction use.
41	    eastern = ts_utc.dt.tz_convert(ZoneInfo("America/New_York"))
42	    return eastern.dt.date.astype("string")
43	
44	
45	def build_daily_features(df: pd.DataFrame, windows: List[int]) -> pd.DataFrame:
46	    # Compute base daily aggregates by (date, ticker)
47	    df = df.copy()
48	    df["date"] = session_date_usa(df["ts_utc"])  # string date key
49	    if "ticker" not in df.columns:
50	        # No per-ticker mapping present
51	        return pd.DataFrame()
52	    grp = df.groupby(["date", "ticker"], as_index=False)
53	    daily = grp.agg(
54	        news_count=("ticker", "count"),
55	        sent_mean=("sentiment", "mean"),
56	        sent_abs_mean=("sentiment", lambda s: np.nanmean(np.abs(s))),
57	        relevance_sum=("relevance", "sum"),
58	    )
59	    if daily.empty:
60	        return pd.DataFrame()
61	    # Convert to date index per ticker for rolling features
62	    out_frames = []
63	    for t, sub in daily.groupby("ticker"):
64	        tmp = sub.drop(columns=["ticker"]).copy()
65	        tmp["date"] = pd.to_datetime(tmp["date"]).dt.tz_localize(None)
66	        tmp = tmp.set_index("date").sort_index()
67	        # Fill missing with 0 for counts, keep means as-is (NaN-safe rolling)
68	        tmp["news_count"] = tmp["news_count"].fillna(0)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
from typing import List

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo


def load_news(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    # Expect columns: time_published (YYYYMMDDTHHMM or YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS), ticker, sentiment, relevance
    if "time_published" not in df.columns:
        raise SystemExit("CSV must have time_published column")
    # Normalize ticker column if present
    if "ticker" in df.columns:
        df["ticker"] = df["ticker"].astype(str).str.strip().str.upper()
    # Parse timestamp as UTC, try multiple formats
    ts = pd.to_datetime(df["time_published"], format="%Y%m%dT%H%M", utc=True, errors="coerce")
    if ts.isna().any():
        ts2 = pd.to_datetime(df["time_published"], format="%Y%m%dT%H%M%S", utc=True, errors="coerce")
        ts = ts.fillna(ts2)
    if ts.isna().any():
        ts3 = pd.to_datetime(df["time_published"], utc=True, errors="coerce")
        ts = ts.fillna(ts3)
    df["ts_utc"] = ts
    # Drop rows without valid timestamp or ticker
    df = df.dropna(subset=["ts_utc"]) 
    if "ticker" in df.columns:
        df = df.dropna(subset=["ticker"]) 
    # Coerce numeric fields
    for c in ("sentiment", "relevance"):
        if c in df.columns:
            df[c] = pd.to_numeric(df[c], errors="coerce")
    return df


def session_date_usa(ts_utc: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    # Map UTC timestamp to US/Eastern calendar date (session date proxy)
    # This bins after-hours news into the same calendar date; good for next-day prediction use.
    eastern = ts_utc.dt.tz_convert(ZoneInfo("America/New_York"))
    return eastern.dt.date.astype("string")


def build_daily_features(df: pd.DataFrame, windows: List[int]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    # Compute base daily aggregates by (date, ticker)
    df = df.copy()
    df["date"] = session_date_usa(df["ts_utc"])  # string date key
    if "ticker" not in df.columns:
        # No per-ticker mapping present
        return pd.DataFrame()
    grp = df.groupby(["date", "ticker"], as_index=False)
    daily = grp.agg(
        news_count=("ticker", "count"),
        sent_mean=("sentiment", "mean"),
        sent_abs_mean=("sentiment", lambda s: np.nanmean(np.abs(s))),
        relevance_sum=("relevance", "sum"),
    )
    if daily.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    # Convert to date index per ticker for rolling features
    out_frames = []
    for t, sub in daily.groupby("ticker"):
        tmp = sub.drop(columns=["ticker"]).copy()
        tmp["date"] = pd.to_datetime(tmp["date"]).dt.tz_localize(None)
        tmp = tmp.set_index("date").sort_index()
        # Fill missing with 0 for counts, keep means as-is (NaN-safe rolling)
        tmp["news_count"] = tmp["news_count"].fillna(0)
        for w in windows:
            tmp[f"news_count_{w}d"] = tmp["news_count"].rolling(w, min_periods=1).sum()
            tmp[f"sent_mean_{w}d"] = tmp["sent_mean"].rolling(w, min_periods=1).mean()
            tmp[f"sent_abs_mean_{w}d"] = tmp["sent_abs_mean"].rolling(w, min_periods=1).mean()
            tmp[f"relevance_sum_{w}d"] = tmp["relevance_sum"].rolling(w, min_periods=1).sum()
        tmp["ticker"] = t
        out_frames.append(tmp.reset_index())
    if not out_frames:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    feats = pd.concat(out_frames, ignore_index=True)
    # Order columns
    base_cols = ["news_count", "sent_mean", "sent_abs_mean", "relevance_sum"]
    roll_cols = [c for c in feats.columns if any(c.startswith(x) for x in ("news_count_", "sent_mean_", "sent_abs_mean_", "relevance_sum_"))]
    feats = feats[["date", "ticker"] + base_cols + roll_cols]
    return feats


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Aggregate raw news CSV into daily per-ticker features for backtesting")
    p.add_argument("--news_csv", type=str, default="news_raw.csv")
    p.add_argument("--out_csv", type=str, default="news_features.csv")
    p.add_argument("--windows", type=str, default="3,5", help="Rolling windows in days, e.g., 3,5,10")
    args = p.parse_args()

    df = load_news(args.news_csv)
    windows = [int(x) for x in args.windows.split(",") if x.strip()]
    feats = build_daily_features(df, windows)
    if feats.empty:
        print("No daily news features produced. Reasons could include: empty input, no valid timestamps, or no ticker mappings in the feed/time range.")
        # Still write an empty file with just headers for traceability
        pd.DataFrame(columns=["date", "ticker"]).to_csv(args.out_csv, index=False)
        return
    feats.to_csv(args.out_csv, index=False)
    print(f"Saved daily news features to {args.out_csv} with columns: {', '.join(feats.columns)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
