The user wants to learn "latency" (or, if blank, you choose the most valuable concept to teach next based on their progress and this project's code). This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

## Memory Ordering

A synchronizes-with relationship between producer and consumer threads is necessary, which can be achieved using acquire/release semantics on the tail variable. Implementations use "release" (and "acquire") memory order while avoiding the default "sequentially-consistent ordering," which offers strict guarantees but shouldn't be needed for SPSC ring buffers.

## Cache Line Padding

Padding is used so the read and write positions occupy different cache lines to avoid false sharing. Boost devs apply padding to avoid False Sharing on the cache line for the reading/writing indices, forcing read_index and write_index to different cache lines.

## Best Practices

Recent implementations (2025-2026) highlight these key practices:

Lock-Free Concurrency uses C++ std::atomic with acquire-release semantics for lockless synchronization, while Cache Optimization employs cache line alignment and power-of-two sizing for efficient wrap-arounds.

Implementing an SPSC queue gives insight on ring buffers, cache lines, atomics and memory barriers.

## Performance Impact

Changing a ring buffer's memory order from seq_cst to release/acquire made it run in about 30 seconds, compared to slower performance with default ordering.

Lesson 0010 Quiz: 0 / 5

Low-Latency C++ Best Practices

Why this matters for HFT_practice: Lesson 0009 cleaned up one hot loop. Real HFT C++ is multi-threaded — a feed thread, a strategy thread, a logger thread — communicating through lock-free rings, pinned to isolated cores, compiled with non-default flags. This is the layer that turns a fast loop into a production system.

1. The production architecture: three threads, two rings

Every serious HFT system in C++ has the same shape, regardless of strategy. The hot path is split across dedicated threads, each doing one thing, each pinned to one core, talking through lock-free queues.

Feed thread Reads market data from the NIC (kernel-bypass or FPGA), parses ticks, pushes onto a ring.
─SPSC─►
Strategy thread Drains ticks from the ring, runs MeanReversion::onTick, decides BUY/HOLD/SELL.
Strategy thread (continued) Emits orders directly to the NIC; pushes trade records onto a log ring.
─SPSC─►
Logger thread Tails the log ring, writes to disk / Kafka / stderr. Not latency-critical.

Why this shape and not "one big main loop"?

  • Isolation. The logger can stall on disk I/O without slowing the strategy.
  • Pinnability. Each thread gets its own dedicated CPU core; the kernel can't context-switch them.
  • Specialization. Each thread can be optimized for its own workload (busy-poll the NIC; batch-flush the disk).

The rings are the only shared state, and they are lock-free. That's the central object of this lesson.

2. The SPSC ring buffer — done right

SPSC = single-producer, single-consumer. The simplest and fastest lock-free queue. One thread always pushes; one thread always pops. No other configuration. (For multi-producer or multi-consumer you need MPSC or MPMC — much more expensive and worth avoiding when you can.)

A correct SPSC has four ingredients that beginners almost always get wrong:

1. Power-of-two capacity

Replace modulo with bitwise-and: idx & (N - 1) instead of idx % N. One instruction instead of an integer division.

2. Acquire/release ordering, not seq_cst

std::atomic's default is memory_order_seq_cst — a full barrier on every access, ~10× slower than necessary. The producer publishes with release; the consumer reads with acquire.

3. Cache-line padding on head/tail

If the producer's write index and the consumer's read index share a cache line, every push ping-pongs that line between cores (false sharing). Force them onto different lines with alignas(64).

4. Storage by value, not pointer

The ring holds the records inline (std::array<T, N>), not pointers to heap-allocated objects. Otherwise you've put the allocator back on the hot path.

Reference implementation

template<typename T, std::size_t N>
class SpscRing {
    static_assert((N & (N - 1)) == 0, "N must be power of 2");
    static constexpr size_t MASK = N - 1;
    static constexpr size_t CACHELINE = 64;

    std::array<T, N> data_{};

    // Each index sits on its own cache line — no false sharing.
    alignas(CACHELINE) std::atomic<std::size_t> head_{0};   // producer writes
    alignas(CACHELINE) std::atomic<std::size_t> tail_{0};   // consumer reads

public:
    // Producer-only.  Returns false if full.
    bool try_push(const T& v) noexcept {
        const auto h = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        const auto t = tail_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
        if (h - t == N) return false;        // full
        data_[h & MASK] = v;                       // store payload
        head_.store(h + 1, std::memory_order_release);  // publish
        return true;
    }

    // Consumer-only.  Returns false if empty.
    bool try_pop(T& out) noexcept {
        const auto t = tail_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        const auto h = head_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
        if (h == t) return false;             // empty
        out = data_[t & MASK];
        tail_.store(t + 1, std::memory_order_release);
        return true;
    }
};

What every memory_order line is doing

LineOrderWhy
head_.load(relaxed) in push relaxed The producer is the only writer of head_ — it owns the value, doesn't need synchronization to read its own write.
tail_.load(acquire) in push acquire Sees the latest tail published by the consumer. Acquire ensures any payload reads the consumer did before publishing are visible — actually unused here but cheap.
head_.store(release) in push release The publish. Guarantees the payload write to data_[h & MASK] is visible to any thread that does an acquire-load of head_. Without release, the consumer could see head_ advance while still reading stale memory.
head_.load(acquire) in pop acquire Pairs with the producer's release. After this load returns a new value, the consumer is guaranteed to see the payload that was written before it.
The seq_cst tax. If you'd written std::atomic<size_t> and used the default operators (head_++, head_ = h+1), you'd silently get memory_order_seq_cst, which inserts a full fence (MFENCE on x86, ~5–10 ns) on every operation. Industry benchmarks show 10×+ speedups by dropping to release/acquire. Always write the orders explicitly.

3. CPU isolation, thread pinning, and the kernel scheduler

A fast hot loop is worthless if Linux can preempt it 10,000 times a second to run cron jobs or background kernel work. HFT systems carve out cores that the kernel won't touch and pin one thread to each.

Kernel boot parameters (set in /etc/default/grub)

GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="isolcpus=4-7 nohz_full=4-7 rcu_nocbs=4-7"
ParameterWhat it does
isolcpus=4-7Tells the scheduler not to place general tasks on cores 4–7. Only threads that explicitly pin to those cores will run there.
nohz_full=4-7Turns off the periodic 1 kHz timer tick on those cores when only one task is runnable. No timer interrupts = no jitter.
rcu_nocbs=4-7Offloads RCU (read-copy-update) callbacks from those cores. Removes another source of kernel work.

Pinning a thread to a core in C++

#include <pthread.h>

void pinThread(std::thread& t, int core_id) {
    cpu_set_t cpus;
    CPU_ZERO(&cpus);
    CPU_SET(core_id, &cpus);
    pthread_setaffinity_np(t.native_handle(), sizeof(cpus), &cpus);
}

// Wire the three threads onto isolated cores:
std::thread feed_thread{feed_loop, &tick_ring};       pinThread(feed_thread, 4);
std::thread strat_thread{strategy_loop, &tick_ring, &log_ring}; pinThread(strat_thread, 5);
std::thread log_thread{log_loop, &log_ring};         pinThread(log_thread, 6);

The strategy thread now runs uninterrupted on core 5: no scheduler preemption, no timer interrupts, no migration to a different cache. Combined with the lock-free ring, the per-tick path is fully deterministic.

Bonus tweaks the experienced teams add: SCHED_FIFO with a high priority (real-time scheduler class), mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE) to prevent paging, transparent-huge-pages disabled, hyperthreading off on the strategy core (so it owns the L1).

4. Build & compiler discipline — the flags that matter

Default compiler settings leave a lot of latency on the table. HFT C++ is typically built with:

FlagWhat it does
-O3Aggressive optimization: inlining, loop unrolling, auto-vectorization.
-march=nativeUses the full instruction set of the build machine (AVX2, AVX-512, FMA). Critical for SIMD wins.
-fltoLink-Time Optimization — lets the compiler inline across translation units and dead-code-eliminate globally.
-fno-exceptionsRemoves exception scaffolding. Pair with explicit error codes.
-fno-rttiRemoves typeid / dynamic_cast machinery. Almost never needed in HFT code.
-fno-pltRemoves one level of indirection for shared-library calls.
-fprofile-use (PGO)Profile-Guided Optimization: build, run with representative load to gather a profile, rebuild using it. The compiler now knows which branches are hot. Real wins: 5–15% on the hot path.

The PGO loop

$ g++ -O3 -march=native -fprofile-generate=./prof  *.cpp -o trader
$ ./trader replay.dat                    # run a representative workload to collect profile
$ g++ -O3 -march=native -flto -fprofile-use=./prof *.cpp -o trader_pgo

The PGO binary lays out hot basic blocks contiguously, predicts branches based on the real profile, and inlines aggressively where the data shows it pays. For a measurement-driven team this is free latency.

SIMD: the bonus you get nearly for free

With -O3 -march=native, the compiler auto-vectorizes simple loops. In Lesson 0009's rewritten MeanReversion::onTick, the running-sum update is already O(1), so SIMD is irrelevant there. But if you batch-process e.g. 1024 ticks for offline backtest replay, the inner loop will be auto-vectorized into AVX-2 (4 doubles/op) or AVX-512 (8 doubles/op) without you writing a single intrinsic. Inspect the assembly with objdump -d or godbolt to confirm.

5. In this project — restructuring the C++ for production

The repo's three C++ files don't yet have any threading. To get production-grade, the responsibilities split this way:

Existing fileHot/coldBecomes…
gradient_boosting_data_fetching.cpp Cold (cURL → REST API) Stays on a worker thread; pushes parsed ticks onto tick_ring. Allocate freely.
sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp Hot Becomes the strategy loop pinned to an isolated core; drains tick_ring, runs onTick (per Lesson 0009), pushes TradeRecord onto log_ring.
main.cpp (ONNX inference) Warm Runs on a parameter-update thread. Refreshes the strategy's weight constants every 100 ms via a single atomic publish. Hot loop reads with memory_order_acquire.

The skeleton

struct Tick { double price; uint64_t ts_ns; };
struct TradeRecord { double price; enum class Side : uint8_t { Buy, Sell } side; uint64_t ts_ns; };

static SpscRing<Tick,        1 << 14> tick_ring;     // 16384 ticks buffered
static SpscRing<TradeRecord, 1 << 14> log_ring;      // 16384 trades buffered

void strategy_loop() noexcept {
    MeanReversion<20> strat;
    Tick tk;
    while (running.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {
        if (!tick_ring.try_pop(tk)) [[unlikely]] {
            // Spin: a few PAUSE instructions, then re-check. No syscalls, no sleep.
            _mm_pause();
            continue;
        }
        auto action = strat.onTick(tk.price);
        if (action != MeanReversion::Action::Hold) [[unlikely]] {
            // Send order to the NIC (kernel-bypass or FPGA path).
            emit_order(tk.price, action);
            log_ring.try_push({tk.price,
                action_to_side(action), tk.ts_ns});
        }
    }
}

What this delivers:

  • Zero allocation per tick — the rings are pre-allocated, strat holds its stack array.
  • Zero I/O per tick — logging is a single try_push of a 24-byte record.
  • Zero syscalls per tick — busy-poll the ring with _mm_pause(); the kernel never sees us.
  • Deterministic per-tick time on the isolated core.
Repo honesty: none of this is implemented yet — the existing C++ is single-threaded and synchronous, and that's the appropriate first cut. The point of this lesson is what the system becomes when you decide to take latency seriously, and to give you the right vocabulary to ask "where would this thread live?" on every line you write.

6. Often confused with

SPSC vs MPSC vs MPMC

SPSC: one producer, one consumer — fastest. MPSC: many producers, one consumer (e.g. logger fed by many strategy threads). MPMC: many of each — most expensive. HFT teams design the system to need only SPSC wherever possible.

seq_cst vs release/acquire

seq_cst: total global order on all atomics — strongest, slowest, default. release/acquire: pairs publish↔read of a specific atomic — enough for queues. relaxed: no synchronization, just atomicity — for indices the thread owns.

Lock-free vs Wait-free

Lock-free: at least one thread always makes progress. Wait-free: every thread completes in bounded steps. SPSC rings written as above are wait-free. Most MPMC queues are only lock-free.

Thread pinning vs Process affinity

Thread pinning (pthread_setaffinity_np): per-thread, fine-grained. Process affinity (taskset): whole-process at launch. HFT pins each thread individually because each plays a different role.

Busy polling vs Sleeping

Busy poll the ring with _mm_pause() — latency-optimal, burns a core. Sleep on a condition variable — energy-friendly, adds tens of µs wakeup latency. HFT busy-polls on the strategy thread, sleeps on the logger.

PGO vs LTO

PGO (Profile-Guided Optimization): uses a real run's branch probabilities to lay out code. LTO (Link-Time Optimization): runs the optimizer across all translation units at link time. They are independent and stack — use both.

7. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. Why does SpscRing use alignas(64) on the head and tail indices?

  • Because std::atomic only guarantees atomicity at 64-byte alignment.
  • To force head_ and tail_ onto different cache lines so that the producer's writes don't invalidate the consumer's cached read of the other variable (false sharing).
  • To make the indices SIMD-vectorizable.
  • Because the heap allocator requires 64-byte alignment.

Q2. The producer publishes a new entry by calling head_.store(h + 1, std::memory_order_release). What does release actually guarantee?

  • That any load after this store also sees the latest data.
  • That any writes the producer did before this store — specifically the payload write into data_[h & MASK] — are visible to any consumer thread that acquire-loads head_.
  • That the producer's own subsequent reads of head_ see the updated value.
  • That a full hardware fence (MFENCE) is inserted on x86 before the store.

Q3. You boot with isolcpus=4-7 nohz_full=4-7 and pin the strategy thread to core 5. Which of the following is the most important consequence?

  • Core 5 automatically runs at a higher clock frequency.
  • Core 5 is no longer subject to general scheduler preemption or the 1 kHz timer tick, eliminating the biggest single source of jitter for the strategy thread.
  • The kernel can no longer schedule any work, so the rest of the system stops.
  • Core 5's L1 and L2 caches double in size because no other process can use them.

Q4. Your team measures a 12% latency win after switching from default-built binaries to -O3 -march=native -flto. They want to push further. What's the highest-impact next step?

  • Rewrite the code in C instead of C++ to remove abstraction overhead.
  • Add Profile-Guided Optimization: build with -fprofile-generate, run a representative workload, rebuild with -fprofile-use.
  • Switch the compiler from g++ to clang++ for better autovectorization.
  • Buy a faster network card to reduce I/O latency.

Q5. The strategy thread busy-polls the tick ring with _mm_pause() instead of sleeping on a condition variable. What's the tradeoff?

  • Busy polling is strictly worse — sleeping is faster.
  • Busy poll gives near-zero wakeup latency (the thread is already running) but burns one core at 100% utilization. Sleeping is energy-efficient but adds ~10–30 µs of wakeup latency per event.
  • Busy polling defeats the memory ordering — the CPU is allowed to reorder freely.
  • Busy polling lets the kernel safely sleep the thread for microseconds at a time.

8. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. You introduce the SpscRing but forget the alignas(64) on head_/tail_. The microbenchmark shows the queue does ~5 M ops/s with both threads on the same physical core, but drops to ~2 M ops/s when the threads are pinned to different cores. Explain.

Classic false sharing. When both threads share a core, they share the L1 cache and the head_/tail_ ping-pong is invisible — same cache, no coherence traffic. When you pin them to different cores, every producer write to head_ invalidates the consumer's cached copy of the same line (because tail_ lives there too). The line ping-pongs between L1s via the L3, costing ~30 ns per round-trip. Fix: alignas(64) on each atomic so they live on separate cache lines. Counter-intuitively, the "more isolated" topology gets slower without the fix.

S2. Your team enables -fno-exceptions and a header-only library you depend on stops compiling because it throws std::runtime_error on bad input. What are your options?

Three workable paths. (a) Wall it off: keep -fno-exceptions on the hot-path TU and link in the library-using TU compiled with exceptions enabled — at the cost of losing some cross-module optimization. (b) Fork the dependency to return error codes; ugly but bounded. (c) Don't use it on the hot path; call it only during setup, where exceptions are fine. The wrong answer is "leave exceptions on globally": you give up the bandwidth/code-size win without solving the root problem, which is that this library was never intended for HFT-hot use.

S3. Two scenarios. (a) The logger ring fills up — the logger is slower than the strategy. (b) The tick ring fills up — the strategy is slower than the feed. What's the right policy for each?

(a) Logger ring full: the strategy must not block. The sane policy is to drop the log record and increment a "dropped_log_count" atomic that the logger reads later. Trades still happen; you lose diagnostic data, not money. (b) Tick ring full: this means the strategy is falling behind real-time. Different problem entirely. Options: drop the oldest tick (latest-is-truth), drop the incoming tick (most-recent-state-is-truth), or escalate to a panic shutdown. The choice depends on whether your strategy needs every tick or just the latest market state — but never block the feed, because the next tick is already arriving on the wire.

Next lesson candidate: Mean-variance portfolio optimization — closes out the modeling → allocation arc the queue has pointed at since Lesson 0006. After that, the lock-free / kernel-bypass / FIX-decoder follow-ups become natural deep dives.

head_.load(acquire) in pop acquire Pairs with the producer's release. After this load returns a new value, the consumer is guaranteed to see the payload that was written before it.
The seq_cst tax. If you'd written std::atomic<size_t> and used the default operators (head_++, head_ = h+1), you'd silently get memory_order_seq_cst, which inserts a full fence (MFENCE on x86, ~5–10 ns) on every operation. Industry benchmarks show 10×+ speedups by dropping to release/acquire. Always write the orders explicitly.

3. CPU isolation, thread pinning, and the kernel scheduler

A fast hot loop is worthless if Linux can preempt it 10,000 times a second to run cron jobs or background kernel work. HFT systems carve out cores that the kernel won't touch and pin one thread to each.

Kernel boot parameters (set in /etc/default/grub)

GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="isolcpus=4-7 nohz_full=4-7 rcu_nocbs=4-7"
ParameterWhat it does
isolcpus=4-7Tells the scheduler not to place general tasks on cores 4–7. Only threads that explicitly pin to those cores will run there.
nohz_full=4-7Turns off the periodic 1 kHz timer tick on those cores when only one task is runnable. No timer interrupts = no jitter.
rcu_nocbs=4-7Offloads RCU (read-copy-update) callbacks from those cores. Removes another source of kernel work.

Pinning a thread to a core in C++

#include <pthread.h>

void pinThread(std::thread& t, int core_id) {
    cpu_set_t cpus;
    CPU_ZERO(&cpus);
    CPU_SET(core_id, &cpus);
    pthread_setaffinity_np(t.native_handle(), sizeof(cpus), &cpus);
}

// Wire the three threads onto isolated cores:
std::thread feed_thread{feed_loop, &tick_ring};       pinThread(feed_thread, 4);
std::thread strat_thread{strategy_loop, &tick_ring, &log_ring}; pinThread(strat_thread, 5);
std::thread log_thread{log_loop, &log_ring};         pinThread(log_thread, 6);

The strategy thread now runs uninterrupted on core 5: no scheduler preemption, no timer interrupts, no migration to a different cache. Combined with the lock-free ring, the per-tick path is fully deterministic.

Bonus tweaks the experienced teams add: SCHED_FIFO with a high priority (real-time scheduler class), mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE) to prevent paging, transparent-huge-pages disabled, hyperthreading off on the strategy core (so it owns the L1).

4. Build & compiler discipline — the flags that matter

Default compiler settings leave a lot of latency on the table. HFT C++ is typically built with:

FlagWhat it does
-O3Aggressive optimization: inlining, loop unrolling, auto-vectorization.
-march=nativeUses the full instruction set of the build machine (AVX2, AVX-512, FMA). Critical for SIMD wins.
-fltoLink-Time Optimization — lets the compiler inline across translation units and dead-code-eliminate globally.
-fno-exceptionsRemoves exception scaffolding. Pair with explicit error codes.
-fno-rttiRemoves typeid / dynamic_cast machinery. Almost never needed in HFT code.
-fno-pltRemoves one level of indirection for shared-library calls.
-fprofile-use (PGO)Profile-Guided Optimization: build, run with representative load to gather a profile, rebuild using it. The compiler now knows which branches are hot. Real wins: 5–15% on the hot path.

The PGO loop

$ g++ -O3 -march=native -fprofile-generate=./prof  *.cpp -o trader
$ ./trader replay.dat                    # run a representative workload to collect profile
$ g++ -O3 -march=native -flto -fprofile-use=./prof *.cpp -o trader_pgo

The PGO binary lays out hot basic blocks contiguously, predicts branches based on the real profile, and inlines aggressively where the data shows it pays. For a measurement-driven team this is free latency.

SIMD: the bonus you get nearly for free

With -O3 -march=native, the compiler auto-vectorizes simple loops. In Lesson 0009's rewritten MeanReversion::onTick, the running-sum update is already O(1), so SIMD is irrelevant there. But if you batch-process e.g. 1024 ticks for offline backtest replay, the inner loop will be auto-vectorized into AVX-2 (4 doubles/op) or AVX-512 (8 doubles/op) without you writing a single intrinsic. Inspect the assembly with objdump -d or godbolt to confirm.

5. In this project — restructuring the C++ for production

The repo's three C++ files don't yet have any threading. To get production-grade, the responsibilities split this way:

Existing fileHot/coldBecomes…
gradient_boosting_data_fetching.cpp Cold (cURL → REST API) Stays on a worker thread; pushes parsed ticks onto tick_ring. Allocate freely.
sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp Hot Becomes the strategy loop pinned to an isolated core; drains tick_ring, runs onTick (per Lesson 0009), pushes TradeRecord onto log_ring.
main.cpp (ONNX inference) Warm Runs on a parameter-update thread. Refreshes the strategy's weight constants every 100 ms via a single atomic publish. Hot loop reads with memory_order_acquire.

The skeleton

struct Tick { double price; uint64_t ts_ns; };
struct TradeRecord { double price; enum class Side : uint8_t { Buy, Sell } side; uint64_t ts_ns; };

static SpscRing<Tick,        1 << 14> tick_ring;     // 16384 ticks buffered
static SpscRing<TradeRecord, 1 << 14> log_ring;      // 16384 trades buffered

void strategy_loop() noexcept {
    MeanReversion<20> strat;
    Tick tk;
    while (running.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {
        if (!tick_ring.try_pop(tk)) [[unlikely]] {
            // Spin: a few PAUSE instructions, then re-check. No syscalls, no sleep.
            _mm_pause();
            continue;
        }
        auto action = strat.onTick(tk.price);
        if (action != MeanReversion::Action::Hold) [[unlikely]] {
            // Send order to the NIC (kernel-bypass or FPGA path).
            emit_order(tk.price, action);
            log_ring.try_push({tk.price,
                action_to_side(action), tk.ts_ns});
        }
    }
}

What this delivers:

  • Zero allocation per tick — the rings are pre-allocated, strat holds its stack array.
  • Zero I/O per tick — logging is a single try_push of a 24-byte record.
  • Zero syscalls per tick — busy-poll the ring with _mm_pause(); the kernel never sees us.
  • Deterministic per-tick time on the isolated core.
Repo honesty: none of this is implemented yet — the existing C++ is single-threaded and synchronous, and that's the appropriate first cut. The point of this lesson is what the system becomes when you decide to take latency seriously, and to give you the right vocabulary to ask "where would this thread live?" on every line you write.

6. Often confused with

SPSC vs MPSC vs MPMC

SPSC: one producer, one consumer — fastest. MPSC: many producers, one consumer (e.g. logger fed by many strategy threads). MPMC: many of each — most expensive. HFT teams design the system to need only SPSC wherever possible.

seq_cst vs release/acquire

seq_cst: total global order on all atomics — strongest, slowest, default. release/acquire: pairs publish↔read of a specific atomic — enough for queues. relaxed: no synchronization, just atomicity — for indices the thread owns.

Lock-free vs Wait-free

Lock-free: at least one thread always makes progress. Wait-free: every thread completes in bounded steps. SPSC rings written as above are wait-free. Most MPMC queues are only lock-free.

Thread pinning vs Process affinity

Thread pinning (pthread_setaffinity_np): per-thread, fine-grained. Process affinity (taskset): whole-process at launch. HFT pins each thread individually because each plays a different role.

Busy polling vs Sleeping

Busy poll the ring with _mm_pause() — latency-optimal, burns a core. Sleep on a condition variable — energy-friendly, adds tens of µs wakeup latency. HFT busy-polls on the strategy thread, sleeps on the logger.

PGO vs LTO

PGO (Profile-Guided Optimization): uses a real run's branch probabilities to lay out code. LTO (Link-Time Optimization): runs the optimizer across all translation units at link time. They are independent and stack — use both.

7. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. Why does SpscRing use alignas(64) on the head and tail indices?

  • Because std::atomic only guarantees atomicity at 64-byte alignment.
  • To force head_ and tail_ onto different cache lines so that the producer's writes don't invalidate the consumer's cached read of the other variable (false sharing).
  • To make the indices SIMD-vectorizable.
  • Because the heap allocator requires 64-byte alignment.

Q2. The producer publishes a new entry by calling head_.store(h + 1, std::memory_order_release). What does release actually guarantee?

  • That any load after this store also sees the latest data.
  • That any writes the producer did before this store — specifically the payload write into data_[h & MASK] — are visible to any consumer thread that acquire-loads head_.
  • That the producer's own subsequent reads of head_ see the updated value.
  • That a full hardware fence (MFENCE) is inserted on x86 before the store.

Q3. You boot with isolcpus=4-7 nohz_full=4-7 and pin the strategy thread to core 5. Which of the following is the most important consequence?

  • Core 5 automatically runs at a higher clock frequency.
  • Core 5 is no longer subject to general scheduler preemption or the 1 kHz timer tick, eliminating the biggest single source of jitter for the strategy thread.
  • The kernel can no longer schedule any work, so the rest of the system stops.
  • Core 5's L1 and L2 caches double in size because no other process can use them.

Q4. Your team measures a 12% latency win after switching from default-built binaries to -O3 -march=native -flto. They want to push further. What's the highest-impact next step?

  • Rewrite the code in C instead of C++ to remove abstraction overhead.
  • Add Profile-Guided Optimization: build with -fprofile-generate, run a representative workload, rebuild with -fprofile-use.
  • Switch the compiler from g++ to clang++ for better autovectorization.
  • Buy a faster network card to reduce I/O latency.

Q5. The strategy thread busy-polls the tick ring with _mm_pause() instead of sleeping on a condition variable. What's the tradeoff?

  • Busy polling is strictly worse — sleeping is faster.
  • Busy poll gives near-zero wakeup latency (the thread is already running) but burns one core at 100% utilization. Sleeping is energy-efficient but adds ~10–30 µs of wakeup latency per event.
  • Busy polling defeats the memory ordering — the CPU is allowed to reorder freely.
  • Busy polling lets the kernel safely sleep the thread for microseconds at a time.

8. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. You introduce the SpscRing but forget the alignas(64) on head_/tail_. The microbenchmark shows the queue does ~5 M ops/s with both threads on the same physical core, but drops to ~2 M ops/s when the threads are pinned to different cores. Explain.

Classic false sharing. When both threads share a core, they share the L1 cache and the head_/tail_ ping-pong is invisible — same cache, no coherence traffic. When you pin them to different cores, every producer write to head_ invalidates the consumer's cached copy of the same line (because tail_ lives there too). The line ping-pongs between L1s via the L3, costing ~30 ns per round-trip. Fix: alignas(64) on each atomic so they live on separate cache lines. Counter-intuitively, the "more isolated" topology gets slower without the fix.

S2. Your team enables -fno-exceptions and a header-only library you depend on stops compiling because it throws std::runtime_error on bad input. What are your options?

Three workable paths. (a) Wall it off: keep -fno-exceptions on the hot-path TU and link in the library-using TU compiled with exceptions enabled — at the cost of losing some cross-module optimization. (b) Fork the dependency to return error codes; ugly but bounded. (c) Don't use it on the hot path; call it only during setup, where exceptions are fine. The wrong answer is "leave exceptions on globally": you give up the bandwidth/code-size win without solving the root problem, which is that this library was never intended for HFT-hot use.

S3. Two scenarios. (a) The logger ring fills up — the logger is slower than the strategy. (b) The tick ring fills up — the strategy is slower than the feed. What's the right policy for each?

(a) Logger ring full: the strategy must not block. The sane policy is to drop the log record and increment a "dropped_log_count" atomic that the logger reads later. Trades still happen; you lose diagnostic data, not money. (b) Tick ring full: this means the strategy is falling behind real-time. Different problem entirely. Options: drop the oldest tick (latest-is-truth), drop the incoming tick (most-recent-state-is-truth), or escalate to a panic shutdown. The choice depends on whether your strategy needs every tick or just the latest market state — but never block the feed, because the next tick is already arriving on the wire.

Next lesson candidate: Mean-variance portfolio optimization — closes out the modeling → allocation arc the queue has pointed at since Lesson 0006. After that, the lock-free / kernel-bypass / FIX-decoder follow-ups become natural deep dives.

### Vtable / Virtual call — `intro`
The dispatch table backing `virtual` methods. Each call requires a pointer
load and an indirect jump (~5–15 ns) and, more importantly, blocks the
compiler from inlining. Replaced by templates/CRTP in HFT code.

---

## Added in Lesson 0010 (Low-Latency C++ Best Practices)

### alignas(64) — `intro`
C++ keyword that forces a variable onto a 64-byte (cache-line) boundary.
Used on SPSC ring head/tail indices to prevent false sharing between
producer and consumer cores.

### Busy polling (CPU side) — `intro`
Spin in user space calling `_mm_pause()` on the data source (a ring, a NIC
queue) instead of sleeping. Near-zero wakeup latency; burns one core at
100% utilization. Used on the strategy thread; not on the logger.

### Cache coherence / Line ping-pong — `intro`
When two cores repeatedly write to the same cache line, the line bounces
between their L1 caches via the L3 (~30 ns per round-trip). The performance
killer that `alignas(64)` defends against.

### CPU isolation (`isolcpus`) — `intro`
Linux kernel boot parameter that tells the scheduler to leave specific
cores free of general tasks. Combined with `nohz_full` (no timer tick) and
`rcu_nocbs` (no RCU callbacks) for true HFT-grade isolation.

### `_mm_pause()` — `intro`
x86 intrinsic that hints to the CPU that this is a spin-wait loop. Slows
speculative execution, conserves power, friendlier to a sibling
hyperthread. Always used in tight polling loops.

### Lock-free vs Wait-free — `intro`
**Lock-free**: at least one thread always makes progress. **Wait-free**:
every thread completes in bounded steps. A correct SPSC ring with the
above pattern is wait-free; most MPMC queues are only lock-free.

### LTO (Link-Time Optimization) — `intro`
Compiler flag (`-flto`) that runs the optimizer at link time across all
translation units, enabling cross-TU inlining and dead-code elimination.
Stacks with PGO.

### `mlockall` — `intro`
Linux syscall that locks all of a process's pages into RAM, preventing the
kernel from paging them out. Used in HFT setups so a memory page fault
can't introduce ms-scale jitter.

### `memory_order_acquire` — `intro`
Atomic load ordering that pairs with `release` on the other side. Ensures
all reads after the acquire-load see writes done before the matching
release-store. Used by the SPSC consumer reading `head_`.

### `memory_order_relaxed` — `intro`
Atomic operation with no synchronization — only atomicity. Cheapest. Used
when the thread owns the variable (e.g. the producer reading its own
`head_`).

### `memory_order_release` — `intro`
Atomic store ordering. Guarantees all writes done before the store are
visible to a thread that acquire-loads the same atomic. The "publish" in
SPSC.

### `memory_order_seq_cst` — `intro`
Atomic ordering that gives a total global order over all seq_cst
operations. Default in `std::atomic`. ~5–10 ns overhead on x86
(MFENCE). Avoid unless you actually need it.

### `nohz_full` — `intro`
Linux boot parameter that disables the 1 kHz scheduling timer on isolated
cores when only one task is runnable. Removes ~1000 interrupts/sec of
jitter from the HFT hot path.

### MPSC / MPMC queue — `intro`
**MPSC**: multi-producer, single-consumer (e.g. many threads feeding one
logger). **MPMC**: multi-producer, multi-consumer. Both are more expensive
than SPSC; design the system to need SPSC wherever possible.

### PGO (Profile-Guided Optimization) — `intro`
Build twice: first with `-fprofile-generate` to instrument, run a
representative workload, then rebuild with `-fprofile-use` so the compiler
knows which branches are hot. 5–15% latency wins on the hot path.

### `pthread_setaffinity_np` — `intro`

## Added in Lesson 0010 (Low-Latency C++ Best Practices)

### alignas(64) — `intro`
C++ keyword that forces a variable onto a 64-byte (cache-line) boundary.
Used on SPSC ring head/tail indices to prevent false sharing between
producer and consumer cores.

### Busy polling (CPU side) — `intro`
Spin in user space calling `_mm_pause()` on the data source (a ring, a NIC
queue) instead of sleeping. Near-zero wakeup latency; burns one core at
100% utilization. Used on the strategy thread; not on the logger.

### Cache coherence / Line ping-pong — `intro`
When two cores repeatedly write to the same cache line, the line bounces
between their L1 caches via the L3 (~30 ns per round-trip). The performance
killer that `alignas(64)` defends against.

### CPU isolation (`isolcpus`) — `intro`
Linux kernel boot parameter that tells the scheduler to leave specific
cores free of general tasks. Combined with `nohz_full` (no timer tick) and
`rcu_nocbs` (no RCU callbacks) for true HFT-grade isolation.

### `_mm_pause()` — `intro`
x86 intrinsic that hints to the CPU that this is a spin-wait loop. Slows
speculative execution, conserves power, friendlier to a sibling
hyperthread. Always used in tight polling loops.

### Lock-free vs Wait-free — `intro`
**Lock-free**: at least one thread always makes progress. **Wait-free**:
every thread completes in bounded steps. A correct SPSC ring with the
above pattern is wait-free; most MPMC queues are only lock-free.

### LTO (Link-Time Optimization) — `intro`
Compiler flag (`-flto`) that runs the optimizer at link time across all
translation units, enabling cross-TU inlining and dead-code elimination.
Stacks with PGO.

### `mlockall` — `intro`
Linux syscall that locks all of a process's pages into RAM, preventing the
kernel from paging them out. Used in HFT setups so a memory page fault
can't introduce ms-scale jitter.

### `memory_order_acquire` — `intro`
Atomic load ordering that pairs with `release` on the other side. Ensures
all reads after the acquire-load see writes done before the matching
release-store. Used by the SPSC consumer reading `head_`.

### `memory_order_relaxed` — `intro`
Atomic operation with no synchronization — only atomicity. Cheapest. Used
when the thread owns the variable (e.g. the producer reading its own
`head_`).

### `memory_order_release` — `intro`
Atomic store ordering. Guarantees all writes done before the store are
visible to a thread that acquire-loads the same atomic. The "publish" in
SPSC.

### `memory_order_seq_cst` — `intro`
Atomic ordering that gives a total global order over all seq_cst
operations. Default in `std::atomic`. ~5–10 ns overhead on x86
(MFENCE). Avoid unless you actually need it.

Linux boot parameter that disables the 1 kHz scheduling timer on isolated
cores when only one task is runnable. Removes ~1000 interrupts/sec of
jitter from the HFT hot path.

representative workload, then rebuild with `-fprofile-use` so the compiler
knows which branches are hot. 5–15% latency wins on the hot path.

Lesson 0010 written. Open it with:

```
xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/0010-low-latency-cpp-best-practices.html
```

## Why this is a distinct lesson from 0009

Lesson 0009 fixed **one hot loop** (per-tick discipline). Lesson 0010 builds the **production system around it**: three threads (feed / strategy / logger), two SPSC rings, CPU isolation, thread pinning, and the build-flag discipline that real HFT teams enforce.

## What you've got

- **`docs/learning/lessons/0010-low-latency-cpp-best-practices.html`** — full production-grade SPSC ring with proper `memory_order_release`/`acquire`/`relaxed` semantics and `alignas(64)` head/tail padding; the `isolcpus`/`nohz_full`/`rcu_nocbs` kernel parameters and `pthread_setaffinity_np` C++ side; busy-poll vs sleep tradeoff; compiler flag menu (`-O3 -march=native -flto -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti`) and the PGO loop; how the repo's three existing C++ files map onto the three-thread architecture. Six "often confused" pairs (SPSC vs MPSC/MPMC, seq_cst vs release/acquire, lock-free vs wait-free, thread pinning vs process affinity, busy-poll vs sleep, PGO vs LTO). 5 quiz, 3 scenarios (false sharing reveal, library throwing exceptions under `-fno-exceptions`, ring-full policies).
- **`docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`** — lesson 0010 logged.
- **`docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md`** — 22 new terms: SPSC ring, all four `memory_order` levels, `alignas(64)`, `_mm_pause()`, `mlockall`, `isolcpus`, `nohz_full`, `rcu_nocbs`, `SCHED_FIFO`, `pthread_setaffinity_np`, PGO, LTO, lock-free vs wait-free, MPSC/MPMC, etc.

## Honest framing in the lesson

None of this architecture is in the repo today — the existing C++ is single-threaded synchronous and that's the appropriate first cut. The point isn't to make you ship a thread-per-core trader tomorrow; it's to give you the vocabulary to ask **"where would this thread live, and which core would own it?"** on every line you write from here on. Also flagged: `release`/`acquire` is the right default; the `seq_cst` you get from default `std::atomic` ops is a ~10× tax most code pays accidentally.

## Knowledge check — answer in chat

1. The producer's `head_.store(h + 1, memory_order_release)` is paired with the consumer's `head_.load(memory_order_acquire)`. In one sentence: what would break if both used `memory_order_relaxed` instead?
2. You forget `alignas(64)` on the SPSC `head_` and `tail_` indices. The ring still works correctly — but throughput collapses when the producer and consumer threads are pinned to **different** physical cores. Why does the bug only show up under pinning?
3. Your strategy thread is pinned to an isolated core (`isolcpus=5`) and busy-polls the tick ring with `_mm_pause()`. Name the single biggest source of jitter this design eliminates compared to a normal `std::condition_variable::wait()`.

Take a swing — then we pick Lesson 0011 (mean-variance is still the standing next-up; the lock-free deep dive in this lesson teed up kernel bypass as a worthy alternative).

- [Writing a Fast and Versatile SPSC Ring Buffer — Kaspar Daugaard](https://www.daugaard.org/blog/writing-a-fast-and-versatile-spsc-ring-buffer--performance-results/)
- [Building a High-Performance Lock-Free Ring Buffer in C++ for Ultra-Low Latency Messaging — DEV](https://dev.to/lakshya_bankey_27825e4908/building-a-high-performance-lock-free-ring-buffer-in-c-for-ultra-low-latency-messaging-19h6)

Once you have the ladder, the techniques that move you down it become straightforward.

Note: per the new repo guidance, code blocks in this lesson are illustrative, not always from the repo. We'll backfill into real code as we build it out.

1. Definitions — there's no formal standard, but a strong industry consensus

"Low-latency" and "ultra-low-latency" are marketing terms with no formal standards body to bless them. But the trading industry has settled on rough conventions that map cleanly onto the technology tiers:

TermTypical tick-to-trade rangeWhat the system looks like
"Fast" / standard milliseconds (1 ms+) Default Python or untuned C++ over kernel TCP. Your FastAPI webapp.
Low-latency (LL) microseconds (1–100 µs) Tuned C++ on Linux with isolated cores, lock-free queues, occasional kernel bypass. This is Lessons 0009–0010 territory.
Ultra-low-latency (ULL) nanoseconds (10 ns – 1 µs) FPGA tick-to-trade, kernel-bypass NICs, colocation, microwave/RF links across cities, hardware timestamping.
The most useful single discriminator: if your hot path crosses the Linux kernel even once, you're in LL territory at best. If your hot path lives entirely on the FPGA or in user-space against a kernel-bypass NIC, you're in ULL territory. The kernel boundary is the rough dividing line.

2. The latency ladder, end-to-end

Each rung swaps a technique for a faster one. Tick-to-trade numbers are representative — they're a moving target as silicon and tooling improve, but the ratios between rungs are stable.

Tier 0 — Web app
Python/Node over public internet. Your FastAPI dev server.
~50 ms
$10/mo
Tier 1 — Retail
Tuned Python or untuned C++ over kernel TCP from a co-region cloud instance.
~1–5 ms
$100/mo
Tier 2 — LL CPU
Tuned C++ + lock-free queues + isolated cores (Lesson 0010). Kernel TCP.
~50–200 µs
~$1k/mo
Tier 3 — Kernel bypass
DPDK or Solarflare OpenOnload — user-space drives the NIC directly.
~750 ns – 5 µs

Tier 4 — FPGA tick-to-trade
Strategy logic synthesized into HDL on the NIC (the repo's fpga/ direction).
~100–300 ns

Tier 5 — Hardware MAC pipeline
Parsing happens inside the PHY/MAC itself; multiple parallel decoders.

Tier 6 — Custom ASIC + microwave

Two things worth noticing about this ladder:

  • The jump from Tier 2 (LL) to Tier 3 (ULL) is ~100× latency. Below Tier 3 every further rung is ~3–10×. The big cliff is the kernel boundary.
  • Cost is roughly geometric. Each rung is order-of-magnitude more expensive than the one above. ULL is a financial decision, not just an engineering one.

3. The six techniques that buy you ULL

Roughly in the order they pay off:

1. Colocation

Rent rack space inside the exchange's data center so your wire to the matching engine is meters, not kilometers. Cuts ~100 µs of fiber latency for free (speed of light is 5 µs/km in glass). Step zero before any of the below makes sense.

2. Kernel bypass (DPDK, OpenOnload)

Route packets from NIC DMA rings directly into your user-space process, skipping the kernel TCP stack (Lesson 0004). Saves ~50 µs per round-trip. Mandatory entry to ULL territory on CPU.

3. FPGA tick-to-trade

Synthesize the strategy into HDL on the NIC itself (Lesson 0002). Parsing → decision → order all happen on-chip in nanoseconds. The biggest single jump in the ladder.

4. CPU/kernel discipline

isolcpus, nohz_full, busy polling, thread pinning, mlockall (Lesson 0010). Cuts jitter — the tail of the latency distribution — to near zero on the CPU paths that remain.

5. Cross-market microwave / RF links

For arbitrage between geographically separated venues, line-of-sight microwave links beat fiber. Light through air ≈ 1.0c; through glass ≈ 0.67c. Chicago↔New Jersey: ~8 ms one-way over microwave vs ~13 ms over fiber — a 5 ms edge that funded an entire industry of tower-builders in the 2010s.

6. Custom silicon (ASIC)

At the top of the ladder, the biggest firms tape out application-specific chips that hard-code parsing, decision, and risk-check in fewer cycles than an FPGA can. Multi-million-dollar capex; only the largest desks justify it.

A worked example — measuring where the time goes

A hypothetical tick-to-trade breakdown at each tier, so you can see what each technique removes:

StageTier 2 (LL CPU)Tier 3 (Kernel bypass)Tier 4 (FPGA)
Packet on wire → host~2 µs~2 µs~25 ns
Kernel network stack~50 µsskippedskipped
User-space parse~1 µs~1 µs~25 ns (on-chip)
Strategy decision~500 ns~500 ns~10 ns
Order encode + TX~5 µs~1 µs~50 ns
Total tick-to-trade~60 µs~5 µs~110 ns

Notice that once kernel and userland are skipped (Tier 4), the parse and decision stages dominate again — and shaving them is exactly what fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd and fpga/market_maker.vhd in this repo do, in nanoseconds.

4. How you actually measure latency — and the numbers that lie

"Our system is 5 µs" is the wrong sentence. The right sentence has a distribution, an endpoint pair, and a clock source.

Distribution, not average

The mean is almost meaningless. HFT lives on the tail. Quote p50 / p99 / p99.9 / p99.99 — the latencies that 50%, 99%, etc. of events come in under. A 5 µs mean with a 500 µs p99.9 will lose money even on a fast median; the tail is the killer.

Endpoint pair (be precise)

Wire-to-wire: last bit of incoming packet → first bit of outgoing order at the NIC. App-to-app: feature extracted → decision made (your code only). Inside-the-FPGA: single-cycle registered output. State which one or comparisons mean nothing.

Clock source

clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) has 10–30 ns resolution but burns a syscall and can step. rdtsc reads the TSC register in ~10 ns but needs tsc_reliable and per-core sync. Hardware timestamps (NIC or FPGA-side) are the only truth at ULL — they have ns resolution and are immune to OS noise.

Jitter, not just latency

Jitter = the variability of latency, often quoted as p99.99 − p50 or as the standard deviation. ULL systems live on low jitter; a deterministic 5 µs beats an "average 1 µs" with a wild tail every time, because risk models price the worst case.

A minimum-viable measurement snippet (illustrative):

struct Sample { uint64_t t_in_ns; uint64_t t_out_ns; };
std::array<Sample, 1 << 20> samples;   // 1M-sample ring of timing pairs

inline uint64_t now_ns() noexcept {
    timespec ts; clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW, &ts);
    return uint64_t(ts.tv_sec) * 1'000'000'000ull + ts.tv_nsec;
}

// Per tick: record entry, do work, record exit, store the pair, never log.
samples[i].t_in_ns  = now_ns();
strategy.onTick(tick);
samples[i].t_out_ns = now_ns();

Offline (cold path), sort the deltas and compute the quantiles. Plot the histogram. The story is always in the tail.

5. The cost cliff — and how to decide what tier you actually need

Each rung of the ladder is ~10× more expensive than the one above. The decision of which tier to target is an economic argument, not a technical one. Ask three questions before committing:

  1. What's your competition's tier? If everyone on your venue is at FPGA tick-to-trade and you're at CPU, your fills will be adversely selected (you trade only when faster traders didn't want to) and your P&L is structurally negative. Conversely, if everyone is at LL CPU, paying for FPGA buys you nothing.
  2. What's your strategy's natural cadence? A daily-rebalance equity model (this repo's GBM) is at Tier 0–1 by design; moving it to Tier 4 is malpractice. A market-making strategy on a liquid futures contract starts to need Tier 3 to be viable and Tier 4 to be competitive.
  3. What's the marginal P&L of one less microsecond? In a market-making strategy, less latency means winning more queue positions, fewer adverse fills, and a bigger fraction of the spread captured. For a directional next-day model: zero marginal P&L from sub-µs latency. Drawing this curve is what justifies the spend.
The single most common HFT-firm misallocation: a junior engineer rebuilds a Tier 1 strategy as a Tier 4 system on the assumption that "faster is better." It's not. Faster is more expensive, harder to debug, and only pays off when the strategy itself is latency-bound. Profile first. Tier the strategy intentionally.

ModuleTodayReasonable target
paper_trading_sim.py / predict_next.pyTier 0–1 (daily Python)Stay there. Daily horizon doesn't reward more.
webapp/main.pyTier 0 (kernel HTTP)Stay there. Web UI; latency irrelevant.
scripts/robinhood_executor.pyTier 0 (HTTPS REST)Tier 0 — Robinhood's API floors it anyway.
gradient_boosting/main.cpp (ONNX inference)Tier 1–2 (CPU C++)Tier 2 with the Lesson 0010 architecture, or Tier 4 via hls4ml.
fpga/*.vhdTier 4 in designTier 4–5 once the 10 GbE UDP + risk pieces from the roadmap are built.

Every module lives at the tier its strategy demands. Mixing tiers is not a sign of inconsistency; it's a sign of intentional design.

6. Often confused with

Latency vs Jitter

Latency: how long one event takes (p50, p99…). Jitter: how variable that is (p99.99 − p50, or stddev). ULL systems often sacrifice average latency for lower jitter; risk models care about the worst case.

Latency vs Throughput

Latency: time per event. Throughput: events per second. HFT optimizes for latency; market-data plants optimize for throughput. They often trade off — busy polling cuts latency by burning a core, lowering throughput per watt.

p50 vs p99 vs p99.99

p50 (median): what the typical event experiences. p99: 1-in-100 events are slower. p99.99: 1-in-10,000 events are slower. At market-data rates of 100k+ messages/sec, p99.99 events happen several times a second.

Round-trip tick-to-trade includes the order leaving your NIC. One-way sometimes refers to wire-to-wire latency or to inbound parsing only. Most published "tick-to-trade" numbers are wire-to-wire round-trip; always confirm.

Real-time in OS terms means "bounded latency" not "fast." A 10 ms deterministic system is real-time; a 100 ns average with a 10 ms tail is not. ULL systems aim to be real-time first and fast second.

Speed vs Edge

Speed is a capability (your tier). Edge is the advantage that capability gives you on a particular strategy. Speed without edge is wasted spend; speed with edge is alpha.

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. What's the single most useful discriminator between LL and ULL?

  • Whether the system is colocated at the exchange.
  • Whether the hot path crosses the Linux kernel even once.
  • Whether the system is written in C++ versus a higher-level language.
  • Whether the system uses application-specific integrated circuits.

Q2. Your daily-rebalance GBM strategy in paper_trading_sim.py takes ~200 ms end-to-end. A teammate proposes rewriting it in FPGA for "ultra-low latency." Best response?

  • "Great idea, faster is always better — the new latency will reduce slippage.
  • "Wrong tier — the strategy acts once per day, so the marginal P&L from sub-µs latency is zero. FPGA cost would be wasted; stay at Tier 0–1.
  • "Sure, but only if we first convert the model to a single decision tree.
  • "Only if the FPGA license is under $1000.

Q3. Two systems are benchmarked. System A: mean 800 ns, p99.99 = 12 µs. System B: mean 1.2 µs, p99.99 = 2 µs. Which would an HFT market-making team typically prefer?

  • System A — it has the lower mean latency.
  • System B — bounded p99.99 is what risk models price; System A's tail will systematically lose money on the tail events.
  • Doesn't matter — both numbers describe the same thing.
  • Whichever has the lower variance, regardless of which metric.

Q4. The Chicago↔NJ microwave link beats fiber by ~5 ms one-way. Why?

  • Because microwaves carry more bandwidth than fiber.
  • Because light travels faster through air than through glass, and the line-of-sight path is shorter than fiber's routed path.
  • Because exchanges process microwave-delivered orders faster than fiber-delivered ones.
  • Because microwaves operate on the nanosecond scale natively.

Q5. Which of these is the cheapest tier-upgrade you can make to a Tier 2 (LL CPU) system to start moving toward ULL?

  • Lease a microwave link to the next data center.
  • Switch to a kernel-bypass NIC + DPDK/OpenOnload so the hot path skips the kernel network stack.
  • Tape out a custom ASIC for parsing the exchange protocol.
  • Add a second strategy thread to run in parallel.

8. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. Your strategy team reports a Sharpe of 2.0 in backtest on a Tier 2 system, but Sharpe of −0.3 when live. The latency was identical to backtest. What's the most likely cause and how does the tier conversation help?

Adverse selection. In backtest, you "fill" every order at the recorded price. Live, faster participants see the same signal microseconds before you and lift the offers you wanted — leaving you with only the bad fills (the ones no one else wanted, where the price was about to move against you). The backtest assumed you were the only player; the market is full of Tier 4 players. Tier conversation: either accept that this strategy needs Tier 3+ to be viable, or pick a different strategy whose alpha doesn't depend on being faster than other participants — e.g. multi-day signals where the first-fill advantage is irrelevant.

S2. You measure p50 = 700 ns and p99.99 = 3 µs on a kernel-bypass system. A new release ships and p50 drops to 500 ns, but p99.99 jumps to 25 µs. Should you ship the new release?

No — and the question is itself a teaching moment about what to optimize. A 200 ns mean win is mathematically beaten by a 22 µs tail blow-up because the tail events happen thousands of times per day at typical market-data rates, and each one likely loses money on adverse selection. The new release also implies you've introduced some jitter source (a new allocation, a new branch on a rare path, a cache eviction pattern, a removed busy-poll). Diagnose what's causing the tail before shipping; revert if necessary. The ULL maxim: median is vanity, tail is sanity.

S3. The repo's fpga/market_maker.vhd targets ~4 ns per stage. If you wrap it in a Linux user-space C++ harness that polls the FPGA over PCIe for every quote, what tier does the combined system actually live at, and why?

Whatever the slowest link is. PCIe Gen3 round-trip from a CPU to a card sitting in a PCIe slot is typically 500 ns – 2 µs, dominated by the driver, the user-space polling pattern, and the bus itself. So even though the FPGA does its arithmetic in ~4 ns, a CPU-in-the-loop system operates at Tier 3 (kernel-bypass-ish, ~µs) — not Tier 4. To live at Tier 4 the orders must leave the FPGA directly over the SFP+ port, with the CPU only used as a slow-path configurator. That's why the README's roadmap groups "10 GbE UDP stack" and "PCIe DMA interface" as separate items: one is the ULL path, the other is the slow-path management interface.

Next lesson in your queue: DMA (Direct Market Access). After that: hardware acceleration, alternative data, order-book dynamics, market making, stat-arb, order-to-trade ratio, more alt-data examples, then the AI/CV concepts (preprocessing, object detection, segmentation, geometric calculus).

  • Switch to a kernel-bypass NIC + DPDK/OpenOnload so the hot path skips the kernel network stack.
  • Tape out a custom ASIC for parsing the exchange protocol.
  • Add a second strategy thread to run in parallel.

8. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. Your strategy team reports a Sharpe of 2.0 in backtest on a Tier 2 system, but Sharpe of −0.3 when live. The latency was identical to backtest. What's the most likely cause and how does the tier conversation help?

Adverse selection. In backtest, you "fill" every order at the recorded price. Live, faster participants see the same signal microseconds before you and lift the offers you wanted — leaving you with only the bad fills (the ones no one else wanted, where the price was about to move against you). The backtest assumed you were the only player; the market is full of Tier 4 players. Tier conversation: either accept that this strategy needs Tier 3+ to be viable, or pick a different strategy whose alpha doesn't depend on being faster than other participants — e.g. multi-day signals where the first-fill advantage is irrelevant.

S2. You measure p50 = 700 ns and p99.99 = 3 µs on a kernel-bypass system. A new release ships and p50 drops to 500 ns, but p99.99 jumps to 25 µs. Should you ship the new release?

No — and the question is itself a teaching moment about what to optimize. A 200 ns mean win is mathematically beaten by a 22 µs tail blow-up because the tail events happen thousands of times per day at typical market-data rates, and each one likely loses money on adverse selection. The new release also implies you've introduced some jitter source (a new allocation, a new branch on a rare path, a cache eviction pattern, a removed busy-poll). Diagnose what's causing the tail before shipping; revert if necessary. The ULL maxim: median is vanity, tail is sanity.

S3. The repo's fpga/market_maker.vhd targets ~4 ns per stage. If you wrap it in a Linux user-space C++ harness that polls the FPGA over PCIe for every quote, what tier does the combined system actually live at, and why?

Whatever the slowest link is. PCIe Gen3 round-trip from a CPU to a card sitting in a PCIe slot is typically 500 ns – 2 µs, dominated by the driver, the user-space polling pattern, and the bus itself. So even though the FPGA does its arithmetic in ~4 ns, a CPU-in-the-loop system operates at Tier 3 (kernel-bypass-ish, ~µs) — not Tier 4. To live at Tier 4 the orders must leave the FPGA directly over the SFP+ port, with the CPU only used as a slow-path configurator. That's why the README's roadmap groups "10 GbE UDP stack" and "PCIe DMA interface" as separate items: one is the ULL path, the other is the slow-path management interface.

Next lesson in your queue: DMA (Direct Market Access). After that: hardware acceleration, alternative data, order-book dynamics, market making, stat-arb, order-to-trade ratio, more alt-data examples, then the AI/CV concepts (preprocessing, object detection, segmentation, geometric calculus).

### Thread pinning — `intro`
Binding a thread to a specific CPU core so the scheduler can't migrate it.
Eliminates cache invalidation from migration and is the in-program half of
`isolcpus`-based isolation.

---

## Added in Lesson 0011 (Low-Latency vs Ultra-Low-Latency)

### Adverse selection (in latency context) — `intro`
Losing money systematically because faster participants see the same signal
microseconds before you and pick off the favorable side. The structural risk
of running at a lower tier than your venue's median competitor.

### App-to-app latency — `intro`
Latency measured between two points inside your application code only
(e.g. signal extracted → decision made). Excludes wire and kernel. Useful
for internal optimization, not for competitive comparison.

### ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) — `intro`
Custom silicon fabricated for one purpose. Faster than FPGAs but multi-
million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen logic. Tier 6 of the latency ladder;
only the largest desks justify it.

### Hardware timestamp — `intro`
A nanosecond-resolution timestamp attached to a packet by the NIC or FPGA at
ingress/egress. The only trustworthy clock at ULL scales — immune to OS
scheduling and clock skew.

### Inside-FPGA latency — `intro`
Latency measured between registers on a single FPGA, i.e. a fixed number of
clock cycles. At 250 MHz, 1 cycle = 4 ns. Fundamentally different unit than
wire-to-wire latency.

### Jitter (latency variability) — `intro`
The variability of latency across events, often quoted as `p99.99 − p50` or
as the standard deviation. ULL systems are judged on jitter as much as on
median latency.

### Latency ladder / tier — `intro`
The 6-rung industry mental model of trading-system latency, from Tier 0
(web app, ms) through Tier 6 (ASIC + microwave, ns + cross-market RF). Each
rung is ~10× more expensive than the one above.

### Latency tail — `intro`
The high-percentile portion of the latency distribution (p99, p99.9,
p99.99). At HFT message rates, tail events happen multiple times per
second; the tail is what loses money, not the mean.

### Low-latency (LL) — `intro`
Industry term for systems with microsecond-scale tick-to-trade (~1–100 µs).
Tuned C++, lock-free queues, kernel TCP. Tier 2 of the ladder.

### Microwave / RF link — `intro`
Line-of-sight wireless link used for cross-market arbitrage. Light through
air ≈ 1.0c vs ~0.67c through glass — a few ms edge over a thousand km. The
basis of the Chicago↔NJ trading corridor.

### One-way latency — `intro`
Time from event ingress to action emission, measured in one direction
(e.g. tick arrival → order on wire). Distinct from round-trip; both are
quoted in HFT and must be specified.

### p50 / p99 / p99.99 — `intro`
Quantiles of the latency distribution: 50%, 99%, 99.99% of events come in
under this latency. HFT systems are evaluated on the higher percentiles.

### Real-time (OS sense) — `intro`
Bounded worst-case latency. Distinct from "fast" — a 10 ms deterministic
system is real-time; a 100 ns average with a 10 ms tail is not. ULL systems
aim to be real-time first.

### Round-trip latency — `intro`
Time from event ingress to action egress through the full pipeline, including
the order leaving your NIC. The headline tick-to-trade number in most
benchmarks is wire-to-wire round-trip.

### Strategy cadence — `intro`
The natural decision rate of a strategy (per day, per second, per tick).
The single most useful input to deciding what tier of latency the strategy
needs.

### TSC (Time-Stamp Counter) — `intro`
x86 CPU register incremented every cycle. Read with `rdtsc` in ~10 ns;
nanosecond resolution but needs `tsc_reliable` and per-core synchronization
on multi-socket systems.

### Ultra-low-latency (ULL) — `intro`
Industry term for systems with nanosecond-scale tick-to-trade (~10 ns – 1
µs). FPGA, kernel-bypass NIC, hardware timestamps, microwave links. Tiers
3–6 of the ladder.

### Wire-to-wire latency — `intro`
Time from the last bit of an inbound packet arriving at the NIC to the
first bit of an outbound order leaving the NIC. The most defensible
endpoint pair for competitive benchmarking.

The user wants to learn "engineering" (or, if blank, you choose the most valuable concept to teach next based on their progress and this project's code). This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7.
