Lesson 0012 Quiz: 0 / 5

RF Engineering in HFT

Why this matters for HFT_practice: Lesson 0011's latency ladder placed cross-market microwave/RF links on Tier 5–6. This lesson opens the box. The physics is simple — light travels faster through air than glass — but the engineering is full of constraints (line-of-sight, weather, FCC licensing, bandwidth) that decide what kinds of strategies can use it and which cannot.

Note: per the new repo guidance, code blocks here are illustrative only — the repo doesn't yet have cross-venue RF infrastructure. They can be retrofitted once we wire one up.

1. The physics — why RF beats fiber over distance

All electromagnetic signals travel at the speed of light c ≈ 299,792,458 m/s in vacuum. The catch is what happens when they enter a medium: glass slows them down dramatically, air barely at all.

MediumRefractive index nEffective speed% of c
Vacuum1.0000299,792 km/s100%
Air (dry, sea level)1.0003~299,700 km/s~99.97%
Hollow-core fiber~1.005~298,300 km/s~99.5%
Conventional silica fiber~1.467~204,400 km/s~68%

That's the entire story. Light through glass moves at about two-thirds the speed of light through air. Over a thousand kilometers between exchanges, those few percent compound into several milliseconds — and several milliseconds is the entire game in cross-market arbitrage. 

# Illustrative: minimum one-way latency for a 1180 km link
def latency_ms(distance_km: float, fraction_of_c: float) -> float:
    c_kms = 299_792.458
    return distance_km / (c_kms * fraction_of_c) * 1000.0

latency_ms(1180, 1.000)   # = 3.94 ms  (vacuum / great-circle floor)
latency_ms(1180, 0.997)   # = 3.95 ms  (microwave through air, line-of-sight)
latency_ms(1180, 0.995)   # = 3.96 ms  (hollow-core fiber, also air-filled)
latency_ms(1180, 0.680)   # = 5.81 ms  (conventional fiber)
Real-world overhead — those are physics minimums. Real fiber routes aren't straight (they follow railroads, highways); real microwave routes aren't straight either but they're close. Real numbers for Chicago↔Carteret one-way: fiber ~6.5–7 ms, microwave ~4.0–4.5 ms. The ~2.5 ms one-way edge is what funded an entire industry of tower-builders.

2. The famous routes, with real numbers

Three corridors dominate the global cross-market HFT business. Each connects venues whose products trade against each other.

ROUTE Endpoints (typical data-center pair) Distance ~MW one-way
CME↔NJ Aurora, IL (CME) ↔ Carteret/Secaucus, NJ (NYSE/NASDAQ) ~1180 km ~4.0 ms
LD4↔FR2 Slough, UK (LSE colo) ↔ Frankfurt (Deutsche Börse) ~660 km ~2.4 ms
TYO↔SGX Tokyo ↔ Singapore (over partial water → mixed RF + fiber) ~5300 km ~25 ms

The CME↔NJ corridor is the most famous because it carries the relationship between futures (e.g. ES, NQ traded in Aurora) and the cash equities they implicitly track (S&P 500, Nasdaq 100 traded in Carteret). A move in the futures contract gives an informational edge on the cash basket — but only to whoever sees it first.

Industry operators (2024–2025): McKay Brothers and Anova Financial Networks are the dominant common-carrier microwave operators on the major US/EU corridors. BSO, Quincy Data, and Jump Trading (in-house) also operate routes. McKay's published target for Aurora↔Carteret is <8.00 ms round-trip end-to-end.

3. The engineering — what actually has to be built

Tower spacing and hops

Microwave links are line-of-sight — the curvature of the Earth eventually puts the receiver behind the horizon. Practical hop length is 40–70 km depending on tower height and terrain. So Chicago↔NJ at 1180 km needs roughly 20–30 hops in series, each adding tower-side repeater latency (~10s of ns per hop).

Frequency bands

BandFrequencyTypical hopBandwidthWeather sensitivity
6 GHz5.9–7.1 GHz60–80 km~30 MbpsVery low (rain fade negligible)
11 GHz10.7–11.7 GHz40–60 km~100 MbpsLow
18 GHz17.7–19.7 GHz20–40 km~300 MbpsModerate (rain fade)
80 GHz (E-band)71–86 GHz5–10 km1–10 GbpsSevere (atmospheric absorption)

For HFT, the lower bands (6, 11 GHz) dominate the long-haul backbone because they survive rain. The higher bands (E-band) are used for last-mile in/out of data centers where higher bandwidth is needed and hops are short. The receiver is typically on the roof of the exchange data center, or on a pole next to it — extra meters of fiber inside the building waste nanoseconds.

Fresnel zone

Between two microwave antennas there's an ellipsoidal volume — the Fresnel zone — that must be roughly 60% clear of obstructions for the link to work. The Fresnel zone is fattest at mid-span. Buildings, trees, and even crops growing in summer can intrude. Tower heights and route planning are designed around this constraint, and an ice storm bending a tower can take a link down for hours.

Modulation and the latency↔bandwidth tradeoff

Higher-order modulations (256-QAM, 1024-QAM) carry more bits per symbol but need higher signal-to-noise ratio and add encoding/decoding latency. HFT operators use lower-order modulations (QPSK, 16-QAM) to minimize latency at each hop, at the cost of usable bandwidth.

4. The fundamental bandwidth tradeoff — and what actually gets sent

A full futures-market data feed is gigabits per second. A long-haul microwave channel delivers ~100 Mbps. The math doesn't work — you cannot ship full market data over microwave.

What HFT firms actually send: highly compressed signals — sometimes just a few critical price ticks, sometimes a single bit ("ES went up or down by more than threshold X"). The remote venue's strategy is pre-loaded with everything else and waits for that one bit.

Illustrative wire-format for a microwave-carried signal:

// 8 bytes total: a tick worth racing across the country
struct __attribute__((packed)) RfSignal {
    uint16_t instrument_id;   // 2 bytes — e.g. ES, NQ, CL
    int16_t  delta_ticks;     // 2 bytes — price change since last frame
    uint32_t ts_remote_ns;    // 4 bytes — sender's hardware timestamp
};

Eight bytes. At 100 Mbps that's a transmission time of ~0.6 microseconds for one message, leaving headroom for ~12 million messages per second on the channel — but in practice you send a few thousand per second because the receiver's strategy only needs the headline moves.

Mental model: microwave isn't a data pipe; it's a messaging channel for compressed alpha. Send the one bit of information that wouldn't fit in your already-known model of the world, and let the receiving end fill in the rest.

5. Economics — the common-carrier model and the tier system

HFT firms rarely build their own networks. The capex (~$10M+ per route), multi-year tower lease negotiations, and FCC/Ofcom licensing make it a specialty business. Instead, common-carrier operators like McKay Brothers and Anova run shared infrastructure and sell access in tiers:

Premium tier

Lowest latency, guaranteed slot, redundant paths. Used by the largest HFT desks for their primary strategies. Annual cost: undisclosed, but in the seven figures per route.

Standard tier

Same wire, but pays slightly higher serialization delay (microseconds, not nanoseconds — but enough to matter). Smaller desks; secondary strategies.

Backup / fiber blend

Hybrid path that falls back to hollow-core or conventional fiber when the microwave link is degraded (storm, alignment loss). Bandwidth is higher; latency reverts to fiber tier.

Why common-carrier works

The towers, licenses, and amplifiers cost the same whether one firm uses them or twenty do. Charging twenty firms tiered access turns a fixed-cost network into a high-margin business.

The hollow-core fiber competitor

Conventional silica fiber slows light to ~0.68c. Hollow-core fiber runs light through an air-filled channel surrounded by photonic-crystal walls — speed is ~99% c. Bandwidth is the same as conventional fiber (~hundreds of Gbps), latency is only slightly worse than microwave, and it doesn't care about rain or line-of-sight.

The current state: hollow-core has been deployed by McKay, DRW, Jump and others for CME↔NJ — about 1 ms slower than microwave one-way but with 1000× more bandwidth. Many HFT firms now run both: microwave for the bit-of-alpha signal, hollow-core for the bulk market data and the rest of the strategy state.

6. In this project

This repo has no cross-venue strategy today — the GBM trades a daily-rebalance long-only equity portfolio from a single market-data source (yfinance), so physics of inter-venue latency is irrelevant. But the natural extension is worth flagging.

A cross-market arbitrage strategy — say, trading the basis between E-mini S&P futures (CME, in Aurora) and the SPY ETF (in Carteret) — would necessarily inhabit Tier 5/6 of the latency ladder. The strategy would need:

  1. Colocation in both Aurora and Carteret.
  2. A microwave or hollow-core path between them (lease, not build).
  3. An FPGA endpoint on each side speaking a compact signal protocol like the 8-byte struct above.
  4. A pre-loaded model on the receiving side that knows what to do when "ES moved by X ticks" arrives.

The decision to take that step is economic before it is technical. A few million dollars per year of operating cost has to be paid back by the spread captured on the arb. That's a question for the strategy team, not the engineering team.

Repo honesty: none of this is in the code today, nor should it be soon. The point of this lesson is to give you the right mental model for when you read about "microwave HFT" — and for the day this repo eventually sprouts a cross-venue branch.

7. Often confused with

Microwave vs Hollow-core fiber

Microwave: ~99.97% c through air, narrow bandwidth (~100 Mbps), weather-sensitive, line-of-sight, cheap per Mbps. Hollow-core: ~99% c through air-filled fiber, wide bandwidth (~Gbps), weather-immune, follows fiber routes (not necessarily straight). Most firms now use both.

Microwave vs Millimeter-wave (E-band)

Microwave (3–30 GHz): long hops, narrow bandwidth, weather-tolerant. Millimeter-wave / E-band (60–80+ GHz): short hops (5–10 km), wide bandwidth (gigabits), severe rain fade. HFT uses E-band for last-mile, microwave for long-haul.

Latency vs Bandwidth (RF specifically)

Microwave gives you the lowest latency available but the smallest usable bandwidth. Fiber gives you the highest bandwidth but slower light. The HFT solution: send tiny signals over microwave, send bulk data over hollow-core fiber, run both in parallel.

Common-carrier vs Private link

Common-carrier (McKay, Anova): shared towers, sold in tiers, multiple HFT firms on the same wire. Private link: a single firm owns the towers and the licenses. The largest desks (Jump, Citadel) sometimes own private routes; most rent from a carrier.

Line-of-sight vs Tropospheric scatter

Line-of-sight: receiver must see the transmitter directly; Earth's curvature limits hops. HFT exclusively uses this. Tropo scatter: bounce signal off the upper atmosphere for longer hops; much higher latency, never used in HFT.

Refractive index vs Group velocity

Refractive index tells you the phase velocity of light in a medium. Group velocity is what carries information and is what matters for latency. In standard fiber they track closely; in exotic media (hollow-core, slow-light fibers) they can diverge.

8. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. The microwave Chicago↔NJ link beats conventional fiber by ~2.5 ms one-way for a single reason at the physics level. What is it?

  • Microwave links carry more bandwidth than fiber, so packets transmit faster.
  • Conventional fiber has refractive index ~1.47 (~0.68c), while microwave travels through air at ~0.9997c — the medium itself is the bottleneck.
  • Microwave signals follow the curvature of the Earth shorter than fiber.
  • Exchanges in Carteret prioritize processing for microwave-delivered packets.

Q2. Why is the data sent over a long-haul microwave link typically a few bytes per message rather than full market data?

  • Because the FCC regulates payload sizes on commercial microwave links.
  • Long-haul microwave delivers ~100 Mbps; full market data is gigabits. You can only ship signals, not full feeds.
  • Because the receiver's decoder can't process more than 8 bytes per message in real time.
  • Because the encryption overhead per message limits the payload size.

Q3. Hollow-core fiber is ~99% c — only slightly slower than microwave (99.97% c). Why do HFT firms still pay for microwave at all?

  • Hollow-core fiber hasn't actually been deployed yet on the major HFT corridors.
  • Even ~1 ms one-way difference between microwave and hollow-core matters at HFT scales; firms typically run both paths in parallel.
  • Microwave is structurally cheaper per route than hollow-core fiber.
  • Hollow-core fiber is reserved for non-trading data only.

Q4. Why are long-haul HFT microwave links built in the 6 and 11 GHz bands rather than 80 GHz, even though 80 GHz carries more bandwidth?

  • Because 80 GHz isn't commercially licensed in the US.
  • At 80 GHz, atmospheric absorption and rain fade limit practical hops to 5–10 km, requiring hundreds of hops on a long route. Lower-frequency bands allow 40–70 km hops and survive weather.
  • Because 80 GHz requires antennas larger than can be mounted on towers.
  • Because 6 GHz signals can't be jammed by weather radar.

Q5. You want to extend this repo from a single-venue daily GBM into a cross-venue (CME futures ↔ NYSE equities) arbitrage strategy. Which infrastructure decision dominates?

  • Train a much faster gradient-boosting model for next-tick prediction.
  • Colocate at both venues, lease a microwave + hollow-core path between them, and put an FPGA endpoint on each side that speaks a compact signal protocol.
  • Move the Python backtests to a cloud region in Chicago for proximity.
  • Subscribe to both venues' public REST APIs over HTTPS.

9. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. A summer ice storm in Pennsylvania bends a microwave tower 2 degrees out of alignment. The link still passes signal but with high error rate. What happens to dependent strategies?

The link's forward error correction will compensate up to a point — but retransmits and dropped messages add latency, and the receiver-side strategy will see inconsistent state ("I got the alpha bit for some seconds, missed it for others"). Most HFT desks running on a primary microwave link have an automatic failover: if error rate or latency crosses a threshold, traffic re-routes to a secondary microwave path or to hollow-core fiber, accepting the ~1 ms penalty. The strategy meanwhile scales itself down or pauses while the failover stabilizes. Tower-alignment alerts are a real operational discipline; carriers like McKay treat them as priority pages.

S2. A teammate proposes "let's bypass McKay and build our own microwave route from Aurora to Carteret." Walk through the major obstacles before they spend any money.

Five hard problems, roughly in cost order. (1) Tower siting: 25+ tower sites must be leased or built across multiple states with land-use approvals — years of permitting per site. (2) FCC licensing: each microwave hop requires individual FCC frequency authorization; the band is already heavily licensed and incumbents have priority. (3) Capex: ~$5–10M for the towers and amplifiers alone, before integration. (4) Operations: 24/7 alignment monitoring, weather response, repair crews; carrier-grade ops is a headcount problem. (5) Time-to-market: 18–36 months assuming no FCC delays. Conclusion: unless you're at the very largest desk (Jump scale) and have a multi-year horizon, renting from McKay or Anova is structurally cheaper, faster, and operationally simpler. The build-it-yourself math almost never works.

S3. You sit at a desk with a Premium-tier McKay subscription on CME↔Carteret. A new firm shows up paying for the same Premium tier. What does that mean for your alpha?

You now share the link's queue with another fast participant who sees the same signal at the same time. The microwave link itself isn't slower, but the population of equally-fast competitors just grew by one. Pre-trade signal value erodes accordingly — what used to be your alpha is now a tied race with the new entrant, with the venue's matching engine being the tiebreaker. Mitigation paths: (a) move faster at the endpoints via FPGA tick-to-trade and queue-priority strategies, (b) move to a more exclusive private microwave route if you can justify the capex, or (c) shift to strategies whose alpha doesn't live on first-fill. The common-carrier model is great for getting onto the link cheaply; the downside is that everyone else on it is just as well-positioned as you are.

Next in your queue: DMA (Direct Market Access) — both the trading sense (sponsored access to exchanges, regulatory implications) and the PCIe sense (how FPGAs and CPUs share data), since the same acronym refers to two very different concepts in HFT engineering.

HFT firms rarely build their own networks. The capex (~$10M+ per route), multi-year tower lease negotiations, and FCC/Ofcom licensing make it a specialty business. Instead, common-carrier operators like McKay Brothers and Anova run shared infrastructure and sell access in tiers:

Premium tier

Lowest latency, guaranteed slot, redundant paths. Used by the largest HFT desks for their primary strategies. Annual cost: undisclosed, but in the seven figures per route.

Standard tier

Same wire, but pays slightly higher serialization delay (microseconds, not nanoseconds — but enough to matter). Smaller desks; secondary strategies.

Backup / fiber blend

Hybrid path that falls back to hollow-core or conventional fiber when the microwave link is degraded (storm, alignment loss). Bandwidth is higher; latency reverts to fiber tier.

Why common-carrier works

The towers, licenses, and amplifiers cost the same whether one firm uses them or twenty do. Charging twenty firms tiered access turns a fixed-cost network into a high-margin business.

The hollow-core fiber competitor

Conventional silica fiber slows light to ~0.68c. Hollow-core fiber runs light through an air-filled channel surrounded by photonic-crystal walls — speed is ~99% c. Bandwidth is the same as conventional fiber (~hundreds of Gbps), latency is only slightly worse than microwave, and it doesn't care about rain or line-of-sight.

The current state: hollow-core has been deployed by McKay, DRW, Jump and others for CME↔NJ — about 1 ms slower than microwave one-way but with 1000× more bandwidth. Many HFT firms now run both: microwave for the bit-of-alpha signal, hollow-core for the bulk market data and the rest of the strategy state.

6. In this project

This repo has no cross-venue strategy today — the GBM trades a daily-rebalance long-only equity portfolio from a single market-data source (yfinance), so physics of inter-venue latency is irrelevant. But the natural extension is worth flagging.

A cross-market arbitrage strategy — say, trading the basis between E-mini S&P futures (CME, in Aurora) and the SPY ETF (in Carteret) — would necessarily inhabit Tier 5/6 of the latency ladder. The strategy would need:

  1. Colocation in both Aurora and Carteret.
  2. A microwave or hollow-core path between them (lease, not build).
  3. An FPGA endpoint on each side speaking a compact signal protocol like the 8-byte struct above.
  4. A pre-loaded model on the receiving side that knows what to do when "ES moved by X ticks" arrives.

The decision to take that step is economic before it is technical. A few million dollars per year of operating cost has to be paid back by the spread captured on the arb. That's a question for the strategy team, not the engineering team.

Repo honesty: none of this is in the code today, nor should it be soon. The point of this lesson is to give you the right mental model for when you read about "microwave HFT" — and for the day this repo eventually sprouts a cross-venue branch.

7. Often confused with

Microwave vs Hollow-core fiber

Microwave: ~99.97% c through air, narrow bandwidth (~100 Mbps), weather-sensitive, line-of-sight, cheap per Mbps. Hollow-core: ~99% c through air-filled fiber, wide bandwidth (~Gbps), weather-immune, follows fiber routes (not necessarily straight). Most firms now use both.

Microwave vs Millimeter-wave (E-band)

Microwave (3–30 GHz): long hops, narrow bandwidth, weather-tolerant. Millimeter-wave / E-band (60–80+ GHz): short hops (5–10 km), wide bandwidth (gigabits), severe rain fade. HFT uses E-band for last-mile, microwave for long-haul.

Latency vs Bandwidth (RF specifically)

Microwave gives you the lowest latency available but the smallest usable bandwidth. Fiber gives you the highest bandwidth but slower light. The HFT solution: send tiny signals over microwave, send bulk data over hollow-core fiber, run both in parallel.

Common-carrier vs Private link

Common-carrier (McKay, Anova): shared towers, sold in tiers, multiple HFT firms on the same wire. Private link: a single firm owns the towers and the licenses. The largest desks (Jump, Citadel) sometimes own private routes; most rent from a carrier.

Line-of-sight vs Tropospheric scatter

Line-of-sight: receiver must see the transmitter directly; Earth's curvature limits hops. HFT exclusively uses this. Tropo scatter: bounce signal off the upper atmosphere for longer hops; much higher latency, never used in HFT.

Refractive index vs Group velocity

Refractive index tells you the phase velocity of light in a medium. Group velocity is what carries information and is what matters for latency. In standard fiber they track closely; in exotic media (hollow-core, slow-light fibers) they can diverge.

8. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load. Read each one — distractors teach too.

Q1. The microwave Chicago↔NJ link beats conventional fiber by ~2.5 ms one-way for a single reason at the physics level. What is it?

  • Microwave links carry more bandwidth than fiber, so packets transmit faster.
  • Conventional fiber has refractive index ~1.47 (~0.68c), while microwave travels through air at ~0.9997c — the medium itself is the bottleneck.
  • Microwave signals follow the curvature of the Earth shorter than fiber.
  • Exchanges in Carteret prioritize processing for microwave-delivered packets.

Q2. Why is the data sent over a long-haul microwave link typically a few bytes per message rather than full market data?

  • Because the FCC regulates payload sizes on commercial microwave links.
  • Long-haul microwave delivers ~100 Mbps; full market data is gigabits. You can only ship signals, not full feeds.
  • Because the receiver's decoder can't process more than 8 bytes per message in real time.
  • Because the encryption overhead per message limits the payload size.

Q3. Hollow-core fiber is ~99% c — only slightly slower than microwave (99.97% c). Why do HFT firms still pay for microwave at all?

  • Hollow-core fiber hasn't actually been deployed yet on the major HFT corridors.
  • Even ~1 ms one-way difference between microwave and hollow-core matters at HFT scales; firms typically run both paths in parallel.
  • Microwave is structurally cheaper per route than hollow-core fiber.
  • Hollow-core fiber is reserved for non-trading data only.

Q4. Why are long-haul HFT microwave links built in the 6 and 11 GHz bands rather than 80 GHz, even though 80 GHz carries more bandwidth?

  • Because 80 GHz isn't commercially licensed in the US.
  • At 80 GHz, atmospheric absorption and rain fade limit practical hops to 5–10 km, requiring hundreds of hops on a long route. Lower-frequency bands allow 40–70 km hops and survive weather.
  • Because 80 GHz requires antennas larger than can be mounted on towers.
  • Because 6 GHz signals can't be jammed by weather radar.

Q5. You want to extend this repo from a single-venue daily GBM into a cross-venue (CME futures ↔ NYSE equities) arbitrage strategy. Which infrastructure decision dominates?

  • Train a much faster gradient-boosting model for next-tick prediction.
  • Colocate at both venues, lease a microwave + hollow-core path between them, and put an FPGA endpoint on each side that speaks a compact signal protocol.
  • Move the Python backtests to a cloud region in Chicago for proximity.
  • Subscribe to both venues' public REST APIs over HTTPS.

9. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. A summer ice storm in Pennsylvania bends a microwave tower 2 degrees out of alignment. The link still passes signal but with high error rate. What happens to dependent strategies?

The link's forward error correction will compensate up to a point — but retransmits and dropped messages add latency, and the receiver-side strategy will see inconsistent state ("I got the alpha bit for some seconds, missed it for others"). Most HFT desks running on a primary microwave link have an automatic failover: if error rate or latency crosses a threshold, traffic re-routes to a secondary microwave path or to hollow-core fiber, accepting the ~1 ms penalty. The strategy meanwhile scales itself down or pauses while the failover stabilizes. Tower-alignment alerts are a real operational discipline; carriers like McKay treat them as priority pages.

S2. A teammate proposes "let's bypass McKay and build our own microwave route from Aurora to Carteret." Walk through the major obstacles before they spend any money.

Five hard problems, roughly in cost order. (1) Tower siting: 25+ tower sites must be leased or built across multiple states with land-use approvals — years of permitting per site. (2) FCC licensing: each microwave hop requires individual FCC frequency authorization; the band is already heavily licensed and incumbents have priority. (3) Capex: ~$5–10M for the towers and amplifiers alone, before integration. (4) Operations: 24/7 alignment monitoring, weather response, repair crews; carrier-grade ops is a headcount problem. (5) Time-to-market: 18–36 months assuming no FCC delays. Conclusion: unless you're at the very largest desk (Jump scale) and have a multi-year horizon, renting from McKay or Anova is structurally cheaper, faster, and operationally simpler. The build-it-yourself math almost never works.

S3. You sit at a desk with a Premium-tier McKay subscription on CME↔Carteret. A new firm shows up paying for the same Premium tier. What does that mean for your alpha?

You now share the link's queue with another fast participant who sees the same signal at the same time. The microwave link itself isn't slower, but the population of equally-fast competitors just grew by one. Pre-trade signal value erodes accordingly — what used to be your alpha is now a tied race with the new entrant, with the venue's matching engine being the tiebreaker. Mitigation paths: (a) move faster at the endpoints via FPGA tick-to-trade and queue-priority strategies, (b) move to a more exclusive private microwave route if you can justify the capex, or (c) shift to strategies whose alpha doesn't live on first-fill. The common-carrier model is great for getting onto the link cheaply; the downside is that everyone else on it is just as well-positioned as you are.

Next in your queue: DMA (Direct Market Access) — both the trading sense (sponsored access to exchanges, regulatory implications) and the PCIe sense (how FPGAs and CPUs share data), since the same acronym refers to two very different concepts in HFT engineering.

## Added in Lesson 0012 (RF Engineering in HFT)

### Anova Financial Networks — `intro`
Major common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT firms. Competitor
to McKay Brothers on the main US/EU corridors.

### Aurora (Aurora, IL) — `intro`
CME Group's data center, the futures venue side of the famous CME↔NJ
arbitrage corridor. Pairs with Carteret/Secaucus for the equity venues.

### Carteret (Carteret, NJ) — `intro`
The equities-side endpoint of the CME↔NJ corridor — Nasdaq's primary
data center. The NYSE-side anchor in Mahwah and Secaucus play the same
role.

### Common-carrier (microwave) — `intro`
Operating model where one company runs the towers, licenses, and antennas
and sells tiered access to multiple HFT firms. McKay Brothers and Anova
are the dominant examples on US/EU routes.

### E-band (millimeter-wave) — `intro`
71–86 GHz licensed band. Carries gigabits but only over 5–10 km hops due
to atmospheric absorption and rain fade. Used for last-mile in/out of
exchange data centers; not for long-haul.

### FCC licensing (microwave) — `intro`
Each individual microwave hop in the US requires an FCC frequency
authorization. The lower bands (6, 11 GHz) are heavily licensed and
incumbents have priority, which is one of the structural reasons HFT
firms rent rather than build.

### Fresnel zone — `intro`
The ellipsoidal volume around the line-of-sight between two microwave
antennas. Must be roughly 60% obstruction-free for the link to work.
Buildings, trees, terrain, and seasonal crops all matter for route planning.

### Great-circle distance — `intro`
Shortest path between two points on Earth's surface, ignoring terrain. The
floor against which any real route — fiber or microwave — is compared.

### Hollow-core fiber — `intro`
Optical fiber where light travels through an air-filled channel inside
photonic-crystal walls, at ~99% c instead of ~68% c through silica. Wider
bandwidth than microwave, weather-immune; ~1 ms slower than microwave one-way
on CME↔NJ. Many HFT firms now run both in parallel.

### Line-of-sight (LOS) — `intro`
Direct visual path between transmitter and receiver. Earth's curvature
limits hop length to 40–70 km on typical towers. HFT microwave links are
always LOS; tropospheric scatter is not used.

### McKay Brothers — `intro`
Dominant common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT corridors,
including a CME↔NJ route with published target of <8 ms round-trip.
Also offers hollow-core fiber and integrated packages.

### Microwave link — `intro`
Wireless point-to-point communication link in the 3–30 GHz range used for
long-haul HFT routes between exchanges. Travels through air at ~99.97% c,
narrow bandwidth (~100 Mbps), weather-sensitive, line-of-sight.

### Modulation (in HFT RF context) — `intro`
The scheme that maps bits onto a radio carrier (QPSK, 16-QAM, 256-QAM,
1024-QAM). Higher orders carry more bits per symbol but need higher SNR
and add encoding latency. HFT uses lower orders to minimize per-hop latency.

### Rain fade — `intro`
Signal attenuation due to rainfall absorbing radio energy. Sharply worse
at higher frequencies (severe at 80 GHz, negligible at 6 GHz). One of the
reasons HFT long-haul stays in lower bands.

### Refractive index — `intro`
Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to speed in a medium. Higher index =
slower light. Air ~1.0003 (~0.997c), hollow-core fiber ~1.005 (~0.995c),
silica fiber ~1.47 (~0.68c). The dominant physics behind the microwave
vs fiber gap.

### Sponsored access / Common carrier vs Private link — `intro`
**Common-carrier**: shared infrastructure rented by multiple HFT desks
(McKay, Anova). **Private link**: a single firm owns the towers and
licenses. Largest desks may build private; everyone else rents.

### Tier (microwave subscription) — `intro`
A pricing/priority level for a common-carrier microwave link. Premium tier
gets the lowest latency and dedicated slots; standard tier pays a slightly
higher serialization delay. Annual cost: undisclosed but in the seven
figures per route at premium.

### Tower spacing / Hop length — `intro`
Practical distance between consecutive microwave repeater towers, typically
40–70 km on long-haul HFT links. Limited by Earth's curvature and tower
height. Each hop adds ~10s of ns of equipment latency.

arbitrage corridor. Pairs with Carteret/Secaucus for the equity venues.

### Carteret (Carteret, NJ) — `intro`
The equities-side endpoint of the CME↔NJ corridor — Nasdaq's primary
data center. The NYSE-side anchor in Mahwah and Secaucus play the same
role.

### Common-carrier (microwave) — `intro`
Operating model where one company runs the towers, licenses, and antennas
and sells tiered access to multiple HFT firms. McKay Brothers and Anova
are the dominant examples on US/EU routes.

### E-band (millimeter-wave) — `intro`
71–86 GHz licensed band. Carries gigabits but only over 5–10 km hops due
to atmospheric absorption and rain fade. Used for last-mile in/out of
exchange data centers; not for long-haul.

### FCC licensing (microwave) — `intro`
Each individual microwave hop in the US requires an FCC frequency
authorization. The lower bands (6, 11 GHz) are heavily licensed and
incumbents have priority, which is one of the structural reasons HFT
firms rent rather than build.

### Fresnel zone — `intro`
The ellipsoidal volume around the line-of-sight between two microwave
antennas. Must be roughly 60% obstruction-free for the link to work.
Buildings, trees, terrain, and seasonal crops all matter for route planning.

### Great-circle distance — `intro`
Shortest path between two points on Earth's surface, ignoring terrain. The
floor against which any real route — fiber or microwave — is compared.

### Hollow-core fiber — `intro`
Optical fiber where light travels through an air-filled channel inside
photonic-crystal walls, at ~99% c instead of ~68% c through silica. Wider
bandwidth than microwave, weather-immune; ~1 ms slower than microwave one-way
on CME↔NJ. Many HFT firms now run both in parallel.

### Line-of-sight (LOS) — `intro`
Direct visual path between transmitter and receiver. Earth's curvature
limits hop length to 40–70 km on typical towers. HFT microwave links are
always LOS; tropospheric scatter is not used.

### McKay Brothers — `intro`
Dominant common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT corridors,
including a CME↔NJ route with published target of <8 ms round-trip.
Also offers hollow-core fiber and integrated packages.

### Microwave link — `intro`
Wireless point-to-point communication link in the 3–30 GHz range used for
long-haul HFT routes between exchanges. Travels through air at ~99.97% c,
narrow bandwidth (~100 Mbps), weather-sensitive, line-of-sight.

### Modulation (in HFT RF context) — `intro`
The scheme that maps bits onto a radio carrier (QPSK, 16-QAM, 256-QAM,
1024-QAM). Higher orders carry more bits per symbol but need higher SNR
and add encoding latency. HFT uses lower orders to minimize per-hop latency.

### Rain fade — `intro`
Signal attenuation due to rainfall absorbing radio energy. Sharply worse
at higher frequencies (severe at 80 GHz, negligible at 6 GHz). One of the
reasons HFT long-haul stays in lower bands.

### Refractive index — `intro`
Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to speed in a medium. Higher index =
slower light. Air ~1.0003 (~0.997c), hollow-core fiber ~1.005 (~0.995c),
silica fiber ~1.47 (~0.68c). The dominant physics behind the microwave
vs fiber gap.

### Sponsored access / Common carrier vs Private link — `intro`
**Common-carrier**: shared infrastructure rented by multiple HFT desks
(McKay, Anova). **Private link**: a single firm owns the towers and
licenses. Largest desks may build private; everyone else rents.

### Tier (microwave subscription) — `intro`
A pricing/priority level for a common-carrier microwave link. Premium tier
gets the lowest latency and dedicated slots; standard tier pays a slightly
higher serialization delay. Annual cost: undisclosed but in the seven
figures per route at premium.

### Tower spacing / Hop length — `intro`
Practical distance between consecutive microwave repeater towers, typically
40–70 km on long-haul HFT links. Limited by Earth's curvature and tower
height. Each hop adds ~10s of ns of equipment latency.

## Overview of DMA and Sponsored Access

Direct market access (DMA) in financial markets is the electronic trading infrastructure that gives investors wishing to trade in financial instruments a way to interact with the order book of an exchange. Investment companies (also known as buy side firms) and other private traders use the information technology infrastructure of sell side firms such as investment banks and the market access that those firms possess, but control the way a trading transaction is managed themselves rather than passing the order over to the broker's own in-house traders for execution.

## Regulatory Oversight

The Market Access Rule topic of the 2025 FINRA Annual Regulatory Oversight Report informs member firms' compliance programs by providing annual insights from FINRA's ongoing regulatory operations. FINRA's Enforcement Department is conducting a review of broker/dealers that provide Direct Market Access, Naked Access, Electronic Access or Sponsored Access ("DMA") to their customers.

## HFT and Sponsored Access

Sponsored access offers particular advantages to HFT firms seeking low latency connectivity to trading venues while avoiding compliance costs associated with maintaining broker-dealer operations. High-frequency trading firms and dedicated algorithmic traders are the most aggressive DMA users, with HFT strategies such as statistical arbitrage, market-making, or latency arbitrage demanding the fastest possible access to market data and order execution.

## Regulatory Concerns

Certain forms of DMA, most notably "sponsored access", have raised substantial regulatory concerns because of the possibility of a malfunction by an investor to cause widespread market disruption.

## FPGA-Based SmartNICs and Zero-Copy Communication

NaNet is an FPGA-based reconfigurable PCIe NIC implementing direct zero-copy communication between network channels and the memory of the host CPUs and NVIDIA GPUs (GPUDirect® RDMA). A high-performance PCIe Gen2/3 DMA engine performs zero-copy data transfers to and from application CPU and GPU memories.

## DMA Ring Buffers

Data are DMA-read from GPU memory; the kernel device driver instructs the NIC by filling a "descriptor" into a dedicated DMA-accessible memory region ("TX ring"). The presence of a new descriptor is notified over PCIe to NaNet by writing on a doorbell register so that the board can issue a "TX done" event in the event queue.

## Modern FPGA DMA Solutions (2025)

Arkville can transport data between FPGA logic and host memory at up to 60 GBytes/s (480 Gbps) in each direction, providing a high-throughput, low-latency conduit between host memory and FPGA fabric logic, offloading CPU core usage, eliminating memory copies, and improving overall efficiency.

## General PCIe DMA Architecture

DMA capabilities enable the FPGA endpoints, such as FPGA-based SmartNICs, to transfer large volumes of data directly to and from host memory without CPU intervention, thus reducing latency and freeing up processing resources for other tasks.

These search results cover practical implementations of zero-copy communication patterns using PCIe DMA with FPGAs and network interfaces.

Lesson 0013 Quiz: 0 / 5

DMA — Direct Market Access & Direct Memory Access

Why this matters for HFT_practice: in trading conversations "DMA" means Direct Market Access — how you reach an exchange. In hardware conversations "DMA" means Direct Memory Access — how a chip reaches host RAM without the CPU. Both are unavoidable in HFT, both constantly come up, and people confuse them constantly. This lesson nails down both.

Illustrative code where the repo doesn't have the real thing yet.

1. The same acronym, two totally different ideas

SenseStands forWhat it's aboutLives in
Trading DMA Direct Market Access A buy-side firm sending orders straight onto an exchange's matching engine, bypassing the broker's manual desk.[1] Business / regulatory layer
Hardware DMA Direct Memory Access A peripheral (NIC, FPGA, GPU) reading/writing host RAM without the CPU running each transfer.[2] Operating-system / silicon layer
Rule of thumb: if the speaker is talking about FINRA, brokers, or "we got direct access to NASDAQ," they mean trading DMA. If they're talking about PCIe, descriptor rings, or "zero-copy from the NIC to our FPGA," they mean hardware DMA. Same letters; rarely the same conversation.

2. Trading DMA — the regulated layer

The basic picture

Traditionally an asset manager phones a broker, the broker enters the order on the manager's behalf. With Direct Market Access, the manager's own algorithm sends the order straight to the exchange's matching engine over the broker's connection.[1] The broker is still legally on the hook for risk checks and trade reporting, but no human sits in the middle.

Three flavors with progressively less broker involvement:

Traditional brokered order

Buy-side sends an order to the broker; broker's trader works it on the exchange. Used for large/illiquid blocks where human discretion adds value. Latency: human-scale.

DMA proper

Buy-side's algo connects through the broker's infrastructure (gateway, risk checks, exchange membership) but submits orders directly. The broker's pre-trade risk filter runs inline on every order.[1]

Sponsored access (SA)

Buy-side gets the broker's MPID and exchange connectivity but skips most of the broker's stack — including, historically, the broker's risk filter. Lowest latency; highest systemic risk; the form regulators care most about.[3]

Exchange membership

Skip the broker entirely. Become a member of the exchange yourself. Highest fixed cost (capital, regulatory, ops); used by the largest HFT firms and proprietary trading shops.

Why HFT firms love sponsored access

Each layer between you and the matching engine adds microseconds and dollars. SA gives HFT firms the regulatory cover of "the broker's customer" without the latency of routing through the broker's order management system. Latency arbitrage, market making, and statistical arbitrage all benefit.[1]

Why regulators were spooked: SEC Rule 15c3-5

Naked sponsored access (broker hands over its connection with no risk checks) was identified as a serious systemic risk after Knight Capital's 2012 incident (different mechanism, same shape of fear: an algo gone wrong dumping orders into a venue with no kill switch). SEC Rule 15c3-5 (the "Market Access Rule", effective 2011) requires the broker to maintain pre-trade risk controls — order size limits, credit limits, kill switches — that cannot be disabled.[4] FINRA's 2025 oversight report continues to treat market-access compliance as a top examination priority.[5]

The practical wire: a FIX session

Most DMA connections use the FIX protocol (or the exchange's binary equivalent: OUCH, ITCH, MITCH, Native, etc.). An illustrative single order: 

8=FIX.4.4|9=145|35=D|49=BUYSIDEALGO|56=EXCHGW|34=42|52=20260610-14:30:00.123|
11=ORD-00012|21=1|55=ESZ6|54=1|60=20260610-14:30:00.122|38=10|40=2|44=4523.25|59=0|10=041|

35=D = NewOrderSingle. 54=1 = Buy. 38=10 contracts. 40=2 Limit. 44=4523.25 at price. The broker's risk filter inspects this before it leaves; HFT firms measure latency through the filter in microseconds and shop brokers accordingly.

3. Hardware DMA — the silicon layer

The basic problem

A NIC receives a packet from the wire. A FPGA wants that packet. Without DMA, the CPU would have to copy every byte from the NIC into user-space buffers via a syscall — which is exactly the kernel-stack cost you saw in Lessons 0004 and 0011 (~50 µs).

Direct Memory Access lets the peripheral (NIC, FPGA, GPU) move data into and out of host RAM by talking directly to the memory controller. The CPU is told when it's done, but isn't involved in the transfer itself.[6]

The standard PCIe DMA pattern

Four objects work together. Every modern NIC, FPGA, and SmartNIC does this in some variation.[7]

1. Descriptor ring

A pre-allocated array of small structs in host memory, mapped so the device can read/write it. Each entry says "DMA this many bytes to/from this physical address."

2. Doorbell register

A memory-mapped register on the device. The CPU writes to it (one PCIe write) to say "I just added a new descriptor — go look."[7]

3. DMA engine on the device

Hardware on the NIC/FPGA that reads descriptors, fetches/writes data to host RAM over PCIe, and updates the descriptor's "done" flag.

4. Completion notification

Either an interrupt (cold path) or the CPU polling the descriptor ring (hot path). HFT uses the polling pattern with kernel-bypass to avoid interrupt cost.

Illustrative receive flow on a kernel-bypass NIC:

// 1. App owns a region of memory (the RX ring) mapped into the NIC's address space.
volatile RxDescriptor* rx_ring = map_dma_region(1024);

// 2. Hot loop: poll the ring head; never wait for an interrupt.
while (running) {
    if (rx_ring[head].status & DESC_DONE) [[likely]] {
        Tick tick = parse(rx_ring[head].payload);   // payload was DMA'd by the NIC
        on_tick(tick);
        rx_ring[head].status = 0;                  // hand the slot back to the NIC
        head = (head + 1) & (1024 - 1);
    } else {
        _mm_pause();                              // busy-poll friendly
    }
}

Notice what this delivers: the packet enters the NIC, is written to host RAM by the NIC's DMA engine, and is read by the application — without ever crossing the kernel. That's the architectural meaning of "kernel bypass" (Lesson 0004) made concrete.

Zero-copy

The slogan "zero-copy" means the bytes are read and written from their final location, never copied between buffers along the way.[8] In the example above, the payload arrives in the application's RX ring and is parsed in place. No memcpy. No allocator. Closest practical embodiment of the "no syscalls, no allocation in the hot path" rule from Lesson 0009.

Modern speeds

PCIe Gen5 x16 DMA engines like Arkville move data between host memory and FPGA fabric at up to ~60 GB/s (≈480 Gbps) per direction with sub-microsecond completion latency.[9] That's gigabit market-data feeds and full LOB snapshots, easily, with budget to spare.

4. Where the two DMAs meet in an HFT stack

The full pipeline of a colocated HFT system, from exchange to strategy, needs both at the same time:

  1. Buy-side firm signs a Trading DMA deal with a broker (or becomes an exchange member). Gets an MPID, a binary-protocol gateway, and a colocation rack.
  2. Inside the rack, market data flows in through a kernel-bypass NIC using Hardware DMA straight into the strategy process's RX ring.
  3. Strategy decides; writes an order descriptor into the TX ring; rings the doorbell.
  4. NIC Hardware DMAs the order onto the wire as a FIX/OUCH/native message, which the exchange treats as the firm's Trading DMA order.

So both flavors of DMA are load-bearing on every single tick of a competitive HFT system. Confusing them in conversation is harmless. Confusing them in design — for example, thinking "if we have Trading DMA we don't need Hardware DMA" — is how slow systems get built.

In this repo today: neither flavor exists. The Robinhood executor (scripts/robinhood_executor.py) uses Robinhood's REST API which is the opposite of Trading DMA — there's a whole broker stack in the middle. Hardware DMA vs PIO

DMA is the mechanism the device uses to access host memory. Zero-copy is the design property of doing so without intermediate buffers. Zero-copy requires DMA; DMA doesn't always achieve zero-copy if the OS still ferries the data into user space.

Trading DMA vs Direct Connect

"Direct connect" usually means a physical fiber to the exchange's matching engine room. Trading DMA is the business and regulatory arrangement on top of that connect. You need both.

Hardware DMA vs RDMA

DMA: device ↔ local host RAM. RDMA (Remote DMA): device ↔ another machine's host RAM, over the network (InfiniBand, RoCE). Common in HPC; some HFT risk systems use it for fast state replication between hosts.

MPID vs ECN / Venue

An MPID (Market Participant Identifier) is the unique 4-character code identifying a broker-dealer on a venue. Buy-side firms using sponsored access trade under their sponsoring broker's MPID — which is why the broker's risk obligations don't go away.

6. Practice — click an answer for instant feedback

Options shuffle on every page load.

Q1. A coworker says "we got DMA last quarter." They mean Trading DMA. What's the most distinctive thing about that arrangement vs traditional brokered orders?

  • "DMA" here means the NIC writes packets straight into host memory.
  • The firm's algorithm sends orders straight to the exchange's matching engine through the broker's pipes, without a human at the broker working the order.
  • The firm became a member of the exchange and no longer needs a broker.
  • The firm now talks to the exchange via a public REST API instead of FIX.

Q2. What does sponsored access get the buy-side firm that ordinary DMA does not?

  • An MPID and full exchange membership.
  • Use of the broker's exchange membership while bypassing most of the broker's order management stack, saving microseconds of latency.
  • Permission to trade without any broker involvement or reporting obligation.
  • An exemption from pre-trade risk checks.

Q3. In the PCIe DMA receive flow, what does the doorbell register actually do?

  • It stores the addresses of buffers the device should write data into.
  • It's a memory-mapped register the CPU writes to as a single PCIe write to notify the device that there's new work in the descriptor ring.
  • It translates between virtual and physical memory addresses on the device side.
  • It is the mechanism by which the device fires an interrupt back at the CPU.

Q4. A teammate sketches a system: "We have Trading DMA, so we don't need Hardware DMA — the orders go straight to the exchange." Why is this wrong?

  • They're right — Trading DMA includes hardware-level acceleration as part of the package.
  • Trading DMA is a regulatory arrangement; Hardware DMA is how packets move on PCIe. Without the latter the kernel stack adds ~50 µs and erases the latency benefit of the former.
  • Hardware DMA is an expensive specialty feature most NICs don't support.
  • Trading DMA actually uses HTTP REST, so there's no DMA at the silicon level anyway.

Q5. SEC Rule 15c3-5 (the Market Access Rule) requires what of a broker that provides sponsored access?

  • The broker must run pre-trade risk and supervisory controls — credit/size limits, kill switches — that cannot be disabled by the sponsored customer.
  • The broker may hand the customer raw connectivity to the exchange with no risk checks ("naked access").
  • The broker must publish round-trip latency for every sponsored customer.
  • The broker must restrict the customer to a limited set of order types.

7. Check your understanding (scenarios)

S1. Your firm is hiring "DMA engineers." Two résumé piles arrive. One contains kernel/PCIe specialists; the other contains FIX/exchange-connectivity specialists. Which is which, and which do you actually want?

The kernel/PCIe pile is Hardware-DMA people: they'll build or tune the NIC drivers, descriptor rings, and zero-copy paths. The FIX pile is Trading-DMA people: they'll handle exchange certification, FIX session negotiation, broker risk-filter integration, and Rule 15c3-5 compliance. You almost certainly want both — but the job posting should be split, because hiring one when you needed the other costs a year.

S2. After a deploy, your sponsored-access connection is suddenly rejecting orders with reason code "PRE_TRADE_RISK_FAIL." Trade volumes are unchanged. What changed and what's the path back?

The sponsoring broker's pre-trade risk filter (the one mandated by Rule 15c3-5) rejected those orders for breaching a configured limit — order size, credit, notional, or kill-switch threshold. The deploy likely changed something the filter cares about: maybe your strategy started placing larger orders, or order rates spiked past a configured cap, or a new instrument lacks a configured limit. The path back is to call the broker's relationship desk, get the rejection logs from their gateway, identify which limit fired, and either roll back the strategy change or negotiate a new limit. You cannot simply turn the filter off — that's illegal.

S3. You profile a kernel-bypass NIC pipeline and see 80% of the per-tick time in a memcpy from the NIC's RX ring into your application's parsing buffer. Diagnose.

You have DMA but not zero-copy. The NIC is correctly DMA'ing the packet into your RX ring, but the application then copies it again into a separate parsing buffer — defeating the point. Fix: parse the payload in place inside the RX ring slot, never copy it. Either restructure the parser to walk a memory range or use a small std::span-like view that the parser consumes from the ring. Confirm with a fresh profile that the memcpy is gone before celebrating; the second-order win is that your L1 cache stops being polluted with duplicated data.

Next in your queue: Hardware Acceleration Practices (FPGA vs GPU vs SmartNIC vs ASIC vs NPU — which workloads go where in an HFT firm).

  1. Direct market access — Wikipedia
  2. High-throughput and Flexible Host Networking for Accelerated Computing — Cornell
  3. Market Access: Direct market access, sponsored access, compliance — CounselStack
  4. Market Access — FINRA
  5. FINRA 2025 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report — Market Access topic
  6. What is direct market access (DMA)? — Databento Microstructure Guide
  7. FPGA-based reconfigurable PCIe NIC with zero-copy DMA — CERN NA62 paper, arXiv:1903.10200
  8. Zero-Copy Memory Access — Intel oneAPI FPGA Add-on Optimization Guide
  9. Arkville FPGA Gen5 PCIe DMA IP — Atomic Rules

The FIX pile is Trading-DMA people: they'll handle exchange certification, FIX session negotiation, broker risk-filter integration, and Rule 15c3-5 compliance. You almost certainly want both — but the job posting should be split, because hiring one when you needed the other costs a year.

S2. After a deploy, your sponsored-access connection is suddenly rejecting orders with reason code "PRE_TRADE_RISK_FAIL." Trade volumes are unchanged. What changed and what's the path back?

The sponsoring broker's pre-trade risk filter (the one mandated by Rule 15c3-5) rejected those orders for breaching a configured limit — order size, credit, notional, or kill-switch threshold. The deploy likely changed something the filter cares about: maybe your strategy started placing larger orders, or order rates spiked past a configured cap, or a new instrument lacks a configured limit. The path back is to call the broker's relationship desk, get the rejection logs from their gateway, identify which limit fired, and either roll back the strategy change or negotiate a new limit. You cannot simply turn the filter off — that's illegal.

S3. You profile a kernel-bypass NIC pipeline and see 80% of the per-tick time in a memcpy from the NIC's RX ring into your application's parsing buffer. Diagnose.

You have DMA but not zero-copy. The NIC is correctly DMA'ing the packet into your RX ring, but the application then copies it again into a separate parsing buffer — defeating the point. Fix: parse the payload in place inside the RX ring slot, never copy it. Either restructure the parser to walk a memory range or use a small std::span-like view that the parser consumes from the ring. Confirm with a fresh profile that the memcpy is gone before celebrating; the second-order win is that your L1 cache stops being polluted with duplicated data.

## Overview of Order-to-Trade Ratio (OTR)

The order-to-trade ratio (OTR) describes the relationship between entry, modification and deletion of orders/quotes and executed transactions. Pursuant to MiFID II RTS 9 Article 2 (DelVO (EU) 2017/566), trading venues are obliged to calculate the ratio between unexecuted orders and trades (order-to-trade ratio) entered into the trading system by trading members for each financial instrument.

## Purpose and Regulatory Framework

Article 51(3) of the proposed Markets in Financial Instruments (MiFID II) draft states that "Member States shall require a regulated market to have in place effective systems, procedures and arrangements to ensure that algorithmic trading systems cannot create or contribute to disorderly trading conditions on the market including systems to limit the ratio of unexecuted orders to transactions that may be entered into the system by a member or participant."

## Implementation Examples

Eurex has recalibrated the Order-to-Trade Ratio (OTR) with effect from 1 January 2021. Main changes compared to the OTR regime until December 2020 are the newly calibrated parameters as well as the provision of intraday periods. The limits for the volume-based OTR are set on the ratio between volume of all order-entries to the trading volume per product and per day, while the limits for the transaction-based OTR are set on the ratio between number of all order entries to the number of trades per product and per day.

## Overview

Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) extends traditional neural network paradigms to non-Euclidean data structures, enabling the effective processing of data that lies on manifolds or graphs. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for modelling relational data by leveraging principles from graph theory and algebraic topology.

## Lie Groups and Neural Networks

Recent work in 2025 is actively exploring the integration of Lie group theory with neural networks. Methods exist for inferring unknown Lie group generators from observed data (e.g., trajectories on a manifold), relying on neural regression to invert the exponential mapping and retrieve latent group actions. Lie group–grounded networks have demonstrated concrete benefits across diverse applications including improved generalization on symmetry-rich domains, superior numerical robustness, reduced training complexity, and increased interpretability.

Lesson 0014Quiz: 0 / 4

Hardware Acceleration Practices in HFT

Why this matters: Lesson 0002 covered FPGAs and 0011 placed them on the latency ladder. This lesson zooms out to the full menu of hardware accelerators a trading firm actually uses — FPGA, GPU, SmartNIC/DPU, ASIC, NPU — and which workload goes where.

Illustrative code where the repo doesn't have the real thing yet.

1. The five-family taxonomy

FamilyWhat it isBest atHFT role
CPUGeneral-purpose serial cores with deep caches and branch prediction.Complex branchy logic, glue code.Strategy logic on tier 2; control plane everywhere.
FPGAReconfigurable logic fabric.[1]Deterministic ns-scale pipelines.Tick-to-trade hot path (this repo's fpga/).
GPUThousands of SIMD cores, deep memory hierarchy.[2]Massively parallel dense math (training, batch inference).Model training, alt-data CV, options pricing. Not hot path.
SmartNIC / DPUNIC with onboard ARM cores + programmable packet engines (BlueField, Pensando).[3]Network offload, in-line risk checks, parsing.Replacing dumb NICs in colocation racks; growing fast.
ASIC / NPUFixed-function silicon for one job. NPUs are AI-specific ASICs.[4]Best $/throughput/watt for one workload.Apex HFT for matching/parsing; AI training at hyperscalers.

2. The decision framework — three questions

1. Determinism vs throughput?

If the workload is "one tick at a time, ns matter" → FPGA/ASIC. If it's "millions of samples, batched" → GPU/NPU. CPUs sit between, mediocre at both.

2. How often does the algorithm change?

Weekly strategy iteration → FPGA (re-synth in hours). Frozen algorithm at scale → ASIC (months of tape-out, then years of use).

3. Is the workload AI?

Training: GPU is still king (NVIDIA H100/B100). Inference at low latency: NPU/Groq LPU offer 10×+ vs GPU on specific shapes.[2] Inference on the trading hot path: hls4ml-style FPGA compile.

The pattern: heterogeneous

2025 production HFT stacks combine all five — CPU control + FPGA hot path + GPU training + SmartNIC for risk/parsing + (rarely) ASIC for matching. Mixing tiers is the design, not a smell.[1]

3. SmartNIC / DPU — the newest entrant worth understanding

A SmartNIC is a NIC plus an embedded CPU complex (typically ARM) and programmable packet engines. NVIDIA BlueField and AMD Pensando are the market leaders; BlueField-4 ships 800 Gbps with 6× compute over its predecessor.[3] The DPU/SmartNIC market reached $1.11B in 2024 and is on a 14.9% CAGR through 2034.[3]

For HFT specifically they fit two niches:

  • Inline risk checks. Run Rule 15c3-5 pre-trade filters on the DPU's ARM cores instead of on the host CPU, saving the PCIe round-trip for rejected orders.
  • Protocol parsing. Strip exchange feeds (ITCH, OUCH, FIX) on the DPU and hand the application a structured tick — same shape as FPGA parsing but cheaper to ship a new schema (no re-synth).

4. The repo today and the realistic next step

The repo's hardware story is the FPGA folder (fpga/*.vhd). Realistic upgrade paths, in order of cost:

  1. Add a GPU for training — the GBM in paper_trading_sim.py stays on CPU; if you ever swap it for a neural net (Lesson 0007), training moves to GPU. Zero hot-path impact.
  2. Add a SmartNIC for the eventual feed handler — when (if) the repo gains a live exchange feed, BlueField-class NICs let you offload parsing without writing HDL.
  3. Compile a small NN onto the FPGA via hls4ml — covered in Lesson 0007. The bridge between Python-trained models and ULL execution.
  4. ASIC: don't. Not at this scale; the economics need billions of messages per day to justify tape-out.

5. Often confused with

DPU vs SmartNIC

The terms are used interchangeably in 2025 marketing. Pedantically: SmartNIC = NIC with some programmability; DPU = SmartNIC with a full CPU complex and OS. NVIDIA/AMD now use "DPU" exclusively.[3]

FPGA vs ASIC

FPGA reprograms in seconds via a new bitstream; ASIC is silicon you taped out and frozen. Same logic on ASIC is 5–10× faster and ~10× cheaper per unit at scale but $10M+ to make.

NPU vs GPU

NPU is an ASIC specialized for the matmul + activation pattern of neural nets. Better $/W on that shape; useless for general parallel code. GPU is more flexible, more power-hungry.[4]

Acceleration vs Offload

Acceleration: doing the same work faster. Offload: moving the work elsewhere so the original processor can do other things. SmartNICs are mostly offload; FPGAs are mostly acceleration.

6. Practice

Q1. You need to run a 7B-parameter LLM for nightly news-sentiment featurization across millions of articles. Which accelerator?

  • FPGA via hls4ml.
  • GPU (or NPU if cost matters).
  • CPU with AVX-512.
  • Custom ASIC.

Lesson 0015Quiz: 0 / 4

Alternative Data — Two Founding Stories

Why this matters: "alt-data" is jargon for "any data source that isn't a price feed or a filing." It's worth a lot of money to whoever sees a signal first. Two famous stories teach the whole concept. (More flavors come in Lesson 0020.)

1. What "alternative data" actually means

Traditional financial data: prices, volumes, filings, broker estimates, central-bank releases. Alternative data: anything else that hints at the same underlying economic reality before it shows up in those traditional channels.[1]

Three properties make a candidate alt-data feed valuable to a hedge fund:

1. It leads the official number

You see it weeks before quarterly earnings or monthly economic releases. The whole point is to know first.

2. It's hard to replicate

Anyone with a Bloomberg terminal sees the same earnings releases. If your alt-data is cheap and ubiquitous, the alpha lasts ~zero seconds after publication.

3. It maps cleanly onto a tradable variable

"Foot traffic at Walmart parking lots" maps to "Walmart same-store sales" which maps to "Walmart Q earnings surprise" which maps to "WMT stock price reaction." Each step is mechanical and modellable.

The decay curve

Once a data source becomes widely known, the alpha decays. The Walmart parking lot story is now textbook — using only parking data buys you nothing. The frontier moved to harder data.

2. Founding story #1: The Walmart parking lot (2010)

In mid-2010 a UBS analyst named Neil Currie published a quarterly research note based on satellite imagery of 100 Walmart parking lots, claiming that car-counts indicated the stock was undervalued. UBS bought the parking-lot counts from a data provider, used the image-derived foot-traffic estimate to triangulate revenues, and was one of the first banks to monetize satellite imagery as an investment signal.[2]

The mechanics:

  1. Source: commercial satellite imagery (Planet, DigitalGlobe-now-Maxar) over a Walmart store on multiple days.
  2. Vendor: a specialist counts cars from the imagery using computer vision and publishes a daily/weekly foot-traffic estimate. Today's vendors include RS Metrics, Orbital Insight, SpaceKnow, Planet Labs.[3]
  3. Signal: car-counts → estimated visits → estimated revenues → revenue-vs-consensus surprise → price reaction.
  4. Trade: long or short WMT before the quarterly print; close after.

In 2014, Tiger Global Management was publicly known to be counting cars in Walmart parking lots from satellite imagery to estimate quarterly sales before earnings.[4] By the late 2010s the trade was crowded; by 2025 it's a textbook example, not an active alpha.

3. Founding story #2: Counting oil drums from space

The "oil drum" example: crude-oil storage tanks have floating roofs that sit on top of the oil itself, so the height of the roof tells you the fill level. From orbit, the shadow cast by the rim onto the roof reveals how high the roof sits — and therefore how much oil is in the tank.[5]

Ursa Space Systems, a New York firm, tracks roughly 11,000 oil-storage tanks worldwide using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites and provides weekly inventory reports to commodity-trading hedge funds.[5] SAR sees through clouds and works at night — a crucial property since traditional oil-storage data is reported weekly by the EIA in the US and monthly by OPEC, with significant lag and self-reporting bias.

The mechanics are the same shape as Walmart:

  1. Source: SAR satellites passing over Cushing, OK (US benchmark), the Strait of Hormuz, China's strategic reserves, etc.
  2. Vendor: image analysis (now mostly automated by CNNs) produces a per-tank fill estimate. Aggregated weekly.
  3. Signal: inventory delta vs expectations → crude price reaction.
  4. Trade: futures on WTI/Brent, or related ETFs/stocks.
Why this is the cleanest example: oil-tank inventory is a single number that maps to a single tradable instrument (the crude futures curve), with a regulatory data release (EIA Petroleum Status Report) as the ground truth. You can backtest the alpha unambiguously.

4. The economics of alt-data

Cost driverTypical 2024–25 range
Mid-tier provider feed (e.g. one retail chain's foot-traffic)$50k–$200k/yr
Comprehensive satellite + geospatial bundle (Orbital Insight, SpaceKnow)$200k–$500k/yr
Premium / exclusive panel (one-of-its-kind data)$1M+/yr

The math fund managers do: an alt-data feed needs to add a few basis points of risk-adjusted return per year on the AUM that uses it. A $1B fund with a 10 bps lift earns $1M — pays for one premium feed and frees the question of whether it's worth a second.

The non-obvious risk: alt-data vendors often sell the same signal to many funds. The first buyer gets the alpha; the tenth pays the same price for an empty signal. Exclusivity riders are negotiated, but expensive — usually only the largest funds can afford them.

5. In this project

The repo's news_features.py + news_fetch.py are a baby alt-data pipeline: news headlines + Alpha Vantage sentiment → daily per-ticker features. The structure (third-party transformation of unstructured data into a tradable signal) is identical to the Walmart parking lot pattern — just with text instead of imagery, and a much cheaper data source. Lesson 0007 noted that the sentiment scalar is silently a transformer's output you don't own; same story here.

A realistic alt-data extension that fits this codebase: foot-traffic data for the S&P 500 retailers via a SafeGraph or Placer.ai-style provider, merged into the GBM features panel via walkforward_sim.py --use_news-style flow. Not built; cleanly conceivable.

6. Often confused with

Alt-data vs Fundamental data

Fundamental: from filings, accounting, official releases. Alt-data: derived from operational or behavioral signals before they appear in fundamentals. Alt-data predicts the fundamental.

Alt-data vs Technical signals

Technical: derived from past prices/volumes (RSI, momentum). Alt-data: derived from outside the market entirely. Technical signals are universally available; alt-data is gated by access.

Walmart pattern vs Oil-drum pattern

Both use satellite imagery. Walmart maps to a single retailer's quarterly earnings (binary event, sparse). Oil drums map to a continuous commodity inventory (frequent, integrable). Different statistical shapes.

Signal vs Data

Raw imagery is data. Counted cars is signal. Funds buy both at different price points; vendor margins are in turning data into signal at scale.

7. Practice

Q1. Why does the floating-roof oil tank work for satellite-based inventory estimation?

  • The roof floats on the oil itself, so its height (visible via shadow length from orbit) directly indicates fill level.
  • The color of the oil changes over time and is visible from space.
  • Tanks broadcast inventory data via GPS.
  • Thermal signature in infrared correlates with fill level.

Q2. The Walmart parking lot signal was profitable in 2010–2014 but became uninteresting by 2025. What's the most likely cause?

  • Satellite imagery quality has gotten worse.
  • Once everyone subscribed to the same data, the alpha was priced in before the earnings release.
  • Walmart stopped being a major retailer.
  • SEC banned the use of alternative data in 2020.

Q3. Three properties make a candidate alt-data source valuable to a hedge fund. Which is NOT one of them?

  • It leads the official number.
  • It's hard for competitors to replicate.
  • It maps cleanly to a tradable variable.
  • It's publicly disclosed in SEC filings.

Q4. A vendor offers an exclusive license on a new geospatial signal for $5M/yr. A non-exclusive license costs $500k/yr. Why might a $10B fund buy the exclusive?

  • Exclusivity prevents competitors from running the same trade, preserving the signal's alpha durability across years.
  • The exclusive license includes higher-resolution data.
  • Better customer support from the vendor.
  • It's required by SEC regulation for large funds.

8. Scenarios

S1. You backtest an alt-data signal and find a Sharpe of 3.0 over 5 years. Two months after going live, Sharpe is 0.4. Diagnose.

Classic alt-data alpha decay — between backtest and live, the vendor probably onboarded several other funds and the signal has been arbitraged into the price. Possible secondary causes: backtest had look-ahead (the data was delivered with delay you didn't model), survivorship bias in the tickers used, or a regime change. The first-line check is to call the vendor and ask about subscriber growth; the second is to redo the backtest with a realistic delivery delay and an exit timing that matches when you can actually act.

S2. You're offered raw satellite imagery for $50k/yr OR pre-processed car counts for $200k/yr. You're a small fund without ML staff. Which is the rational choice?

The pre-processed counts — you're paying the vendor's price for their ML infrastructure (CNN models, validation labels, ops team running the pipeline) which would cost you much more than $150k/yr to build and maintain. Raw imagery is the right buy only if you have a CV team, want signal differentiation from other subscribers, and can extract value the vendor's standard pipeline misses. For a small fund, vendor margin on processed signal is real but cheap relative to do-it-yourself cost.

Sources

  1. Alternative Data for Hedge Funds Guide — VertData
  2. How Satellite Imagery Is Helping Hedge Funds Outperform — International Banker
  3. Satellite Data For Investors: Top Alternative Data Providers — Paragon Intel
  4. How hedge funds use satellite images to beat Wall Street — UC Berkeley Haas
  5. How Hedge Funds Use SAR + AIS Data — PierSight

Lesson 0016Quiz: 0 / 4

Order-Book Dynamics

Why this matters: Lesson 0001 introduced the limit order book. This lesson goes deeper — price-time priority, queue position, the lifecycle of an order, and what every event in the book actually means.

1. The LOB as a state machine

A limit order book (LOB) is a continuously updated data structure tracking every resting buy and sell order, sorted by price then by arrival time. At any instant it has:

  • A bid side: buy orders, sorted descending by price (highest bid at top).
  • An ask side: sell orders, sorted ascending by price (lowest ask at top).
  • A best bid and best ask — the inside quote.
  • A spread = best ask − best bid.
  • A mid = (best bid + best ask) / 2.

Illustrative top-of-book snapshot for ES (E-mini S&P futures):

BIDS (size × price)
PX
ASKS (price × size)
4523.50
4523.50 × 18
4523.25
4523.25 × 47
12 × 4523.00
4523.00
85 × 4522.75
4522.75
120 × 4522.50
4522.50

Best bid 4523.00, best ask 4523.25. Spread = $0.25. Mid = 4523.125. The "12" on the best bid means 12 contracts are waiting at that level — sorted internally by arrival time.

2. Price-time priority — the rule that runs everything

When a marketable order arrives (an order that crosses the spread), it matches against resting orders by price first, then by time of arrival:

  1. Match against the best available price first (4523.25 ask, 47 contracts).
  2. Within that price level, match against orders in FIFO order — the order that arrived first gets filled first.
  3. If the incoming order exceeds the size at one level, walk up the book to the next price level.

The single most important consequence: queue position matters as much as price. If you posted a buy at 4523.00 first, you're at the front of the line; you fill first when a marketable sell hits.
