Lesson 0017Quiz: 0 / 4

Market Making

Why this matters: fpga/market_maker.vhd is named for this strategy. Lessons 0001 and 0016 sketched the idea; this lesson formalizes it — the P&L model, the two killers (adverse selection + inventory risk), and the canonical Avellaneda-Stoikov framework.

1. The strategy in one sentence

A market maker continuously posts both a bid (to buy) and an ask (to sell) on a venue and earns the spread when both sides fill before the underlying price moves.[1]

Toy P&L

// Post bid at 99.99, ask at 100.01 — 2-cent spread.
// Buyer hits your ask: +1 unit at 100.01, P&L = +100.01 short
// Seller hits your bid: -1 unit at 99.99,  P&L = -99.99   long
// Net inventory back to flat. Net P&L = +$0.02 per round-trip.

Multiply that 2-cent edge across millions of round-trips per day. That's the entire economic engine of a high-frequency market maker.

2. The two killers

Killer 1: Adverse selection

The trader who lifted your offer at 100.01 may have known something you didn't — informed flow that's about to push the price to 100.10. You sold low; the market moved against you; the spread you earned (2¢) gets wiped out by the loss on inventory (9¢).

Adverse selection is the reason market makers cancel orders aggressively. If new information arrives (a related instrument moved, a news headline hit, the order-book imbalance flipped), the market maker pulls its quotes faster than the competing takers can lift them.[1] Cancellation speed is half of why latency matters.

Killer 2: Inventory risk

When fills are imbalanced — many buy fills, few sell fills — the market maker accumulates inventory (long or short). That inventory has mark-to-market exposure: if the price drifts, P&L moves with it, unhedged.

The fix is to skew quotes based on current inventory: if you're long 100 contracts, lower your bid (less aggressive on buying more) and lower your ask (more aggressive on selling). The optimal quote is no longer symmetric around the mid.

3. The Avellaneda-Stoikov framework

The canonical mathematical treatment.[2] Given mid-price s, inventory q, volatility σ, risk-aversion γ, and time-to-horizon T-t, the optimal quotes are:

reservation_price = s - q * γ * σ² * (T - t)         // skewed by inventory
optimal_spread    = γ * σ² * (T - t) + (2/γ) * ln(1 + γ/k)

bid = reservation_price - optimal_spread / 2
ask = reservation_price + optimal_spread / 2

Three intuitions packed in:

  • Reservation price ≠ mid. When long inventory, your "fair value" shifts down to reflect that you want to sell.
  • Spread grows with volatility. Higher σ → higher adverse-selection risk → wider quotes needed to compensate.
  • Spread grows with risk aversion. Higher γ → you tolerate less inventory risk → wider quotes.
The repo's market_maker.vhd doesn't do any of this. It computes a simple mid ± spread/2 with constant spread and zero inventory tracking. That's the arithmetic shell of market making; the actual strategy needs inventory state and adverse-selection awareness. Adding those is the obvious next step.

4. Where market makers earn the rest of their money

Beyond the headline spread capture, three secondary income streams matter:

Maker rebates

Most exchanges pay liquidity providers a rebate per filled lot — typically a fraction of a cent per share or a few cents per futures contract. For high-volume MMs this is a major revenue stream.

Designated market maker (DMM) fees

Some venues pay a fixed monthly fee to MMs that meet quoting obligations (e.g. quote 90% of the day in size X). Stable, lower-margin business; floor for the strategy.

Order-flow analytics

Seeing your own fill pattern gives a window into broader market microstructure. Not directly monetized; informs other strategies inside the firm.

Cross-venue arbitrage

MMs often see slight price differences between venues (NASDAQ vs ARCA vs IEX) and capture the basis. Adjacent strategy that shares the same infrastructure.

5. Often confused with

Market making vs Stat arb

MM: directionally neutral, earns spread, worries about inventory. Stat arb: directional bet based on a statistical signal (Lesson 0018). Different P&L drivers, different risk profile.

Designated MM vs Voluntary MM

Designated: has formal obligations (continuous quoting, max spread, min size) in exchange for benefits. Voluntary: makes markets when conditions are favorable, leaves when they aren't.

Quote vs Order

A quote is a market maker's intent to buy/sell at a price. An order is the exchange-level message that makes the quote real (NewOrderSingle in FIX terms).

Spread capture vs Mid-price prediction

An MM doesn't predict the mid; they make money on the round-trip. Stat arb predicts the mid. Both can be wrong about direction; the MM survives if inventory stays flat.

6. Practice

Q1. A market maker quotes 99.99/100.01 in size 10. A buyer lifts the ask, taking 10 lots at 100.01. Within 50ms the mid moves to 100.10. What just happened?

  • The MM made $0.02 × 10 = $0.20 risk-free.
  • Adverse selection: the MM captured 2¢ spread but lost 9¢ on the short position when mid moved against them — net -7¢/lot.
  • The MM is risk-free because the fill happens in 50 ms.
  • Both sides profit because the MM holds inventory only briefly.

Q2. In the Avellaneda-Stoikov framework, the reservation price is shifted away from the mid by what?

  • By inventory q multiplied by risk aversion γ, volatility σ² and time-to-horizon.
  • By the order-book imbalance only.
  • By the spread the MM expects to capture on the next round-trip.
  • By the time of day (more skew at the open).

Q3. Why do market makers cancel orders far more than they execute them?

  • Because exchanges encourage cancellation as a fee model.
  • Because adverse selection means stale quotes that don't reflect new information are negative-EV — the MM cancels faster than the taker can lift.
  • Because they're spoofing — placing orders they don't intend to execute.
  • Because cancellation is essentially free and faster to fix than to leave alone.

Q4. fpga/market_maker.vhd computes mid ± spread/2 with constant spread and no inventory tracking. What's the most important missing piece for a real strategy?

  • An inventory accumulator and inventory-based quote skewing (reservation price), so quotes shift as inventory accumulates.
  • A wider spread to compensate for being slow.
  • An LLM-based quote-optimization layer.
  • Cross-venue routing.

7. Scenarios

S1. A MM strategy backtest shows steady spread capture but live P&L is negative. Diagnose.

Almost certainly adverse selection. The backtest assumed the MM was filled at the recorded prices, but in reality only the unfavorable fills happen — the favorable ones get arbitraged away by faster participants. Common test: split historical fills into "MM was at the front of the queue" vs "MM was not." The backtest implicitly assumes the former; live skews toward the latter. Fix: model queue position explicitly and assume you only fill when you're at the front, or reduce the strategy to a tier where queue position is achievable (slower instrument, less competitive venue).

S2. You add inventory-aware skewing to market_maker.vhd. After deployment, fill rate drops 40% but P&L per fill is much better. Should you ship it?

Probably yes, but verify with a P&L attribution. Lower fill rate means the new quotes don't sit at the inside as often — that's expected when you skew defensively. The key questions: (1) Is the per-fill P&L improvement coming from reduced adverse selection, or just from a small sample? Need ~10× more fills than the variance suggests. (2) Are exchange rebates also dropping? In some venues maker rebates are a significant revenue stream that's proportional to fill count. (3) Is the overall realized Sharpe better? That's the headline. If yes to all three, ship.

Sources

  1. High-frequency trading in a limit order book — Avellaneda & Stoikov (Cornell)
  2. Optimal High-Frequency Market Making — Stanford MS&E 448 report

Statistical Arbitrage

Why this matters: this repo's GBM strategy is closer to stat arb than to anything else — it ranks tickers cross-sectionally and bets on the top-N. This lesson formalizes the family: pairs trading, cointegration, mean-reversion, and what makes a stat-arb strategy "statistical" rather than "arbitrage."

1. The definition

Statistical arbitrage: a strategy that exploits statistical patterns in price relationships, expecting profits over a large number of trades on average even if individual trades can lose. Not arbitrage in the textbook sense (which is risk-free profit from a price mismatch). The "statistical" qualifier means: relies on the law of large numbers, not on a strict mispricing.

2. The canonical example: pairs trading

Coca-Cola (KO) and Pepsi (PEP) sell similar products to similar customers under similar economic conditions. Their prices tend to move together. Over a 1-year window, the ratio price(KO) / price(PEP) has some long-run mean — say 1.5. When the ratio deviates significantly (say to 1.7), the strategy bets it will revert: short KO, long PEP, with sizes chosen so the position is dollar-neutral.

# Toy pairs strategy (illustrative)
spread = np.log(price_KO) - beta * np.log(price_PEP)
z      = (spread - spread.rolling(60).mean()) / spread.rolling(60).std()

# Trade signals:
# z > +2  → short KO, long PEP (spread too high, expect mean reversion)
# z < -2  → long  KO, short PEP
# |z| < 0.5 → close

The profit doesn't require KO or PEP to move in any particular direction — only for the spread between them to revert. That's the "market-neutral" property.

3. Cointegration — the math behind "they move together"

Two price series are cointegrated if a linear combination of them is stationary (mean-reverting), even though each individual series is non-stationary (random walk). Formally: there exists a β such that log(P_KO) - β·log(P_PEP) is a stationary process.

This is testable. The standard procedure (Engle-Granger):

  1. Regress log(P_KO) on log(P_PEP) to estimate β.
  2. Compute residuals.
  3. Test residuals for stationarity using an Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test.
  4. If ADF rejects the unit-root hypothesis at the desired significance level → pair is cointegrated.
Cointegration breaks. The relationship between two companies can shift permanently (M&A, business model change, regulatory shock). What was a tradable pair becomes a one-way bet on a permanent regime change. Re-test cointegration regularly; have rules to retire pairs that break.

4. The broader family

Pairs trading is the textbook example, but modern stat arb runs at much larger scale:

Pairs trading

Two related assets, one spread, mean reversion. Capacity is small but risk profile is clean.

Basket / sector arb

Long one stock, short an ETF or basket of competitors. Removes the broad sector risk while keeping idiosyncratic alpha.

Cross-sectional momentum

Rank N stocks by recent performance; long top decile, short bottom decile. The dominant equity quant strategy globally. Closely related to this repo's GBM ranking.

Index arbitrage

S&P 500 futures vs the cash basket of constituents — when prices diverge, trade both legs. The classic Chicago↔NJ trade from Lesson 0012.

Convertible / Capital-structure arb

Trade equity vs bonds vs convertibles of the same issuer. Hedges out company risk, captures pricing inefficiency between instruments.

ML-driven cross-sectional

Train a model to rank tickers by predicted return. This repo's GBM. Mechanically the same as cross-sectional momentum, just with a more flexible signal.

5. Stat arb vs Market making — the same toolbox, different P&L drivers

PropertyMarket making (Lesson 0017)Statistical arbitrage
Directional?No — earns spread, neutral on price directionYes — bets that A goes up relative to B
HorizonMicroseconds–secondsMinutes–days, sometimes weeks
P&L sourceSpread + rebatesMean reversion of price relationships
Main riskAdverse selection + inventoryPersistent regime change (cointegration breaks)
Number of betsMillions/day, small10s–1000s/day, larger
Latency tierTier 4–6 (ULL essential)Tier 1–3 typically; some flavors push lower

6. In this project

The repo's setup is a cross-sectional stat-arb scaffold dressed in ML clothing. paper_trading_sim.py ranks tickers by predicted next-day return and takes the top-N — that's the mechanics of cross-sectional momentum / mean-reversion stat arb. The fact that the predictor is a GBM rather than a hand-coded ratio doesn't change the strategy family; it just makes the signal flexible.

Things missing for true production stat arb:

  • Short side: a real stat arb book is long-short, not long-only. The repo's meanvar_long_only enforces long-only — half the dispersion-capturing power is left on the table.
  • Factor neutrality: ensuring the portfolio is neutral to market, sector, and size factors (so the alpha is idiosyncratic stock-picking, not just market timing). Not done here.
  • Risk model: BARRA-style factor risk decomposition. Not done; the --risk_overlay in walkforward_sim.py is a much simpler stress detector.

7. Often confused with

Statistical arbitrage vs True arbitrage

True arbitrage: risk-free profit from a guaranteed mispricing (e.g. triangular FX). Rare. Stat arb: probabilistic profit from a statistical pattern. Loss is possible on any individual trade.

Stat arb vs Macro

Stat arb: many small bets driven by statistical patterns, holding period of days. Macro: few large bets driven by economic narratives, holding period of months. Different shops, different talent.

Cointegration vs Correlation

Correlation: linear association of returns. Two random walks can be highly correlated yet diverge forever. Cointegration: their levels stay tethered — the spread is mean-reverting. Stat arb uses cointegration, not raw correlation.

Stat arb vs HFT

Overlapping but not synonymous. Some stat arb is HFT (Tier 3+), most is not. The repo's GBM is stat arb but not HFT — daily horizon, Tier 0–1 latency.

8. Practice

Q1. Why does pairs trading work even if both KO and PEP are random walks?

  • Because both KO and PEP are mean-reverting individually.
  • Because the spread between them is cointegrated and mean-reverting, even though each price is a random walk.
  • Because their daily returns are highly correlated.
  • Because they're in the same industry and that automatically makes them tradable.

Q2. The biggest single risk in pairs trading is:

  • Transaction costs eating the spread profit.
  • The pair's cointegration breaking due to a permanent regime change in one company, leaving the strategy long a one-way bet.
  • An overnight increase in market volatility.
  • Margin requirements doubling overnight.

Q3. The repo's paper_trading_sim.py picks the top-N predicted returns and goes long equal-weight. Why is that a stat-arb strategy?

  • Because it operates at HFT speeds and earns spread on every fill.
  • It places many bets based on the statistical ranking of a cross-section of tickers, relying on the model being right on average rather than on any single bet.
  • Because each individual trade is risk-free.
  • Because it exploits a guaranteed mispricing.

Q4. A teammate suggests "make the GBM strategy market-neutral by shorting the index." What's the benefit?

  • It doubles the gross returns of the strategy.
  • It isolates the strategy's cross-sectional alpha from broad market moves, so you can measure stock-picking skill independent of market timing.
  • It reduces operational complexity by removing the need for a risk model.
  • It makes the strategy completely risk-free.

9. Scenarios

S1. You test 4000 stock pairs for cointegration at 95% confidence and find 200 cointegrated pairs. Should you trade all of them?

No — that's exactly the number you'd expect from pure randomness. At 95% significance, 5% of pairs will appear cointegrated by chance alone, which is 200 out of 4000. This is the multiple-testing problem in disguise. Practical fix: use a much stricter significance level (e.g. 99.9%) and/or require multiple supporting tests (Engle-Granger + Johansen + economic rationale). Trading the raw 200 will produce a strategy that looks great in backtest and dies live as the spurious correlations decay.

S2. You add a short side to paper_trading_sim.py (short the bottom-N predictions). Backtest Sharpe goes UP but max drawdown also gets worse. Diagnose.

Probably a sector concentration effect. When the long and short sides are not factor-neutralized, both can be loading on the same underlying factor exposures (e.g. you accidentally are long growth and short value, or long mega-cap and short small-cap). When that factor reverses sharply you lose on both legs. Fix: add a constraint that the long and short books have matching sector weights and matching market-cap distributions, or use a proper risk model to decompose factor exposures. The Sharpe up + MaxDD up pattern is a classic signature of hidden factor concentration.

Sources

  1. High-frequency trading in a limit order book — Avellaneda & Stoikov
  2. Databento Microstructure Guide

Lesson 0019Quiz: 0 / 4

Order-to-Trade Ratio (OTR)

Why this matters: Lesson 0016 noted that market makers cancel orders 50–500× more than they execute. Regulators noticed. This lesson covers the headline metric exchanges use to throttle aggressive quoting and the rule framework around it.

1. The definition

The Order-to-Trade Ratio (OTR) is the ratio of order-entries (including modifications and cancels) to executions on a venue, measured per participant per instrument per day.[1] Two common flavors:

OTR_transactions = (orders + modifications + cancellations) / number of trades
OTR_volume       = total order volume / total traded volume

An OTR of 100 means you sent 100 messages for every 1 trade you executed. Market makers easily hit 200–500. The metric was designed during MiFID II to identify and meter participants whose system load is disproportionate to their economic contribution.[2]

2. The regulatory background — MiFID II RTS 9

Article 51(3) of MiFID II requires regulated venues to "have in place effective systems, procedures and arrangements to ensure that algorithmic trading systems cannot create or contribute to disorderly trading conditions … including systems to limit the ratio of unexecuted orders to transactions."[3]

RTS 9 (Regulatory Technical Standard 9, DelVO (EU) 2017/566) operationalizes the obligation:[1]

  • Each venue computes the OTR per member per instrument per day.
  • Venues set per-instrument limits (different for an illiquid small-cap vs an active blue-chip).
  • Exceeding limits triggers fees, throttling, or in extreme cases participant suspension.

Eurex example — the most public regime

Eurex publishes its OTR parameters publicly. In 2021 it recalibrated parameters and introduced intra-day periods.[4] Limits are set both on:

  • Volume-based OTR: ratio of total order-entry volume to traded volume per product per day.
  • Transaction-based OTR: ratio of order-entry message count to trade count per product per day.

A participant exceeding the limit pays an Excessive System Usage (ESU) fee.[5] Other major venues (Borsa Istanbul, Vienna, BME) operate similar schemes; thresholds vary by venue and instrument.[6]

3. What the metric is trying to discourage

Spoofing

Posting large orders with no intention to fill, to influence the book, then canceling. Already illegal; high OTR is a noisy proxy.

Quote stuffing

Flooding the venue with messages to slow competitors' systems. Outright denial-of-service against the matching engine.

Excessive system load

Honest but very high-cancel strategies that consume disproportionate matching-engine capacity. The bulk of what OTR actually polices.

What it doesn't catch

Strategies that send fewer total messages but with manipulative intent. OTR is structural, not behavioral. Spoofing prosecutions rely on intent evidence (emails, code).

4. The market-maker exemption

Real market makers have legitimately high OTRs — that's the nature of the strategy. Most venues offer relaxed OTR limits to participants registered as designated market makers (DMMs) or who meet specific quoting-obligation criteria.[1] This is the regulatory compromise: let the people who provide liquidity be aggressive about quoting; throttle the rest.

5. Practical tooling

An HFT shop's pre-trade risk system typically tracks OTR in real-time per venue per instrument and can:

  • Throttle or pause the strategy when projected daily OTR approaches the venue limit.
  • Reroute quoting to a different (less constrained) venue.
  • Tighten the strategy's own internal cancel logic (e.g. wait for a bigger price move before re-quoting).
// Illustrative pre-trade check
if (running_otr_today > 0.9 * venue_otr_limit) {
    strategy.throttle();           // reduce quote update rate
}
if (running_otr_today > 0.99 * venue_otr_limit) {
    strategy.pause_quoting();      // stop until next day's reset
}

6. In this project

Robinhood (the only execution venue this repo touches via scripts/robinhood_executor.py) is a retail brokerage with low order rates; OTR limits don't bite at the volumes a daily-rebalance strategy generates. If the repo ever connects to a real exchange, OTR tracking goes into the same pre-trade risk module as Rule 15c3-5 checks (Lesson 0013) and inventory limits.

7. Often confused with

OTR vs Cancel-to-fill ratio

OTR: every order-entry message (add, modify, cancel) divided by trades. Cancel ratio: just cancels divided by something. OTR is the regulatory metric; cancel ratio is internal diagnostics.

OTR limit vs Spoofing prosecution

Hitting an OTR limit costs a fee. Spoofing is a criminal/civil prosecution requiring intent evidence. Very different consequences for behaviors that can look similar on the wire.

Venue OTR vs Broker OTR

Venue: tracks per-member, enforces fees. Broker: tracks per-client, may impose its own limits to protect its own venue-side standing. Both can throttle you independently.

OTR vs Rule 15c3-5

OTR: an EU-rooted venue-side metric. Rule 15c3-5: a US broker-dealer obligation (Lesson 0013). Different jurisdictions, different layers; many HFT firms must comply with both.

8. Practice

Q1. A typical market-maker on a liquid instrument might run an OTR of:

  • ~1 (one order per trade).
  • ~5–10.
  • 100–500.
  • 10,000+.

Q2. Why do most venues exempt registered market makers from the strictest OTR limits?

  • Because DMMs pay venue fees.
  • Because real market making structurally requires high OTRs, and capping them would destroy MM liquidity provision. Exemption comes with quoting obligations.
  • Because MM software is slower to react to news.
  • Because they were grandfathered in from pre-MiFID II rules.

Q3. Your strategy's OTR is approaching the venue limit by 14:00 each day. Which response is operationally sane?

  • Double the order rate to fill the book with quotes before the limit hits.
  • Tighten the strategy's internal re-quote logic (require larger price moves to update) so message count drops while keeping the strategy active.
  • Spoof additional sells to mark them as orders, lifting the denominator.
  • Disable the pre-trade risk check so orders get through faster.

Q4. OTR catches some bad behaviors but not all. Which is it NOT designed to catch?

  • Quote stuffing — flooding the venue with messages.
  • Sophisticated spoofing with low total message counts but manipulative intent.
  • Excessive system usage by honest high-cancel strategies.
  • Sudden order-rate spikes during news events.

9. Scenarios

S1. The strategy team complains "the OTR limit is killing our edge." How do you respond as the engineer?

First, check whether the strategy qualifies for designated market-maker status on the venue — if it provides genuine liquidity, the relaxed DMM limits may apply, in exchange for quoting obligations. Second, look at message efficiency: are the canceled orders adding economic value, or are they spurious re-quotes from poor signal stability? Smoothing the strategy's quote-update logic often drops OTR significantly without reducing alpha. Third, consider venue choice: some venues have higher limits for the same instrument. The "OTR limit is killing our edge" framing usually has a 30–50% operational improvement on top before any regulatory conversation is needed.

S2. Eurex changes its OTR parameters effective next quarter. The new transaction-based limit on your main instrument drops from 500 to 200. What's the operational plan?

Three weeks of preparation, broadly: (1) Modify the strategy's internal quote-update threshold so projected daily OTR comes in safely under 180 (with a 10% headroom for spikes). (2) Add real-time OTR monitoring to the dashboard so the trading desk sees the running count. (3) Run a one-week shadow deploy where the new logic is active but trades are unchanged, to validate that the OTR projection model matches reality. (4) Update the kill-switch logic so the strategy pauses at 95% of the new limit rather than 99% (more headroom). (5) Communicate to risk and compliance that the change is being made and update the playbook for what to do if the limit is hit.

Sources

  1. Order-to-Trade Ratio — Eurex regulations page
  2. ESMA draft RTS on Microstructural Issues — MiFID II / algo trading
  3. Order to trade ratios and their impact on the Italian stock market — UK Government Office for Science
  4. Redesign of the OTR in the context of MiFID II — Eurex circular
  5. HFT Act: ESU Fee and OTR enhancements — Eurex circular
  6. Borsa Istanbul OTR Information Note

Venue: tracks per-member, enforces fees. Broker: tracks per-client, may impose its own limits to protect its own venue-side standing. Both can throttle you independently.

OTR vs Rule 15c3-5

OTR: an EU-rooted venue-side metric. Rule 15c3-5: a US broker-dealer obligation (Lesson 0013). Different jurisdictions, different layers; many HFT firms must comply with both.

8. Practice

Q1. A typical market-maker on a liquid instrument might run an OTR of:

  • ~1 (one order per trade).
  • ~5–10.
  • 100–500.
  • 10,000+.

Q2. Why do most venues exempt registered market makers from the strictest OTR limits?

  • Because DMMs pay venue fees.
  • Because real market making structurally requires high OTRs, and capping them would destroy MM liquidity provision. Exemption comes with quoting obligations.
  • Because MM software is slower to react to news.
  • Because they were grandfathered in from pre-MiFID II rules.

Q3. Your strategy's OTR is approaching the venue limit by 14:00 each day. Which response is operationally sane?

  • Double the order rate to fill the book with quotes before the limit hits.
  • Tighten the strategy's internal re-quote logic (require larger price moves to update) so message count drops while keeping the strategy active.
  • Spoof additional sells to mark them as orders, lifting the denominator.
  • Disable the pre-trade risk check so orders get through faster.

Q4. OTR catches some bad behaviors but not all. Which is it NOT designed to catch?

  • Quote stuffing — flooding the venue with messages.
  • Sophisticated spoofing with low total message counts but manipulative intent.
  • Excessive system usage by honest high-cancel strategies.
  • Sudden order-rate spikes during news events.

9. Scenarios

S1. The strategy team complains "the OTR limit is killing our edge." How do you respond as the engineer?

First, check whether the strategy qualifies for designated market-maker status on the venue — if it provides genuine liquidity, the relaxed DMM limits may apply, in exchange for quoting obligations. Second, look at message efficiency: are the canceled orders adding economic value, or are they spurious re-quotes from poor signal stability? Smoothing the strategy's quote-update logic often drops OTR significantly without reducing alpha. Third, consider venue choice: some venues have higher limits for the same instrument. The "OTR limit is killing our edge" framing usually has a 30–50% operational improvement on top before any regulatory conversation is needed.

S2. Eurex changes its OTR parameters effective next quarter. The new transaction-based limit on your main instrument drops from 500 to 200. What's the operational plan?

Three weeks of preparation, broadly: (1) Modify the strategy's internal quote-update threshold so projected daily OTR comes in safely under 180 (with a 10% headroom for spikes). (2) Add real-time OTR monitoring to the dashboard so the trading desk sees the running count. (3) Run a one-week shadow deploy where the new logic is active but trades are unchanged, to validate that the OTR projection model matches reality. (4) Update the kill-switch logic so the strategy pauses at 95% of the new limit rather than 99% (more headroom). (5) Communicate to risk and compliance that the change is being made and update the playbook for what to do if the limit is hit.

  2. ESMA draft RTS on Microstructural Issues — MiFID II / algo trading
  3. Order to trade ratios and their impact on the Italian stock market — UK Government Office for Science
  4. Redesign of the OTR in the context of MiFID II — Eurex circular
  5. HFT Act: ESU Fee and OTR enhancements — Eurex circular
  6. Borsa Istanbul OTR Information Note

Lesson 0020Quiz: 0 / 4

Alternative Data — Four More Concrete Examples

Why this matters: Lesson 0015 covered the framework with Walmart parking lots and oil tanks. This lesson walks through four more concrete alt-data flavors that fund managers actually buy in 2024–25: cell-phone location, satellite parking lots, crop color (NDVI), and cargo-port activity (AIS).

1. Cell-phone location data

Aggregated, anonymized location pings from smartphone apps. Foursquare's CEO Jeff Glueck famously predicted in March 2016 that Chipotle Q1 sales would fall ~30%, based on declining foot-traffic at restaurants observed via Foursquare check-ins (in the wake of the E. coli outbreak).[1] The prediction was almost exactly right; the actual decline was 29.7%. Funds with the data shorted Chipotle into earnings.

Modern flavors:

  • Vendors: SafeGraph, Placer.ai, Veraset, Foursquare. Pricing: $50k–$500k/yr depending on coverage.
  • Signal: weekly per-store foot-traffic counts → daily/weekly retailer revenue estimates → quarterly print predictions.
  • Hot trades: retailers, restaurants, theme parks, gyms — anywhere foot-traffic correlates with revenue.
Privacy & legal: the data is aggregated and anonymized, but the supply chain (apps → data brokers → fund) has been under scrutiny since 2020. Multiple vendor shutdowns and FTC actions have happened. Future regulatory tightening is a real strategy-side risk.

2. Satellite parking-lot counts

The Lesson 0015 Walmart story refined for 2024–25. Modern vendors automate the CV pipeline with CNN-based car counting at scale, applied to hundreds of retail chains globally. Key providers include RS Metrics, Orbital Insight, SpaceKnow, and Planet Labs.[2]

Three improvements over the 2010-era version:

Sub-meter resolution

Commercial satellites at Maxar/Planet level can now resolve individual car make/model in good lighting, opening up demographic segmentation (luxury vs economy cars in the lot → customer mix shift).

Multi-temporal stacks

Same lot imaged daily; full time series of foot-traffic. Earlier vendors gave weekly snapshots; modern feeds are near-daily.

Cross-asset integration

Fused with the cell-phone data above — when both signals agree, the conviction is higher. When they disagree, that itself can be a tradable signal (one source has structural bias).

Decay is fast

The Walmart-style signal is now firmly textbook. Modern alpha is in newer angles: EV-charger usage as auto-industry leading indicator, drone footage of cattle herds, etc.

3. Crop color from satellites (NDVI)

NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) is calculated from satellite multispectral imagery:

NDVI = (NIR - RED) / (NIR + RED)        // values in [-1, +1]
                                          // healthy vegetation → ~0.6-0.9
                                          // stressed crops     → ~0.2-0.4
                                          // bare soil          → ~0

By imaging crop fields throughout the growing season, hedge funds can estimate yields for corn, soy, wheat, and other commodities weeks before USDA crop reports. The trade is on agricultural commodity futures or related stocks (Bunge, ADM, fertilizer companies, ag-equipment makers).[2]

The data flow:

  1. Satellites (Sentinel-2 is free; Planet/Maxar provide higher cadence) image crop regions weekly.
  2. NDVI computed pixel-by-pixel; aggregated by USDA crop region.
  3. Compared to historical NDVI trajectories at the same point in the season.
  4. Yield estimate published; commodity trader acts before USDA's monthly WASDE report.

4. Cargo-port activity (AIS + SAR)

Every commercial ship over 300 GT is required to broadcast its position via AIS (Automatic Identification System). Companies (MarineTraffic, Spire, Orbital Insight) ingest AIS feeds plus SAR satellite imagery to track:[3]

  • Ship-by-ship cargo capacity and route.
  • Port congestion (number of ships anchored vs berthed).
  • Ship-to-ship transfers (offshore transfers of crude oil, LNG) which often indicate sanctions-evasion or arbitrage activity.
  • Port-level inflows/outflows of specific cargo categories (containers, dry bulk, crude).

Trades downstream of cargo-port data:

  • Shipping rates (Baltic Dry Index futures): port congestion → tighter capacity → higher rates.
  • Commodity inventories: ship-tracked crude unloading at Cushing → inventory delta vs EIA expectations.
  • Retailer earnings: container throughput at LA/Long Beach → US import flow → earnings of import-heavy retailers.
  • Geopolitical: ship-to-ship transfers near sanctioned countries → real-time monitoring of sanctions efficacy.

5. The pattern repeated, with sharper edges

SignalDecay horizonCapacityHot use
Cell phoneDays–weeksMedium (retailers limited)Restaurant/retail earnings
Parking lotsNow textbookSmall (alpha eroded)Cross-validation with cell phone
NDVI / cropsWeeksMedium (commodities)Pre-WASDE positioning
AIS / cargoDaysLarge (multiple commodity classes)Shipping rates + commodity flow

6. In this project

The repo doesn't currently ingest any of these. A realistic build-out would target one signal end-to-end (say cargo-port AIS for the Drewry container-rate index) and fit it as an additional column in build_features alongside the technical features. Backtesting honestly requires the signal to have realistic delivery delay (satellite imagery isn't real-time; an AIS-derived inventory estimate may have 24-48h vendor processing lag), or the backtested alpha will be optimistic.

7. Often confused with

Cell-phone location vs Credit-card transactions

Both are "consumer behavior" alt-data. Location data is foot-traffic (people walking in). Transaction data is actual purchases (people checking out). The two correlate but aren't identical; using both reduces noise.

NDVI vs Soil-moisture

NDVI: vegetation health from visible/near-IR. Soil-moisture: ground water content from microwave bands or in-situ sensors. Complementary; both feed yield estimates.

AIS vs SAR for ships

AIS: broadcast positions ships report themselves. Can be spoofed/turned off. SAR: radar imagery from satellites, independent of ship cooperation. Combining catches "dark fleet" behavior AIS alone misses.

Alt-data vs Web-scraped data

Web scraping (Glassdoor reviews, Indeed job posts, eBay completed sales) is a subset of alt-data. The same framework applies — leads the official number, hard to replicate at scale, maps to a tradable.

8. Practice

Q1. What did Foursquare's CEO predict about Chipotle in March 2016, and what was the signal?

  • A menu price increase based on credit-card data.
  • A ~30% Q1 same-store sales decline, based on Foursquare check-in foot-traffic data.
  • A second E. coli outbreak based on health-app data.
  • A modest single-digit revenue beat based on earnings models.

Q2. NDVI is computed as (NIR - RED) / (NIR + RED). Why does this single ratio map to crop health?

  • Healthy chlorophyll absorbs red light and reflects near-infrared; NDVI captures that contrast as a single number that scales with photosynthetic activity.
  • It measures crop temperature.
  • It measures the soil's water content directly.
  • It compares this season's image to last season's at the same pixel.

Q3. Why do cargo-port analytics firms combine AIS and SAR data instead of using AIS alone?

  • Because AIS is only available in coastal waters.
  • Because ships can spoof or switch off AIS; SAR imagery sees them anyway, catching the 'dark fleet' for sanctions / arbitrage tracking.
  • Because SAR is cheaper per ship-day than AIS.
  • Because SEC rules require dual-source validation of marine data.

Q4. You backtest an NDVI-based corn yield signal and get Sharpe 2.5 over 2015–2024. Going live in 2025 the Sharpe is 0.4. Most likely cause?

  • The USDA changed its WASDE reporting schedule, making the signal late.
  • Standard alt-data alpha decay: more funds subscribed to similar NDVI signals between backtest end and live, so the alpha is now priced in faster than the model can react.
  • Satellite resolution has degraded since 2024.
  • A climate-driven shift in agronomy invalidating the historical model.

9. Scenarios

S1. A vendor pitches cell-phone foot-traffic data on 500 mid-cap retailers. Backtest looks great. What do you check before signing?

Three things. (1) Vendor exclusivity: ask how many other funds already subscribe. If the number is >5, alpha is probably already decayed. If it's 0 or under exclusivity, you may have a real edge. (2) Survivorship bias in the backtest: were the 500 names selected because they happened to have signal, or were they predetermined? Re-run on a frozen 2015 universe. (3) Realistic delivery delay: the data has processing lag (typically 1-3 days). Was the backtest using next-day-available data or future-cheating perfect-information? Re-backtest with realistic lag before you trust the Sharpe.

S2. You build a port-congestion signal and start trading container-rate futures. After 6 months your Sharpe is 1.5. Should you scale up the position size?

Cautiously. The strategy works but you have only 6 months of live performance — barely enough to distinguish skill from luck at Sharpe 1.5 (need ~2 years for statistical significance). Three checks before scaling: (1) Does the live P&L match the predicted-from-backtest P&L? Big divergence = something is different in live. (2) Has any new vendor entered the same niche? Decay is real. (3) Position scaling needs market-impact analysis: doubling your size in a thin futures contract may make your own trades move the price against you. The right move is usually a 20-30% size increase plus a 6-month re-evaluation, not a doubling.

Sources

  1. Your Mobile Phone as a Gold Mine (for hedge funds) — DataDrivenInvestor
  2. Satellite Data For Investors: Top Alternative Data Providers — Paragon Intel
  3. SAR + AIS Data for Hedge Funds — PierSight

Lesson 0021Quiz: 0 / 4

AI Preprocessing

Why this matters: the four-lesson AI mini-arc (preprocessing → object detection → segmentation → geometric calculus) prepares you to read modern CV/ML papers and tie them back to alt-data and HFT use cases. We start with the unsexy but load-bearing first step: preprocessing.

1. Why preprocessing is half the job

A common saying among ML engineers: "the model is 20% of the work; the data and preprocessing are 80%." Models are commoditized; getting clean, normalized, well-shaped inputs is where most of the real engineering happens. Preprocessing covers six operations, applied in roughly this order:

StepWhy
1. CleaningDrop NaN/Inf, fix dtypes, handle outliers, fix obvious errors (negative prices, dates in the future).
2. Normalization / scalingGet features onto comparable scales so gradient-based optimizers converge.
3. EncodingTurn non-numeric data (text, categories) into numbers the model can consume.
4. AugmentationSynthetic perturbations of training data to improve generalization (CV mostly).
5. Batching / shardingGroup examples into batches; shuffle for SGD; pad/truncate sequences.
6. SplittingTrain / val / test splits — chronological for time series; stratified for class imbalance.

2. Cleaning — small fixes, big impact

# In this repo's spirit: cleaning the OHLCV panel before training
def clean(df):
    df = df.dropna(subset=["Close"])             # drop rows missing the target driver
    df = df[df["Close"] > 0]                     # reject impossible prices
    df = df[df["Volume"] >= 0]
    df = df[df.index.duplicated(keep="last") == False]  # dedupe
    return df

The repo already does some of this via dropna() in build_features. Missed cases (negative volume, duplicates from data-vendor merges, dtype confusion when a column is loaded as string) are the ones that bite.

3. Normalization — the four common flavors

Min-max scaling

x_norm = (x - min) / (max - min)
Output ∈ [0,1]. Sensitive to outliers — one outlier crushes the rest of the range. Use only when bounds are known.

Standardization (z-score)

x_std = (x - mean) / std
Output has mean 0, std 1. Default for most tabular ML. Less outlier-sensitive than min-max.

Robust scaling

x_rob = (x - median) / IQR
Uses median and interquartile range. Resistant to outliers. Common for financial data with heavy tails.

Log transform

x_log = log(x + ε)
For strictly positive variables with right-skewed distributions (volume, price). Compresses tails before any other scaling.

The cardinal preprocessing sin in time-series ML: computing the normalization statistics (mean, std, max) using the entire dataset. This leaks future information into the training set. Always fit the scaler on training data only, then apply to validation/test/live. The repo's walkforward_sim.py structure (refit periodically using only past data) is the right shape.

4. Encoding categorical features

  • One-hot: sector="Tech" → [0,0,1,0,0,...]. Simple, works with any model, but expands dimensionality.
  • Target encoding: replace each category with the mean target value for that category. Powerful for high-cardinality features (e.g. ticker symbols) but introduces leakage if computed naively.
  • Embedding: learn a dense d-dimensional vector per category. The standard NN approach.
  • Ordinal: simple integer mapping. Useful only when categories have a meaningful order.

5. Augmentation — the CV staple

For image-based alt-data (satellite imagery, parking lots, oil tanks), augmentation creates synthetic training examples by perturbing real ones:

  • Geometric: rotate, flip, crop, scale. Teaches the model rotation invariance — important for satellite images where there's no canonical orientation.
  • Photometric: brightness, contrast, hue shifts. Handles different times of day, atmospheric conditions.
  • Cutout / mixup: mask random regions or blend two examples. Reduces overfitting on backgrounds.
  • Domain-specific: cloud occlusion for satellite imagery; SAR-vs-optical pairings.

For tabular data (this repo's GBM), augmentation is rare — the standard trick is feature engineering instead (lagged returns, rolling windows). Boosting models tend to overfit augmentation patterns more easily than NNs.

6. Batching, sharding, time-series splitting

NN training requires batches of fixed shape. For sequences (LOB snapshots, NLP):

  • Pad: short sequences padded to max length; masking tells the model to ignore padding.
  • Truncate: long sequences cut to max length.
  • Bucket: group sequences of similar length to minimize padding waste.

For time series, splits MUST be chronological:

def walkforward_split(df, train_end, test_end):
    train = df.loc[:train_end]
    test  = df.loc[train_end:test_end]
    return train, test

Random shuffles or k-fold are wrong for time series — they leak future into the past. The repo's walkforward_sim.py is the correct shape.

7. In this project

paper_trading_sim.py:build_features already does a small preprocessing pipeline: pct_change (transformation), rolling stats (feature engineering), dropna (cleaning), implicit scaling because gradient-boosted trees are scale-invariant (which is why the repo doesn't need a StandardScaler). The _rsi normalization by /100.0 is a manual range-shift to roughly [0,1].

What's missing for production: explicit outlier handling on returns (a single 200% jump from a data-vendor glitch can poison features for days), and chronological refit of any computed statistic. The walkforward_sim.py:--rolling_retrain path does the latter.

8. Often confused with

Preprocessing vs Feature engineering

Preprocessing: mechanical transformations (scale, encode, clean). Feature engineering: domain-driven creation of new features (rolling vol, RSI, moving averages). Different skill sets; overlapping in practice.

Normalization vs Standardization

Loose terms used interchangeably. Strictly: normalization = min-max to [0,1]; standardization = z-score to mean 0/std 1. Always check what the speaker means.

Augmentation vs Synthetic data

Augmentation: small perturbations of real examples. Synthetic data: entirely generated examples (GAN, simulator). Augmentation is mainstream; synthetic data is controversial in finance because the distribution it generates is itself a modeling choice.

Leakage vs Look-ahead bias

Leakage: features include information they shouldn't (e.g. target itself in features, computed scaler stats from test set). Look-ahead: target is shifted incorrectly so today's row uses tomorrow's information. Both result in optimistic backtests.

9. Practice

Q1. You fit a StandardScaler on the entire 10-year dataset, then split into train/test chronologically. What did you just do wrong?

  • You should have used min-max scaling instead.
  • You leaked future statistics (mean, std) into the training set via the scaler — the model's training-time transformation used information from the test period.
  • StandardScaler assumes Gaussian data, which financial returns aren't.
  • You spent compute on something the model already does internally.

Q2. Which preprocessing is LEAST relevant for the repo's GBM (gradient-boosted trees)?

  • Cleaning NaN and dtype issues.
  • Standardization (z-scoring) of input features.
  • Encoding categorical features.
  • Chronological train/test splitting.

Q3. You have satellite imagery for crop NDVI prediction. What's the right augmentation strategy?

  • Geometric (rotation, flip) + photometric (brightness, contrast) + cloud-occlusion simulation.
  • No augmentation — it would distort the NDVI signal.
  • Apply the augmentations at test time too for consistency.
  • Mixup — blend two random crop images for every training example.

Q4. The cardinal preprocessing sin in time-series ML is:

  • Applying log transform to prices.
  • Computing normalization statistics (mean, std, max) across the entire dataset rather than train-only.
  • Removing outliers before training.
  • Using one-hot encoding instead of embeddings.

10. Scenarios

S1. Your NN training loss plateaus at a suspiciously high value. You discover one feature has range [0, 1e6] while others are [0, 1]. What happened?

S2. A teammate adds 50 lagged features (return_1d, return_2d, ..., return_50d) to the GBM. Out-of-sample R² doesn't improve. Why?

Two likely causes. (1) Most of those lagged returns are highly correlated with each other (autocorrelation in returns is small but the features themselves are nearly redundant), so the model gets little new information. (2) The total feature count went from 7 to 57, multiplying the search space the GBM has to explore; on a small dataset (~10k rows) the model may not fit cleanly. The fix is feature selection: use feature_importances_ or SHAP to identify which lags contribute, drop the rest. Often a small set of strategically chosen lags (1, 5, 21) beats 50 of them.

Why this matters: the four-lesson AI mini-arc (preprocessing → object detection → segmentation → geometric calculus) prepares you to read modern CV/ML papers and tie them back to alt-data and HFT use cases. We start with the unsexy but load-bearing first step: preprocessing.

1. Why preprocessing is half the job

A common saying among ML engineers: "the model is 20% of the work; the data and preprocessing are 80%." Models are commoditized; getting clean, normalized, well-shaped inputs is where most of the real engineering happens. Preprocessing covers six operations, applied in roughly this order:

StepWhy
1. CleaningDrop NaN/Inf, fix dtypes, handle outliers, fix obvious errors (negative prices, dates in the future).
2. Normalization / scalingGet features onto comparable scales so gradient-based optimizers converge.
3. EncodingTurn non-numeric data (text, categories) into numbers the model can consume.
4. AugmentationSynthetic perturbations of training data to improve generalization (CV mostly).
5. Batching / shardingGroup examples into batches; shuffle for SGD; pad/truncate sequences.
6. SplittingTrain / val / test splits — chronological for time series; stratified for class imbalance.

2. Cleaning — small fixes, big impact

# In this repo's spirit: cleaning the OHLCV panel before training
def clean(df):
    df = df.dropna(subset=["Close"])             # drop rows missing the target driver
    df = df[df["Close"] > 0]                     # reject impossible prices
    df = df[df["Volume"] >= 0]
    df = df[df.index.duplicated(keep="last") == False]  # dedupe
    return df

The repo already does some of this via dropna() in build_features. Missed cases (negative volume, duplicates from data-vendor merges, dtype confusion when a column is loaded as string) are the ones that bite.

3. Normalization — the four common flavors

Min-max scaling

x_norm = (x - min) / (max - min)
Output ∈ [0,1]. Sensitive to outliers — one outlier crushes the rest of the range. Use only when bounds are known.

Standardization (z-score)

x_std = (x - mean) / std
Output has mean 0, std 1. Default for most tabular ML. Less outlier-sensitive than min-max.

Robust scaling

x_rob = (x - median) / IQR
Uses median and interquartile range. Resistant to outliers. Common for financial data with heavy tails.

Log transform

x_log = log(x + ε)
For strictly positive variables with right-skewed distributions (volume, price). Compresses tails before any other scaling.

The cardinal preprocessing sin in time-series ML: computing the normalization statistics (mean, std, max) using the entire dataset. This leaks future information into the training set. Always fit the scaler on training data only, then apply to validation/test/live. The repo's walkforward_sim.py structure (refit periodically using only past data) is the right shape.

4. Encoding categorical features

  • One-hot: sector="Tech" → [0,0,1,0,0,...]. Simple, works with any model, but expands dimensionality.
  • Target encoding: replace each category with the mean target value for that category. Powerful for high-cardinality features (e.g. ticker symbols) but introduces leakage if computed naively.
  • Embedding: learn a dense d-dimensional vector per category. The standard NN approach.
  • Ordinal: simple integer mapping. Useful only when categories have a meaningful order.

5. Augmentation — the CV staple

For image-based alt-data (satellite imagery, parking lots, oil tanks), augmentation creates synthetic training examples by perturbing real ones:

  • Geometric: rotate, flip, crop, scale. Teaches the model rotation invariance — important for satellite images where there's no canonical orientation.
  • Photometric: brightness, contrast, hue shifts. Handles different times of day, atmospheric conditions.
  • Cutout / mixup: mask random regions or blend two examples. Reduces overfitting on backgrounds.
  • Domain-specific: cloud occlusion for satellite imagery; SAR-vs-optical pairings.

For tabular data (this repo's GBM), augmentation is rare — the standard trick is feature engineering instead (lagged returns, rolling windows). Boosting models tend to overfit augmentation patterns more easily than NNs.

6. Batching, sharding, time-series splitting

NN training requires batches of fixed shape. For sequences (LOB snapshots, NLP):

  • Pad: short sequences padded to max length; masking tells the model to ignore padding.
  • Truncate: long sequences cut to max length.
  • Bucket: group sequences of similar length to minimize padding waste.

For time series, splits MUST be chronological:

def walkforward_split(df, train_end, test_end):
    train = df.loc[:train_end]
    test  = df.loc[train_end:test_end]
    return train, test

Random shuffles or k-fold are wrong for time series — they leak future into the past. The repo's walkforward_sim.py is the correct shape.

7. In this project

paper_trading_sim.py:build_features already does a small preprocessing pipeline: pct_change (transformation), rolling stats (feature engineering), dropna (cleaning), implicit scaling because gradient-boosted trees are scale-invariant (which is why the repo doesn't need a StandardScaler). The _rsi normalization by /100.0 is a manual range-shift to roughly [0,1].

What's missing for production: explicit outlier handling on returns (a single 200% jump from a data-vendor glitch can poison features for days), and chronological refit of any computed statistic. The walkforward_sim.py:--rolling_retrain path does the latter.

8. Often confused with

Preprocessing vs Feature engineering

Preprocessing: mechanical transformations (scale, encode, clean). Feature engineering: domain-driven creation of new features (rolling vol, RSI, moving averages). Different skill sets; overlapping in practice.

Normalization vs Standardization

Loose terms used interchangeably. Strictly: normalization = min-max to [0,1]; standardization = z-score to mean 0/std 1. Always check what the speaker means.

Augmentation vs Synthetic data

Augmentation: small perturbations of real examples. Synthetic data: entirely generated examples (GAN, simulator). Augmentation is mainstream; synthetic data is controversial in finance because the distribution it generates is itself a modeling choice.

Leakage vs Look-ahead bias

Leakage: features include information they shouldn't (e.g. target itself in features, computed scaler stats from test set). Look-ahead: target is shifted incorrectly so today's row uses tomorrow's information. Both result in optimistic backtests.

Lesson 0022Quiz: 0 / 4

AI: Object Detection

Why this matters: the alt-data lessons (0015, 0020) leaned on "count cars in parking lots" and "count ships in ports." That counting is object detection. This lesson formalizes what object detection is, the three modern model families, and what you'd actually deploy on a satellite-imagery pipeline.

1. Classification vs Detection vs Segmentation

TaskOutputExample
ClassificationOne label for the whole image."this image contains a parking lot"
Object detectionA list of bounding boxes, each with a class label and confidence score."car at (x=120, y=340, w=80, h=40), confidence 0.95"
Semantic segmentationA class label for every pixel."these pixels are cars, those are asphalt, those are grass" (Lesson 0023)
Instance segmentationA mask + class for every individual object."this clump of pixels is car #1, that clump is car #2" (Lesson 0023)

For an alt-data pipeline that counts cars at Walmart parking lots, you'd typically use object detection (boxes + count) for speed, falling back to instance segmentation (Lesson 0023) when cars are partially occluded or touching.

2. The three model families

Family 1: Two-stage detectors (R-CNN, Faster R-CNN)

Stage 1: a Region Proposal Network suggests ~1000 candidate boxes where objects might be. Stage 2: a classifier inspects each candidate. Accurate but slow because of the two passes. Production has largely moved on from this family — too slow for real-time, no clear accuracy advantage over modern alternatives.

Family 2: Single-stage detectors (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet)

One pass: the model directly emits boxes + classes for the whole image in a single forward pass. The YOLO ("You Only Look Once") series dominates production:

  • YOLOv5–YOLOv11: Ultralytics-maintained PyTorch implementations. Fast, accurate, easy to fine-tune. Default choice for most production pipelines in 2024–25.
  • YOLOv8/v11: native instance-segmentation head bolted on, blurring the line with the segmentation lesson.

YOLO's appeal: a small image-tiles → boxes pipeline, ~30 FPS on a commodity GPU, easy to fine-tune on 100s of labeled examples.

Family 3: Transformer-based (DETR, RT-DETR, Grounding DINO)

DETR ("DEtection TRansformer", Facebook 2020): treats detection as a set-prediction problem solved by a transformer over image patches. Simpler pipeline (no anchors, no NMS) but slower convergence. Modern variants (RT-DETR from Baidu, 2023) have caught up to YOLO on speed and surpass it on accuracy for many tasks.

Grounding DINO (2023): open-vocabulary detection. Give a text prompt ("car", "ship", "shipping container") and the model finds all instances. Hugely valuable for alt-data because you can detect arbitrary new classes without retraining.

3. The standard detection output

# Each detection is a 6-tuple
detection = {
    "x": 120,           # top-left x in pixels
    "y": 340,           # top-left y in pixels
    "w": 80,            # width
    "h": 40,            # height
    "class_id": 2,      # 2 = car (per training-set ontology)
    "confidence": 0.95  # model's certainty in [0, 1]
}

Two key concepts on top of this output:

  • NMS (Non-Maximum Suppression): the model often emits multiple overlapping boxes for the same object. NMS keeps the highest-confidence box and suppresses overlapping ones with IoU above a threshold (typically 0.5).
  • IoU (Intersection over Union): metric for box overlap = area of intersection / area of union. 1.0 = identical boxes; 0 = no overlap.

4. Evaluation metrics

MetricDefinitionWhen to use
Precision(true positives) / (true positives + false positives)When false alarms are costly.
Recall(true positives) / (true positives + false negatives)When missing real objects is costly.
AP@IoU=0.5Average Precision at IoU threshold 0.5Headline benchmark metric.
mAP@[0.5:0.95]Mean AP averaged across IoU thresholds 0.5–0.95COCO standard, harder metric.

5. Production: counting cars at Walmart (illustrative)

from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolov11m.pt")                # pretrained on COCO
results = model("walmart_2025-06-10.png",    # satellite tile
                classes=[2],                  # COCO class 2 = 'car'
                conf=0.3,                      # confidence threshold
                iou=0.5)                       # NMS IoU threshold

car_count = len(results[0].boxes)
print(f"Cars detected: {car_count}")

That's the entire engineering of an alt-data signal in 8 lines. The real work is:

  1. Domain-shift fine-tuning — COCO is street-level cars; satellite cars look completely different (top-down, small, low contrast). Fine-tune on a few thousand labeled satellite tiles.
  2. Tiling — a satellite image of a parking lot is huge (10000×10000 pixels). Cut into overlapping tiles, run YOLO on each, merge results.
  3. Calibration — your model emits raw counts; you need a calibration function that maps counts → estimated revenue → trade signal.
  4. Drift monitoring — accuracy degrades over time as fashions, vehicle shapes, and parking layouts change. Need ongoing retraining.

6. Often confused with

Object detection vs Classification

Classification: one label for the image. Detection: many objects, each with a box and label. Detection subsumes classification when there's one detection per image.

YOLO vs DETR

YOLO: convnet-based, single-stage, NMS-based. Mature, fast. DETR: transformer-based, set-prediction, no NMS. Cleaner conceptually; slower to train; modern variants competitive.

Detection vs Tracking

Detection: per-frame, no memory. Tracking: maintains object identity across frames. For static satellite imagery, detection is enough; for video of port activity, tracking is needed.

Closed-set vs Open-vocabulary

Closed-set: model knows N predefined classes; can only output those. Open-vocabulary: detect any class described by a text prompt (Grounding DINO). The latter is transformative for alt-data exploration.

7. Practice

Q1. Why does object detection use NMS (Non-Maximum Suppression)?

  • To regularize training when the model overfits to common classes.
  • To collapse multiple overlapping predictions for the same object down to one, keeping the highest-confidence box.
  • To augment training data with rotated copies of each image.
  • To reduce GPU memory usage during training.

Q2. You use a YOLO model pretrained on COCO to count cars in satellite imagery. Performance is poor. Most likely cause?

  • YOLO doesn't natively output bounding boxes.
  • COCO's cars are street-level and large; satellite views are top-down and small — pretrained features don't transfer. Fine-tuning on satellite-specific data is required.
  • YOLO can only process images up to 640x640 pixels.
  • Satellite imagery is grayscale while YOLO expects color.

Q3. What makes Grounding DINO different from a standard YOLO-style detector?

  • It's faster at inference.
  • It's open-vocabulary: given a text prompt, it detects arbitrary classes without retraining. Standard YOLO has a fixed ontology.
  • It doesn't require any training data.
  • It runs only on quantum hardware.

Q4. mAP@[0.5:0.95] is a stricter metric than AP@0.5. Why?

  • It averages over more classes.
  • It requires tighter box localization at IoU thresholds up to 0.95, where small box errors fail.
  • It uses a stricter confidence threshold.
  • It evaluates on a held-out test set instead of validation.

8. Scenarios

S1. Your YOLO car-counter trained on suburban malls performs poorly on dense urban parking garages. Why?

Distribution shift. The training set's cars were spaced out on open asphalt; in urban garages they're packed tightly, often partially occluded, and the lighting is much different. YOLO's anchor-based proposal density doesn't handle very dense overlapping objects well. Three responses: (1) fine-tune on labeled urban-garage data; (2) lower the NMS IoU threshold so densely packed cars aren't suppressed by their neighbors; (3) switch to an instance-segmentation model (Lesson 0023) that's better at touching-but-distinct objects. Option 1 is the cleanest and the others are emergency fixes.

S2. You want a single model that detects cars, trucks, ships, and storage tanks at a hedge fund. Build one big model or four specialized ones?

Probably four specialized ones, then a shared inference framework. Reasons: (1) the optimal image resolution differs — cars need fine resolution, storage tanks are fine at lower res; (2) the fine-tuning datasets are sourced separately and have very different sizes; (3) deploying changes to one class won't risk regressing the others; (4) model size scales sub-linearly with class count, so four small models is comparable cost to one large one. Single multi-task models are seductive but practically fragile for production alt-data pipelines.

Sources

  1. Ultralytics YOLOv8/v11 documentation
  2. DETR — End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers (Carion et al, 2020)
  3. Grounding DINO — open-vocabulary detection (Liu et al, 2023)
  4. COCO dataset and evaluation metrics

Lesson 0023Quiz: 0 / 4

AI: Segmentation

Why this matters: object detection (Lesson 0022) draws boxes around objects. Segmentation goes a level deeper — it labels every pixel. For alt-data pipelines like crop NDVI (Lesson 0020) or oil-tank fill detection (Lesson 0015), segmentation is the natural tool because the question is "what is this pixel?" not "where is this object?"

1. The three segmentation tasks

TaskOutputDistinguishes individual instances?
Semantic segmentationEvery pixel gets a class label.No. All "car" pixels are the same class.
Instance segmentationEvery pixel gets a class + instance ID.Yes. "Car 1" and "Car 2" are separate.
Panoptic segmentationCombines the two. "Things" (countable: cars, ships) get instance IDs; "stuff" (uncountable: sky, road, water) gets only a class.For things, yes; for stuff, no.

2. Why segmentation for alt-data

Crop NDVI (Lesson 0020)

You want the NDVI only over crop pixels, not over roads, buildings, or water. Semantic segmentation produces a crop mask which you then apply to the NDVI map.

Oil-tank fill detection

The tank's outline is needed to measure the shadow length of the floating roof. Semantic segmentation gives the tank's boundary; analysis runs on the bounded region.

Port activity

Counting ships needs instance segmentation — touching ships need to be distinguished from one another. Box-based detection alone fails when ships are docked side-by-side.

Building footprint extraction

Urbanization signals for property markets. Semantic seg gives building/non-building pixels; instance seg gives individual buildings.

3. The model families

(a) U-Net (2015): the OG semantic segmentation architecture

An encoder-decoder convnet with skip connections between corresponding encoder and decoder layers. The encoder downsamples (gathering context); the decoder upsamples (recovering resolution); skip connections preserve fine detail. Still a strong baseline for satellite imagery; trivially small to train.[1]

(b) Mask R-CNN (2017): instance segmentation by extension

Take Faster R-CNN's two-stage detection, add a mask-prediction head on top of each detected box. Outputs per-instance pixel masks. Slower than YOLO but the standard baseline for instance segmentation in research.

(c) SAM — Segment Anything Model (Meta, 2023)

A foundation model for segmentation. Trained on 11M images with 1.1B masks. Given a prompt (a point, a box, or text), SAM produces a high-quality mask for the indicated region — without per-domain fine-tuning.[2]

SAM is a step-change for alt-data:

  • You can prompt with a point ("segment whatever's here") and SAM produces a mask.
  • Combine with Grounding DINO (Lesson 0022) for text-driven prompts → fully open-vocabulary instance segmentation.
  • Fine-tuning is optional for many tasks; it works zero-shot.

(d) Transformer-based (Mask2Former, SegFormer)

Adopt the DETR-style set-prediction approach for segmentation. Strong on panoptic tasks; competitive with CNNs in 2024–25.

4. The standard output

# Semantic segmentation output: a 2D array same size as the input image,
# each cell holds an integer class label.
mask = model(image)            # shape: (H, W), values in [0, num_classes-1]

# Instance segmentation output: a list of (binary_mask, class_id, confidence)
instances = model(image)
for inst in instances:
    binary_mask = inst["mask"]   # shape: (H, W), boolean
    class_id    = inst["cls"]
    score       = inst["score"]

MetricDefinitionUse
Pixel accuracyFraction of pixels classified correctly.Bad for imbalanced classes (background dominates).
mIoU (mean IoU)Mean of IoU across all classes.Headline metric for semantic segmentation.
Dice coefficient2·|A∩B| / (|A|+|B|). Equivalent to F1 for binary masks.Common in medical imaging; also fine for satellite.
AP@maskAverage precision computed on mask-IoU rather than box-IoU.Instance segmentation benchmark.

6. Illustrative pipeline: oil-tank fill from satellite

# 1. Detect tanks (box-level) with a YOLO-family model.
boxes = yolo(satellite_tile, classes=["oil_tank"])

for box in boxes:
    # 2. Crop to the tank box, run SAM with the box as prompt → fine mask.
    tank_crop = crop(satellite_tile, box)
    mask      = sam(tank_crop, prompt=box)

    # 3. Find the floating-roof shadow inside the tank mask.
    shadow_mask = detect_shadow(tank_crop, mask)

    # 4. Convert shadow length + tank diameter + sun angle → roof height → fill level.
    fill_pct = geometry(shadow_mask, box.w, sun_elevation)
    emit(box.center_latlon, fill_pct)

That's the structure of one of the most lucrative alt-data feeds in the industry — Ursa Space's oil-tank inventory product (Lesson 0015) is a polished production version of this pattern.

Semantic vs Instance segmentation

Semantic: all "car" pixels look identical in the output. Instance: each individual car has its own ID. Counting requires instance.

Panoptic vs Instance

Panoptic: includes "stuff" classes (sky, road) for which instance IDs make no sense. Instance: typically only outputs masks for the things you care about, ignoring backgrounds.

SAM vs U-Net

SAM: prompt-driven foundation model, zero-shot for many tasks. U-Net: train per task, much smaller, deployable on edge devices.

Mask R-CNN vs YOLO-seg

Both do instance segmentation. Mask R-CNN: two-stage, more accurate, slower. YOLO-seg (v8/v11): single-stage, fast, real-time. YOLO-seg has largely supplanted Mask R-CNN in production.

8. Practice

Q1. You need to count ships in a satellite image of a port. Two ships are docked side-by-side. Which task is the minimum required?

  • Semantic segmentation.
  • Instance segmentation.
  • Image classification.
  • Object detection with NMS.

Q2. SAM (Segment Anything Model) is described as a "foundation model for segmentation." What does that mean operationally?

  • It produces high-quality masks zero-shot or with simple prompts (point, box, text) across many domains without per-task training.
  • It achieves 100% accuracy on any imagery domain.
  • It's so small it fits on embedded hardware.
  • It learns segmentation without any labeled data.

Q3. For crop NDVI estimation, you need to mask out non-crop pixels (roads, buildings, water) before averaging NDVI. Which segmentation task is the right fit?

  • Semantic segmentation — a binary crop/non-crop mask per pixel.
  • Instance segmentation of every individual field.
  • Object detection with bounding boxes around each field.
  • Image classification: 'this image contains crops or it doesn't'.

Q4. Why is pixel accuracy a misleading metric for satellite segmentation tasks?

  • Satellite images are too high-resolution.
  • Background classes typically dominate, so a model that predicts everything as background scores ~90% pixel accuracy without learning anything. mIoU and Dice are robust to imbalance.
  • It doesn't measure what you actually want to measure.
  • It's too expensive to compute at scale.

9. Scenarios

S1. You build a SAM-based pipeline for cargo-container counting at a port. Throughput is too slow for daily updates over global ports. How do you accelerate?

Two-stage cascade. Use a fast lightweight detector (YOLO) to box candidate ports/containers; only run SAM on the cropped boxes. SAM is computationally expensive at full image scale but cheap on small crops. Expected speedup: 10–100× depending on how empty the imagery is. Second-line speedup: use SAM's smaller variants (MobileSAM, FastSAM) which trade some mask quality for big speed wins.

S2. Your panoptic segmentation model trained on aerial urban imagery shows excellent mIoU but the segmentation looks visually wrong on edges. What's wrong with the metric?

mIoU is averaged across the whole mask area. A large object with a slightly wrong boundary loses very little IoU because the boundary pixels are a small fraction of the total. So the model can have great mIoU and ugly edges. Two fixes: (1) use the boundary-IoU metric explicitly, which penalizes boundary errors; (2) add a boundary-aware loss term during training (DiceBoundaryLoss, Focal-edge). For applications like building-footprint extraction the boundary IS the product, so this matters a lot.

Sources

  1. U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation (Ronneberger et al, 2015)
  2. Segment Anything (Kirillov et al, Meta AI, 2023)
  3. Ultralytics YOLO segmentation docs
