AI: Geometric Calculus & Geometric Deep Learning

Why this matters: "geometric calculus" in modern ML usage points at geometric deep learning — neural networks built on non-Euclidean structures (graphs, manifolds, Lie groups). This is where the most rigorous structural-prior ML work lives in 2025, and it's directly relevant to quant: portfolios are graphs, returns live on manifolds, symmetries matter.

1. The big idea

Classical neural networks assume data lives in flat Euclidean space ℝⁿ. A lot of real data does not.[1]

Data typeActual structureSymmetry the model should respect
ImagesPixels on a 2D gridTranslation (object can move)
3D moleculesAtoms in ℝ³Rotation + translation (chemistry doesn't depend on orientation)
Social networkGraph of nodes + edgesNode permutation (relabeling shouldn't change meaning)
Robot poseElement of SE(3) — Lie group of rigid motionsLie group composition
Stock returnsPoints on the simplex (weights sum to 1) or on the cone of positive-definite covariance matricesRiemannian structure of these manifolds

Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) is the program of designing neural networks that are equivariant to the natural symmetries of the data. A model is equivariant to a transformation if applying the transformation to the input and applying it to the output give the same result.

2. The four pillars (Bronstein-style taxonomy)

1. CNNs — grids

Translation-equivariant by design. The convolution operation produces the same response whether the dog is in the upper-left or center-right of the image. The foundational geometric DL architecture, although it predated the framing.

2. GNNs — graphs

Permutation-equivariant by message passing. The graph is the data; nodes pass messages to neighbors; aggregation must be order-independent (sum, max, mean). PyTorch Geometric is the workhorse library.[2]

3. Group-equivariant networks — Lie groups

Generalization of CNNs to arbitrary symmetry groups. For 3D molecules: SE(3)-equivariant networks (e3nn, SEGNN). Used in AlphaFold and modern protein-structure prediction.[3]

4. Manifold networks — Riemannian

Networks that operate on data lying on curved manifolds (sphere, hyperbolic space, SPD matrices). Geomstats is the standard library; used in covariance-matrix learning, hyperbolic embeddings of hierarchies.[4]

3. "Geometric calculus" specifically

The phrase has two flavors in 2024–25 usage:

Flavor A: differential geometry on neural nets

Treating the loss landscape, the data manifold, or the parameter space as Riemannian objects. Practical artifacts:

  • Riemannian optimizers: Adam/SGD adapted to non-Euclidean parameter spaces. Used when weights are constrained to live on a manifold (orthogonal matrices, SPD covariances).
  • Information geometry: the Fisher information matrix turns the parameter space into a Riemannian manifold; natural gradient descent moves along its geodesics.
  • Neural ODEs on manifolds: extend the ResNet → neural-ODE bridge to curved spaces. 2025 active research direction with extensions to Lie groups.[5]

Flavor B: geometric algebra in neural nets

The Clifford / geometric-algebra formalism — multivectors, the geometric product — applied as neural network operations. Promising for physics-informed ML and for rotation-equivariant networks; not yet mainstream.

4. Why a quant should care

Three concrete touchpoints, none yet in this repo:

(a) GNN for portfolio risk modeling

The "graph of stocks" is naturally encoded as a GNN — nodes are tickers, edges encode sector / supply-chain / correlation relationships. Message passing learns embeddings that respect graph structure. Used by some quant funds as a feature-engineering step for cross-sectional ranking.

(b) SPD-manifold learning for covariance matrices

The covariance matrix Σ from Lesson 0006 lives on the cone of symmetric positive-definite matrices — a Riemannian manifold, not a Euclidean space. Standard ML treats it as a flat vector and loses structure. Riemannian methods (e.g. log-Euclidean metric) train portfolio optimization more stably. Direct application to predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only.

(c) Lie-group equivariance for time-series symmetries

Some time-series have natural group symmetries (e.g. time-shifting, sign reversal under sign of return). Equivariant networks exploit these explicitly; standard CNNs ignore them. Active research direction in 2025.[3]

5. Illustrative GNN code (PyTorch Geometric)

from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv
import torch.nn as nn

class PortfolioGNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hid_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = GCNConv(in_dim, hid_dim)
        self.conv2 = GCNConv(hid_dim, hid_dim)
        self.head  = nn.Linear(hid_dim, 1)         # predicted return per node

    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        # x: [num_tickers, features], edge_index: [2, num_edges]
        h = self.conv1(x, edge_index).relu()
        h = self.conv2(h, edge_index).relu()
        return self.head(h).squeeze(-1)        # shape: [num_tickers]

The model is permutation-equivariant: relabeling the tickers gives a relabeled output. The cross-sectional prediction GBM in this repo also has that property (it doesn't use ticker identity), but GBM doesn't exploit edge structure; the GNN does.

6. Often confused with

Equivariant vs Invariant

Equivariant: f(g·x) = g·f(x). The output transforms predictably. Invariant: f(g·x) = f(x). The output ignores the transformation. Image-classification networks are translation-invariant; segmentation networks are translation-equivariant.

GNN vs Transformer

A transformer is technically a fully-connected GNN with attention as message-passing. Modern GNN research often borrows attention from transformers. The line is blurry; "GNN" usually implies sparse graphs.

Riemannian vs Euclidean optimization

Euclidean: SGD/Adam in ℝⁿ. Riemannian: SGD/Adam along geodesics of a curved manifold. Required when weights are constrained (orthogonal, SPD).

Geometric DL vs Physics-informed ML

Geometric DL: respect data symmetries via architecture. Physics-informed: respect physical laws via loss-function constraints. Different mechanisms, overlapping goals.

7. Practice

Q1. Why is a CNN considered translation-equivariant rather than translation-invariant?

  • Because they use padding and stride.
  • Because shifting the input shifts the feature maps correspondingly; the network's response transforms with the transformation, rather than ignoring it.
  • Because of skip connections.
  • Because pixels are permutation-equivariant.

Q2. The covariance matrix in predict_next.py lives on the cone of SPD matrices, a Riemannian manifold. Why might Riemannian ML be relevant?

  • Riemannian methods respect the SPD constraint by construction; Euclidean treatment can produce non-SPD outputs that break downstream optimization.
  • Because Riemannian methods are computationally faster.
  • Because they make the covariance matrix easier to interpret.
  • Because they reduce the bandwidth of market-data feeds.

Q3. Equivariance vs Invariance — which is correct?

  • Equivariant means the output is unchanged by the transformation.
  • Invariant: the output ignores the transformation. Equivariant: the output transforms with the input in a predictable way.
  • Equivariant and invariant are synonyms in this context.
  • Invariant only applies to RNNs; equivariant only to CNNs.

Q4. A teammate proposes using a GNN to predict stock returns where nodes are tickers and edges encode sector and supply-chain relationships. What's the structural advantage over the repo's GBM?

  • GNNs train faster than gradient-boosted trees.
  • It explicitly models inter-ticker relationships via message passing on the graph, capturing sector and supply-chain co-movement that the GBM ignores.
  • It automatically reduces overfitting by adding more parameters.
  • It produces inference at lower latency than tree ensembles.

8. Scenarios

S1. You implement a GNN for portfolio prediction with sector-edge graphs. It performs WORSE than the simple GBM. Diagnose the most likely causes.

Three usual suspects. (1) Graph topology is wrong: sector classifications are coarse and miss real economic relationships. Try edge weights based on returns-correlation or supply-chain data rather than industry codes. (2) Insufficient data: GNNs have more parameters than GBMs and need more rows. With 10k daily samples, the GNN may underfit while the GBM works on the same data. (3) Wrong aggregation: simple message-passing averages neighbors. Maybe you need attention-based aggregation (GAT) or skip connections. (4) Most boringly: the GBM was already exploiting all the signal there is. Sometimes the simpler model is just right; geometric structure isn't always available alpha.

S2. Your covariance-matrix-on-SPD-manifold work seems mathematically elegant but doesn't improve Sharpe in backtest. Should you ship it?

Probably not, but the framing matters. Riemannian SPD methods do improve numerical stability of the mean-variance optimization (the matrix inverse used in Σ⁻¹μ can blow up with naïve estimation). If your existing covariance pipeline already shrinks toward diagonal and adds regularization (as the repo's --shrink does), the numerical benefit is small. The mathematical elegance doesn't automatically translate to Sharpe. Either way, the right metric is Sharpe + drawdown + stability under regime change, not aesthetic appeal. Ship only if the empirical evidence is there.

Sources

  1. A Friendly Primer on Geometric Deep Learning — Patrick Nicolas (Substack)
  2. PyTorch Geometric documentation
  3. Lie Group-Based Neural Networks — EmergentMind
  4. Geomstats — Riemannian geometry for ML
  5. Geometric Neural ODEs: From Manifolds to Lie Groups — MDPI Entropy (2025)

        return self.head(h).squeeze(-1)        # shape: [num_tickers]

The model is permutation-equivariant: relabeling the tickers gives a relabeled output. The cross-sectional prediction GBM in this repo also has that property (it doesn't use ticker identity), but GBM doesn't exploit edge structure; the GNN does.

6. Often confused with

Equivariant vs Invariant

Equivariant: f(g·x) = g·f(x). The output transforms predictably. Invariant: f(g·x) = f(x). The output ignores the transformation. Image-classification networks are translation-invariant; segmentation networks are translation-equivariant.

GNN vs Transformer

A transformer is technically a fully-connected GNN with attention as message-passing. Modern GNN research often borrows attention from transformers. The line is blurry; "GNN" usually implies sparse graphs.

Riemannian vs Euclidean optimization

Euclidean: SGD/Adam in ℝⁿ. Riemannian: SGD/Adam along geodesics of a curved manifold. Required when weights are constrained (orthogonal, SPD).

Geometric DL vs Physics-informed ML

Geometric DL: respect data symmetries via architecture. Physics-informed: respect physical laws via loss-function constraints. Different mechanisms, overlapping goals.

7. Practice

Q1. Why is a CNN considered translation-equivariant rather than translation-invariant?

  • Because they use padding and stride.
  • Because shifting the input shifts the feature maps correspondingly; the network's response transforms with the transformation, rather than ignoring it.
  • Because of skip connections.
  • Because pixels are permutation-equivariant.

Q2. The covariance matrix in predict_next.py lives on the cone of SPD matrices, a Riemannian manifold. Why might Riemannian ML be relevant?

  • Riemannian methods respect the SPD constraint by construction; Euclidean treatment can produce non-SPD outputs that break downstream optimization.
  • Because Riemannian methods are computationally faster.
  • Because they make the covariance matrix easier to interpret.
  • Because they reduce the bandwidth of market-data feeds.

Q3. Equivariance vs Invariance — which is correct?

  • Equivariant means the output is unchanged by the transformation.
  • Invariant: the output ignores the transformation. Equivariant: the output transforms with the input in a predictable way.
  • Equivariant and invariant are synonyms in this context.
  • Invariant only applies to RNNs; equivariant only to CNNs.

Q4. A teammate proposes using a GNN to predict stock returns where nodes are tickers and edges encode sector and supply-chain relationships. What's the structural advantage over the repo's GBM?

  • GNNs train faster than gradient-boosted trees.
  • It explicitly models inter-ticker relationships via message passing on the graph, capturing sector and supply-chain co-movement that the GBM ignores.
  • It automatically reduces overfitting by adding more parameters.
  • It produces inference at lower latency than tree ensembles.

8. Scenarios

S1. You implement a GNN for portfolio prediction with sector-edge graphs. It performs WORSE than the simple GBM. Diagnose the most likely causes.

Three usual suspects. (1) Graph topology is wrong: sector classifications are coarse and miss real economic relationships. Try edge weights based on returns-correlation or supply-chain data rather than industry codes. (2) Insufficient data: GNNs have more parameters than GBMs and need more rows. With 10k daily samples, the GNN may underfit while the GBM works on the same data. (3) Wrong aggregation: simple message-passing averages neighbors. Maybe you need attention-based aggregation (GAT) or skip connections. (4) Most boringly: the GBM was already exploiting all the signal there is. Sometimes the simpler model is just right; geometric structure isn't always available alpha.

S2. Your covariance-matrix-on-SPD-manifold work seems mathematically elegant but doesn't improve Sharpe in backtest. Should you ship it?

Probably not, but the framing matters. Riemannian SPD methods do improve numerical stability of the mean-variance optimization (the matrix inverse used in Σ⁻¹μ can blow up with naïve estimation). If your existing covariance pipeline already shrinks toward diagonal and adds regularization (as the repo's --shrink does), the numerical benefit is small. The mathematical elegance doesn't automatically translate to Sharpe. Either way, the right metric is Sharpe + drawdown + stability under regime change, not aesthetic appeal. Ship only if the empirical evidence is there.

Sources

  1. A Friendly Primer on Geometric Deep Learning — Patrick Nicolas (Substack)
  2. PyTorch Geometric documentation
  3. Lie Group-Based Neural Networks — EmergentMind
  4. Geomstats — Riemannian geometry for ML
  5. Geometric Neural ODEs: From Manifolds to Lie Groups — MDPI Entropy (2025)

### Tower spacing / Hop length — `intro`
Practical distance between consecutive microwave repeater towers, typically
40–70 km on long-haul HFT links. Limited by Earth's curvature and tower
height. Each hop adds ~10s of ns of equipment latency.

---

## Added in Lessons 0013–0024 (batch update, 2026-06-10)

Compact form: one-line definitions grouped by source lesson. Promote to fuller
entries as terms get used in conversation.

### From Lesson 0013 (DMA)

- **Direct Market Access (Trading DMA)** — Buy-side firm submits orders directly to the exchange matching engine through a broker's infrastructure, no human in between.
- **Sponsored Access** — Lowest-latency form of DMA where the buy-side uses the broker's MPID and connectivity but skips most of the broker's order-management stack.
- **Naked access** — Pre-2011 sponsored access with no pre-trade risk filter. Prohibited by Rule 15c3-5.
- **MPID** — Market Participant Identifier, the 4-character code identifying a broker on a venue. Sponsored customers trade under their sponsor's MPID.
- **FIX protocol** — The dominant exchange messaging protocol for orders. NewOrderSingle = 35=D.
- **SEC Rule 15c3-5** — US Market Access Rule (2011). Requires brokers to maintain undisableable pre-trade risk controls on customer order flow.
- **Direct Memory Access (Hardware DMA)** — Peripheral (NIC, FPGA, GPU) reads/writes host RAM via PCIe without CPU executing every transfer.
- **Descriptor ring** — Pre-allocated array in host memory; entries describe DMA transfers. The mailbox between CPU and device.
- **Doorbell register** — Memory-mapped register on device; CPU writes to it as a single PCIe write to signal "new work in the ring."
- **Zero-copy** — Design property where data is read/written from its final location, no intermediate buffers. Requires DMA but isn't synonymous with it.
- **RDMA** — Remote DMA. Device accesses another machine's host memory over the network (InfiniBand, RoCE).
- **PIO** — Programmed I/O. CPU executes load/store instructions to copy every byte. The pre-DMA way.

### From Lesson 0014 (Hardware Acceleration)

- **DPU** — Data Processing Unit. SmartNIC with full ARM CPU complex and OS. NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando.
- **SmartNIC** — NIC with programmable packet engines and embedded compute. DPU is the marketing term.
- **NPU** — Neural Processing Unit. ASIC specialized for matmul + activation patterns of neural nets.
- **TPU** — Tensor Processing Unit. Google's NPU for training and inference.
- **Acceleration vs Offload** — Acceleration: same work, faster. Offload: same work, elsewhere so the original CPU is freed.

### From Lesson 0015 + 0020 (Alternative Data)

- **Alternative data (alt-data)** — Any non-traditional data source that hints at economic reality before official numbers. Must lead the official metric, be hard to replicate, and map to a tradable.
- **SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar)** — Satellite imaging technique that sees through clouds and at night. Used by Ursa Space for oil tanks and by ship trackers.
- **Ursa Space Systems** — NY firm tracking ~11,000 oil tanks worldwide via SAR.
- **Foursquare** — Geolocation provider; famous 2016 Chipotle revenue prediction from check-in foot-traffic.
- **NDVI** — Normalized Difference Vegetation Index: (NIR − RED) / (NIR + RED). Crop-health signal from satellite multispectral imagery.
- **AIS (Automatic Identification System)** — Mandatory ship position broadcast (ships >300 GT). Combined with SAR to catch dark-fleet behavior.
- **Alpha decay** — The phenomenon where alt-data signals lose value as more funds subscribe. The frontier always moves to harder data.
- **SafeGraph / Placer.ai / Veraset** — Major commercial geolocation data vendors for foot-traffic analytics.
- **RS Metrics / Orbital Insight / SpaceKnow / Planet Labs** — Major satellite alt-data providers.

### From Lesson 0016 (Order-Book Dynamics)

- **Limit Order Book (LOB)** — Continuously updated structure tracking all resting buy/sell orders, sorted by price-time priority.
- **Price-time priority** — Match incoming marketable orders first by price, then by FIFO arrival time within each price level.
- **Order-book imbalance** — `(bid_size − ask_size) / (bid_size + ask_size)`. Microstructure signal predicting short-term mid drift.
- **Top of book** — Best bid + best ask only. L1 data.
- **Queue position** — Where your order sits in the FIFO at its price level. Determines fill priority.
- **LOB events** — ADD, CANCEL, MODIFY, TRADE, NEW LEVEL.

### From Lesson 0017 (Market Making)

- **Reservation price** — In Avellaneda-Stoikov: the inventory-skewed "fair" price the MM uses as the center of its quotes. Not the mid when inventory ≠ 0.
- **Avellaneda-Stoikov framework** — Canonical mathematical treatment of optimal MM quoting under inventory risk and adverse selection.
- **Maker rebate** — Per-fill rebate paid by venues to liquidity-providing orders. Significant secondary income for MMs.
- **Designated Market Maker (DMM)** — MM with formal quoting obligations on a venue in exchange for benefits (relaxed OTR, rebates, sometimes flat fees).
- **Spread capture** — MM revenue mechanism: earn the bid-ask spread on round-trip fills.

### From Lesson 0018 (Statistical Arbitrage)

- **Statistical arbitrage** — Strategy family exploiting statistical patterns across many bets, profitable on average even if individual trades can lose. Not true arbitrage.
- **Pairs trading** — Long one asset, short a related one, trade the spread on mean reversion.
- **Cointegration** — Two non-stationary series whose linear combination is stationary. The math behind pairs trading.
- **Engle-Granger procedure** — Two-step test for cointegration: regress + ADF on residuals.
- **ADF (Augmented Dickey-Fuller) test** — Statistical test for unit root / non-stationarity.
- **Market-neutral** — Portfolio with zero net market beta exposure. Achieved by hedging out the index.
- **Factor neutrality** — Portfolio neutral to specific risk factors (sector, size, value, momentum). Tighter than market-neutral.

### From Lesson 0019 (Order-to-Trade Ratio)

- **Order-to-Trade Ratio (OTR)** — (orders + modifications + cancellations) / executions, per participant per instrument per day. Venue-enforced regulatory metric.
- **MiFID II RTS 9** — EU regulation operationalizing OTR limits at trading venues.
- **Article 51(3) MiFID II** — Requires venues to have systems limiting OTR to prevent disorderly trading.
- **ESU fee** — Excessive System Usage fee. Eurex's mechanism for charging participants who exceed OTR limits.
- **Quote stuffing** — Flooding venue with messages to slow competitors. Targeted by OTR caps.
- **Spoofing** — Posting orders with no intent to fill, to manipulate the book. Illegal; OTR is a noisy proxy.

### From Lesson 0021 (AI Preprocessing)

- **StandardScaler** — Z-score: (x − mean)/std. Default normalization for NNs.
- **RobustScaler** — (x − median)/IQR. Outlier-resistant.
- **Min-max scaling** — (x − min)/(max − min). Bounded to [0,1] but outlier-sensitive.
- **One-hot encoding** — Categorical → sparse binary vector. Simple, dimensionality-expanding.
- **Target encoding** — Categorical → mean target for that category. Powerful but leakage-prone.
- **Embedding (categorical)** — Learned dense vector per category. Standard NN approach.
- **Data augmentation** — Synthetic perturbations of training examples. Geometric, photometric, cutout, mixup. Mostly CV.
- **Walkforward split** — Chronological train/test split that respects time-series causality. Opposite of k-fold.
- **Leakage** — Future information accidentally present in training. Cardinal preprocessing sin.

### From Lesson 0022 (Object Detection)

- **YOLO** — "You Only Look Once" detector family. Production default for object detection.
- **DETR** — DEtection TRansformer. Set-prediction approach without anchors or NMS.
- **Grounding DINO** — Open-vocabulary detector: detects any class described by a text prompt.
- **NMS (Non-Maximum Suppression)** — Post-processing that collapses overlapping high-IoU detections to one.
- **IoU (Intersection over Union)** — Area of overlap / area of union. Box overlap metric in [0,1].
- **mAP** — Mean Average Precision. Standard detection benchmark. mAP@[0.5:0.95] is the strictest variant.
- **COCO** — Common Objects in Context. Reference dataset and metric standard.

### From Lesson 0023 (Segmentation)

- **Semantic segmentation** — Per-pixel class label. Doesn't distinguish individual instances.
- **Instance segmentation** — Per-pixel class + instance ID. Required for counting touching objects.
- **Panoptic segmentation** — Semantic + instance. "Things" get IDs; "stuff" (background) only gets class.
- **U-Net** — Encoder-decoder with skip connections. Foundational semantic-segmentation architecture.
- **Mask R-CNN** — Detection + per-instance mask head. Two-stage, accurate, slow.
- **SAM (Segment Anything Model)** — Meta 2023 foundation model for segmentation. Prompt-driven, zero-shot.
- **mIoU** — Mean IoU averaged across classes. Standard semantic-segmentation metric.
- **Dice coefficient** — 2·|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|). Boundary-friendly mask metric.

### From Lesson 0024 (Geometric Deep Learning)

- **Geometric Deep Learning (GDL)** — ML on non-Euclidean data (graphs, manifolds, Lie groups). Bronstein et al's framing.
- **Equivariance** — `f(g·x) = g·f(x)`. Output transforms predictably with input.
- **Invariance** — `f(g·x) = f(x)`. Output ignores transformation.
- **GNN (Graph Neural Network)** — Permutation-equivariant network on graphs. Message-passing over nodes/edges.
- **Lie group** — Continuous symmetry group (rotations SO(3), rigid motions SE(3), translations).
- **Group-equivariant network** — NN respecting a specified symmetry group's transformations.
- **Manifold network** — NN operating on data lying on a curved manifold (sphere, hyperbolic, SPD).
- **SPD manifold** — Symmetric Positive-Definite matrix cone. Where covariance matrices live.
- **Riemannian optimizer** — SGD/Adam variants that respect manifold structure of constrained parameter spaces.
- **PyTorch Geometric** — Standard PyTorch library for GNNs.
- **Geomstats** — Standard Python library for Riemannian computations and manifold-aware ML.

40–70 km on long-haul HFT links. Limited by Earth's curvature and tower
height. Each hop adds ~10s of ns of equipment latency.
+## Added in Lessons 0013–0024 (batch update, 2026-06-10)
+Compact form: one-line definitions grouped by source lesson. Promote to fuller
+entries as terms get used in conversation.
+### From Lesson 0013 (DMA)
+- **Direct Market Access (Trading DMA)** — Buy-side firm submits orders directly to the exchange matching engine through a broker's infrastructure, no human in between.
+- **Sponsored Access** — Lowest-latency form of DMA where the buy-side uses the broker's MPID and connectivity but skips most of the broker's order-management stack.
+- **Naked access** — Pre-2011 sponsored access with no pre-trade risk filter. Prohibited by Rule 15c3-5.
+- **MPID** — Market Participant Identifier, the 4-character code identifying a broker on a venue. Sponsored customers trade under their sponsor's MPID.
+- **FIX protocol** — The dominant exchange messaging protocol for orders. NewOrderSingle = 35=D.
+- **SEC Rule 15c3-5** — US Market Access Rule (2011). Requires brokers to maintain undisableable pre-trade risk controls on customer order flow.
+- **Direct Memory Access (Hardware DMA)** — Peripheral (NIC, FPGA, GPU) reads/writes host RAM via PCIe without CPU executing every transfer.
+- **Descriptor ring** — Pre-allocated array in host memory; entries describe DMA transfers. The mailbox between CPU and device.
+- **Doorbell register** — Memory-mapped register on device; CPU writes to it as a single PCIe write to signal "new work in the ring."
+- **Zero-copy** — Design property where data is read/written from its final location, no intermediate buffers. Requires DMA but isn't synonymous with it.
+- **RDMA** — Remote DMA. Device accesses another machine's host memory over the network (InfiniBand, RoCE).
+- **PIO** — Programmed I/O. CPU executes load/store instructions to copy every byte. The pre-DMA way.
+### From Lesson 0014 (Hardware Acceleration)
+- **DPU** — Data Processing Unit. SmartNIC with full ARM CPU complex and OS. NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando.
+- **SmartNIC** — NIC with programmable packet engines and embedded compute. DPU is the marketing term.
+- **NPU** — Neural Processing Unit. ASIC specialized for matmul + activation patterns of neural nets.
+- **TPU** — Tensor Processing Unit. Google's NPU for training and inference.
+- **Acceleration vs Offload** — Acceleration: same work, faster. Offload: same work, elsewhere so the original CPU is freed.
+### From Lesson 0015 + 0020 (Alternative Data)

+- **Alternative data (alt-data)** — Any non-traditional data source that hints at economic reality before official numbers. Must lead the official metric, be hard to replicate, and map to a tradable.
+- **SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar)** — Satellite imaging technique that sees through clouds and at night. Used by Ursa Space for oil tanks and by ship trackers.
+- **Ursa Space Systems** — NY firm tracking ~11,000 oil tanks worldwide via SAR.
+- **Foursquare** — Geolocation provider; famous 2016 Chipotle revenue prediction from check-in foot-traffic.
+- **NDVI** — Normalized Difference Vegetation Index: (NIR − RED) / (NIR + RED). Crop-health signal from satellite multispectral imagery.
+- **AIS (Automatic Identification System)** — Mandatory ship position broadcast (ships >300 GT). Combined with SAR to catch dark-fleet behavior.
+- **Alpha decay** — The phenomenon where alt-data signals lose value as more funds subscribe. The frontier always moves to harder data.
+- **SafeGraph / Placer.ai / Veraset** — Major commercial geolocation data vendors for foot-traffic analytics.
+- **RS Metrics / Orbital Insight / SpaceKnow / Planet Labs** — Major satellite alt-data providers.
+### From Lesson 0016 (Order-Book Dynamics)
+- **Limit Order Book (LOB)** — Continuously updated structure tracking all resting buy/sell orders, sorted by price-time priority.
+- **Price-time priority** — Match incoming marketable orders first by price, then by FIFO arrival time within each price level.
+- **Order-book imbalance** — `(bid_size − ask_size) / (bid_size + ask_size)`. Microstructure signal predicting short-term mid drift.
+- **Top of book** — Best bid + best ask only. L1 data.
+- **Queue position** — Where your order sits in the FIFO at its price level. Determines fill priority.
+- **LOB events** — ADD, CANCEL, MODIFY, TRADE, NEW LEVEL.
+### From Lesson 0017 (Market Making)
+- **Reservation price** — In Avellaneda-Stoikov: the inventory-skewed "fair" price the MM uses as the center of its quotes. Not the mid when inventory ≠ 0.
+- **Avellaneda-Stoikov framework** — Canonical mathematical treatment of optimal MM quoting under inventory risk and adverse selection.
+- **Maker rebate** — Per-fill rebate paid by venues to liquidity-providing orders. Significant secondary income for MMs.
+- **Designated Market Maker (DMM)** — MM with formal quoting obligations on a venue in exchange for benefits (relaxed OTR, rebates, sometimes flat fees).
+- **Spread capture** — MM revenue mechanism: earn the bid-ask spread on round-trip fills.
+### From Lesson 0018 (Statistical Arbitrage)
+- **Statistical arbitrage** — Strategy family exploiting statistical patterns across many bets, profitable on average even if individual trades can lose. Not true arbitrage.
+- **Pairs trading** — Long one asset, short a related one, trade the spread on mean reversion.
+- **Cointegration** — Two non-stationary series whose linear combination is stationary. The math behind pairs trading.
+- **Engle-Granger procedure** — Two-step test for cointegration: regress + ADF on residuals.
+- **ADF (Augmented Dickey-Fuller) test** — Statistical test for unit root / non-stationarity.
+- **Market-neutral** — Portfolio with zero net market beta exposure. Achieved by hedging out the index.
+- **Factor neutrality** — Portfolio neutral to specific risk factors (sector, size, value, momentum). Tighter than market-neutral.
+### From Lesson 0019 (Order-to-Trade Ratio)
+- **Order-to-Trade Ratio (OTR)** — (orders + modifications + cancellations) / executions, per participant per instrument per day. Venue-enforced regulatory metric.
+- **MiFID II RTS 9** — EU regulation operationalizing OTR limits at trading venues.
+- **Article 51(3) MiFID II** — Requires venues to have systems limiting OTR to prevent disorderly trading.
+- **ESU fee** — Excessive System Usage fee. Eurex's mechanism for charging participants who exceed OTR limits.
+- **Quote stuffing** — Flooding venue with messages to slow competitors. Targeted by OTR caps.
+- **Spoofing** — Posting orders with no intent to fill, to manipulate the book. Illegal; OTR is a noisy proxy.
+### From Lesson 0021 (AI Preprocessing)
+- **StandardScaler** — Z-score: (x − mean)/std. Default normalization for NNs.
+- **RobustScaler** — (x − median)/IQR. Outlier-resistant.
+- **Min-max scaling** — (x − min)/(max − min). Bounded to [0,1] but outlier-sensitive.
+- **One-hot encoding** — Categorical → sparse binary vector. Simple, dimensionality-expanding.
+- **Target encoding** — Categorical → mean target for that category. Powerful but leakage-prone.
+- **Embedding (categorical)** — Learned dense vector per category. Standard NN approach.
+- **Data augmentation** — Synthetic perturbations of training examples. Geometric, photometric, cutout, mixup. Mostly CV.
+- **Walkforward split** — Chronological train/test split that respects time-series causality. Opposite of k-fold.
+- **Leakage** — Future information accidentally present in training. Cardinal preprocessing sin.
+### From Lesson 0022 (Object Detection)
+- **YOLO** — "You Only Look Once" detector family. Production default for object detection.
+- **DETR** — DEtection TRansformer. Set-prediction approach without anchors or NMS.
+- **Grounding DINO** — Open-vocabulary detector: detects any class described by a text prompt.
+- **NMS (Non-Maximum Suppression)** — Post-processing that collapses overlapping high-IoU detections to one.
+- **IoU (Intersection over Union)** — Area of overlap / area of union. Box overlap metric in [0,1].
+- **mAP** — Mean Average Precision. Standard detection benchmark. mAP@[0.5:0.95] is the strictest variant.
+- **COCO** — Common Objects in Context. Reference dataset and metric standard.
+### From Lesson 0023 (Segmentation)
+- **Semantic segmentation** — Per-pixel class label. Doesn't distinguish individual instances.
+- **Instance segmentation** — Per-pixel class + instance ID. Required for counting touching objects.
+- **Panoptic segmentation** — Semantic + instance. "Things" get IDs; "stuff" (background) only gets class.
+- **U-Net** — Encoder-decoder with skip connections. Foundational semantic-segmentation architecture.
+- **Mask R-CNN** — Detection + per-instance mask head. Two-stage, accurate, slow.
+- **SAM (Segment Anything Model)** — Meta 2023 foundation model for segmentation. Prompt-driven, zero-shot.
+- **mIoU** — Mean IoU averaged across classes. Standard semantic-segmentation metric.
+- **Dice coefficient** — 2·|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|). Boundary-friendly mask metric.
+### From Lesson 0024 (Geometric Deep Learning)
+- **Geometric Deep Learning (GDL)** — ML on non-Euclidean data (graphs, manifolds, Lie groups). Bronstein et al's framing.
+- **Equivariance** — `f(g·x) = g·f(x)`. Output transforms predictably with input.
+- **Invariance** — `f(g·x) = f(x)`. Output ignores transformation.
+- **GNN (Graph Neural Network)** — Permutation-equivariant network on graphs. Message-passing over nodes/edges.
+- **Lie group** — Continuous symmetry group (rotations SO(3), rigid motions SE(3), translations).
+- **Group-equivariant network** — NN respecting a specified symmetry group's transformations.
+- **Manifold network** — NN operating on data lying on a curved manifold (sphere, hyperbolic, SPD).
+- **SPD manifold** — Symmetric Positive-Definite matrix cone. Where covariance matrices live.
+- **Riemannian optimizer** — SGD/Adam variants that respect manifold structure of constrained parameter spaces.
+- **PyTorch Geometric** — Standard PyTorch library for GNNs.
+- **Geomstats** — Standard Python library for Riemannian computations and manifold-aware ML.

skills.name: teach
skills.content:
The user wants to learn "engineering" (or, if blank, you choose the most valuable concept to teach next based on their progress and this project's code). This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.

### 5. **Exercises / Practice Directories**

- **None found.** No `exercises/`, `practice/`, or similar teaching-focused module directories.
- **Learning materials only:** `docs/learning/` contains 24+ HTML lessons (0001–0024) + GLOSSARY.md and PROGRESS.md, but these are read-only documentation/interactive lessons.

- **docker-compose.yml exists** but is for local development/testing, not CI

---

### **Summary for Planning**

**Suitable locations for new testable HFT modules:**
- **Python:** Add to `/tests/test_*.py` following existing pytest patterns (fixtures in `conftest.py`)
- **C++:** Add to `/tests/cpp/` with CMake integration (no framework overhead)

Design an implementation plan (research/planning only — do NOT write code) for adding "testable HFT practice material" to the repo at /home/node/work/normal_work/HFT_practice.

## Background

This repo is an algorithmic-trading research platform (daily-frequency Python quant code, some C++ ONNX inference in gradient_boosting/, three VHDL modules in fpga/). The user has completed 24 self-paced HTML lessons in docs/learning/lessons/ covering HFT concepts. Many lessons (0009–0019) use "illustrative" code examples because the repo lacks real HFT code. The user now wants exercism-style practice exercises: skeleton modules with TODOs they implement themselves, graded by pre-written test suites, with reference solutions kept separately to peek at after attempting.

## Confirmed scope (user-selected)

**Format**: fill-in exercises + tests. Layout the user approved:
```
exercises/
├── 01_order_book/
│   ├── order_book.py        # stubs + docstrings, user fills in
│   └── README.md            # spec + link to lesson 0016
├── 02_spsc_ring/ (C++)
solutions/                   # reference impls
tests/exercises/
│   └── test_01_order_book.py
```
Run via `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 01`.

**Languages**: Python, C++, AND VHDL testbenches.

**Building blocks** (all four, each maps to a lesson):
1. Order book — price-time priority LOB with add/cancel/execute, BBO, imbalance signal (lesson 0016). Python.
2. Market maker — inventory-aware Avellaneda-Stoikov-style quoting; the existing fpga/market_maker.vhd quotes mid±spread/2 with NO inventory tracking, a flagged gap (lesson 0017). Python.
3. SPSC ring + O(1) moving average — C++ lock-free SPSC ring with release/acquire ordering and alignas(64) padding; O(1) ring-buffer MA (lessons 0009/0010). The repo's gradient_boosting/sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp has an O(window) MA its own comments admit should be O(1).
4. Stat-arb + risk utils — cointegration/pairs utilities (lesson 0018), CUSUM detector (lesson 0006, exists conceptually in walkforward_sim.py), OTR tracker (lesson 0019), walk-forward split helpers. Python.

VHDL: testbenches for the three existing fpga/*.vhd modules (market_maker.vhd, linear_regression_predictor.vhd, moving_average_trader.vhd) — likely as a fill-in exercise too (stub testbench the user completes) or write-the-testbench exercises. No simulation infra exists; fpga/README.md mentions GHDL as the open-source path. Note GHDL may not be installed in the user's environment — plan should handle that (e.g., document install, make VHDL tests opt-in, NOT part of default pytest run).

## Existing infrastructure facts (verified)

- pyproject.toml: flat py-modules layout + packages `scripts`, `webapp`; pytest config `testpaths = ["tests"]`; dev deps pytest>=8.0, pytest-cov>=5.0. Package manager is `uv` exclusively.
- tests/: 4 test files + conftest.py with seeded-rng fixtures (sample_prices_df etc.). Plain pytest, fixtures, unittest-style Test classes, no parametrize, no HTTP mocking infra.
- tests/cpp/: test_algorithms.cpp (standalone C++17, custom ASSERT macro, no framework), CMakeLists.txt (CMake 3.14+), run_tests.sh builds+runs.
- No CI (.github/workflows absent).
- CLAUDE.md conventions: `uv run pytest tests/ -v`, every new Python function needs ≥1 test, never hit live APIs in tests.

## Key design questions for you to resolve in the plan

1. **How tests find user code vs solutions**: tests/exercises/ must import from exercises/ by default, but it's valuable to be able to run the same tests against solutions/ to prove the suite is solvable (e.g., an env var like HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions, or a conftest.py fixture that switches import path). Recommend a clean mechanism.
2. **Default pytest run**: should `uv run pytest tests/` start failing because exercise stubs are unimplemented? That would break the existing green suite. Recommend how to isolate (separate testpath not in default testpaths, marker + addopts, or skip-if-not-implemented sentinel like raising NotImplementedError → xfail/skip semantics). The user should get clear "not yet implemented" vs "wrong answer" feedback.
3. **C++ exercise build**: how the SPSC/MA exercise plugs into tests/cpp/ CMake or gets its own CMakeLists + run script; how user-code-vs-solution switching works there (e.g., include path switch).
4. **VHDL**: structure of GHDL-based testbench exercises, a run script, opt-in mechanism, and what the user fills in (stimulus process? assertions?).
5. **Per-exercise difficulty progression**: each exercise dir should have a README with spec, acceptance criteria, link to its lesson HTML, and hints. Recommend the ordering/numbering of all exercises (Python + C++ + VHDL), keeping it incremental.
6. **Solutions**: ensure solutions are importable for the verify-against-solutions run, and that nothing in production code imports exercises.
7. What needs updating in pyproject.toml (if anything), CLAUDE.md (test command for exercises), and docs/learning/PROGRESS.md (the lessons↔exercises map). Lessons themselves will be retrofitted to real code LATER — out of scope now, but the plan can note the linkage.

# Implementation Plan: Testable HFT Practice Exercises

## Directory tree

```
exercises/
├── README.md                      # how exercises work, run commands, workflow
├── 01_order_book/
│   ├── README.md                  # spec, acceptance criteria, hints, link to lesson 0016
│   └── order_book.py              # stubs raising NotImplementedError
├── 02_market_maker/

│   └── market_maker.py
├── 03_stat_arb_risk/
│   ├── README.md                  # lessons 0018, 0006, 0019
│   ├── pairs.py                   # cointegration utils
│   └── risk.py                    # CUSUM, OTR, walk-forward splits
├── 04_spsc_ring/                  # C++
│   ├── README.md                  # lessons 0009, 0010
│   ├── ring_ma.hpp                # Part A: O(1) moving average (fixes the O(window) flaw
│   │                              #   admitted in gradient_boosting/sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp:62)
│   └── spsc_ring.hpp              # Part B: lock-free SPSC ring
└── 05_vhdl_testbench/             # VHDL, opt-in
    ├── README.md                  # lesson 0002; GHDL install instructions
    ├── tb_market_maker.vhd        # scaffold: entity/arch/clock done; stimulus + asserts are TODOs
    ├── tb_moving_average_trader.vhd
    └── tb_linear_regression_predictor.vhd

solutions/                         # mirrors exercises/ exactly (same dirs, same filenames)
├── 01_order_book/order_book.py
├── 02_market_maker/market_maker.py
├── 03_stat_arb_risk/{pairs.py,risk.py}
├── 04_spsc_ring/{ring_ma.hpp,spsc_ring.hpp}
└── 05_vhdl_testbench/tb_*.vhd     # complete testbenches

tests/exercises/
├── __init__.py
├── conftest.py                    # loader + NotImplementedError→skip + auto-markers
├── test_01_order_book.py
├── test_02_market_maker.py
├── test_03_stat_arb_risk.py
├── test_04_spsc_ring.py          # pytest wrapper: shells out to run_cpp.sh
├── test_05_vhdl.py               # pytest wrapper: skips unless ghdl installed
└── cpp/
    ├── test_ring_ma.cpp           # custom ASSERT macro, mirroring tests/cpp/test_algorithms.cpp style
    ├── test_spsc_ring.cpp
    └── run_cpp.sh                 # g++ direct build (no cmake — it isn't installed)

scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh          # ghdl -a/-e/-r driver
```

## Q1 — Test targeting (exercises vs solutions)

Because `01_order_book` isn't a valid package name, tests load modules **by file path** via a conftest helper, and because `solutions/` mirrors `exercises/` exactly, switching is one env var:

```python
# tests/exercises/conftest.py
TARGET = os.environ.get("HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET", "exercises")  # or "solutions"

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def load_exercise():
    def _load(exercise_dir: str, module: str):
        path = REPO_ROOT / TARGET / exercise_dir / f"{module}.py"
        spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(f"{TARGET}_{exercise_dir}_{module}", path)
        mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
        return mod
    return _load
```

Tests do `ob = load_exercise("01_order_book", "order_book")`. The same `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET` is read by `run_cpp.sh` (sets the `-I` include dir) and `run_vhdl_tests.sh` (selects which `tb_*.vhd` to analyze alongside `fpga/*.vhd`). One mechanism, three languages.

## Q2 — Keeping the default suite green

Place `tests/exercises/` **inside** the existing `testpaths`, but make stubs raise `NotImplementedError` and convert that to a skip in `tests/exercises/conftest.py`:

```python
@pytest.hookimpl(wrapper=True)
def pytest_runtest_call(item):
    try:
        return (yield)
    except NotImplementedError:
        pytest.skip("Exercise not implemented yet — fill in the TODO")
```

Result: `uv run pytest tests/` stays green ("N passed, M skipped"), the skip count is a visible progress bar, and once a stub is filled, wrong answers surface as normal assertion failures — clean "not implemented" vs "wrong answer" separation. Also auto-apply markers in `pytest_collection_modifyitems` (`exercise` on everything in the dir, plus `cpp`/`vhdl` on the wrappers) so `-m "not exercise"` filters them out when wanted. C++/VHDL wrappers map a sentinel exit code 42 (stub throws `std::logic_error("not implemented")`; VHDL stub hits a `report ... severity failure` TODO sentinel) to the same skip.

## Exercise contents and test coverage

**01_order_book** (`OrderBook` class): `add_limit(order_id, side, price, qty)`, `cancel(order_id)`, `execute_market(side, qty) -> list[Fill]`, `best_bid()/best_ask()/bbo()`, `imbalance(levels)`. Tests: empty-book BBO is `None`; add updates BBO; price priority across levels; **FIFO at same price** (older order fills first); partial fill leaves remainder at front of queue; cancel removes order and BBO re-derives; cancel of unknown id raises `KeyError`; market order walks multiple levels; imbalance ∈ [−1, 1] with hand-computed cases.

**02_market_maker** (`InventoryAwareQuoter`, Avellaneda-Stoikov-lite): `reservation_price(mid, inventory)`, `optimal_spread()`, `quote(mid, inventory) -> (bid, ask)` with `gamma, sigma, horizon, max_inventory` params. Tests: zero inventory → symmetric quotes; long inventory → reservation price below mid (both quotes skew down); short → up; spread widens monotonically with `gamma` and `sigma`; quotes never cross; at `±max_inventory` quoting goes one-sided. README explicitly contrasts with `fpga/market_maker.vhd`'s inventory-blind mid±spread/2.

**03_stat_arb_risk** (numpy-only — statsmodels is not a dependency): `pairs.py`: `hedge_ratio` (OLS), `spread_series`, `zscore`, `dickey_fuller_stat` (lag-0 DF t-stat: regress Δe on e₋₁), `half_life` (AR(1)). `risk.py`: `CUSUMDetector` (per lesson 0006 / `walkforward_sim.py` concept), `OTRTracker` (`record_order/record_cancel/record_trade`, `ratio()`, `breached(threshold)` — lesson 0019), `walkforward_splits(n, train, test, embargo)`. Tests: constructed cointegrated pair (y = 2x + stationary AR noise, seeded rng like `tests/conftest.py`) → DF stat below critical value; two independent random walks → not; CUSUM fires on injected mean shift, silent on noise; OTR arithmetic and breach flag; splits non-overlapping, chronological, embargo gap respected.

**04_spsc_ring** (header-only C++20, `-pthread`): Part A `RingMA<N>`: O(1) push/average via running sum, fixed array, no heap. Part B `SpscRing<T, N>` (N power-of-two, `static_assert`): `try_push/try_pop` with release/acquire `std::atomic<size_t>` head/tail and `alignas(64)` separation. Tests: MA matches naive recomputation across wraparound; ring single-thread FIFO order; full/empty detection; `offsetof` check that head/tail are ≥64 bytes apart; two-thread test moving 1M sequenced items intact.

**05_vhdl_testbench**: stubs ship with entity, DUT instantiation, and clock process complete; the user writes the stimulus process (drive Q16.16 bid/ask, pulse the valid handshake) and `assert` checks (buy = mid − spread/2, sell = mid + spread/2, valid latency in cycles; ramp prices vs MA signal; known-weights dot product → 2-bit signal for the LR predictor).

## Q3 — C++ build

`cmake` is not installed; `g++` is. `tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh` compiles directly:

```bash
TARGET=${HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET:-exercises}
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -pthread -I "$ROOT/$TARGET/04_spsc_ring" test_ring_ma.cpp -o build/test_ring_ma && ./build/test_ring_ma
# (same for test_spsc_ring.cpp)
```

`test_04_spsc_ring.py` runs it via `subprocess`, skipping if `g++` is absent, mapping exit 42 → skip. Note in the README that `tests/cpp/run_tests.sh` still covers the legacy cmake path; optionally add a `CMakeLists.txt` stanza later, but don't depend on it.

## Q4 — VHDL (opt-in)

`scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh`: for each tb, `ghdl -a fpga/<dut>.vhd $TARGET/05_vhdl_testbench/tb_<dut>.vhd && ghdl -e tb_<dut> && ghdl -r tb_<dut> --assert-level=error`. `test_05_vhdl.py` skips with "GHDL not installed — see exercises/05_vhdl_testbench/README.md" when `shutil.which("ghdl")` is None, so VHDL never breaks the default run. README documents `apt-get install ghdl` (and gtkwave for waveforms).

## Q5 — Ordering rationale

Python ramp first (01 LOB → 02 MM builds on LOB concepts → 03 stat-arb/risk, breadth), then 04 C++ (Part A easy, Part B hard), then 05 VHDL (new toolchain). Each README ends with a relative link to its lesson HTML (e.g., `../../docs/learning/lessons/0016-order-book-dynamics.html`) and a "peek policy" pointer to `solutions/`.

## Q6 — Solutions isolation

`solutions/` mirrors `exercises/` and is loaded only via the path-based loader — neither directory is in `[tool.setuptools] packages`/`py-modules`, so nothing installable or in production code can import them. Verified: current pyproject packages only `scripts` and `webapp`.

## Q7 — Config/doc updates

- **pyproject.toml**: only add `markers = ["exercise: ...", "cpp: ...", "vhdl: ..."]` to `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`. `testpaths` unchanged.
- **CLAUDE.md** Testing section: `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 01 -v` (one exercise), `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v` (verify suite), `bash scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh` (opt-in).
- **docs/learning/PROGRESS.md**: add a "Lessons ↔ exercises map" table (0016→01, 0017→02, 0006/0018/0019→03, 0009/0010→04, 0002→05) and note lessons 0009–0019 will be retrofitted to this real code later (per the existing "illustrative" guidance block).

## Implementation sequence

1. `tests/exercises/conftest.py` (loader + skip hook + markers) and pyproject marker registration.
2. Exercise 01: write `solutions/01_order_book/order_book.py` **first**, then the test suite against it, then derive the stub by hollowing the solution (keep signatures/docstrings, body → `raise NotImplementedError`). Repeat per exercise — this guarantees stubs and solutions never drift.
3. Exercises 02, 03 the same way.
4. Exercise 04: headers + C++ tests + `run_cpp.sh` + pytest wrapper.
5. Exercise 05: solution testbenches + hollowed stubs + `run_vhdl_tests.sh` + wrapper.
6. READMEs, CLAUDE.md, PROGRESS.md.

## Verification

1. `uv run pytest tests/ -v` → all pre-existing tests pass; every exercise test **skipped** with the "not implemented" message; zero failures.
2. `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v` → all Python + C++ wrapper tests **pass** (proves solvability); VHDL skipped if ghdl absent.
3. `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh` → both binaries pass; default target exits 42.
4. Sabotage check: implement one stub method wrongly → its test **fails** (not skips), confirming the skip hook doesn't mask real errors.

├── README.md                      # workflow, run commands, peek policy
├── 01_order_book/{README.md, order_book.py}          # lesson 0016
├── 02_market_maker/{README.md, market_maker.py}      # lesson 0017
├── 03_stat_arb_risk/{README.md, pairs.py, risk.py}   # lessons 0018/0006/0019
├── 04_spsc_ring/{README.md, ring_ma.hpp, spsc_ring.hpp}   # lessons 0009/0010
└── 05_vhdl_testbench/{README.md, tb_market_maker.vhd,
        tb_moving_average_trader.vhd, tb_linear_regression_predictor.vhd}  # lesson 0002

solutions/                         # mirrors exercises/ exactly (same dirs/filenames)

tests/exercises/

├── conftest.py                    # path-based loader + NotImplementedError→skip + markers
├── test_01_order_book.py
├── test_02_market_maker.py
├── test_03_stat_arb_risk.py
├── test_04_spsc_ring.py           # subprocess wrapper → cpp/run_cpp.sh
├── test_05_vhdl.py                # skips unless ghdl on PATH

```

## Core mechanisms

# Testable HFT Practice Exercises

## Context

The 24 HTML lessons in `docs/learning/` teach HFT concepts, but lessons 0009–0019 use *illustrative* code because the repo lacks real HFT building blocks. The user wants hands-on, exercism-style practice: skeleton modules with TODOs they implement, graded by pre-written pytest suites, with reference solutions to peek at after attempting. Scope confirmed: Python + C++ + VHDL, covering order book, market maker, stat-arb/risk utils, and SPSC ring / O(1) MA. Once solutions land, lessons can later be retrofitted with real repo code (existing standing instruction — out of scope here, but noted in PROGRESS.md).

Toolchain facts (verified): `g++` and `make` installed; `cmake` and `ghdl` are **not**; `statsmodels` is not a dep (stat-arb utils must be numpy-only).

## Directory tree

```
exercises/
├── README.md                      # workflow, run commands, peek policy
├── 01_order_book/{README.md, order_book.py}          # lesson 0016
├── 02_market_maker/{README.md, market_maker.py}      # lesson 0017
├── 03_stat_arb_risk/{README.md, pairs.py, risk.py}   # lessons 0018/0006/0019
├── 04_spsc_ring/{README.md, ring_ma.hpp, spsc_ring.hpp}   # lessons 0009/0010
└── 05_vhdl_testbench/{README.md, tb_market_maker.vhd,
        tb_moving_average_trader.vhd, tb_linear_regression_predictor.vhd}  # lesson 0002

solutions/                         # mirrors exercises/ exactly (same dirs/filenames)

tests/exercises/
├── __init__.py
├── conftest.py                    # path-based loader + NotImplementedError→skip + markers
├── test_01_order_book.py
├── test_02_market_maker.py
├── test_03_stat_arb_risk.py
├── test_04_spsc_ring.py           # subprocess wrapper → cpp/run_cpp.sh
├── test_05_vhdl.py                # skips unless ghdl on PATH
└── cpp/{test_ring_ma.cpp, test_spsc_ring.cpp, run_cpp.sh}

scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh          # ghdl -a/-e/-r driver
```

Stubs are derived by hollowing solutions (keep signatures + docstrings, body → `raise NotImplementedError`) so they never drift.

## Core mechanisms

**Targeting (exercises vs solutions)** — exercise dirs like `01_order_book` aren't valid package names, so `tests/exercises/conftest.py` provides a `load_exercise(dir, module)` fixture that loads by file path via `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location`, rooted at `$HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET` (default `exercises`, set to `solutions` to verify the suite is solvable). `run_cpp.sh` reads the same env var for its `-I` include dir; `run_vhdl_tests.sh` for which `tb_*.vhd` to analyze. One mechanism, three languages.

**Default suite stays green** — stubs raise `NotImplementedError`; a `pytest_runtest_call` wrapper hook in `tests/exercises/conftest.py` converts that to `pytest.skip("Exercise not implemented yet — fill in the TODO")`. So `uv run pytest tests/` shows "N passed, M skipped" (skip count = progress bar), and a filled-but-wrong stub fails normally — clean "not implemented" vs "wrong answer" separation. C++/VHDL stubs signal not-implemented via sentinel exit code 42 (`std::logic_error` / `report ... severity failure` TODO), which the pytest wrappers map to skip. Auto-apply `exercise` / `cpp` / `vhdl` markers via `pytest_collection_modifyitems` so `-m "not exercise"` reproduces today's suite.

**C++ build** — no cmake; `run_cpp.sh` compiles directly: `g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -pthread -I "$ROOT/$TARGET/04_spsc_ring" test_*.cpp`. Wrapper skips if `g++` absent. C++ tests use the custom ASSERT-macro style from `tests/cpp/test_algorithms.cpp`.

**VHDL opt-in** — `test_05_vhdl.py` skips when `shutil.which("ghdl")` is None. README documents `apt-get install ghdl` + gtkwave. Script: `ghdl -a fpga/<dut>.vhd $TARGET/05_vhdl_testbench/tb_<dut>.vhd && ghdl -e ... && ghdl -r ... --assert-level=error`.

## Exercise specs and test coverage

**01 — Order book** (`OrderBook`): `add_limit(order_id, side, price, qty)`, `cancel(order_id)`, `execute_market(side, qty) -> list[Fill]`, `best_bid()/best_ask()/bbo()`, `imbalance(levels)`. Tests: empty-book BBO None; BBO updates on add; price priority; FIFO at same price; partial fill leaves remainder at queue front; cancel re-derives BBO; unknown cancel → `KeyError`; market order walks levels; imbalance ∈ [−1,1] hand-computed.

**02 — Market maker** (`InventoryAwareQuoter`, Avellaneda-Stoikov-lite; params `gamma, sigma, horizon, max_inventory`): `reservation_price(mid, inventory)`, `optimal_spread()`, `quote(mid, inventory)`. Tests: zero inventory → symmetric; long → skew down, short → up; spread monotone in gamma and sigma; quotes never cross; one-sided at ±max_inventory. README contrasts with the inventory-blind `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

**03 — Stat-arb + risk** (numpy-only). `pairs.py`: `hedge_ratio` (OLS), `spread_series`, `zscore`, `dickey_fuller_stat` (lag-0 DF: regress Δe on e₋₁), `half_life` (AR(1)). `risk.py`: `CUSUMDetector`, `OTRTracker` (`record_order/record_cancel/record_trade`, `ratio()`, `breached(threshold)`), `walkforward_splits(n, train, test, embargo)`. Tests: constructed cointegrated pair (seeded rng, like `tests/conftest.py`) → DF stat passes, independent random walks don't; CUSUM fires on injected shift, silent on noise; OTR arithmetic + breach; splits chronological, non-overlapping, embargo respected.

**04 — C++** (header-only, C++20). Part A `RingMA<N>`: O(1) push/average, fixed array, no heap — fixes the O(window) flaw admitted in `gradient_boosting/sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp`. Part B `SpscRing<T,N>` (power-of-two `static_assert`): `try_push/try_pop`, release/acquire atomics, `alignas(64)` head/tail separation. Tests: MA matches naive recompute across wraparound; FIFO order; full/empty; `offsetof` ≥64-byte check; 2-thread 1M-item sequenced transfer.

**05 — VHDL testbenches**: stubs ship with entity, DUT instantiation, clock process complete; user writes the stimulus process (Q16.16 prices, valid handshake pulses) and `assert` checks (MM: buy=mid−spread/2, sell=mid+spread/2, latency cycles; MA: ramp vs signal; LR: known-weights dot product → signal).

## Config/doc updates

- `pyproject.toml`: add `markers = [...]` to `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` only. `testpaths` unchanged; `exercises/`/`solutions/` are never packaged (setuptools lists explicit py-modules/packages already).
- `CLAUDE.md` Testing section: add `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 01 -v`, `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v`, `bash scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh`.
- `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: add "Lessons ↔ exercises" map (0016→01, 0017→02, 0006/0018/0019→03, 0009/0010→04, 0002→05) + note that lesson retrofitting comes later.

## Implementation sequence

1. `tests/exercises/conftest.py` (loader + skip hook + markers) + pyproject markers.
2. Per Python exercise (01→02→03): write solution first, then tests against it, then hollow the solution into the stub.
3. Exercise 04: headers (solution + stub), C++ tests, `run_cpp.sh`, pytest wrapper.
4. Exercise 05: solution testbenches, hollowed stubs, `scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh`, pytest wrapper.
5. READMEs (top-level + per-exercise with spec/criteria/hints/lesson link), CLAUDE.md, PROGRESS.md.

## Verification

2. `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v` → all Python + C++ tests **pass** (proves solvability); VHDL skipped if ghdl absent.
3. `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh` → binaries pass; default target exits 42.
4. Sabotage check: implement one stub method wrongly → its test **fails**, not skips.
5. `uv run pytest tests/ -m "not exercise"` → identical to today's green suite.

## Key reference files

- `tests/conftest.py` — seeded-rng fixture style to copy
- `tests/cpp/test_algorithms.cpp` — ASSERT-macro style for C++ tests
- `fpga/market_maker.vhd` — DUT ports / Q16.16 format for exercise 05; inventory-gap framing for 02

"""Shared pytest fixtures for the HFT_practice test suite."""
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def sample_prices_df() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """100-row OHLCV DataFrame starting at price 100, random walk."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
    n = 100
    # Random walk on close prices
    steps = rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)
    close = 100.0 + np.cumsum(steps)
    # Build OHLC around close
    noise = rng.uniform(0.1, 0.5, n)
    high = close + noise
    low = close - noise
    open_ = close + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3, n)
    volume = rng.integers(100_000, 1_000_000, n).astype(float)

    df = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Open": open_,
            "High": high,
            "Low": low,
            "Close": close,
            "Volume": volume,
        }
    )
    return df


@pytest.fixture
def sample_equity_df() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """250-row DataFrame with DatetimeIndex and 'equity' column, random walk upward."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=7)
    n = 250
    dates = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=n, freq="B")
    # Slight upward drift of 0.03% per day + noise
    daily_returns = rng.normal(0.0003, 0.01, n)
    equity = 100_000.0 * np.cumprod(1 + daily_returns)
    df = pd.DataFrame({"equity": equity}, index=dates)
    return df


@pytest.fixture
def sample_news_df() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """50-row DataFrame with columns [time_published, ticker, sentiment, relevance]."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=99)
    n = 50
    tickers = ["AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOG", "AMZN", "NVDA"]
    # Timestamps in YYYYMMDDTHHMM format (what load_news expects)
    base = pd.Timestamp("2023-01-01 09:00", tz="UTC")
    ts_list = [
        (base + pd.Timedelta(hours=int(i * 3.7))).strftime("%Y%m%dT%H%M")
        for i in range(n)
    ]
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "time_published": ts_list,
            "ticker": [tickers[i % len(tickers)] for i in range(n)],
            "sentiment": rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, n).round(4),
            "relevance": rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0, n).round(4),
        }
    )
    return df

2	-- @file    market_maker.vhd
3	-- @brief   Fixed-point market-making spread engine
4	-- @detail  Given a live bid price and ask price, computes the mid-price and
5	--          derives a buy quote and a sell quote separated by a configurable
6	--          spread.  Arithmetic uses Q16.16 fixed-point (signed 32-bit integers
7	--          where the lower 16 bits represent the fractional part).
8	--
9	--          Formula:
10	--            mid_price  = (bid_price_in + ask_price_in) / 2
11	--            buy_price  = mid_price - spread_in / 2
12	--            sell_price = mid_price + spread_in / 2

15	--          valid_in asserted for exactly one cycle triggers one output cycle.

18	-- @version 1.0
19	--
20	-- @note    Q16.16 encoding:
21	--            real_value = integer_signal / 65536
22	--            e.g. $100.50  ->  100.50 * 65536 = 6_586_368  (0x0064_8000)
23	--                 spread $0.01 ->  0.01 * 65536 =       655  (0x0000_028F)
24	--
25	-- @note    Synthesizable with Vivado 2022.1+; targets Artix-7 / Kintex-7 /
26	--          UltraScale+ devices.  No floating-point DSP required.

-- =============================================================================
-- @file    market_maker.vhd
-- @brief   Fixed-point market-making spread engine
-- @detail  Given a live bid price and ask price, computes the mid-price and
--          derives a buy quote and a sell quote separated by a configurable
--          spread.  Arithmetic uses Q16.16 fixed-point (signed 32-bit integers
--          where the lower 16 bits represent the fractional part).
--
--          Formula:
--            mid_price  = (bid_price_in + ask_price_in) / 2
--            buy_price  = mid_price - spread_in / 2
--            sell_price = mid_price + spread_in / 2
--
--          Pipeline: 1 clock cycle latency.
--          valid_in asserted for exactly one cycle triggers one output cycle.
--
-- @author  HFT Practice Project
-- @version 1.0
--
-- @note    Q16.16 encoding:
--            real_value = integer_signal / 65536
--            e.g. $100.50  ->  100.50 * 65536 = 6_586_368  (0x0064_8000)
--                 spread $0.01 ->  0.01 * 65536 =       655  (0x0000_028F)
--
-- @note    Synthesizable with Vivado 2022.1+; targets Artix-7 / Kintex-7 /
--          UltraScale+ devices.  No floating-point DSP required.
-- =============================================================================

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

-- =============================================================================
-- Entity
-- =============================================================================
entity market_maker is
    port (
        -- Clock / reset
        clk          : in  std_logic;                     -- Rising-edge clock
        rst_n        : in  std_logic;                     -- Active-low sync reset

        -- Input prices (Q16.16 fixed-point, signed 32-bit)
        bid_price_in : in  signed(31 downto 0);           -- Best bid price
        ask_price_in : in  signed(31 downto 0);           -- Best ask price
        spread_in    : in  signed(31 downto 0);           -- Desired order spread

        -- Input handshake
        valid_in     : in  std_logic;                     -- Input data valid

        -- Output quotes (Q16.16 fixed-point, signed 32-bit)
        buy_price_out  : out signed(31 downto 0);         -- Computed buy  quote
        sell_price_out : out signed(31 downto 0);         -- Computed sell quote

        -- Output handshake
        order_valid_out : out std_logic                   -- Output data valid
    );
end entity market_maker;

-- =============================================================================
-- Architecture
-- =============================================================================
architecture rtl of market_maker is

    -- Internal registered pipeline signals
    signal mid_price   : signed(31 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal half_spread : signed(31 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal buy_price_r : signed(31 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal sell_price_r: signed(31 downto 0) := (others => '0');
    signal valid_r     : std_logic            := '0';

    -- Wider accumulator to avoid overflow during (bid + ask) addition
    signal bid_plus_ask : signed(32 downto 0) := (others => '0');

begin

    -- =========================================================================
    -- Registered 1-cycle pipeline
    -- All arithmetic is performed combinatorially then registered on the
    -- rising edge, giving a clean single-cycle latency with no glitching.
    -- =========================================================================
    pipeline_reg : process(clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            if rst_n = '0' then
                mid_price    <= (others => '0');
                half_spread  <= (others => '0');
                buy_price_r  <= (others => '0');
                sell_price_r <= (others => '0');
                valid_r      <= '0';
            else
                valid_r <= valid_in;

                if valid_in = '1' then
                    -- Extend by one bit to hold the carry from addition, then
                    -- arithmetic right-shift by 1 to divide by 2.
                    bid_plus_ask <= resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33);
                    mid_price    <= resize(
                                        shift_right(
                                            resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33),
                                            1),
                                        32);

                    -- half_spread = spread_in / 2  (arithmetic right shift)
                    half_spread  <= shift_right(spread_in, 1);

                    -- buy  quote = mid - half_spread
                    -- sell quote = mid + half_spread
                    buy_price_r  <= shift_right(
                                        resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33),
                                        1)(31 downto 0)
                                    - shift_right(spread_in, 1);

                    sell_price_r <= shift_right(
                                        resize(bid_price_in, 33) + resize(ask_price_in, 33),
                                        1)(31 downto 0)
                                    + shift_right(spread_in, 1);
                end if;
            end if;
        end if;
    end process pipeline_reg;

    -- Drive output ports from registered values
    buy_price_out   <= buy_price_r;
    sell_price_out  <= sell_price_r;
    order_valid_out <= valid_r;

end architecture rtl;
