## Added in Lesson 0010 (Low-Latency C++ Best Practices)

### alignas(64) — `intro`
C++ keyword that forces a variable onto a 64-byte (cache-line) boundary.
Used on SPSC ring head/tail indices to prevent false sharing between
producer and consumer cores.

### Busy polling (CPU side) — `intro`
Spin in user space calling `_mm_pause()` on the data source (a ring, a NIC
queue) instead of sleeping. Near-zero wakeup latency; burns one core at
100% utilization. Used on the strategy thread; not on the logger.

### Cache coherence / Line ping-pong — `intro`
When two cores repeatedly write to the same cache line, the line bounces
between their L1 caches via the L3 (~30 ns per round-trip). The performance
killer that `alignas(64)` defends against.

### CPU isolation (`isolcpus`) — `intro`
Linux kernel boot parameter that tells the scheduler to leave specific
cores free of general tasks. Combined with `nohz_full` (no timer tick) and
`rcu_nocbs` (no RCU callbacks) for true HFT-grade isolation.

### `_mm_pause()` — `intro`
x86 intrinsic that hints to the CPU that this is a spin-wait loop. Slows
speculative execution, conserves power, friendlier to a sibling
hyperthread. Always used in tight polling loops.

### Lock-free vs Wait-free — `intro`
**Lock-free**: at least one thread always makes progress. **Wait-free**:
every thread completes in bounded steps. A correct SPSC ring with the
above pattern is wait-free; most MPMC queues are only lock-free.

### LTO (Link-Time Optimization) — `intro`
Compiler flag (`-flto`) that runs the optimizer at link time across all
translation units, enabling cross-TU inlining and dead-code elimination.
Stacks with PGO.

### `mlockall` — `intro`
Linux syscall that locks all of a process's pages into RAM, preventing the
kernel from paging them out. Used in HFT setups so a memory page fault
can't introduce ms-scale jitter.

### `memory_order_acquire` — `intro`
Atomic load ordering that pairs with `release` on the other side. Ensures
all reads after the acquire-load see writes done before the matching
release-store. Used by the SPSC consumer reading `head_`.

### `memory_order_relaxed` — `intro`
Atomic operation with no synchronization — only atomicity. Cheapest. Used
when the thread owns the variable (e.g. the producer reading its own
`head_`).

### `memory_order_release` — `intro`
Atomic store ordering. Guarantees all writes done before the store are
visible to a thread that acquire-loads the same atomic. The "publish" in
SPSC.

### `memory_order_seq_cst` — `intro`
Atomic ordering that gives a total global order over all seq_cst
operations. Default in `std::atomic`. ~5–10 ns overhead on x86
(MFENCE). Avoid unless you actually need it.

### `nohz_full` — `intro`
Linux boot parameter that disables the 1 kHz scheduling timer on isolated
cores when only one task is runnable. Removes ~1000 interrupts/sec of
jitter from the HFT hot path.

### MPSC / MPMC queue — `intro`
**MPSC**: multi-producer, single-consumer (e.g. many threads feeding one
logger). **MPMC**: multi-producer, multi-consumer. Both are more expensive
than SPSC; design the system to need SPSC wherever possible.

### PGO (Profile-Guided Optimization) — `intro`
Build twice: first with `-fprofile-generate` to instrument, run a
representative workload, then rebuild with `-fprofile-use` so the compiler
knows which branches are hot. 5–15% latency wins on the hot path.

### `pthread_setaffinity_np` — `intro`
POSIX call that pins a thread to a specific CPU core via a `cpu_set_t`
mask. The C++-side mechanism for the per-thread pinning that pairs with
`isolcpus`.

### `rcu_nocbs` — `intro`
Linux boot parameter that offloads RCU (read-copy-update) callbacks off
the specified cores. Removes a class of kernel work from the HFT cores.

### `SCHED_FIFO` — `intro`
Linux real-time scheduling class. A `SCHED_FIFO` thread runs until it
voluntarily blocks; preempts lower-priority work. Used for the strategy
thread.

### SPSC ring buffer — `intro`
Single-producer / single-consumer lock-free queue using a power-of-two
circular array and atomic head/tail indices with release/acquire ordering.
The HFT-grade inter-thread communication primitive.

### Synchronizes-with relationship — `intro`
The C++ memory-model term for the formal guarantee that a release-store on
one thread "synchronizes with" an acquire-load that reads its value on
another thread. The reason SPSC rings need release/acquire to be correct.

### Thread pinning — `intro`
Binding a thread to a specific CPU core so the scheduler can't migrate it.
Eliminates cache invalidation from migration and is the in-program half of
`isolcpus`-based isolation.

## Added in Lesson 0011 (Low-Latency vs Ultra-Low-Latency)

### Adverse selection (in latency context) — `intro`
Losing money systematically because faster participants see the same signal
microseconds before you and pick off the favorable side. The structural risk
of running at a lower tier than your venue's median competitor.

### App-to-app latency — `intro`
Latency measured between two points inside your application code only
(e.g. signal extracted → decision made). Excludes wire and kernel. Useful
for internal optimization, not for competitive comparison.

### ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) — `intro`
Custom silicon fabricated for one purpose. Faster than FPGAs but multi-
million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen logic. Tier 6 of the latency ladder;
only the largest desks justify it.

### Hardware timestamp — `intro`
A nanosecond-resolution timestamp attached to a packet by the NIC or FPGA at
ingress/egress. The only trustworthy clock at ULL scales — immune to OS
scheduling and clock skew.

### Inside-FPGA latency — `intro`
Latency measured between registers on a single FPGA, i.e. a fixed number of
clock cycles. At 250 MHz, 1 cycle = 4 ns. Fundamentally different unit than
wire-to-wire latency.

### Jitter (latency variability) — `intro`
The variability of latency across events, often quoted as `p99.99 − p50` or
as the standard deviation. ULL systems are judged on jitter as much as on
median latency.

### Latency ladder / tier — `intro`
The 6-rung industry mental model of trading-system latency, from Tier 0
(web app, ms) through Tier 6 (ASIC + microwave, ns + cross-market RF). Each
rung is ~10× more expensive than the one above.

### Latency tail — `intro`
The high-percentile portion of the latency distribution (p99, p99.9,
p99.99). At HFT message rates, tail events happen multiple times per
second; the tail is what loses money, not the mean.

### Low-latency (LL) — `intro`
Industry term for systems with microsecond-scale tick-to-trade (~1–100 µs).
Tuned C++, lock-free queues, kernel TCP. Tier 2 of the ladder.

### Microwave / RF link — `intro`
Line-of-sight wireless link used for cross-market arbitrage. Light through
air ≈ 1.0c vs ~0.67c through glass — a few ms edge over a thousand km. The
basis of the Chicago↔NJ trading corridor.

### One-way latency — `intro`
Time from event ingress to action emission, measured in one direction
(e.g. tick arrival → order on wire). Distinct from round-trip; both are
quoted in HFT and must be specified.

### p50 / p99 / p99.99 — `intro`
Quantiles of the latency distribution: 50%, 99%, 99.99% of events come in
under this latency. HFT systems are evaluated on the higher percentiles.

### Real-time (OS sense) — `intro`
Bounded worst-case latency. Distinct from "fast" — a 10 ms deterministic
system is real-time; a 100 ns average with a 10 ms tail is not. ULL systems
aim to be real-time first.

### Round-trip latency — `intro`
Time from event ingress to action egress through the full pipeline, including
the order leaving your NIC. The headline tick-to-trade number in most
benchmarks is wire-to-wire round-trip.

### Strategy cadence — `intro`
The natural decision rate of a strategy (per day, per second, per tick).
The single most useful input to deciding what tier of latency the strategy
needs.

### TSC (Time-Stamp Counter) — `intro`
x86 CPU register incremented every cycle. Read with `rdtsc` in ~10 ns;
nanosecond resolution but needs `tsc_reliable` and per-core synchronization
on multi-socket systems.

### Ultra-low-latency (ULL) — `intro`
Industry term for systems with nanosecond-scale tick-to-trade (~10 ns – 1
µs). FPGA, kernel-bypass NIC, hardware timestamps, microwave links. Tiers
3–6 of the ladder.

### Wire-to-wire latency — `intro`
Time from the last bit of an inbound packet arriving at the NIC to the
first bit of an outbound order leaving the NIC. The most defensible
endpoint pair for competitive benchmarking.

## Added in Lesson 0012 (RF Engineering in HFT)

### Anova Financial Networks — `intro`
Major common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT firms. Competitor
to McKay Brothers on the main US/EU corridors.

### Aurora (Aurora, IL) — `intro`
CME Group's data center, the futures venue side of the famous CME↔NJ
arbitrage corridor. Pairs with Carteret/Secaucus for the equity venues.

### Carteret (Carteret, NJ) — `intro`
The equities-side endpoint of the CME↔NJ corridor — Nasdaq's primary
data center. The NYSE-side anchor in Mahwah and Secaucus play the same
role.

### Common-carrier (microwave) — `intro`
Operating model where one company runs the towers, licenses, and antennas
and sells tiered access to multiple HFT firms. McKay Brothers and Anova
are the dominant examples on US/EU routes.

### E-band (millimeter-wave) — `intro`
71–86 GHz licensed band. Carries gigabits but only over 5–10 km hops due
to atmospheric absorption and rain fade. Used for last-mile in/out of
exchange data centers; not for long-haul.

### FCC licensing (microwave) — `intro`
Each individual microwave hop in the US requires an FCC frequency
authorization. The lower bands (6, 11 GHz) are heavily licensed and
incumbents have priority, which is one of the structural reasons HFT
firms rent rather than build.

### Fresnel zone — `intro`
The ellipsoidal volume around the line-of-sight between two microwave
antennas. Must be roughly 60% obstruction-free for the link to work.
Buildings, trees, terrain, and seasonal crops all matter for route planning.

### Great-circle distance — `intro`
Shortest path between two points on Earth's surface, ignoring terrain. The
floor against which any real route — fiber or microwave — is compared.

### Hollow-core fiber — `intro`
Optical fiber where light travels through an air-filled channel inside
photonic-crystal walls, at ~99% c instead of ~68% c through silica. Wider
bandwidth than microwave, weather-immune; ~1 ms slower than microwave one-way
on CME↔NJ. Many HFT firms now run both in parallel.

### Line-of-sight (LOS) — `intro`
Direct visual path between transmitter and receiver. Earth's curvature
limits hop length to 40–70 km on typical towers. HFT microwave links are
always LOS; tropospheric scatter is not used.

### McKay Brothers — `intro`
Dominant common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT corridors,
including a CME↔NJ route with published target of <8 ms round-trip.
Also offers hollow-core fiber and integrated packages.

### Microwave link — `intro`
Wireless point-to-point communication link in the 3–30 GHz range used for
long-haul HFT routes between exchanges. Travels through air at ~99.97% c,
narrow bandwidth (~100 Mbps), weather-sensitive, line-of-sight.

### Modulation (in HFT RF context) — `intro`
The scheme that maps bits onto a radio carrier (QPSK, 16-QAM, 256-QAM,
1024-QAM). Higher orders carry more bits per symbol but need higher SNR
and add encoding latency. HFT uses lower orders to minimize per-hop latency.

### Rain fade — `intro`
Signal attenuation due to rainfall absorbing radio energy. Sharply worse
at higher frequencies (severe at 80 GHz, negligible at 6 GHz). One of the
reasons HFT long-haul stays in lower bands.

### Refractive index — `intro`
Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to speed in a medium. Higher index =
slower light. Air ~1.0003 (~0.997c), hollow-core fiber ~1.005 (~0.995c),
silica fiber ~1.47 (~0.68c). The dominant physics behind the microwave
vs fiber gap.

### Sponsored access / Common carrier vs Private link — `intro`
**Common-carrier**: shared infrastructure rented by multiple HFT desks
(McKay, Anova). **Private link**: a single firm owns the towers and
licenses. Largest desks may build private; everyone else rents.

### Tier (microwave subscription) — `intro`
A pricing/priority level for a common-carrier microwave link. Premium tier
gets the lowest latency and dedicated slots; standard tier pays a slightly
higher serialization delay. Annual cost: undisclosed but in the seven
figures per route at premium.

### Tower spacing / Hop length — `intro`
Practical distance between consecutive microwave repeater towers, typically
40–70 km on long-haul HFT links. Limited by Earth's curvature and tower
height. Each hop adds ~10s of ns of equipment latency.

## Added in Lessons 0013–0024 (batch update, 2026-06-10)

Compact form: one-line definitions grouped by source lesson. Promote to fuller
entries as terms get used in conversation.

### From Lesson 0013 (DMA)

- **Direct Market Access (Trading DMA)** — Buy-side firm submits orders directly to the exchange matching engine through a broker's infrastructure, no human in between.
- **Sponsored Access** — Lowest-latency form of DMA where the buy-side uses the broker's MPID and connectivity but skips most of the broker's order-management stack.
- **Naked access** — Pre-2011 sponsored access with no pre-trade risk filter. Prohibited by Rule 15c3-5.
- **MPID** — Market Participant Identifier, the 4-character code identifying a broker on a venue. Sponsored customers trade under their sponsor's MPID.
- **FIX protocol** — The dominant exchange messaging protocol for orders. NewOrderSingle = 35=D.
- **SEC Rule 15c3-5** — US Market Access Rule (2011). Requires brokers to maintain undisableable pre-trade risk controls on customer order flow.
- **Direct Memory Access (Hardware DMA)** — Peripheral (NIC, FPGA, GPU) reads/writes host RAM via PCIe without CPU executing every transfer.
- **Descriptor ring** — Pre-allocated array in host memory; entries describe DMA transfers. The mailbox between CPU and device.
- **Doorbell register** — Memory-mapped register on device; CPU writes to it as a single PCIe write to signal "new work in the ring."
- **Zero-copy** — Design property where data is read/written from its final location, no intermediate buffers. Requires DMA but isn't synonymous with it.
- **RDMA** — Remote DMA. Device accesses another machine's host memory over the network (InfiniBand, RoCE).
- **PIO** — Programmed I/O. CPU executes load/store instructions to copy every byte. The pre-DMA way.

### From Lesson 0014 (Hardware Acceleration)

- **DPU** — Data Processing Unit. SmartNIC with full ARM CPU complex and OS. NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando.
- **SmartNIC** — NIC with programmable packet engines and embedded compute. DPU is the marketing term.
- **NPU** — Neural Processing Unit. ASIC specialized for matmul + activation patterns of neural nets.
- **TPU** — Tensor Processing Unit. Google's NPU for training and inference.
- **Acceleration vs Offload** — Acceleration: same work, faster. Offload: same work, elsewhere so the original CPU is freed.

### From Lesson 0015 + 0020 (Alternative Data)

- **Alternative data (alt-data)** — Any non-traditional data source that hints at economic reality before official numbers. Must lead the official metric, be hard to replicate, and map to a tradable.
- **SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar)** — Satellite imaging technique that sees through clouds and at night. Used by Ursa Space for oil tanks and by ship trackers.
- **Ursa Space Systems** — NY firm tracking ~11,000 oil tanks worldwide via SAR.
- **Foursquare** — Geolocation provider; famous 2016 Chipotle revenue prediction from check-in foot-traffic.
- **NDVI** — Normalized Difference Vegetation Index: (NIR − RED) / (NIR + RED). Crop-health signal from satellite multispectral imagery.
- **AIS (Automatic Identification System)** — Mandatory ship position broadcast (ships >300 GT). Combined with SAR to catch dark-fleet behavior.
- **Alpha decay** — The phenomenon where alt-data signals lose value as more funds subscribe. The frontier always moves to harder data.
- **SafeGraph / Placer.ai / Veraset** — Major commercial geolocation data vendors for foot-traffic analytics.
- **RS Metrics / Orbital Insight / SpaceKnow / Planet Labs** — Major satellite alt-data providers.

### From Lesson 0016 (Order-Book Dynamics)

- **Limit Order Book (LOB)** — Continuously updated structure tracking all resting buy/sell orders, sorted by price-time priority.
- **Price-time priority** — Match incoming marketable orders first by price, then by FIFO arrival time within each price level.
- **Order-book imbalance** — `(bid_size − ask_size) / (bid_size + ask_size)`. Microstructure signal predicting short-term mid drift.
- **Top of book** — Best bid + best ask only. L1 data.
- **Queue position** — Where your order sits in the FIFO at its price level. Determines fill priority.
- **LOB events** — ADD, CANCEL, MODIFY, TRADE, NEW LEVEL.

### From Lesson 0017 (Market Making)

- **Reservation price** — In Avellaneda-Stoikov: the inventory-skewed "fair" price the MM uses as the center of its quotes. Not the mid when inventory ≠ 0.
- **Avellaneda-Stoikov framework** — Canonical mathematical treatment of optimal MM quoting under inventory risk and adverse selection.
- **Maker rebate** — Per-fill rebate paid by venues to liquidity-providing orders. Significant secondary income for MMs.
- **Designated Market Maker (DMM)** — MM with formal quoting obligations on a venue in exchange for benefits (relaxed OTR, rebates, sometimes flat fees).
- **Spread capture** — MM revenue mechanism: earn the bid-ask spread on round-trip fills.

### From Lesson 0018 (Statistical Arbitrage)

- **Statistical arbitrage** — Strategy family exploiting statistical patterns across many bets, profitable on average even if individual trades can lose. Not true arbitrage.
- **Pairs trading** — Long one asset, short a related one, trade the spread on mean reversion.
- **Cointegration** — Two non-stationary series whose linear combination is stationary. The math behind pairs trading.
- **Engle-Granger procedure** — Two-step test for cointegration: regress + ADF on residuals.
- **ADF (Augmented Dickey-Fuller) test** — Statistical test for unit root / non-stationarity.
- **Market-neutral** — Portfolio with zero net market beta exposure. Achieved by hedging out the index.
- **Factor neutrality** — Portfolio neutral to specific risk factors (sector, size, value, momentum). Tighter than market-neutral.

### From Lesson 0019 (Order-to-Trade Ratio)

- **Order-to-Trade Ratio (OTR)** — (orders + modifications + cancellations) / executions, per participant per instrument per day. Venue-enforced regulatory metric.
- **MiFID II RTS 9** — EU regulation operationalizing OTR limits at trading venues.
- **Article 51(3) MiFID II** — Requires venues to have systems limiting OTR to prevent disorderly trading.
- **ESU fee** — Excessive System Usage fee. Eurex's mechanism for charging participants who exceed OTR limits.
- **Quote stuffing** — Flooding venue with messages to slow competitors. Targeted by OTR caps.
- **Spoofing** — Posting orders with no intent to fill, to manipulate the book. Illegal; OTR is a noisy proxy.

### From Lesson 0021 (AI Preprocessing)

- **StandardScaler** — Z-score: (x − mean)/std. Default normalization for NNs.
- **RobustScaler** — (x − median)/IQR. Outlier-resistant.
- **Min-max scaling** — (x − min)/(max − min). Bounded to [0,1] but outlier-sensitive.
- **One-hot encoding** — Categorical → sparse binary vector. Simple, dimensionality-expanding.
- **Target encoding** — Categorical → mean target for that category. Powerful but leakage-prone.
- **Embedding (categorical)** — Learned dense vector per category. Standard NN approach.
- **Data augmentation** — Synthetic perturbations of training examples. Geometric, photometric, cutout, mixup. Mostly CV.
- **Walkforward split** — Chronological train/test split that respects time-series causality. Opposite of k-fold.
- **Leakage** — Future information accidentally present in training. Cardinal preprocessing sin.

### From Lesson 0022 (Object Detection)

- **YOLO** — "You Only Look Once" detector family. Production default for object detection.
- **DETR** — DEtection TRansformer. Set-prediction approach without anchors or NMS.
- **Grounding DINO** — Open-vocabulary detector: detects any class described by a text prompt.
- **NMS (Non-Maximum Suppression)** — Post-processing that collapses overlapping high-IoU detections to one.
- **IoU (Intersection over Union)** — Area of overlap / area of union. Box overlap metric in [0,1].
- **mAP** — Mean Average Precision. Standard detection benchmark. mAP@[0.5:0.95] is the strictest variant.
- **COCO** — Common Objects in Context. Reference dataset and metric standard.

### From Lesson 0023 (Segmentation)

- **Semantic segmentation** — Per-pixel class label. Doesn't distinguish individual instances.
- **Instance segmentation** — Per-pixel class + instance ID. Required for counting touching objects.
- **Panoptic segmentation** — Semantic + instance. "Things" get IDs; "stuff" (background) only gets class.
- **U-Net** — Encoder-decoder with skip connections. Foundational semantic-segmentation architecture.
- **Mask R-CNN** — Detection + per-instance mask head. Two-stage, accurate, slow.
- **SAM (Segment Anything Model)** — Meta 2023 foundation model for segmentation. Prompt-driven, zero-shot.
- **mIoU** — Mean IoU averaged across classes. Standard semantic-segmentation metric.
- **Dice coefficient** — 2·|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|). Boundary-friendly mask metric.

### From Lesson 0024 (Geometric Deep Learning)

- **Geometric Deep Learning (GDL)** — ML on non-Euclidean data (graphs, manifolds, Lie groups). Bronstein et al's framing.
- **Equivariance** — `f(g·x) = g·f(x)`. Output transforms predictably with input.
- **Invariance** — `f(g·x) = f(x)`. Output ignores transformation.
- **GNN (Graph Neural Network)** — Permutation-equivariant network on graphs. Message-passing over nodes/edges.
- **Lie group** — Continuous symmetry group (rotations SO(3), rigid motions SE(3), translations).
- **Group-equivariant network** — NN respecting a specified symmetry group's transformations.
- **Manifold network** — NN operating on data lying on a curved manifold (sphere, hyperbolic, SPD).
- **SPD manifold** — Symmetric Positive-Definite matrix cone. Where covariance matrices live.
- **Riemannian optimizer** — SGD/Adam variants that respect manifold structure of constrained parameter spaces.
- **PyTorch Geometric** — Standard PyTorch library for GNNs.
- **Geomstats** — Standard Python library for Riemannian computations and manifold-aware ML.

1 2 3 Lesson 0024 — AI: Geometric Calculus & Geometric Deep Learning 4
8
Lesson 0024Quiz: 0 / 4
9

AI: Geometric Calculus & Geometric Deep Learning

10

Why this matters: "geometric calculus" in modern ML usage points at geometric deep learning — neural networks built on non-Euclidean structures (graphs, manifolds, Lie groups). This is where the most rigorous structural-prior ML work lives in 2025, and it's directly relevant to quant: portfolios are graphs, returns live on manifolds, symmetries matter.

11 12

1. The big idea

13

Classical neural networks assume data lives in flat Euclidean space ℝⁿ. A lot of real data does not.[1]

14 15 16 17 18 19 20 21
Data typeActual structureSymmetry the model should respect
ImagesPixels on a 2D gridTranslation (object can move)
3D moleculesAtoms in ℝ³Rotation + translation (chemistry doesn't depend on orientation)
Social networkGraph of nodes + edgesNode permutation (relabeling shouldn't change meaning)
Robot poseElement of SE(3) — Lie group of rigid motionsLie group composition
Stock returnsPoints on the simplex (weights sum to 1) or on the cone of positive-definite covariance matricesRiemannian structure of these manifolds
22 23

Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) is the program of designing neural networks that are equivariant to the natural symmetries of the data. A model is equivariant to a transformation if applying the transformation to the input and applying it to the output give the same result.

24 25

2. The four pillars (Bronstein-style taxonomy)

26
27

1. CNNs — grids

Translation-equivariant by design. The convolution operation produces the same response whether the dog is in the upper-left or center-right of the image. The foundational geometric DL architecture, although it predated the framing.

28

2. GNNs — graphs

Permutation-equivariant by message passing. The graph is the data; nodes pass messages to neighbors; aggregation must be order-independent (sum, max, mean). PyTorch Geometric is the workhorse library.[2]

29

3. Group-equivariant networks — Lie groups

Generalization of CNNs to arbitrary symmetry groups. For 3D molecules: SE(3)-equivariant networks (e3nn, SEGNN). Used in AlphaFold and modern protein-structure prediction.[3]

30

4. Manifold networks — Riemannian

Networks that operate on data lying on curved manifolds (sphere, hyperbolic space, SPD matrices). Geomstats is the standard library; used in covariance-matrix learning, hyperbolic embeddings of hierarchies.[4]

31
32 33

3. "Geometric calculus" specifically

34

The phrase has two flavors in 2024–25 usage:

35 36

Flavor A: differential geometry on neural nets

37

Treating the loss landscape, the data manifold, or the parameter space as Riemannian objects. Practical artifacts:

38
    39
  • Riemannian optimizers: Adam/SGD adapted to non-Euclidean parameter spaces. Used when weights are constrained to live on a manifold (orthogonal matrices, SPD covariances).
    • 40
  • Information geometry: the Fisher information matrix turns the parameter space into a Riemannian manifold; natural gradient descent moves along its geodesics.
    • 41
  • Neural ODEs on manifolds: extend the ResNet → neural-ODE bridge to curved spaces. 2025 active research direction with extensions to Lie groups.[5]
    • 42
43 44

Flavor B: geometric algebra in neural nets

45

The Clifford / geometric-algebra formalism — multivectors, the geometric product — applied as neural network operations. Promising for physics-informed ML and for rotation-equivariant networks; not yet mainstream.

46 47

4. Why a quant should care

48

Three concrete touchpoints, none yet in this repo:

49 50

(a) GNN for portfolio risk modeling

51

The "graph of stocks" is naturally encoded as a GNN — nodes are tickers, edges encode sector / supply-chain / correlation relationships. Message passing learns embeddings that respect graph structure. Used by some quant funds as a feature-engineering step for cross-sectional ranking.

52 53

(b) SPD-manifold learning for covariance matrices

54

The covariance matrix Σ from Lesson 0006 lives on the cone of symmetric positive-definite matrices — a Riemannian manifold, not a Euclidean space. Standard ML treats it as a flat vector and loses structure. Riemannian methods (e.g. log-Euclidean metric) train portfolio optimization more stably. Direct application to predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only.

55 56

(c) Lie-group equivariance for time-series symmetries

57

Some time-series have natural group symmetries (e.g. time-shifting, sign reversal under sign of return). Equivariant networks exploit these explicitly; standard CNNs ignore them. Active research direction in 2025.[3]

58 59

5. Illustrative GNN code (PyTorch Geometric)

60 
from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv
61	import torch.nn as nn
62	
63	class PortfolioGNN(nn.Module):
64	    def __init__(self, in_dim, hid_dim):
65	        super().__init__()
66	        self.conv1 = GCNConv(in_dim, hid_dim)
67	        self.conv2 = GCNConv(hid_dim, hid_dim)
68	        self.head  = nn.Linear(hid_dim, 1)         # predicted return per node
69	
70	    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
71	        # x: [num_tickers, features], edge_index: [2, num_edges]
72	        h = self.conv1(x, edge_index).relu()
73	        h = self.conv2(h, edge_index).relu()
74	        return self.head(h).squeeze(-1)        # shape: [num_tickers]
75
76

The model is permutation-equivariant: relabeling the tickers gives a relabeled output. The cross-sectional prediction GBM in this repo also has that property (it doesn't use ticker identity), but GBM doesn't exploit edge structure; the GNN does.

77 78

6. Often confused with

79
80

Equivariant vs Invariant

Equivariant: f(g·x) = g·f(x). The output transforms predictably. Invariant: f(g·x) = f(x). The output ignores the transformation. Image-classification networks are translation-invariant; segmentation networks are translation-equivariant.

81

GNN vs Transformer

A transformer is technically a fully-connected GNN with attention as message-passing. Modern GNN research often borrows attention from transformers. The line is blurry; "GNN" usually implies sparse graphs.

82

Riemannian vs Euclidean optimization

Euclidean: SGD/Adam in ℝⁿ. Riemannian: SGD/Adam along geodesics of a curved manifold. Required when weights are constrained (orthogonal, SPD).

83

Geometric DL vs Physics-informed ML

Geometric DL: respect data symmetries via architecture. Physics-informed: respect physical laws via loss-function constraints. Different mechanisms, overlapping goals.

84
85 86

7. Practice

87

Q1. Why is a CNN considered translation-equivariant rather than translation-invariant?

    88
  • Because they use padding and stride.
    • 89
  • Because shifting the input shifts the feature maps correspondingly; the network's response transforms with the transformation, rather than ignoring it.
    • 90
  • Because of skip connections.
    • 91
  • Because pixels are permutation-equivariant.
    • 92

93 94

Q2. The covariance matrix in predict_next.py lives on the cone of SPD matrices, a Riemannian manifold. Why might Riemannian ML be relevant?

    95
  • Riemannian methods respect the SPD constraint by construction; Euclidean treatment can produce non-SPD outputs that break downstream optimization.
    • 96
  • Because Riemannian methods are computationally faster.
    • 97
  • Because they make the covariance matrix easier to interpret.
    • 98
  • Because they reduce the bandwidth of market-data feeds.
    • 99

100 101

Q3. Equivariance vs Invariance — which is correct?

    102
  • Equivariant means the output is unchanged by the transformation.
    • 103
  • Invariant: the output ignores the transformation. Equivariant: the output transforms with the input in a predictable way.
    • 104
  • Equivariant and invariant are synonyms in this context.
    • 105
  • Invariant only applies to RNNs; equivariant only to CNNs.
    • 106

107 108

Q4. A teammate proposes using a GNN to predict stock returns where nodes are tickers and edges encode sector and supply-chain relationships. What's the structural advantage over the repo's GBM?

    109
  • GNNs train faster than gradient-boosted trees.
    • 110
  • It explicitly models inter-ticker relationships via message passing on the graph, capturing sector and supply-chain co-movement that the GBM ignores.
    • 111
  • It automatically reduces overfitting by adding more parameters.
    • 112
  • It produces inference at lower latency than tree ensembles.
    • 113

114 115

8. Scenarios

116
S1. You implement a GNN for portfolio prediction with sector-edge graphs. It performs WORSE than the simple GBM. Diagnose the most likely causes. 117

Three usual suspects. (1) Graph topology is wrong: sector classifications are coarse and miss real economic relationships. Try edge weights based on returns-correlation or supply-chain data rather than industry codes. (2) Insufficient data: GNNs have more parameters than GBMs and need more rows. With 10k daily samples, the GNN may underfit while the GBM works on the same data. (3) Wrong aggregation: simple message-passing averages neighbors. Maybe you need attention-based aggregation (GAT) or skip connections. (4) Most boringly: the GBM was already exploiting all the signal there is. Sometimes the simpler model is just right; geometric structure isn't always available alpha.

118 119
S2. Your covariance-matrix-on-SPD-manifold work seems mathematically elegant but doesn't improve Sharpe in backtest. Should you ship it? 120

Probably not, but the framing matters. Riemannian SPD methods do improve numerical stability of the mean-variance optimization (the matrix inverse used in Σ⁻¹μ can blow up with naïve estimation). If your existing covariance pipeline already shrinks toward diagonal and adds regularization (as the repo's --shrink does), the numerical benefit is small. The mathematical elegance doesn't automatically translate to Sharpe. Either way, the right metric is Sharpe + drawdown + stability under regime change, not aesthetic appeal. Ship only if the empirical evidence is there.

121 122

Sources

123
    124
  1. A Friendly Primer on Geometric Deep Learning — Patrick Nicolas (Substack)
    2. 125
  2. PyTorch Geometric documentation
    3. 126
  3. Lie Group-Based Neural Networks — EmergentMind
    4. 127
  4. Geomstats — Riemannian geometry for ML
    5. 128
  5. Geometric Neural ODEs: From Manifolds to Lie Groups — MDPI Entropy (2025)
    6. 129

1	"""Reference solution — Exercise 03 (part 1): pairs-trading utilities.
2	
3	Numpy-only (no statsmodels): OLS hedge ratio, spread, z-score, a lag-0
4	Dickey-Fuller t-statistic, and an AR(1) half-life.
5	
6	Peek policy: attempt exercises/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py first.
7	"""
8	import numpy as np
9	
10	
11	def _ols(y: np.ndarray, X: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
12	    """OLS of y on X (X already includes any intercept column).
13	
14	    Returns (coefficients, standard errors).
15	    """
16	    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
17	    resid = y - X @ beta
18	    dof = len(y) - X.shape[1]
19	    sigma2 = float(resid @ resid) / dof
20	    cov = sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
21	    return beta, np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))
22	
23	
24	def hedge_ratio(y, x) -> float:
25	    """OLS slope of y on x (with intercept): how many units of x hedge one
26	    unit of y."""
27	    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
28	    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
29	    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
30	    beta, _ = _ols(y, X)
31	    return float(beta[1])
32	
33	
34	def spread_series(y, x, beta: float) -> np.ndarray:
35	    """Residual spread e_t = y_t - beta * x_t."""
36	    return np.asarray(y, dtype=float) - beta * np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
37	
38	
39	def zscore(spread) -> np.ndarray:
40	    """Standardized spread: (e - mean(e)) / std(e), sample std (ddof=1)."""
41	    e = np.asarray(spread, dtype=float)
42	    return (e - e.mean()) / e.std(ddof=1)
43	
44	
45	def dickey_fuller_stat(e) -> float:

"""Reference solution — Exercise 03 (part 1): pairs-trading utilities.

Numpy-only (no statsmodels): OLS hedge ratio, spread, z-score, a lag-0
Dickey-Fuller t-statistic, and an AR(1) half-life.

Peek policy: attempt exercises/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py first.
"""
import numpy as np


def _ols(y: np.ndarray, X: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """OLS of y on X (X already includes any intercept column).

    Returns (coefficients, standard errors).
    """
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    resid = y - X @ beta
    dof = len(y) - X.shape[1]
    sigma2 = float(resid @ resid) / dof
    cov = sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
    return beta, np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))


def hedge_ratio(y, x) -> float:
    """OLS slope of y on x (with intercept): how many units of x hedge one
    unit of y."""
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    beta, _ = _ols(y, X)
    return float(beta[1])


def spread_series(y, x, beta: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Residual spread e_t = y_t - beta * x_t."""
    return np.asarray(y, dtype=float) - beta * np.asarray(x, dtype=float)


def zscore(spread) -> np.ndarray:
    """Standardized spread: (e - mean(e)) / std(e), sample std (ddof=1)."""
    e = np.asarray(spread, dtype=float)
    return (e - e.mean()) / e.std(ddof=1)


def dickey_fuller_stat(e) -> float:
    """Lag-0 Dickey-Fuller t-statistic (with constant).

    Regress de_t = alpha + delta * e_{t-1} + eps and return t = delta / se.
    Strongly negative values reject the unit root (the spread mean-reverts);
    the 5% critical value with a constant is about -2.86.
    """
    e = np.asarray(e, dtype=float)
    de = np.diff(e)
    lag = e[:-1]
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(lag)), lag])
    beta, se = _ols(de, X)
    return float(beta[1] / se[1])


def half_life(e) -> float:
    """Mean-reversion half-life from an AR(1) fit.

    de_t = alpha + delta * e_{t-1} implies rho = 1 + delta and
    half_life = -ln(2) / ln(rho). Returns inf when the series does not
    mean-revert (delta >= 0).
    """
    e = np.asarray(e, dtype=float)
    de = np.diff(e)
    lag = e[:-1]
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(lag)), lag])
    beta, _ = _ols(de, X)
    delta = float(beta[1])
    if delta >= 0:
        return float("inf")
    return float(-np.log(2.0) / np.log(1.0 + delta))

Lesson 0025Quiz: 0 / 5

Gradient Boosting: A Deep Dive

Why this matters: GradientBoostingRegressor is the flagship model of this repo — every backtest in paper_trading_sim.py and walkforward_sim.py rides on it, with all-default hyperparameters. This lesson opens the black box: what each boosting round actually computes, why the defaults are what they are, and which knob you'd turn first on noisy financial data. (Lesson 0003 introduced the idea; this is the mechanics.)

1. The big idea: descent in function space

Ordinary gradient descent improves a parameter vector: w ← w − η·∇L(w). Gradient boosting improves a function. The model is a running sum:

Fm(x) = Fm−1(x) + ν · hm(x)   where each hm is a small regression tree fit to the negative gradient of the loss evaluated at the current predictions.[1]

For squared-error loss L = ½(y − F(x))², the negative gradient is just y − F(x) — the residual. So the procedure reads plainly:

  1. Start with the dumbest possible model: F₀(x) = mean(y).
  2. Compute what it got wrong on every row: r = y − F₀(x).
  3. Fit a shallow tree h₁ to predict those residuals.
  4. Add a shrunk copy of it: F₁ = F₀ + ν·h₁ (ν = learning rate, default 0.1).
  5. Repeat from step 2, M times (default M = 100).

Every round attacks whatever error pattern is still left. Different losses just change what "what it got wrong" means — absolute error gives sign-of-residual, Huber blends the two — which is why the same machinery handles robust regression for free.

2. Worked example — three rounds by hand

Five points, one feature, depth-1 trees (stumps), and ν = 0.5 so the arithmetic stays visible (sklearn's default is 0.1 — same mechanics, smaller steps, more rounds).

x12345
y246810

Round 0 — the constant

F₀ = mean(y) = 6 everywhere. Residuals r = y − 6 = [−4, −2, 0, 2, 4]. Sum of squared residuals (SSE): 40.

Round 1 — first stump

A stump on the residuals picks the best single split. Here that's x ≤ 2.5: left leaf predicts the left residual mean (−3), right leaf the right mean (+2). Shrink by ν=0.5 and add:

x12345
F₁ = 6 + 0.5·h₁4.54.5777
new residual y − F₁−2.5−0.5−1+1+3

SSE: 6.25 + 0.25 + 1 + 1 + 9 = 17.5.

Round 2 — second stump

Refit on the new residuals. The best split is now x ≤ 3.5 (left mean −4/3 ≈ −1.33, right mean +2) — a different split than round 1, because the error pattern changed. Add 0.5 of it:

x12345
F₂3.833.836.3388
residual y − F₂−1.83+0.17−0.330+2

SSE: ≈ 7.5. The trend 40 → 17.5 → 7.5 is the whole story: each round provably shrinks training error. That guarantee is also the danger — run long enough and the ensemble will fit pure noise, which is why the test error curve is U-shaped while training error only falls.

Key observation: the stump in round 2 chose a different split point than round 1. Boosting builds a staircase of corrections, each shaped by what's left to explain. That's fundamentally different from fitting one deep tree to y directly — the ensemble allocates its capacity where the remaining error is.

3. The three knobs and what they trade

Parametersklearn default[2]What raising it doesOn noisy financial data
n_estimators (M)100More rounds = lower training error, eventually overfittingUse early stopping (n_iter_no_change) on a chronological validation split rather than guessing M
learning_rate (ν)0.1Bigger steps = fewer trees needed, worse generalizationLower ν (0.01–0.05) + more trees almost always generalizes better; ν and M trade off roughly multiplicatively
max_depth3Deeper trees capture higher-order feature interactionsDaily-bar alpha signals rarely support depth > 4 — interactions deeper than 3 features are mostly noise at this signal-to-noise ratio

Two more worth knowing: subsample < 1.0 turns it into stochastic gradient boosting (each tree sees a random row sample — cheap variance reduction), and loss="huber" caps the influence of fat-tailed return outliers, which financial targets have in abundance.

4. In this project

paper_trading_sim.py:113–125 — the trainer

def train_model(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> GradientBoostingRegressor:
    model = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=42)   # all defaults: M=100, ν=0.1, depth=3
    model.fit(X, y)
    return model

Three things to notice:

  • The defaults are untuned. 100 trees × depth 3 × ν 0.1 is sklearn's general-purpose setting, not a choice made for daily equity returns. The first experiment worth running on this repo: ν=0.05 with early stopping, scored on the walk-forward Sharpe rather than in-sample R².
  • random_state=42 matters even without subsampling — feature-split ties are broken pseudo-randomly, so this pin is what makes a retrain reproducible.
  • The target is brutal. fwd_ret_1d (built in build_features, line 68, via shift(-1)) has a signal-to-noise ratio so low that train R² of a few percent is normal. The repo never needs the predictions to be accurate — only their daily ranking has to be better than random, because the backtest takes the top-N by predicted return (Lesson 0003's cross-sectional ranking argument).

walkforward_sim.py:224 — same model, different lifecycle

The walk-forward simulator can refit the same all-default GBM on a rolling window (--rolling_retrain, default 756 trading days ≈ 3 years, monthly cadence). That's the project's answer to non-stationarity: the feature→return mapping drifts as regimes change, so the ensemble is periodically rebuilt on recent history only. Note what this implies — the *hyperparameters* stay frozen across refits while the *trees* are entirely replaced. Tuning and retraining are different time scales.

The model bundle

{ "model": GradientBoostingRegressor, "features": ["close", "ret_1d", "ma_5", "ma_10", "ma_gap", "vol_10", "rsi_14"] }

Trees address features by column index, not by name. The features list in the saved bundle is the contract that keeps inference columns in training order — feed the columns shuffled and the model silently produces garbage. This is also why CLAUDE.md insists on retraining after any build_features change.

5. Often confused with

Gradient boosting vs Random forest

Both are tree ensembles; the resemblance ends there. Random forest: many deep trees trained independently on bootstrap samples, then averaged — variance reduction by averaging. Boosting: many shallow trees trained sequentially, each on the previous ensemble's residuals — bias reduction by correction. RF parallelizes trivially and barely overfits with more trees; boosting can't parallelize across trees and will overfit if you let M grow unchecked.

Boosting vs Gradient descent

Both follow a negative gradient, in different spaces. Gradient descent updates a fixed-length parameter vector. Boosting takes a step in function space: the "step direction" is itself a fitted tree approximating the gradient at every training point. Each boosting round = one gradient step where the step is a function.

GradientBoostingRegressor vs HistGradientBoosting / XGBoost / LightGBM

Same algorithm family, different engineering. The histogram-based variants bucket feature values into 256 bins before splitting, making training 10–100× faster on large data, and add niceties (native NaN handling, better regularization). At this repo's data size (~thousands of rows per training set) the classic implementation is fine; at S&P-500 × 10-years × minute-bars scale it wouldn't be.

Residual vs Gradient

For squared error they coincide (up to sign/scale), which is why "fit the residuals" is the standard intuition. For any other loss they differ — with absolute error each tree fits sign(y − F), with log-loss (classification) it fits y − p. "Fit the negative gradient" is the general truth; "fit the residuals" is the squared-error special case.

6. Practice

Q1. In the worked example, round 1's stump split at x ≤ 2.5 but round 2's split at x ≤ 3.5. Why did the split move?

  • Random tie-breaking from the seed chose a different split.
  • Round 2 fits a different target — the residuals left after round 1's correction — so the best split is wherever the remaining error now concentrates.
  • The tree got deeper in round 2, allowing more splits.
  • The learning rate shifted the split threshold.

Q2. You halve the learning rate from 0.1 to 0.05 and keep n_estimators at 100. What's the most likely immediate effect?

  • Stronger overfitting, since each tree now matters more.
  • Underfitting — the ensemble hasn't taken enough total correction with only 100 half-sized steps; you'd typically raise n_estimators to compensate.
  • Training becomes twice as fast.
  • Feature importance becomes concentrated on fewer features.

Q3. Why does this repo tolerate a model whose predictions of fwd_ret_1d are individually almost worthless (R² of a few percent)?

  • Because the strategy only consumes the cross-sectional ranking of predictions, not their values — small ordering skill compounds across many picks.
  • Because the risk overlay corrects the predictions downstream.
  • It doesn't — low R² means the model is broken and should be discarded.
  • Because adding more trees would push R² to acceptable levels.

Q4. Gradient boosting vs random forest — which statement is correct?

  • Random forests use shallow sequential trees; boosting uses deep independent trees.
  • Boosting parallelizes across trees more easily than random forests.
  • Random forests average independent deep trees to cut variance; boosting chains shallow trees to cut bias, so more rounds can eventually overfit.
  • Random forests are for classification and boosting is for regression.

Q5. After adding a new feature to build_features, a teammate loads the old saved model bundle and runs inference with the new 8-column frame. What happens?

  • The model transparently ignores the extra column.
  • Best case a shape error; worst case (same count, different order) silently wrong predictions — the bundle's feature list exists to prevent exactly this.
  • The model uses the new feature for splits it already has.
  • sklearn automatically refits the model on the new schema.

7. Scenarios

S1. You tune the GBM and training R² jumps from 4% to 35%, but walk-forward Sharpe drops from 1.1 to 0.4. What happened and what do you check?

Classic overfitting signature on a low signal-to-noise target. The extra in-sample fit is mostly memorized noise, and memorized noise doesn't repeat out-of-sample — but it does displace the small real signal in the ranking. Check: (1) which knob moved — deeper trees (max_depth > 4) and more estimators without early stopping are the usual suspects; (2) whether the validation used for tuning was chronological — a shuffled split leaks future rows into training and rewards exactly this kind of memorization (Lesson 0021's cardinal sin); (3) re-tune scoring on the walk-forward metric directly, not on R². On financial data, the right amount of fit usually feels insultingly small.

S2. The C++ ONNX path (gradient_boosting/main.cpp) must produce identical predictions to the Python model. After a retrain, Python and C++ disagree. List the likely causes in order.

(1) Stale export — the .onnx file was not regenerated after retraining; it still encodes the old trees (python gradient_boosting/model_to_onnx.py is the mandated step). (2) Feature-order drift — the C++ side builds its input vector by hand; if build_features changed order or added a column, the ONNX graph receives features at wrong indices and produces garbage with no error. (3) Float precision — ONNX Runtime evaluates in float32 while sklearn uses float64; tiny per-tree differences are normal, but they only matter if a comparison threshold sits exactly on a leaf boundary — disagreement beyond ~1e-6 relative means cause (1) or (2), not this. The fix discipline is in CLAUDE.md: retrain → re-export → rebuild together, never separately.

Sources

  1. scikit-learn User Guide §1.11 — Gradient boosting (algorithm, shrinkage, subsampling)
  2. sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingRegressor — API reference (defaults: n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, loss='squared_error')
  3. J. Friedman (2001), "Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine" — the original paper

Lesson 0026Quiz: 0 / 5

Linear Regression: OLS From First Principles

Why this matters: this repo now uses ordinary least squares in three genuinely different roles — as a hedge-ratio estimator (solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py, the stat-arb exercise you'll implement), as a hypothesis test (the Dickey-Fuller stat in the same file), and as an inference engine in silicon (fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd). One piece of math, three jobs. Lesson 0003 introduced the model; this lesson derives it.

1. The problem and the solution

Given n observations of a target y and p features (stacked into a matrix X with a leading column of 1s for the intercept), find the coefficient vector β that minimizes the sum of squared errors:

minβ ‖y − Xβ‖². Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations: XᵀXβ = Xᵀy, hence β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy.[1]

Why squared error? Three reasons stack: it makes the objective differentiable and convex (one global minimum, closed form); it equals the maximum-likelihood answer when noise is Gaussian; and it makes the residual vector orthogonal to every feature column — the fitted plane absorbs all linear structure, leaving residuals that no feature can explain linearly. That orthogonality is what stat-arb exploits: the pairs-trading spread is defined as an OLS residual.

The one-feature special case (worth memorizing)

slope β₁ = cov(x, y) / var(x),   intercept β₀ = ȳ − β₁x̄.

You will meet this exact formula again in Lesson 0028, where x = market returns and β₁ gets the famous name beta.

2. Worked example — by hand

Three points: x = [1, 2, 3], y = [2, 3, 5].

  • Means: x̄ = 2, ȳ = 10/3.
  • Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) = (−1)(−4/3) + 0 + (1)(5/3) = 3.  Σ(x−x̄)² = 2.
  • β₁ = 3/2 = 1.5,   β₀ = 10/3 − 1.5·2 = 1/3.
  • Fitted: ŷ = [1.83, 3.33, 4.83]. Residuals: [+0.17, −0.33, +0.17] — note they sum to zero (intercept guarantees it) and correlate zero with x (slope guarantees it).

How good is the fit? R²

R² = 1 − SSR/TSS, the fraction of y's variance the line explains. Here SSR = 1/6 ≈ 0.167 and TSS = Σ(y−ȳ)² = 42/9 ≈ 4.667, so R² ≈ 0.964. Calibration for trading: an R² of 0.96 happens in textbooks; predicting next-day returns, 0.01–0.05 out-of-sample is a good year. High R² on a return target is usually a leakage alarm, not a victory.

How sure are we? Standard errors

Each coefficient comes with a standard error from σ̂²(XᵀX)⁻¹, where σ̂² = SSR/(n−p) is the residual variance (degrees-of-freedom corrected). The ratio β̂/SE is a t-statistic — "how many standard errors from zero is this coefficient?" This single idea powers the Dickey-Fuller test below.

3. In this project

solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py:11–21 — the engine, 8 lines of numpy

def _ols(y: np.ndarray, X: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)   # solve min ||y - Xb||² stably
    resid = y - X @ beta
    dof = len(y) - X.shape[1]                       # n - p degrees of freedom
    sigma2 = float(resid @ resid) / dof              # residual variance σ̂²
    cov = sigma2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)            # coefficient covariance σ̂²(XᵀX)⁻¹
    return beta, np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))               # (coefficients, standard errors)

Note what it does not do: it never forms (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy directly. lstsq solves the least-squares problem via SVD, which stays accurate when feature columns are nearly collinear — exactly the case where explicitly inverting XᵀX amplifies rounding error. The normal equations are how you understand OLS; lstsq (or QR) is how you compute it.[2]

Same file — three callers, three jobs

CallerRegression ofWhat's consumed
hedge_ratio(y, x)price series y on price series x (+ intercept)the slope — how many shares of x hedge one of y
spread_series / zscore(uses the slope from above)the residual e = y − βx — the mean-reverting thing you trade
dickey_fuller_stat(e)Δe on lagged e (+ intercept)the t-statistic β̂/SE — strongly negative ⇒ spread mean-reverts (5% critical ≈ −2.86)

That's the full anatomy of OLS output put to work: slope, residual, and standard error each carry a different trade-worthy fact.

fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd — inference is just four numbers

constant W0   : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(  50, 32);  -- intercept 0.05 (×1000)
constant W_F0 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 300, 32);  -- weight 0.30
constant W_F1 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed(-100, 32);  -- weight -0.10
constant W_F2 : signed(31 downto 0) := to_signed( 200, 32);  -- weight 0.20

This is the payoff of the parametric property from Lesson 0003: training produces a fixed, tiny parameter set, so inference is three multiplies and three adds — each * maps to a DSP slice, the whole prediction completes in 2 pipeline stages. Compare: shipping the 100-tree GBM to hardware means evaluating 100 tree traversals (the hls4ml problem). A linear model is the only model family where "deploy to FPGA" is trivially cheap — that's why it's the one living in fpga/ despite being the weakest predictor.

4. Often confused with

Correlation vs Regression slope

Related but not interchangeable: β₁ = corr(x,y) · σ_y/σ_x. Correlation is symmetric and unitless in [−1,1]; the slope has units of y-per-x and changes if you swap x and y. A pair can be 0.95-correlated with a hedge ratio of 0.3 or 3.0 — for hedging you need the slope, not the correlation.

Regressing y-on-x vs x-on-y

Not inverses! Slope(y on x) = cov/var(x) but slope(x on y) = cov/var(y); their product is corr², not 1. In pairs trading the choice of which leg is "y" changes the hedge ratio and therefore the spread. Convention: regress the leg you'll trade against the leg you'll hedge with — and test both directions for cointegration.

R² in-sample vs out-of-sample

In-sample R² never decreases when you add features — even pure-noise features. Out-of-sample R² (compute SSR on data the fit never saw) is the honest number and can be negative (worse than predicting the mean). Trading models live and die on the out-of-sample version.

lstsq vs normal equations

Same minimizer, different numerics. Forming (XᵀX)⁻¹ squares the condition number of X — with collinear features (think ma_5 and ma_10, correlated ~0.99) precision loss is real. SVD/QR-based solvers (np.linalg.lstsq) avoid it. Write the formula in your notebook; call the solver in your code.

5. Practice

Q1. For x = [1,2,3], y = [2,3,5], we found β₁ = 1.5 and β₀ = 1/3. What must be true of the residuals, by construction?

  • They are each smaller than 0.1 in absolute value.
  • They sum to zero and are uncorrelated with x.
  • They are normally distributed.
  • They are all positive.

Q2. Why does _ols in pairs.py call np.linalg.lstsq instead of computing inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y?

  • lstsq returns more coefficients.
  • Numerical stability — inverting XᵀX amplifies rounding error when features are nearly collinear; lstsq's SVD route doesn't.
  • lstsq is orders of magnitude faster.
  • The normal equations give a different (wrong) answer mathematically.

Q3. Stock A and stock B have return correlation 0.9. σ_A = 4%/day, σ_B = 1%/day. You're long 1 share-dollar of A; the hedge ratio from regressing A on B is…

  • ≈ 0.9 — same as the correlation.
  • ≈ 3.6 — correlation times the volatility ratio σ_A/σ_B.
  • ≈ 0.225 — correlation times σ_B/σ_A.
  • Exactly 1.0 — hedges are share-for-share.

Q4. The Dickey-Fuller test in pairs.py regresses Δe on lagged e and reports β̂/SE. Why is the standard error essential — why not just check whether β̂ is negative?

  • A random walk's estimated δ̂ comes out slightly negative by chance in most samples — only the size of δ̂ relative to its noise (the t-stat) separates real mean reversion from luck.
  • The SE corrects the bias in β̂.
  • Dividing by SE converts the units to percent.
  • It isn't essential; a negative β̂ already proves mean reversion.

Q5. Why is linear regression the model family in fpga/, when the GBM clearly predicts better?

  • Tree models are proprietary and can't be shipped to hardware.
  • Parametric compactness: four fixed constants synthesize to a few DSP slices with deterministic latency, while 100 trees would cost orders of magnitude more area and cycles.
  • Linear regression is more accurate on this data.
  • VHDL cannot express if-else logic, which trees need.

6. Scenarios

S1. You regress next-day returns on the repo's 7 features and get in-sample R² = 0.31. Celebrate or investigate?

Investigate, with leakage as the prime suspect. Daily equity returns are ~95%+ noise; honest models live at R² of a few percent. A 0.31 means one of: (1) a feature secretly contains the future — e.g. a moving average computed with a window that includes tomorrow's close, or the target shifted the wrong direction (the .shift(-1) discipline from Lesson 0003); (2) you computed R² on training data with many features relative to rows (in-sample R² inflates mechanically); (3) the data includes duplicated or overlapping rows. The test: walk-forward out-of-sample R². If it collapses to ~0 (or negative), it was leakage or overfit. If it genuinely holds out-of-sample at 0.31 on daily returns — you've made one of the great discoveries in finance, which is to say: check again.

S2. Your pairs spread y − 2.0x passed the DF test on 2023 data. In 2025 the hedge ratio re-estimates to 3.1 and the old spread trends. What's happening and what's the fix discipline?

The relationship drifted — cointegration is a property of a sample period, not a law of nature. Corporate actions, index reweighting, or a business-model change can permanently shift the equilibrium ratio. Holding the stale β means your "spread" now contains 1.1x of unhedged market exposure, which trends instead of mean-reverting — you're directionally long without intending it. Discipline: (1) re-estimate β on a rolling window (the same non-stationarity answer as walkforward_sim.py --rolling_retrain); (2) keep re-running the DF test — if the t-stat decays toward −2.86 and beyond, retire the pair; (3) size by the spread's recent half-life (half_life in pairs.py): if the half-life balloons from 5 days to 50, mean reversion has effectively left even if the test still scrapes by.

Sources

  1. Ordinary least squares — derivation of the normal equations, properties of residuals
  2. numpy.linalg.lstsq — SVD-based least-squares solver documentation
  3. statsmodels OLS documentation — reference implementation with full inference output (this repo deliberately re-implements the minimal core in numpy)

Lesson 0027Quiz: 0 / 5

Logistic Regression — and How It Differs From Linear

Why this matters: this repo contains zero logistic regressions, and that absence is a design decision worth understanding. Lesson 0003 asserted "regression beats classification for ranking"; this lesson gives you the machinery to defend that claim — and to recognize the cases where logistic regression is exactly the right tool.

1. The model: a linear core wearing a sigmoid

Logistic regression computes the same linear score as linear regression — z = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … + β_px_p — and then squashes it through the sigmoid (logistic) function:

P(y = 1 | x) = σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e−z)   — output is a probability in (0, 1), never a raw number.[1]

Anchor points worth memorizing: σ(0) = 0.5, σ(2) ≈ 0.88, σ(−2) ≈ 0.12, and σ is symmetric: σ(−z) = 1 − σ(z). Equivalently, the model says the log-odds are linear in the features: ln(p/(1−p)) = z. Each coefficient moves the log-odds, not the probability, by a fixed amount — that's the price of bounded output.

The loss: log-loss, not squared error

Training maximizes the likelihood of the observed labels, equivalent to minimizing log-loss: −[y·ln(p̂) + (1−y)·ln(1−p̂)]. Feel the asymmetry: predicting p̂ = 0.9 when y = 1 costs −ln(0.9) ≈ 0.105; the same p̂ = 0.9 when y = 0 costs −ln(0.1) ≈ 2.30 — twenty-two times more. Confident wrongness is punished brutally, which is what forces the probabilities to be calibrated rather than just ordered.

Unlike OLS there is no closed form: the first-order conditions are nonlinear in β, so fitting is iterative (Newton's method / IRLS, or gradient descent). Convexity still guarantees one global optimum — logistic regression keeps most of linear regression's tractability, just not its one-line solution.

2. The contrast (the point of this lesson)

Linear regressionLogistic regression
Shared coreidentical linear score z = Xβ; both parametric (p+1 numbers); both convex fits; both "regression" by name
Targetcontinuous number (e.g. fwd_ret_1d)probability of a discrete label (e.g. "up day")
Output range(−∞, ∞)(0, 1)
Losssquared errorlog-loss (negative log-likelihood)
Fitclosed form (normal equations / lstsq)iterative (no closed form)
Coefficient meaningΔy per unit ΔxΔlog-odds per unit Δx
Decision boundary—the hyperplane z = 0 (p = 0.5); linear, just like LDA's
The name trap: "logistic regression" is a classifier. The name survives from statistics, where "regression" means modeling a conditional expectation — here E[y|x] = P(y=1|x). When an interviewer asks "is logistic regression a regression or a classification model?", the expected answer covers both: it regresses the probability, which you then threshold to classify.

3. Why this repo deliberately has neither label nor sigmoid

You could absolutely rebuild this repo's pipeline as classification. Illustratively (illustrative — not in the repo):

# What the classification version of paper_trading_sim would look like:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
y_label = (feat["fwd_ret_1d"] > 0).astype(int)      # +2.0% day and +0.01% day → both just "1"
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y_label)
p_up = clf.predict_proba(X_today)[:, 1]              # P(up) per ticker
picks = p_up.argsort()[-5:]                          # top-5 by probability

The line that should bother you is the first one. Thresholding at zero throws away magnitude: a +4% day and a +0.02% day become the same label, and a −0.02% day becomes maximally different from the +0.02% day it's economically identical to. The strategy's P&L, however, is paid in magnitudes. A stock that's 55%-likely to go up 0.1% is a worse pick than one 45%-likely to go up 3% — the regression's expected-return ranking gets this right; P(up) ranking gets it wrong. That's the precise content of Lesson 0003's slogan.

# walkforward_sim.py:307 — regime filter, NOT logistic regression
probs = gm.predict_proba(arr)     # gm is a GaussianMixture

Same method name, different species. The GMM is unsupervised: nobody gave it labels; it invented its own clusters from return/vol shape and reports membership probabilities (Lesson 0005's "filtering"). Logistic regression is supervised: you define the label, it learns the boundary. Probability output is a property of many models — seeing predict_proba tells you nothing about which one you're holding.

Logistic regression vs Linear regression on 0/1 labels

You CAN fit OLS to a 0/1 target (the "linear probability model"). It sort of works, but predictions escape [0,1], the constant-variance assumption breaks, and squared error under-penalizes confident wrongness. Logistic is the same linear machinery with the right link and loss for probabilities.

Sigmoid: one number → probability of one binary event. Softmax: a vector of scores → a probability distribution over K classes. Probability vs Calibrated probability

A model can RANK well (high AUC) while its probabilities are miscalibrated — "0.9" events happening 70% of the time. The fitted model outputs probabilities; the 0.5 threshold is a DECISION, not part of the model. With asymmetric costs (false-buy vs missed-buy), the right threshold moves — and in trading you often skip thresholding entirely and size positions by probability × magnitude.

5. Practice

Q1. A logistic model gives z = 2 for a ticker. What is P(up), roughly, and what would z = −2 give?

Both, depending on the layer. Same: identical linear score z = Xβ — same features, same parametric form, same coefficient count, both convex to fit, both members of the generalized linear model family. Different: the link and the loss. Linear uses the identity link with squared error, modeling E[y|x] directly for a continuous y; logistic uses the logit link with log-loss, modeling P(y=1|x) for a binary y. Lesson 0028Quiz: 0 / 5

Alpha and Beta in Finance

Why this matters: this repo's headline claim — the best model bundle made ~27.19% annualized out-of-sample — is incomplete until you ask: how much of that was just market exposure? Alpha and beta are the decomposition that answers it, and they're literally the linear regression you derived in Lesson 0026, pointed at returns.

1. The model: CAPM as a regression

Regress your strategy's (excess) returns on the market's:

rstrategy,t = α + β · rmarket,t + εt[1]  — estimated by OLS, so  β = cov(r_s, r_m) / var(r_m)  and  α = r̄_s − β·r̄_m — slope and intercept from Lesson 0026's one-feature formula, verbatim.

QuantityWhat it measuresReading it
β (beta)Sensitivity to the market: on a day the market moves +1%, the strategy moves +β% on averageβ=1: index-like · β>1: amplified · 0<β<1: damped · β≈0: market-neutral · β<0: hedge-like
α (alpha)The intercept — average return left over after the market's contribution is subtracted out (Jensen's alpha[2])The part of performance you can't get by just buying the index with leverage. The thing quant funds are paid for.
ε (residual)Day-to-day noise uncorrelated with the marketIts volatility is your idiosyncratic risk; diversification attacks this term

(The textbook CAPM uses returns in excess of the risk-free rate, r − r_f. This repo's convention is r_f = 0 — same as its Sharpe in analyze_equity.py — so the simple form above is consistent.)

Worked example

Your backtest returns 20%/yr. SPY did 15%. Sounds like +5% of skill — but the regression says β = 1.3. Then:

  • Market's contribution: β × r_m = 1.3 × 15% = 19.5%.
  • α = 20% − 19.5% = +0.5%.

Almost the entire "outperformance" was just holding 1.3× of market risk — achievable with index futures for a few basis points. The strategy's actual skill content is half a percent, before asking whether even that is statistically distinguishable from zero (the α's t-stat, via the standard errors from Lesson 0026, answers that — and for most strategies on a few years of data, it isn't).

Why anyone pays 2-and-20: leverage scales β for nearly free, so the market's return is a commodity. α is the scarce thing — uncorrelated return that improves a portfolio no matter what else is in it. "Hedge fund" originally meant exactly this: hedge out β, keep α.

2. In this project

analyze_equity.py:compute_metrics — what's missing and the 10-line fix

The function reports CAGR, vol, Sharpe, MaxDD — all absolute metrics. Nothing compares the equity curve to a benchmark, so a bull-market backtest gets credit for the bull market. The addition would look like this (illustrative — not yet in the repo):

def alpha_beta(strategy_ret: pd.Series, market_ret: pd.Series) -> dict:
    # align the two return series on shared dates
    df = pd.concat([strategy_ret, market_ret], axis=1, keys=["s", "m"]).dropna()
    beta = df["s"].cov(df["m"]) / df["m"].var()      # Lesson 0026: slope = cov/var
    alpha_daily = df["s"].mean() - beta * df["m"].mean()
    return {"alpha_annual": alpha_daily * 252, "beta": beta}

Feed it the walk-forward equity curve's pct_change() and SPY's daily returns over the same dates. Until that number exists, "27.19% annualized 2020–2025" is unresolved: 2020–2025 contained a historic bull run, and a long-only top-5 momentum-flavored portfolio plausibly carries β near 1. The honest brag is "X% alpha at β = Y", not total return.

The exercise-03 connection: a hedge ratio is a beta

hedge_ratio(y, x) in solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py computes cov/var of two assets — mathematically the same slope, asked a different question: "how much of x offsets one unit of y?" Pairs trading in Lesson 0018 is now expressible in one sentence of this lesson's vocabulary: short the pair-beta, harvest the spread's mean reversion as alpha. Likewise "market-neutral" from that lesson just means engineering portfolio β to ≈ 0 — e.g. holding the repo's top-5 longs against a short index position sized by the portfolio's measured β.

Why a regulator-grade version uses the same machinery

Everything here generalizes: replace the single market factor with several (size, value, momentum — Fama-French style[3]) and the multi-feature OLS of Lesson 0026 decomposes returns into many betas plus a residual alpha. Factor neutrality (Lesson 0018's glossary entry) = driving those betas to zero too. One regression, the whole risk-attribution industry.

3. Often confused with

Alpha vs Total return

Total return = α + β·(market) + luck. A 30% year with β = 2 in a 15% market is ZERO alpha. Conversely a +4% year with β = 0 in a −20% market is heroic. Never evaluate a strategy's return without asking what its β bought for free.

Alpha vs Sharpe

Both are "skill" metrics with different denominators. Sharpe = return per unit of TOTAL volatility — it doesn't care whether the volatility is market or idiosyncratic. Alpha = return orthogonal to a BENCHMARK. A leveraged index fund has the same Sharpe as the index but zero alpha; a market-neutral book can have modest Sharpe and pure alpha. Allocators want both numbers.

Beta (CAPM) vs Beta (hedge ratio) vs β̂ (regression)

All the same OLS slope wearing different hats. Regression β̂: generic coefficient. CAPM beta: that slope when x = market returns. Hedge ratio: that slope when x = the other leg of a pair, used to size the offset. When a quant says "beta" unqualified, context decides — usually CAPM.

Market-neutral vs Hedged vs Flat

Flat: no positions. Hedged: some specific risk offset (maybe only partially). Market-neutral: measured portfolio β ≈ 0 — you can be massively invested long and short while having no net market exposure. Neutrality is a measured property, re-estimated continuously, not a label you set once.

4. Practice

Q1. Strategy returns 20%/yr with β = 1.3; the market returned 15%. (r_f = 0.) The alpha is…

  • +5% — it beat the market by five points.
  • +0.5% — the market explains 1.3 × 15% = 19.5% of the 20%.
  • −6.5%.
  • Can't be computed without the Sharpe ratio.

Q2. β = cov(r_s, r_m)/var(r_m). Where have you literally seen this formula before in this repo's code?

  • In solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py:hedge_ratio — the pairs-trading hedge ratio is the same OLS slope with a different x.
  • In analyze_equity.py:compute_metrics.
  • In fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd.
  • In paper_trading_sim.py:build_features.

Q3. A market-neutral fund returns +6% in a year the index drops −20%. A long-only fund returns +25% in a year the index gains +30% (β ≈ 1). Which showed more alpha?

  • The long-only fund — +25% beats +6%.
  • The market-neutral fund — +6% with β≈0 is +6% alpha, while the long-only fund's alpha is roughly −5%.
  • Roughly equal alpha.
  • Alpha can't compare funds with different strategies.

Q4. Sharpe vs alpha — a 2× leveraged S&P index fund has, relative to the index itself…

  • Higher Sharpe and positive alpha.
  • About the same Sharpe and zero alpha (β = 2).
  • Double the Sharpe, zero alpha.
  • β = 2 and meaningfully negative alpha.

Q5. The repo's best bundle shows 27.19% annualized over 2020–2025 (long-only top-5 daily picks). Before celebrating, the single most important missing number is…

  • The maximum drawdown.
  • Its β to the market over the same window — without it you can't say how much of the 27% was just the 2020–2025 bull market.
  • The model's n_estimators.
  • The training R².

5. Scenarios

S1. You add alpha_beta() to analyze_equity.py and the walk-forward strategy shows α = +9%/yr, β = 0.85, but the α's t-stat is 1.4. An allocator asks: "so do you have alpha or not?" What's the honest answer?

"The point estimate is +9% but the data can't yet rule out zero." A t-stat of 1.4 means the α is 1.4 standard errors from zero — below the conventional ~2 threshold, so a luck-only explanation survives. This is the normal condition for young strategies: with daily data, the t-stat grows roughly with √years × (information ratio), so a true α of this size might need 6–10 years of live-like history to clear significance. What you CAN say honestly: the β is well-estimated (slopes pin down much faster than intercepts), so the strategy is demonstrably not just leveraged market; and the α estimate is positive across subperiods (show it). What you cannot say: "we have proven 9% alpha." Allocators have heard that one before — Lesson 0026's standard-error discipline is exactly what separates the credible pitch.

S2. To make the strategy market-neutral, you short SPY futures sized at β = 0.85 of the book. Six months later the book is down on flat markets and the re-measured β of the *hedged* book is −0.4. What happened?

The hedge overshot because β drifted — and you kept paying for stale neutrality. β is an estimate from a window, not a constant: the portfolio's composition changes daily (top-5 picks rotate through sectors with different betas), and the picks' own betas move with regimes. If the book's true β fell toward 0.45 while you stayed short 0.85-worth of futures, the net position is β ≈ −0.4: you're now short the market, and "down on flat markets" is the bleed of negative carry plus noise on an unintended directional bet. Fix discipline: (1) re-estimate β on a rolling window (e.g. 60–120 days) and rebalance the hedge on a schedule or a drift threshold; (2) measure the hedged book's β continuously — neutrality is verified, never assumed; (3) consider beta-forecasting rather than trailing estimation if turnover is high. Same non-stationarity lesson as rolling retrains and rolling hedge ratios — parameters in finance are subscriptions, not purchases.

Sources

  1. Capital Asset Pricing Model — Sharpe (1964) / Lintner (1965); the security market line and beta
  2. Jensen's alpha — Jensen (1968), alpha as the regression intercept over CAPM-expected return
  3. Fama–French three-factor model — the multi-factor generalization of the single-beta decomposition
