  • α = 20% − 19.5% = +0.5%.

Almost the entire "outperformance" was just holding 1.3× of market risk — achievable with index futures for a few basis points. The strategy's actual skill content is half a percent, before asking whether even that is statistically distinguishable from zero (the α's t-stat, via the standard errors from Lesson 0026, answers that — and for most strategies on a few years of data, it isn't).

Why anyone pays 2-and-20: leverage scales β for nearly free, so the market's return is a commodity. α is the scarce thing — uncorrelated return that improves a portfolio no matter what else is in it. "Hedge fund" originally meant exactly this: hedge out β, keep α.

2. In this project

analyze_equity.py:compute_metrics — what's missing and the 10-line fix

The function reports CAGR, vol, Sharpe, MaxDD — all absolute metrics. Nothing compares the equity curve to a benchmark, so a bull-market backtest gets credit for the bull market. The addition would look like this (illustrative — not yet in the repo):

def alpha_beta(strategy_ret: pd.Series, market_ret: pd.Series) -> dict:
    # align the two return series on shared dates
    df = pd.concat([strategy_ret, market_ret], axis=1, keys=["s", "m"]).dropna()
    beta = df["s"].cov(df["m"]) / df["m"].var()      # Lesson 0026: slope = cov/var
    alpha_daily = df["s"].mean() - beta * df["m"].mean()
    return {"alpha_annual": alpha_daily * 252, "beta": beta}

Feed it the walk-forward equity curve's pct_change() and SPY's daily returns over the same dates. Until that number exists, "27.19% annualized 2020–2025" is unresolved: 2020–2025 contained a historic bull run, and a long-only top-5 momentum-flavored portfolio plausibly carries β near 1. The honest brag is "X% alpha at β = Y", not total return.

The exercise-03 connection: a hedge ratio is a beta

hedge_ratio(y, x) in solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py computes cov/var of two assets — mathematically the same slope, asked a different question: "how much of x offsets one unit of y?" Pairs trading in Lesson 0018 is now expressible in one sentence of this lesson's vocabulary: short the pair-beta, harvest the spread's mean reversion as alpha. Likewise "market-neutral" from that lesson just means engineering portfolio β to ≈ 0 — e.g. holding the repo's top-5 longs against a short index position sized by the portfolio's measured β.

Why a regulator-grade version uses the same machinery

Everything here generalizes: replace the single market factor with several (size, value, momentum — Fama-French style[3]) and the multi-feature OLS of Lesson 0026 decomposes returns into many betas plus a residual alpha. Factor neutrality (Lesson 0018's glossary entry) = driving those betas to zero too. One regression, the whole risk-attribution industry.

3. Often confused with

Alpha vs Total return

Total return = α + β·(market) + luck. A 30% year with β = 2 in a 15% market is ZERO alpha. Conversely a +4% year with β = 0 in a −20% market is heroic. Never evaluate a strategy's return without asking what its β bought for free.

Alpha vs Sharpe

Both are "skill" metrics with different denominators. Sharpe = return per unit of TOTAL volatility — it doesn't care whether the volatility is market or idiosyncratic. Alpha = return orthogonal to a BENCHMARK. A leveraged index fund has the same Sharpe as the index but zero alpha; a market-neutral book can have modest Sharpe and pure alpha. Allocators want both numbers.

Beta (CAPM) vs Beta (hedge ratio) vs β̂ (regression)

All the same OLS slope wearing different hats. Regression β̂: generic coefficient. CAPM beta: that slope when x = market returns. Hedge ratio: that slope when x = the other leg of a pair, used to size the offset. When a quant says "beta" unqualified, context decides — usually CAPM.

Market-neutral vs Hedged vs Flat

Flat: no positions. Hedged: some specific risk offset (maybe only partially). Market-neutral: measured portfolio β ≈ 0 — you can be massively invested long and short while having no net market exposure. Neutrality is a measured property, re-estimated continuously, not a label you set once.

4. Practice

Q1. Strategy returns 20%/yr with β = 1.3; the market returned 15%. (r_f = 0.) The alpha is…

  • +5% — it beat the market by five points.
  • +0.5% — the market explains 1.3 × 15% = 19.5% of the 20%.
  • −6.5%.
  • Can't be computed without the Sharpe ratio.

Q2. β = cov(r_s, r_m)/var(r_m). Where have you literally seen this formula before in this repo's code?

  • In solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py:hedge_ratio — the pairs-trading hedge ratio is the same OLS slope with a different x.
  • In analyze_equity.py:compute_metrics.
  • In fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd.
  • In paper_trading_sim.py:build_features.

Q3. A market-neutral fund returns +6% in a year the index drops −20%. A long-only fund returns +25% in a year the index gains +30% (β ≈ 1). Which showed more alpha?

  • The long-only fund — +25% beats +6%.
  • The market-neutral fund — +6% with β≈0 is +6% alpha, while the long-only fund's alpha is roughly −5%.
  • Roughly equal alpha.
  • Alpha can't compare funds with different strategies.

Q4. Sharpe vs alpha — a 2× leveraged S&P index fund has, relative to the index itself…

  • Higher Sharpe and positive alpha.
  • About the same Sharpe and zero alpha (β = 2).
  • Double the Sharpe, zero alpha.
  • β = 2 and meaningfully negative alpha.

Q5. The repo's best bundle shows 27.19% annualized over 2020–2025 (long-only top-5 daily picks). Before celebrating, the single most important missing number is…

  • The maximum drawdown.
  • Its β to the market over the same window — without it you can't say how much of the 27% was just the 2020–2025 bull market.
  • The model's n_estimators.
  • The training R².

5. Scenarios

S1. You add alpha_beta() to analyze_equity.py and the walk-forward strategy shows α = +9%/yr, β = 0.85, but the α's t-stat is 1.4. An allocator asks: "so do you have alpha or not?" What's the honest answer?

"The point estimate is +9% but the data can't yet rule out zero." A t-stat of 1.4 means the α is 1.4 standard errors from zero — below the conventional ~2 threshold, so a luck-only explanation survives. This is the normal condition for young strategies: with daily data, the t-stat grows roughly with √years × (information ratio), so a true α of this size might need 6–10 years of live-like history to clear significance. What you CAN say honestly: the β is well-estimated (slopes pin down much faster than intercepts), so the strategy is demonstrably not just leveraged market; and the α estimate is positive across subperiods (show it). What you cannot say: "we have proven 9% alpha." Allocators have heard that one before — Lesson 0026's standard-error discipline is exactly what separates the credible pitch.

S2. To make the strategy market-neutral, you short SPY futures sized at β = 0.85 of the book. Six months later the book is down on flat markets and the re-measured β of the *hedged* book is −0.4. What happened?

The hedge overshot because β drifted — and you kept paying for stale neutrality. β is an estimate from a window, not a constant: the portfolio's composition changes daily (top-5 picks rotate through sectors with different betas), and the picks' own betas move with regimes. If the book's true β fell toward 0.45 while you stayed short 0.85-worth of futures, the net position is β ≈ −0.4: you're now short the market, and "down on flat markets" is the bleed of negative carry plus noise on an unintended directional bet. Fix discipline: (1) re-estimate β on a rolling window (e.g. 60–120 days) and rebalance the hedge on a schedule or a drift threshold; (2) measure the hedged book's β continuously — neutrality is verified, never assumed; (3) consider beta-forecasting rather than trailing estimation if turnover is high. Same non-stationarity lesson as rolling retrains and rolling hedge ratios — parameters in finance are subscriptions, not purchases.

Sources

  1. Capital Asset Pricing Model — Sharpe (1964) / Lintner (1965); the security market line and beta
  2. Jensen's alpha — Jensen (1968), alpha as the regression intercept over CAPM-expected return
  3. Fama–French three-factor model — the multi-factor generalization of the single-beta decomposition

### From Lessons 0025–0028 (Regression suite + Alpha/Beta, added 2026-06-11)

- **OLS (Ordinary Least Squares)** — Fit β to minimize Σ(y − Xβ)². Closed form via the normal equations β = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy; computed stably via `np.linalg.lstsq` in `solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py:_ols`.
- **Normal equations** — XᵀXβ = Xᵀy, the first-order conditions of OLS. Conceptual form only; invert XᵀX in code and collinear features amplify rounding error.
- **R² (coefficient of determination)** — 1 − SSR/TSS, fraction of target variance explained. In-sample R² only grows with features; out-of-sample R² is the honest number and can be negative. A few percent is good on daily returns.
- **Standard error (coefficient)** — Uncertainty of an OLS coefficient, from σ̂²(XᵀX)⁻¹. β̂/SE is the t-statistic; powers the Dickey-Fuller test and the "is the alpha real?" question.
- **Shrinkage (learning rate ν, boosting)** — Scaling each boosted tree's contribution by ν before adding (default 0.1 in sklearn). Lower ν + more trees = better generalization. Distinct from covariance shrinkage (Lesson 0006).
- **Stochastic gradient boosting (subsample)** — Fitting each boosting round on a random row sample (`subsample < 1`), trading a little bias for variance reduction.
- **Function-space gradient descent** — Boosting's framing: each round adds a tree approximating the negative loss-gradient at every training point — a "gradient step" where the step is a function.
- **Sigmoid (logistic function)** — σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), maps a linear score to (0,1). σ(0)=0.5, σ(±2)≈0.88/0.12. The link function of logistic regression and a classic NN activation.
- **Log-loss (cross-entropy)** — −[y·ln p̂ + (1−y)·ln(1−p̂)]. Unbounded penalty for confident wrongness; forces calibrated probabilities. The loss logistic regression minimizes.
- **Logistic regression** — Linear score + sigmoid, fit by log-loss; a *classifier* despite the name. Not used in this repo by design — binarizing `fwd_ret_1d` would destroy the magnitudes the top-N ranking needs.
- **Linear probability model** — OLS fit directly to a 0/1 label. Works crudely; predictions escape [0,1]. The "why logistic exists" foil.
- **Calibration (probability)** — Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies ("0.9 events happen 90% of the time"). Distinct from ranking quality (AUC).
- **CAPM** — r_s = α + β·r_m + ε. Single-factor model decomposing strategy returns into market exposure and skill. Estimated with the same OLS as everything else.
- **Beta (β, market)** — cov(r_s, r_m)/var(r_m): the OLS slope of strategy returns on market returns. β≈0 = market-neutral. Same formula as `hedge_ratio` in exercise 03 — different x.
- **Alpha (α, Jensen's)** — The CAPM regression intercept: average return left after subtracting β×market. The scarce, paid-for part of performance; leverage replicates β but not α.
- **Market-neutral (measured)** — Portfolio whose *measured* β ≈ 0, re-estimated on a rolling basis. A maintained property, not a one-time label.
- **Factor model (multi-beta)** — CAPM generalized to several regressors (size, value, momentum — Fama-French). Multi-feature OLS; factor neutrality = driving all those betas to zero.

# Algo-Trading Learning Roadmap — from daily rebalancing to nanosecond HFT

A leveled curriculum built on THIS repo. Every level has three kinds of files:

1. **Working files** — real, runnable code already in the repo (the reference
   you read and run).
2. **Practice files** — the same components with bodies removed
   (`exercises/…` — you implement, an automated suite grades you).
3. **Tested references** — complete solutions (`solutions/…`) verified by the
   same suite, for after you've attempted the practice.

The grading machinery already exists: `exercises/` + `solutions/` +
`tests/exercises/` (see `exercises/README.md`). Unimplemented stubs show as
**skipped**, wrong answers **fail**, done means **green** — the pytest skip
count is your progress bar. C++ exercises compile and run via
`tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh`; VHDL via `scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh` (ghdl).

```bash
uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v                         # grade everything
HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v   # prove suites solvable
```

---

## The ladder at a glance

Latency classes follow Lesson 0011's tier ladder. "Theoretical speed" is the
per-decision software latency the level's techniques can reach.

| Level | Domain | Decision cadence | Theoretical speed | Repo assets | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L0** | Daily-frequency ML trading (what you have) | 1/day | seconds per run (offline) | `paper_trading_sim.py`, `walkforward_sim.py`, `predict_next.py`, `analyze_equity.py`, `tests/` | ✅ working + tested |
| **L1** | Quant math: regression, stat-arb, risk | 1/day–1/min | ms (numpy) | exercise **03** (pairs/CUSUM/OTR/walk-forward splits); lessons 0006, 0018, 0019, 0026, 0028 | ✅ practice ready |
| **L2** | Market microstructure in Python | per-tick (simulated) | µs–ms (Python) | exercise **01** (order book), **02** (inventory-aware market maker); lessons 0016, 0017 | ✅ practice ready |
| **L3** | Low-latency C++ building blocks | per-tick | ~10–100 **ns** per op | exercise **04** (O(1) MA + lock-free SPSC ring), `gradient_boosting/` ONNX C++, `tests/cpp/`; lessons 0009, 0010 | ✅ practice ready |
| **L4** | Ultra-low-latency C++ systems | millions of msgs/sec | ~100 ns–1 µs tick-to-trade (CPU) | **proposed batch 06–08** (C++ order book, binary feed handler, latency benchmark harness); lessons 0011, 0013 | 🔜 to build |
| **L5** | Hardware (FPGA/VHDL) | per-tick, wire-rate | ~4–50 ns (cycles, deterministic) | exercise **05** (GHDL testbenches), `fpga/*.vhd`; **proposed batch 09** (inventory-aware MM in VHDL); lessons 0002, 0014 | ✅ practice ready / 🔜 extension |
| **L6** | Capstone: tick-to-trade integration | end-to-end | measured p50/p99/p99.99 | **proposed batch 10** (replay → book → strategy → order, with hardware-style latency report) | 🔜 to build |

Career mapping (roughly): L0–L1 → quant research / data roles; L2 →
trading-systems & quant dev; L3–L4 → low-latency C++ developer (the classic
high-comp HFT software role); L5 → FPGA engineer; L6 is the portfolio piece
that ties the interview story together.

---

## Level 0 — Daily-frequency ML trading (your existing system)

**Working files:** `paper_trading_sim.py` (GBM training + backtest),
`walkforward_sim.py` (rolling retrain + risk overlay), `predict_next.py`
(inference + mean-variance allocation), `analyze_equity.py` (metrics).
**Tests:** `tests/` (run `uv run pytest tests/ -m "not exercise"`).

**Goal:** read every one of these end-to-end and be able to answer: where
could look-ahead bias enter? why regression instead of classification? what
does the risk overlay gate on?

**Complexity/speed profile:** pandas + sklearn, seconds-to-minutes per run.
Speed is irrelevant here — correctness of the *time discipline* (no future
leakage) is everything. This is also where the money-math lives that every
interview at every level asks about (Sharpe, drawdown, alpha/beta — lessons
0006 and 0028).

**Suggested self-assignments (no scaffolding needed):**
- Add `alpha_beta()` to `analyze_equity.py` (spec in lesson 0028 §2) and
  report the flagship bundle's β to SPY.
- Re-tune the GBM (lesson 0025 §3) scoring on walk-forward Sharpe, not R².

## Level 1 — Quant math (exercise 03)

**Practice:** `exercises/03_stat_arb_risk/{pairs.py, risk.py}` —
OLS hedge ratio, spread z-score, Dickey-Fuller, AR(1) half-life, CUSUM
detector, OTR tracker, walk-forward splits with embargo.
**Grade:** `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 03 -v`

**Complexity ranking:** all O(n) or O(n·p²) numpy — the intellectual
difficulty is statistical (why a t-stat needs a different critical value
under a unit-root null), not computational.

## Level 2 — Microstructure in Python (exercises 01–02)

**Practice:** `exercises/01_order_book/` (price-time-priority LOB: add,
cancel, market execution with FIFO fills, imbalance) and
`exercises/02_market_maker/` (Avellaneda-Stoikov-lite inventory-aware
quoting — deliberately fixing the inventory-blindness of
`fpga/market_maker.vhd`).
**Grade:** `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k "01 or 02" -v`

**Complexity ranking:** the order book is the first place data-structure
choice = P&L: best-bid lookup O(P) with a dict-of-levels (acceptable here),
O(log P) with a heap/tree, O(1) amortized with the array-of-price-levels
trick real engines use. Internalize the operations now in Python; L4 makes
them fast.

## Level 3 — Low-latency C++ (exercise 04)

**Practice:** `exercises/04_spsc_ring/ring_ma.hpp` (O(1) running-sum moving
average — fixes the O(window) flaw in
`gradient_boosting/sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp`) and `spsc_ring.hpp`
(lock-free single-producer/single-consumer queue: release/acquire ordering,
power-of-two indexing, `alignas(64)` anti-false-sharing — the tests include a
2-thread, 1M-message sequenced transfer and a `sizeof` check that catches a
forgotten `alignas`).
**Grade:** `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 04 -v` or
`bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh` (compiles with g++ -std=c++20 -O2).

**Theoretical speed ranking (the numbers interviewers expect):**
ring-MA push ≈ a handful of ns (two adds, an index mask, all L1-resident);
SPSC push/pop ≈ 10–20 ns uncontended (one relaxed load, one acquire load, one
release store); a mutex-based queue ≈ 50–200+ ns and unbounded tail under
contention. Being able to *explain why* (cache lines, memory ordering, false
sharing — lessons 0009/0010) is the L3→L4 interview gate.

## Level 4 — ULL C++ systems (proposed exercise batches 06–08)

The "millions of messages per second" tier. Not yet scaffolded — say the word
and these get built in the same exercises/solutions/tests pattern:

| # | Exercise | What you build | Speed target / ranking |
|---|---|---|---|
| 06 | **C++ order book** | The L2 book re-done for speed: flat arrays indexed by price tick, intrusive FIFO queues, O(1) best-bid maintenance | ~50–200 ns per event; handles 10⁶–10⁷ events/sec single-threaded |
| 07 | **Binary feed handler** | Parse an ITCH-flavored binary message stream (fixed-width structs, no allocation, no branching on the hot path) into book events | wire-rate parsing, ~10–30 ns/msg; teaches the L13 DMA/zero-copy ideas in software |
| 08 | **Latency benchmark harness** | rdtsc-based timing of 06+07, histogram, p50/p99/p99.99 + jitter report; experiments: enable/disable `alignas`, `[[likely]]`, -O0 vs -O2 vs PGO | the *measuring* skill from lesson 0011 — honest percentiles, not averages |

Each ships with a working solution, a hollowed stub, and a test binary that
checks both correctness *and* (loosely) performance ceilings.

## Level 5 — FPGA (exercise 05 + proposed batch 09)

**Practice now:** `exercises/05_vhdl_testbench/` — write GHDL testbenches for
all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules (clocking idiom, fixed-point encodings,
pipeline-latency assertions). `bash scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh` (needs
`apt-get install ghdl`; auto-skipped otherwise).

**Proposed batch 09:** port your L2 Python market maker into VHDL — an
inventory-aware quoting module (the reservation-price skew in Q16.16
fixed-point) replacing the inventory-blind `market_maker.vhd`, verified by
the same testbench machinery.

**Speed ranking:** 1–2 pipeline stages at a 250 MHz clock = 4–8 ns,
*deterministically* — the jitter-free property no CPU can offer (lesson
0002). This is the floor of the software→hardware ladder.

## Level 6 — Capstone (proposed batch 10)

One binary: replay a recorded message stream → feed handler (07) → order
book (06) → strategy (your MM from 02, in C++) → order events out, with the
benchmark harness (08) reporting tick-to-trade percentiles. The deliverable
is a README table of p50/p99/p99.99 before/after each optimization — exactly
the artifact to talk through in a low-latency interview.

---

## Working order

1. **L0 reading + the two self-assignments** (you have lessons 0001–0028 as
   the theory track).
2. **Exercises 01 → 02 → 03** (Python; recommended order in
   `exercises/README.md`).
3. **Exercise 04** (C++), then re-read lessons 0009/0010 against your own
   code.
4. **Exercise 05** (VHDL testbenches; install ghdl).
5. Ask for **batches 06–08** when 04 is green — they assume your SPSC ring
   and MA exist.
6. **Batch 09–10** last.

## Rules of the road

- Attempt before peeking: `solutions/` is for *after* the suite has judged
  your attempt (wrong-answer failures are the most instructive moment).
- Keep the default repo suite green: stubs skip, they never fail. If
  `uv run pytest tests/` shows failures, you broke something real.
- Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`'s exercises table as levels go green —
  it's the shared map between sessions.

2. Key Technical Concepts:

- **Gradient Boosting:** Stagewise additive modeling — F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + ν·h_m(x); each shallow tree h_m fits the negative gradient of the loss (residuals for squared error). Key knobs: n_estimators (default 100), learning_rate ν (default 0.1), max_depth (default 3). GBR vs Random Forest distinction (sequential residual-fitting vs parallel bagging).
- **OLS Linear Regression:** Normal equations β̂ = (X'X)⁻¹X'y; three-use-case architecture in this repo (hedge ratio slope, spread residual, Dickey-Fuller t-statistic); lstsq vs normal equations for numerical stability.

# Algo-Trading Learning Roadmap — from daily rebalancing to nanosecond HFT

A leveled curriculum built on THIS repo. Every level has three kinds of files:

1. **Working files** — real, runnable code already in the repo (the reference
   you read and run).
2. **Practice files** — the same components with bodies removed
   (`exercises/…` — you implement, an automated suite grades you).
3. **Tested references** — complete solutions (`solutions/…`) verified by the
   same suite, for after you've attempted the practice.

The grading machinery already exists: `exercises/` + `solutions/` +
`tests/exercises/` (see `exercises/README.md`). Unimplemented stubs show as
**skipped**, wrong answers **fail**, done means **green** — the pytest skip
count is your progress bar. C++ exercises compile and run via
`tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh`; VHDL via `scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh` (ghdl).

```bash
uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v                         # grade everything
HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v   # prove suites solvable
```

---

## The ladder at a glance

Latency classes follow Lesson 0011's tier ladder. "Theoretical speed" is the
per-decision software latency the level's techniques can reach.

| Level | Domain | Decision cadence | Theoretical speed | Repo assets | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **L0** | Daily-frequency ML trading (what you have) | 1/day | seconds per run (offline) | `paper_trading_sim.py`, `walkforward_sim.py`, `predict_next.py`, `analyze_equity.py`, `tests/` | ✅ working + tested |
| **L1** | Quant math: regression, stat-arb, risk | 1/day–1/min | ms (numpy) | exercise **03** (pairs/CUSUM/OTR/walk-forward splits); lessons 0006, 0018, 0019, 0026, 0028 | ✅ practice ready |
| **L2** | Market microstructure in Python | per-tick (simulated) | µs–ms (Python) | exercise **01** (order book), **02** (inventory-aware market maker); lessons 0016, 0017 | ✅ practice ready |
| **L3** | Low-latency C++ building blocks | per-tick | ~10–100 **ns** per op | exercise **04** (O(1) MA + lock-free SPSC ring), `gradient_boosting/` ONNX C++, `tests/cpp/`; lessons 0009, 0010 | ✅ practice ready |
| **L4** | Ultra-low-latency C++ systems | millions of msgs/sec | ~100 ns–1 µs tick-to-trade (CPU) | **proposed batch 06–08** (C++ order book, binary feed handler, latency benchmark harness); lessons 0011, 0013 | 🔜 to build |
| **L5** | Hardware (FPGA/VHDL) | per-tick, wire-rate | ~4–50 ns (cycles, deterministic) | exercise **05** (GHDL testbenches), `fpga/*.vhd`; **proposed batch 09** (inventory-aware MM in VHDL); lessons 0002, 0014 | ✅ practice ready / 🔜 extension |
| **L6** | Capstone: tick-to-trade integration | end-to-end | measured p50/p99/p99.99 | **proposed batch 10** (replay → book → strategy → order, with hardware-style latency report) | 🔜 to build |

Career mapping (roughly): L0–L1 → quant research / data roles; L2 →
trading-systems & quant dev; L3–L4 → low-latency C++ developer (the classic
high-comp HFT software role); L5 → FPGA engineer; L6 is the portfolio piece
that ties the interview story together.

---

## Level 0 — Daily-frequency ML trading (your existing system)

**Working files:** `paper_trading_sim.py` (GBM training + backtest),
`walkforward_sim.py` (rolling retrain + risk overlay), `predict_next.py`
(inference + mean-variance allocation), `analyze_equity.py` (metrics).
**Tests:** `tests/` (run `uv run pytest tests/ -m "not exercise"`).

**Goal:** read every one of these end-to-end and be able to answer: where
could look-ahead bias enter? why regression instead of classification? what
does the risk overlay gate on?

**Complexity/speed profile:** pandas + sklearn, seconds-to-minutes per run.
Speed is irrelevant here — correctness of the *time discipline* (no future
leakage) is everything. This is also where the money-math lives that every
interview at every level asks about (Sharpe, drawdown, alpha/beta — lessons
0006 and 0028).

**Suggested self-assignments (no scaffolding needed):**
- Add `alpha_beta()` to `analyze_equity.py` (spec in lesson 0028 §2) and
  report the flagship bundle's β to SPY.
- Re-tune the GBM (lesson 0025 §3) scoring on walk-forward Sharpe, not R².

## Level 1 — Quant math (exercise 03)

**Practice:** `exercises/03_stat_arb_risk/{pairs.py, risk.py}` —
OLS hedge ratio, spread z-score, Dickey-Fuller, AR(1) half-life, CUSUM
detector, OTR tracker, walk-forward splits with embargo.
**Grade:** `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 03 -v`

**Complexity ranking:** all O(n) or O(n·p²) numpy — the intellectual
difficulty is statistical (why a t-stat needs a different critical value
under a unit-root null), not computational.

## Level 2 — Microstructure in Python (exercises 01–02)

**Practice:** `exercises/01_order_book/` (price-time-priority LOB: add,
cancel, market execution with FIFO fills, imbalance) and
`exercises/02_market_maker/` (Avellaneda-Stoikov-lite inventory-aware
quoting — deliberately fixing the inventory-blindness of
`fpga/market_maker.vhd`).
**Grade:** `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k "01 or 02" -v`

**Complexity ranking:** the order book is the first place data-structure
choice = P&L: best-bid lookup O(P) with a dict-of-levels (acceptable here),
O(log P) with a heap/tree, O(1) amortized with the array-of-price-levels
trick real engines use. Internalize the operations now in Python; L4 makes
them fast.

## Level 3 — Low-latency C++ (exercise 04)

**Practice:** `exercises/04_spsc_ring/ring_ma.hpp` (O(1) running-sum moving
average — fixes the O(window) flaw in
`gradient_boosting/sample_with_gradient_boosting.cpp`) and `spsc_ring.hpp`
(lock-free single-producer/single-consumer queue: release/acquire ordering,
power-of-two indexing, `alignas(64)` anti-false-sharing — the tests include a
2-thread, 1M-message sequenced transfer and a `sizeof` check that catches a
forgotten `alignas`).
**Grade:** `uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 04 -v` or
`bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh` (compiles with g++ -std=c++20 -O2).

**Theoretical speed ranking (the numbers interviewers expect):**
ring-MA push ≈ a handful of ns (two adds, an index mask, all L1-resident);
SPSC push/pop ≈ 10–20 ns uncontended (one relaxed load, one acquire load, one
release store); a mutex-based queue ≈ 50–200+ ns and unbounded tail under
contention. Being able to *explain why* (cache lines, memory ordering, false
sharing — lessons 0009/0010) is the L3→L4 interview gate.

## Level 4 — ULL C++ systems (proposed exercise batches 06–08)

The "millions of messages per second" tier. Not yet scaffolded — say the word
and these get built in the same exercises/solutions/tests pattern:

| # | Exercise | What you build | Speed target / ranking |
|---|---|---|---|
| 06 | **C++ order book** | The L2 book re-done for speed: flat arrays indexed by price tick, intrusive FIFO queues, O(1) best-bid maintenance | ~50–200 ns per event; handles 10⁶–10⁷ events/sec single-threaded |
| 07 | **Binary feed handler** | Parse an ITCH-flavored binary message stream (fixed-width structs, no allocation, no branching on the hot path) into book events | wire-rate parsing, ~10–30 ns/msg; teaches the L13 DMA/zero-copy ideas in software |
| 08 | **Latency benchmark harness** | rdtsc-based timing of 06+07, histogram, p50/p99/p99.99 + jitter report; experiments: enable/disable `alignas`, `[[likely]]`, -O0 vs -O2 vs PGO | the *measuring* skill from lesson 0011 — honest percentiles, not averages |

Each ships with a working solution, a hollowed stub, and a test binary that
checks both correctness *and* (loosely) performance ceilings.

## Level 5 — FPGA (exercise 05 + proposed batch 09)

**Practice now:** `exercises/05_vhdl_testbench/` — write GHDL testbenches for
all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules (clocking idiom, fixed-point encodings,
pipeline-latency assertions). `bash scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh` (needs
`apt-get install ghdl`; auto-skipped otherwise).

**Proposed batch 09:** port your L2 Python market maker into VHDL — an
inventory-aware quoting module (the reservation-price skew in Q16.16
fixed-point) replacing the inventory-blind `market_maker.vhd`, verified by
the same testbench machinery.

**Speed ranking:** 1–2 pipeline stages at a 250 MHz clock = 4–8 ns,
*deterministically* — the jitter-free property no CPU can offer (lesson
0002). This is the floor of the software→hardware ladder.

## Level 6 — Capstone (proposed batch 10)

One binary: replay a recorded message stream → feed handler (07) → order
book (06) → strategy (your MM from 02, in C++) → order events out, with the
benchmark harness (08) reporting tick-to-trade percentiles. The deliverable
is a README table of p50/p99/p99.99 before/after each optimization — exactly
the artifact to talk through in a low-latency interview.

---

## Working order

1. **L0 reading + the two self-assignments** (you have lessons 0001–0028 as
   the theory track).
2. **Exercises 01 → 02 → 03** (Python; recommended order in
   `exercises/README.md`).
3. **Exercise 04** (C++), then re-read lessons 0009/0010 against your own
   code.
4. **Exercise 05** (VHDL testbenches; install ghdl).
5. Ask for **batches 06–08** when 04 is green — they assume your SPSC ring
   and MA exist.
6. **Batch 09–10** last.

## Rules of the road

- Attempt before peeking: `solutions/` is for *after* the suite has judged
  your attempt (wrong-answer failures are the most instructive moment).
- Keep the default repo suite green: stubs skip, they never fail. If
  `uv run pytest tests/` shows failures, you broke something real.
- Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`'s exercises table as levels go green —
  it's the shared map between sessions.

# Four New Lessons: Gradient Boosting, Linear Regression, Logistic vs Linear, Alpha & Beta

## Context

The user queued four /teach topics: **ML (Gradient Boosting)**, **ML (Linear Regression)**, **Logistic Regression and difference from Linear Regression**, and **Alpha and Beta in finance**. The teaching workspace (`docs/learning/`) has 24 lessons; these become **0025–0028**, following the established format (self-contained HTML, inline CSS/JS, Fisher-Yates-shuffled quizzes with `data-correct` attributes, section-complete checkboxes, no localStorage).

Lesson 0003 already covers ML algorithms broadly (boosting mechanics at intro level, the three-model split, look-ahead bias). The new lessons go **deeper on each model** and ground in code that didn't exist when 0003 was written — notably the new `solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py` OLS implementation from the exercises batch.

## Exploration findings (grounding facts, verified)

- Highest lesson is 0024; GLOSSARY.md exists; **alpha/beta/CAPM are nowhere** in lessons or glossary (0006 covers Sharpe/CAGR/drawdown/covariance only; `analyze_equity.py` computes no benchmark-relative metrics — Sharpe with rf=0 is the repo convention).
- `paper_trading_sim.py:123` — `GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=42)` all-default hyperparams (100 trees, depth 3, lr 0.1, squared error); `build_features` (lines 48–69): close, ret_1d, ma_5, ma_10, ma_gap, vol_10, rsi_14; target `fwd_ret_1d` via `shift(-1)`.
- `walkforward_sim.py:224` — same model but optional `--rolling_retrain` (756-day window, monthly).
- **No logistic regression anywhere** (only `gm.predict_proba` at walkforward_sim.py:307 — a GaussianMixture regime filter, a useful "often confused with" hook).
- `solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py:24` — `hedge_ratio` is textbook OLS via `np.linalg.lstsq` (the hedge ratio IS a beta — perfect bridge to lesson 0028).
- `fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd` — 4 hardcoded ×1000 fixed-point weights (W0=50, W=[300,−100,200]), inference-only linear model in silicon.

## The four lessons

### 0025-gradient-boosting-deep-dive.html
- **Concept:** stagewise additive modeling — each tree fits the *negative gradient of the loss* (residuals, for squared error); why shallow trees + small learning rate + many trees beats one deep tree (bias/variance, shrinkage as regularization).
- **Worked example:** tiny 5-point numeric walkthrough of 3 boosting rounds (initial prediction = mean, residuals, tree fits, shrinkage) — hand-computable numbers.
- **In this project:** `paper_trading_sim.py` train_model (defaults are sklearn's, untuned — discuss what tuning n_estimators/max_depth/learning_rate would trade off on noisy financial data); `walkforward_sim.py` rolling retrain as the answer to non-stationarity; the model bundle format (features list ordering).
- **Often confused with:** gradient boosting vs random forest (sequential residual-fitting vs parallel bagging); boosting vs gradient descent (descent in *function space* vs parameter space).

### 0026-linear-regression.html
- **Concept:** OLS from first principles — minimize Σ(y−Xβ)², normal equations β=(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, why lstsq is preferred numerically; residuals, R², standard errors of coefficients.
- **In this project (three real call sites):** `solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py` `_ols`/`hedge_ratio` (walk the lstsq + SE code line by line); `fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd` (a trained linear model is just 4 numbers → trivially synthesizable, ×1000 fixed point); `pairs.py` `dickey_fuller_stat` as regression reused for hypothesis testing.
- **Often confused with:** correlation vs regression slope; interpolation vs extrapolation risk in trading features.

### 0027-logistic-vs-linear-regression.html
- **Concept:** logistic regression = linear model pushed through a sigmoid, output is P(class); log-loss vs squared error; decision boundaries; why there's no closed form (iterative MLE).
- **The contrast (core of the lesson, per the request):** what they share (linear in parameters, same feature vector, both "regression" by name) vs where they diverge (continuous target vs probability of a label; loss function; output range; calibration). When each fails in finance: thresholding returns into up/down labels throws away magnitude — exactly why this repo uses *regression* for ranking (ties back to 0003's argument, now with the math).
- **In this project:** honest framing — the repo deliberately has **no** logistic regression; show illustratively (tagged as such, per standing convention) what classifying `fwd_ret_1d > 0` would look like and what's lost. Contrast with the one real `predict_proba` in the repo (`walkforward_sim.py:307`, GaussianMixture regimes) — probability output ≠ logistic regression.

### 0028-alpha-and-beta-in-finance.html
- **Concept:** CAPM — r_strategy = α + β·r_market + ε estimated by OLS; β = cov(r_s, r_m)/var(r_m); alpha as benchmark-adjusted skill; market-neutral as β≈0; beta-hedging.
- **Bridge from 0026:** beta is literally the OLS slope the user just learned — and `hedge_ratio` in the stat-arb exercise is a beta between two assets (pairs trading = betting on α of the spread with β hedged out).
- **In this project:** `analyze_equity.py` computes Sharpe with rf=0 but **no alpha/beta** — show the ~10-line addition that would regress the equity-curve returns against SPY (illustrative, tagged); the model bundle's "27.19% annualized" claim needs a beta to know how much is market exposure vs alpha.
- **Often confused with:** alpha vs total return; beta (CAPM) vs beta (hedge ratio) — same math, different question; Sharpe vs alpha (volatility-adjusted vs benchmark-adjusted).

## Cross-cutting work

1. **Web grounding** (teach skill step 2): verify sklearn `GradientBoostingRegressor` current defaults/docs and standard CAPM/Jensen's-alpha references; footnote sources in lessons (existing convention).
2. **Quiz mechanics:** each lesson gets 4–5 shuffled questions (`data-correct` + per-option `data-why`, Fisher-Yates on load) + scenario "check your understanding" + per-section complete buttons with score display — copy the structural pattern from lesson 0024 (latest).
3. **GLOSSARY.md:** add OLS / normal equations, R², sigmoid / log-loss, CAPM, alpha, beta, shrinkage (learning rate) — definitions consistent with existing entries.
4. **PROGRESS.md:** append the four lessons to the completed table (Grasp: TBD), note the lesson 0026 ↔ exercise 03 cross-link, suggest next concept.
5. **Open commands:** print `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/0025-...` lines (Linux).
6. **In-chat knowledge check:** close with 2–3 questions spanning the four lessons (e.g. "your backtest returns 20%/yr with β=1.3 to SPY which did 15% — what's your alpha, roughly?").

## Files to create / modify

- Create: `docs/learning/lessons/0025-gradient-boosting-deep-dive.html`, `0026-linear-regression.html`, `0027-logistic-vs-linear-regression.html`, `0028-alpha-and-beta-in-finance.html`
- Edit: `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md`, `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`

## Verification

- Each HTML file: open-able standalone (no external refs — grep for `http` in src/href attributes other than footnote links), quiz JS shuffles on load and grades via `data-correct` (not position), section progress + quiz score render.
- Quick numeric sanity on every worked example (boosting-round arithmetic, CAPM alpha example) — hand-check the numbers shown.
- GLOSSARY/PROGRESS diffs are append-only and consistent with the existing format.

*(Unrelated carry-over: the practice-exercises verification (task #8) remains blocked by the Bash classifier outage — retry `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v` when it recovers; not part of this plan.)*

skills.content:
The user wants to learn "engineering" (or, if blank, you choose the most valuable concept to teach next based on their progress and this project's code). This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. Perfect. I have all three files. Let me provide you with a comprehensive report on the order book semantics for your C++ port.

## API & Method Signatures

**Class: `OrderBook`**

1. `__init__() -> None`
   - Initializes empty order book with no orders

2. `add_limit(order_id: int, side: str, price: float, qty: int) -> None`
   - Rests a limit order in the book
   - `side`: "buy" or "sell" (raises ValueError otherwise)
   - `price`, `qty`: must be positive (raises ValueError if not)
   - Raises ValueError if order_id already exists (duplicate prevention)

3. `cancel(order_id: int) -> None`
   - Removes a resting order
   - Raises KeyError if order_id not found
   - Must clean up empty price levels (critical for BBO re-derivation)

4. `best_bid() -> float | None`
   - Returns highest resting bid price, or None if no bids

5. `best_ask() -> float | None`
   - Returns lowest resting ask price, or None if no asks

6. `bbo() -> tuple[float | None, float | None]`
   - Returns (best_bid, best_ask)

7. `level_qty(side: str, price: float) -> int`
   - Returns total resting quantity at a price level
   - Returns 0 if level absent (no exception)

8. `execute_market(side: str, qty: int) -> list[Fill]`
   - Executes market order for aggressor `side`
   - "buy" lifts asks (lowest price first); "sell" hits bids (highest price first)
   - FIFO within levels
   - Partial fills allowed (order fills until book runs out of liquidity)
   - Returns list of Fill objects

**Class: `Fill`** (frozen dataclass)
- `order_id: int`
- `price: float`
- `qty: int`

---

## Data Structures

The solution uses:

```python
self._bids: dict[float, deque[list]]       # price -> deque of [order_id, qty]
self._asks: dict[float, deque[list]]       # price -> deque of [order_id, qty]
self._orders: dict[int, tuple[str, price]] # order_id -> (side, price)
```

**Key design choices:**
- **Dict of deques** for each side: `dict[float, deque[list]]`
- Price levels map to deques of `[order_id, remaining_qty]` lists
- Deque for FIFO ordering within a price level (append on add, popleft on fill)
- Separate `_orders` dict tracks order metadata for O(1) cancel lookup
- Lists used for order entries (mutable to track remaining qty during partial fills)
- No explicit sorted container; best_bid/ask computed on-demand via `max()`/`min()`

---

## FIFO Ordering Within Price Level

Each price level is a `deque[list]` where each entry is `[order_id, remaining_qty]`:

1. **Adding**: `book.setdefault(price, deque()).append([order_id, qty])`
   - New orders go to the back (append)

2. **Market execution**: Fill from front (FIFO)
   - Take min(remaining_qty, market_qty)
   - Decrement `entry[1]` in place
   - Only popleft when fully filled (`entry[1] == 0`)
   - Partially filled orders stay at front for next execution

3. **Cancellation**: Linear search through level to find and remove entry
   ```python
   for entry in level:
       if entry[0] == order_id:
           level.remove(entry)
           break
   ```

---

## Imbalance Calculation Formula

```
imbalance(levels=1) = (bid_qty - ask_qty) / (bid_qty + ask_qty)
```

Where:
- `bid_qty` = sum of quantities in top `levels` bid price levels (highest prices first)
- `ask_qty` = sum of quantities in top `levels` ask price levels (lowest prices first)
- Returns **0.0** when both sides empty
- Result is **always in [-1, 1]**:
  - +1.0: all bids, no asks (buy imbalance)
  - -1.0: all asks, no bids (sell imbalance)
  - 0.0: equal or both empty

Implementation:
```python
top_bids = sorted(self._bids, reverse=True)[:levels]      # highest levels first
top_asks = sorted(self._asks)[:levels]                     # lowest levels first
bid_qty = sum(self.level_qty("buy", p) for p in top_bids)
ask_qty = sum(self.level_qty("sell", p) for p in top_asks)
total = bid_qty + ask_qty
return (bid_qty - ask_qty) / total if total > 0 else 0.0
```

---

## Test Coverage Breakdown

**TestBBO** (lines 18-35):
- Empty book returns (None, None)
- Adding orders updates BBO
- Price priority: highest bid, lowest ask win

**TestAddAndCancel** (lines 38-59):
- Cancel removes order and re-derives BBO correctly
- Cancel on unknown ID raises KeyError
- Duplicate order_id raises ValueError
- Invalid side raises ValueError

**TestMarketExecution** (lines 61-102):
- **FIFO within level**: Same-price orders fill in arrival order (test_fifo_at_same_price)
- **Partial fill behavior**: Partially filled order stays at front of queue (test_partial_fill_leaves_remainder_at_queue_front)
  - Critical detail: Next execution continues from the same order, not skipping to next
- **Level walking**: Market order crosses multiple price levels until liquidity exhausted (test_market_order_walks_levels)
- **Opposite side direction**: "sell" hits highest bid first, "buy" lifts lowest ask first (test_sell_market_hits_best_bid_first)
- **Partial fills allowed**: Insufficient liquidity returns partial Fill list (test_insufficient_liquidity_fills_partially)

**TestImbalance** (lines 104-128):
- Empty book returns 0.0
- Hand-computed top-1 level: (30 - 10) / 60 = 0.5 ✓
- Multi-level with bounds: Correctly sums multiple levels and respects level limit
- One-sided book saturates at ±1.0

---

## Critical C++ Port Considerations

1. **Deque with mutable entries**: The Python code stores `[order_id, qty]` lists that are mutated during partial fills. In C++, consider a struct/pair that can be modified in-place within the deque.

2. **Price level cleanup**: Both cancel and market execution must explicitly delete empty price levels from the dict to keep BBO derivation correct.

3. **Order metadata dict**: The `_orders` dict is essential for cancel performance (O(1) lookup of side/price before searching the level deque).

4. **No rebalancing**: The data structure doesn't maintain sorted levels; best_bid/ask are computed O(n) on-demand. For C++, you might use `std::map` for automatic ordering.

5. **Fill list semantics**: Fills must preserve order and quantity exactly as they occurred during market execution (price-level order, then FIFO within level).

## Summary: C++ Exercise 04 Structure & Patterns

Based on my analysis of the exercise 04 files, here's the exact structure and patterns you should replicate for exercises 06-08:

### Directory Layout
```
exercises/04_spsc_ring/
  ├── README.md              (problem description + acceptance criteria)
  ├── ring_ma.hpp            (exercise stub - header-only template)
  └── spsc_ring.hpp          (exercise stub - header-only template)

solutions/04_spsc_ring/

  └── spsc_ring.hpp          (reference solution)

tests/exercises/cpp/
  ├── test_ring_ma.cpp       (grading test binary for Part A)
  ├── test_spsc_ring.cpp     (grading test binary for Part B)
  ├── run_cpp.sh             (build & run orchestrator)
  └── build/                 (compiled binaries written here)

tests/exercises/
  └── test_04_spsc_ring.py   (pytest wrapper that calls run_cpp.sh)
```

### TODO/Stub Pattern in Exercise Files

**Marking TODOs** (in exercise stubs):
- Each unimplemented method has a comment block with `// TODO` marking what needs to be filled
- The method body throws `std::logic_error("not implemented")` immediately
- Example from `ring_ma.hpp`:
  ```cpp
  void push(double x) {
      (void)x;
      throw std::logic_error("not implemented");  // TODO
  }
  ```
- The `(void)x;` prevents unused-parameter warnings during compilation

**Additional TODO markers** (for data members):
```cpp
private:
    // TODO: fixed storage (std::array — no heap on the hot path),
    // a running sum, a head index, and a count.
    std::array<double, N> buf_{};
```

### Exit Code 42 Stub Detection

The test detection works through exception handling:
1. Each test binary (`test_ring_ma.cpp` and `test_spsc_ring.cpp`) wraps all test execution in a `try-catch`:
   ```cpp
   try {
       // ... run tests ...
       return 0;  // all pass
   } catch (const std::logic_error& e) {
       std::cout << "NOT IMPLEMENTED: " << e.what() << "\n";
       return 42;  // not implemented
   }
   ```
2. When a stub method throws `std::logic_error`, it propagates to `main()` and returns exit code 42
3. The pytest wrapper checks `proc.returncode == 42` and skips the test if true
4. If exit code is 1, the test failed; if 0, it passed

### Test Compilation & Execution Flow

**`run_cpp.sh` script behavior:**
```bash
TARGET="${HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET:-exercises}"  # default: use exercise stubs
INC="$ROOT/$TARGET/04_spsc_ring"            # include dir switches based on env var
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -pthread -I "$INC" "$HERE/$t.cpp" -o "$BUILD/$t"
```

Key points:
- Single environment variable `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET` controls stub vs solution
- Default: `exercises/` (student stubs)
- Override: `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions bash run_cpp.sh` (reference)
- `-I` flag points at the exercise directory with the headers
- All headers are `#include "name.hpp"` (not paths), so `-I` controls which version is used
- Compiled binaries written to `tests/exercises/cpp/build/`
- Exit codes: 0=pass, 1=fail/compile error, 42=not implemented

### Solution Files vs Stubs

**Stub files** (exercises/):
- Minimal file size (~1.8-2.1 KB)
- All methods throw `std::logic_error` immediately
- Data members are bare stubs with `// TODO` comments
- Include comprehensive documentation comments explaining the requirements and hints
- Methods lack `noexcept` (since they throw)

**Solution files** (solutions/):
- Fully implemented (~1.4-1.9 KB, often smaller due to no stub comments)
- All methods have `noexcept` applied (added after the TODO version works)
- Data members fully declared with correct types
- Comments explain the design rationale (e.g., why alignas(64) is needed)
- Example from solution spsc_ring.hpp:
  ```cpp
  bool try_push(const T& v) noexcept {  // <-- noexcept added
      const std::size_t head = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
      // ... actual implementation ...
      head_.store(next, std::memory_order_release);
      return true;
  }
  ```

### Test Structure Pattern

Both test files follow identical structure:
1. **Header section** with comments describing exit codes
2. **ASSERT macro** for test assertions:
   ```cpp
   #define ASSERT(cond, msg) \
       do { if (!(cond)) { std::cerr << "FAIL: " << msg << "\n"; return 1; } } while (0)
   ```
3. **Individual test functions** returning `int` (0=pass, 1=fail)
4. **Main function** with:
   - Test array of `{name, function_ptr}` pairs
   - Loop running each test and tracking failures
   - Try-catch around entire loop to catch `std::logic_error` and return 42

### For Exercises 06-08, Replicate This Pattern:

1. **Create directories:**
   ```
   exercises/0X_name/
   solutions/0X_name/
   ```

2. **Create header stub files** with:
   - Detailed doc comments explaining requirements
   - `// TODO` comments for each unimplemented section
   - Throw statements: `throw std::logic_error("not implemented");`
   - Data member stubs with `// TODO` explaining what to add

3. **Create matching solution files** with:
   - Same class/method signatures
   - Full implementations
   - `noexcept` on all hot-path methods
   - Explanatory comments on why design choices were made

4. **Create test files** in `tests/exercises/cpp/`:
   - `test_0X_name.cpp` with comprehensive test coverage
   - Use ASSERT macro pattern
   - Include threading tests for concurrency
   - Wrap main in try-catch for exit code 42 detection

5. **Create `run_cpp.sh` entry** (or extend existing):
   - Add test name to the default tests array
   - Uses same `-I "$INC"` pattern to switch between stubs/solutions

6. **Create pytest wrapper** in `tests/exercises/`:
   - `test_0X_name.py` calling `run_cpp.sh` with appropriate test names
   - Use the `_run_cpp_test()` helper function pattern

**Additional TODO markers** (for data members):
```cpp
private:
    // TODO: fixed storage (std::array — no heap on the hot path),
    // a running sum, a head index, and a count.
    std::array<double, N> buf_{};
```

### Exit Code 42 Stub Detection

The test detection works through exception handling:
1. Each test binary (`test_ring_ma.cpp` and `test_spsc_ring.cpp`) wraps all test execution in a `try-catch`:
   ```cpp
   try {
       // ... run tests ...
       return 0;  // all pass
   } catch (const std::logic_error& e) {
       std::cout << "NOT IMPLEMENTED: " << e.what() << "\n";
       return 42;  // not implemented
   }
   ```
2. When a stub method throws `std::logic_error`, it propagates to `main()` and returns exit code 42
3. The pytest wrapper checks `proc.returncode == 42` and skips the test if true
4. If exit code is 1, the test failed; if 0, it passed

### Test Compilation & Execution Flow

**`run_cpp.sh` script behavior:**
```bash
TARGET="${HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET:-exercises}"  # default: use exercise stubs
INC="$ROOT/$TARGET/04_spsc_ring"            # include dir switches based on env var
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -pthread -I "$INC" "$HERE/$t.cpp" -o "$BUILD/$t"
```

Key points:
- Single environment variable `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET` controls stub vs solution
- Default: `exercises/` (student stubs)
- Override: `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions bash run_cpp.sh` (reference)
- `-I` flag points at the exercise directory with the headers
- All headers are `#include "name.hpp"` (not paths), so `-I` controls which version is used
- Compiled binaries written to `tests/exercises/cpp/build/`
- Exit codes: 0=pass, 1=fail/compile error, 42=not implemented

### Solution Files vs Stubs

**Stub files** (exercises/):
- Minimal file size (~1.8-2.1 KB)
- All methods throw `std::logic_error` immediately
- Data members are bare stubs with `// TODO` comments
- Include comprehensive documentation comments explaining the requirements and hints
- Methods lack `noexcept` (since they throw)

**Solution files** (solutions/):
- Fully implemented (~1.4-1.9 KB, often smaller due to no stub comments)
- All methods have `noexcept` applied (added after the TODO version works)
- Data members fully declared with correct types
- Comments explain the design rationale (e.g., why alignas(64) is needed)
- Example from solution spsc_ring.hpp:
  ```cpp
  bool try_push(const T& v) noexcept {  // <-- noexcept added
      const std::size_t head = head_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
      // ... actual implementation ...
      head_.store(next, std::memory_order_release);
      return true;
  }
  ```

### Test Structure Pattern

Both test files follow identical structure:
1. **Header section** with comments describing exit codes
2. **ASSERT macro** for test assertions:
   ```cpp
   #define ASSERT(cond, msg) \
       do { if (!(cond)) { std::cerr << "FAIL: " << msg << "\n"; return 1; } } while (0)
   ```
3. **Individual test functions** returning `int` (0=pass, 1=fail)
4. **Main function** with:
   - Test array of `{name, function_ptr}` pairs
   - Loop running each test and tracking failures
   - Try-catch around entire loop to catch `std::logic_error` and return 42

### For Exercises 06-08, Replicate This Pattern:

1. **Create directories:**
   ```
   exercises/0X_name/
   solutions/0X_name/
   ```

2. **Create header stub files** with:
   - Detailed doc comments explaining requirements
   - `// TODO` comments for each unimplemented section
   - Throw statements: `throw std::logic_error("not implemented");`
   - Data member stubs with `// TODO` explaining what to add

3. **Create matching solution files** with:
   - Same class/method signatures
   - Full implementations
   - `noexcept` on all hot-path methods
   - Explanatory comments on why design choices were made

4. **Create test files** in `tests/exercises/cpp/`:
   - `test_0X_name.cpp` with comprehensive test coverage
   - Use ASSERT macro pattern
   - Include threading tests for concurrency
   - Wrap main in try-catch for exit code 42 detection

5. **Create `run_cpp.sh` entry** (or extend existing):
   - Add test name to the default tests array
   - Uses same `-I "$INC"` pattern to switch between stubs/solutions

6. **Create pytest wrapper** in `tests/exercises/`:
   - `test_0X_name.py` calling `run_cpp.sh` with appropriate test names
   - Use the `_run_cpp_test()` helper function pattern

This structure allows students to work on stubs while the grading system can swap in solutions via the `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET` environment variable.

# Exercises 06–10: L4–L6 HFT Practice (C++ ULL + VHDL + Capstone)

## Context

The roadmap (`docs/learning/ROADMAP.md`) defines a 7-level curriculum. Exercises 01–05 are already built and green. Levels 4–6 (the C++ ultra-low-latency tier, VHDL extension, and integration capstone) are marked "🔜 to build." This plan implements them using the identical exercises/solutions/tests/exercises pattern already established.

Pattern recap (from existing exercise 04):
- `exercises/0N_name/` — stub headers; unimplemented bodies throw `std::logic_error("not implemented")` → `main()` catches → exit 42 → pytest skips
- `solutions/0N_name/` — full implementations; same API
- `tests/exercises/cpp/test_0N_name.cpp` — ASSERT-macro test binary; exit 0/1/42
- `tests/exercises/test_0N_name.py` — pytest wrapper that calls `run_cpp.sh`
- `tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh` — existing orchestrator, needs each new exercise appended to its tests array

---

## Exercise 06 — C++ Order Book (`06_cpp_order_book`)

**Goal:** Port the Python LOB (exercise 01) to C++ — same semantics, faster data structures.

### Files

```
exercises/06_cpp_order_book/
  order_book.hpp        (stub)
solutions/06_cpp_order_book/
  order_book.hpp        (solution)
tests/exercises/cpp/
  test_06_order_book.cpp
tests/exercises/
  test_06_cpp_order_book.py
```

### Structs (both stub and solution share these in a common block)

```cpp
struct Order  { int64_t order_id; int64_t price_ticks; int32_t qty; };
struct Fill   { int64_t order_id; int64_t price_ticks; int32_t qty; };
```

Price is represented as **integer ticks** (×10000 of dollars; e.g. $100.25 → 1002500) — no float equality bugs and trivial to compare.

### Class `OrderBook` — required interface

```cpp
void add_limit(int64_t order_id, char side, int64_t price_ticks, int32_t qty);
void cancel(int64_t order_id);
std::vector<Fill> execute_market(char side, int32_t qty);
int64_t best_bid() const noexcept;   // returns INT64_MIN if empty
int64_t best_ask() const noexcept;   // returns INT64_MAX if empty
int32_t level_qty(char side, int64_t price_ticks) const noexcept;
double  imbalance(int levels = 1) const noexcept;
```

### Solution data structures

```cpp
// bids: largest price first → std::map with reverse iterator for O(log P) BBO
std::map<int64_t, std::deque<Order>, std::greater<int64_t>> bids_;
// asks: smallest price first → std::map with forward iterator
std::map<int64_t, std::deque<Order>>                        asks_;
// order index for O(1) cancel lookup
std::unordered_map<int64_t, std::pair<char, int64_t>>       order_index_;
```

### Stub TODOs (what the student fills in)

1. Define `bids_`, `asks_`, `order_index_` data members (hint in comment)
2. Implement `add_limit` (route by side, append to level deque, update index)
3. Implement `cancel` (index lookup, remove from deque, erase empty level)
4. Implement `execute_market` (walk levels FIFO, produce Fill list, erase empty levels)
5. Implement `best_bid` / `best_ask` (1 line each using `rbegin`/`begin`)
6. Implement `imbalance` (top-N level sum, formula = (bid_qty − ask_qty) / total)

### Tests (test_06_order_book.cpp) — mirrors Python test suite

- BBO on empty book returns sentinels
- Price priority: highest bid / lowest ask wins
- FIFO within level: two same-price orders; first placed gets first fill
- Partial fill stays at front of queue
- Market order walks multiple levels
- Cancel removes and re-derives BBO; cancel unknown ID exits 1 (not 42)
- Imbalance hand-computed value check (same numbers as Python test)
- A **throughput smoke test**: 1,000,000 add+cancel cycles should complete in < 2 s (wall clock via `std::chrono`) — loose ceiling, catches O(n²) bugs only

### Speed ranking to explain in exercise README

| Data structure | BBO | Insert | Cancel | Execute |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `std::map` (exercise) | O(log P) | O(log P) | O(log P + L) | O(log P × fills) |
| Flat array of levels (L4 optimization) | O(1) amortized | O(1) | O(L) | O(fills) |

---

## Exercise 07 — Binary Feed Handler (`07_feed_handler`)

**Goal:** Parse a fixed-width binary message stream into `OrderBook` events with zero heap allocation on the hot path.

### Message format (ITCH-inspired, packed structs)

All fields little-endian (host byte order for simplicity; note for student that real ITCH uses network/big-endian).

```cpp
#pragma pack(push, 1)
struct MsgAdd    { char type; uint64_t oid; char side; int64_t price_ticks; int32_t qty; }; // type='A'
struct MsgCancel { char type; uint64_t oid; };                                               // type='X'
struct MsgExec   { char type; uint64_t oid; int32_t qty; };                                  // type='E'
struct MsgTrade  { char type; int64_t price_ticks; int32_t qty; };                           // type='P'
#pragma pack(pop)
```

### Class `FeedHandler` — required interface

```cpp
struct BookEvent { char type; uint64_t oid; char side; int64_t price; int32_t qty; };

class FeedHandler {
public:
    // parse one message from buf[0..]; advance *pos by the message length.
    // writes one event to *out; returns true if a book-relevant event was written.
    bool parse_one(const uint8_t* buf, size_t buf_len, size_t* pos, BookEvent* out);

    // parse all messages in buf; calls callback(event) for each book event.
    template<typename Fn>
    size_t parse_all(const uint8_t* buf, size_t buf_len, Fn callback);
};
```

### Stub TODOs

1. Fill in the `switch(type)` dispatch in `parse_one` for each message type
2. Implement `memcpy`-based field extraction (no reinterpret_cast of misaligned ptr)
3. Implement `parse_all` loop (advance `pos` until `buf_len` exhausted)

### Tests (test_07_feed_handler.cpp)

- Round-trip: encode a known sequence of 4 message types → parse → verify events match
- Buffer boundary: message split across two buffers is handled correctly (partial read returns false, no advance)
- Throughput: parse 1,000,000 Add messages in < 0.5 s — catches any accidental allocation

---

## Exercise 08 — Latency Benchmark Harness (`08_latency_bench`)

**Goal:** Measure and report p50/p99/p99.9 latency of exercises 06 + 07 with an rdtsc-based timer.

### Files

```
exercises/08_latency_bench/
  latency.hpp        (rdtsc wrapper + histogram class — stub)
  bench.cpp          (benchmark driver, partially filled; students add timed sections)
solutions/08_latency_bench/
  latency.hpp
  bench.cpp
tests/exercises/cpp/
  test_08_latency.cpp
tests/exercises/
  test_08_latency.py
```

### `latency.hpp` — required interface

```cpp
inline uint64_t rdtsc() noexcept; // __rdtsc() or fallback clock_gettime

class Histogram {
    static constexpr int BUCKETS = 64; // bucket i covers [2^i, 2^(i+1)) cycles
    uint64_t counts_[BUCKETS]{};
public:
    void record(uint64_t cycles) noexcept;
    uint64_t percentile(double p) const noexcept; // p in [0,1]; returns cycles
    void print(double mhz = 3000.0) const;        // converts cycles → ns using MHz
};
```

### `bench.cpp` — the experiment script (partial pre-fill)

Pre-filled sections: setup, warm-up loop, MHz calibration.
Student TODOs:
1. Insert `rdtsc()` start/stop around `add_limit` calls and `record()` to histogram
2. Insert start/stop around `execute_market` calls
3. Print the two histograms (already provided: `hist.print(mhz)`)
4. Add a second experimental run with `alignas(64)` stripped (compile flag) — instructions in README

### Tests (test_08_latency.cpp)

- `Histogram::percentile(0.5)` on a known set of 1024 recorded values returns within 1 bucket of expected median
- `rdtsc()` monotonically increases over 1000 calls
- `bench.cpp` compiles and produces valid output (stdout contains "p50", "p99") — test captures output and parses

---

## Exercise 09 — Inventory-Aware VHDL Market Maker (`09_vhdl_inv_mm`)

**Goal:** Port the Python inventory-aware market maker (exercise 02's `reservation_price` formula) into VHDL, replacing the inventory-blind `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### Files

```
exercises/09_vhdl_inv_mm/
  inv_market_maker.vhd      (stub — reservation price skew left unimplemented)
solutions/09_vhdl_inv_mm/
  inv_market_maker.vhd
tests/exercises/
  test_09_vhdl.py           (ghdl driver, auto-skips if ghdl absent)
```

### VHDL interface

```vhdl
entity inv_market_maker is
  port(
    clk        : in  std_logic;
    mid_price  : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- Q16.16 fixed-point
    inventory  : in  signed(15 downto 0);  -- signed units held
    max_inv    : in  signed(15 downto 0);  -- max units (always positive)
    gamma      : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- risk aversion ×1000
    sigma      : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- volatility ×1000
    T          : in  signed(31 downto 0);  -- time horizon ×1000
    bid_price  : out signed(31 downto 0);
    ask_price  : out signed(31 downto 0)
  );
end inv_market_maker;
```

Stub leaves the reservation-price skew `r = mid - q*γ*σ²*T` and spread `s = γ*σ²*T + (2/γ)*ln(1+γ/k)` as unimplemented (all zeros). Student fills in the fixed-point arithmetic.

---

## Exercise 10 — Capstone: Tick-to-Trade Integration (`10_tick_to_trade`)

**Goal:** Wire exercises 06 + 07 + strategy (market maker from 02, ported to C++) into a single binary that replays a message stream, maintains a live book, generates quotes, and reports tick-to-trade latency.

This is a **reading + integration exercise** — no stubs, but a guided TODO list in a `main.cpp` scaffold:

1. Instantiate `FeedHandler`, `OrderBook`, `MarketMakerStrategy`
2. Load a pre-generated test message file (`data/sample_feed.bin`, generated by a Python helper)
3. Parse all messages, update book, tick strategy, record `rdtsc` latency per event
4. Print p50/p99/p99.99 from `Histogram`
5. Print a before/after table when recompiled with `-O0` vs `-O2` (Makefile target provided)

The deliverable is a README results table — the interview artifact.

---

## Implementation order

1. **Exercise 06** first — the most impactful standalone piece; the hardest core logic.
2. **Exercise 07** second — fast once 06 exists (feed handler dispatches to book).
3. **Exercise 08** third — depends on 06+07 being testable.
4. **Exercise 09** after 06–08 (independent track, needs ghdl).
5. **Exercise 10** last (depends on all above).

Build 06–08 in one session; 09 independently; 10 in a final session.

---

## Changes to existing files

- `tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh` — append `06_order_book`, `07_feed_handler`, `08_latency` to the test list
- `exercises/README.md` — add rows for 06–10 to the exercise table
- `docs/learning/ROADMAP.md` — update status column from "🔜 to build" to "✅ practice ready" as each batch lands
- `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — add to the lessons↔exercises map table

---

## Verification per batch

**Exercise 06:**
```bash
HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/test_06_cpp_order_book.py -v
# expect: all tests pass
uv run pytest tests/exercises/test_06_cpp_order_book.py -v
# expect: 1 skipped (not implemented)
```

**Exercise 07:**
```bash
HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh
# expect: test_07_feed_handler PASS
```

tests/exercises/test_06_cpp_order_book.py

struct Order { int64_t order_id; int64_t price_ticks; int32_t qty; };

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Build and run the C++ exercise tests directly with g++ (no cmake needed).
#
# Usage:
#   bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh                  # both tests
#   bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh test_ring_ma     # one test
#
# HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions switches the include dir from the user stubs
# in exercises/04_spsc_ring to the reference implementations.
#
# Exit codes: 0 = pass, 1 = compile error or test failure,
#             42 = exercise not implemented yet (stub threw).
set -u

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
ROOT="$(cd "$HERE/../../.." && pwd)"
TARGET="${HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET:-exercises}"
INC="$ROOT/$TARGET/04_spsc_ring"
BUILD="$HERE/build"
mkdir -p "$BUILD"

if [ $# -gt 0 ]; then
    tests=("$@")
else
    tests=(test_ring_ma test_spsc_ring)
fi

status=0
for t in "${tests[@]}"; do
    if ! g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -pthread -I "$INC" "$HERE/$t.cpp" -o "$BUILD/$t"; then
        echo "$t: COMPILE FAILED"
        exit 1
    fi
    "$BUILD/$t"
    rc=$?
    if [ "$rc" -eq 42 ]; then
        echo "$t: NOT IMPLEMENTED"
        if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then status=42; fi
    elif [ "$rc" -ne 0 ]; then
        echo "$t: FAILED (exit $rc)"
        exit 1
    else
        echo "$t: PASSED"
    fi
done
exit "$status"

# HFT Practice Exercises

Hands-on, graded companions to the lessons in
[`docs/learning/`](../docs/learning/). Each exercise is a skeleton module
full of TODOs; a pre-written test suite grades your implementation; a
reference solution lives in [`solutions/`](../solutions/) for after you've
attempted it.

## Workflow

1. Read the exercise's `README.md` and the linked lesson.
2. Implement the stubs (replace `raise NotImplementedError` / the C++
   `throw` placeholders / the VHDL sentinel).
3. Run the tests. Unimplemented parts show as **skipped** ("Exercise not
   implemented yet"); wrong answers **fail**; done means all green.
4. Compare with the solution and read its comments.

## Commands

```bash
uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v                  # grade everything
uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 01 -v            # one exercise
uv run pytest tests/ -m "not exercise"             # repo suite without exercises

# prove the test suites are solvable (runs them against solutions/):
HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v

# language-specific direct runners:
bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh                # C++ (needs g++)
bash scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh                     # VHDL (needs ghdl; opt-in)
```

## The exercises

| # | Exercise | Language | Lesson(s) | What you build |
|---|----------|----------|-----------|----------------|
| 01 | [Order book](01_order_book/) | Python | 0016 | Price-time priority LOB: add/cancel/execute, BBO, imbalance |
| 02 | [Market maker](02_market_maker/) | Python | 0017 | Inventory-aware quoting (Avellaneda-Stoikov-lite) — fixes the gap in `fpga/market_maker.vhd` |
| 03 | [Stat-arb + risk](03_stat_arb_risk/) | Python | 0018, 0006, 0019 | Cointegration utils, CUSUM detector, OTR tracker, walk-forward splits |
| 04 | [SPSC ring + O(1) MA](04_spsc_ring/) | C++20 | 0009, 0010 | Lock-free SPSC queue with release/acquire + cache-line padding; O(1) moving average |
| 05 | [VHDL testbenches](05_vhdl_testbench/) | VHDL | 0002 | GHDL testbenches for all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules |

Recommended order: 01 → 02 → 03 (Python ramp), then 04 (C++), then 05
(new toolchain). 03 is independent if you want to jump around.

## How grading works

- Tests load your code from `exercises/` by file path; setting
  `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions` points the same tests at the reference
  implementations instead.
- Python stubs raise `NotImplementedError` → reported as a skip, so the
  repo-wide `uv run pytest tests/` stays green while you work. The skip
  count is your progress bar.
- C++ placeholders throw (`exit 42` from the harness) and the VHDL stubs
  hit a `severity failure` sentinel — both map to the same skip.
- Exercises and solutions are never imported by production code and are
  not part of the installed package.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Build and run C++ exercise tests directly with g++ (no cmake needed).
#
# Usage:
#   bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh                  # all tests
#   bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh test_ring_ma     # one test
#
# HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions switches every include dir from exercises/
# to solutions/.  Default is exercises/ (student stubs).
#
# Exit codes: 0 = all pass, 1 = compile error or test failure,
#             42 = exercise not implemented yet (stub threw).
set -u

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
ROOT="$(cd "$HERE/../../.." && pwd)"
TARGET="${HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET:-exercises}"
BUILD="$HERE/build"
mkdir -p "$BUILD"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Map a test name to the include directories it needs (space-separated).
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
get_inc_dirs() {
    case "$1" in
        test_ring_ma|test_spsc_ring)
            echo "$ROOT/$TARGET/04_spsc_ring" ;;
        test_06_order_book)
            echo "$ROOT/$TARGET/06_cpp_order_book" ;;
        test_07_feed_handler)
            echo "$ROOT/$TARGET/07_feed_handler" ;;
        test_08_latency)
            echo "$ROOT/$TARGET/08_latency_bench" ;;
        *)
            echo "" ;;
    esac
}

if [ $# -gt 0 ]; then
    tests=("$@")
else
    tests=(test_ring_ma test_spsc_ring
           test_06_order_book
           test_07_feed_handler
           test_08_latency)
fi

status=0
for t in "${tests[@]}"; do
    # Build -I flags from the whitespace-separated directory list
    INC_FLAGS=""
    for d in $(get_inc_dirs "$t"); do
        INC_FLAGS="$INC_FLAGS -I$d"
    done

    if ! g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -pthread $INC_FLAGS "$HERE/$t.cpp" -o "$BUILD/$t" 2>&1; then
        echo "$t: COMPILE FAILED"
        exit 1
    fi
    "$BUILD/$t"
    rc=$?
    if [ "$rc" -eq 42 ]; then
        echo "$t: NOT IMPLEMENTED"
        if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then status=42; fi
    elif [ "$rc" -ne 0 ]; then
        echo "$t: FAILED (exit $rc)"
        exit 1
    else
        echo "$t: PASSED"
    fi
done
exit "$status"

# HFT Practice Exercises

Hands-on, graded companions to the lessons in
[`docs/learning/`](../docs/learning/). Each exercise is a skeleton module
full of TODOs; a pre-written test suite grades your implementation; a
reference solution lives in [`solutions/`](../solutions/) for after you've
attempted it.

## Workflow

1. Read the exercise's `README.md` and the linked lesson.
2. Implement the stubs (replace `raise NotImplementedError` / the C++
   `throw` placeholders / the VHDL sentinel).
3. Run the tests. Unimplemented parts show as **skipped** ("Exercise not
   implemented yet"); wrong answers **fail**; done means all green.
4. Compare with the solution and read its comments.

## Commands

```bash
uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v                  # grade everything
uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -k 01 -v            # one exercise
uv run pytest tests/ -m "not exercise"             # repo suite without exercises

# prove the test suites are solvable (runs them against solutions/):
HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions uv run pytest tests/exercises/ -v

# language-specific direct runners:
bash tests/exercises/cpp/run_cpp.sh                # C++ (needs g++)
bash scripts/run_vhdl_tests.sh                     # VHDL (needs ghdl; opt-in)
```

## The exercises

| # | Exercise | Language | Lesson(s) | What you build |
|---|----------|----------|-----------|----------------|
| 01 | [Order book](01_order_book/) | Python | 0016 | Price-time priority LOB: add/cancel/execute, BBO, imbalance |
| 02 | [Market maker](02_market_maker/) | Python | 0017 | Inventory-aware quoting (Avellaneda-Stoikov-lite) — fixes the gap in `fpga/market_maker.vhd` |
| 03 | [Stat-arb + risk](03_stat_arb_risk/) | Python | 0018, 0006, 0019 | Cointegration utils, CUSUM detector, OTR tracker, walk-forward splits |
| 04 | [SPSC ring + O(1) MA](04_spsc_ring/) | C++20 | 0009, 0010 | Lock-free SPSC queue with release/acquire + cache-line padding; O(1) moving average |
| 05 | [VHDL testbenches](05_vhdl_testbench/) | VHDL | 0002 | GHDL testbenches for all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules |

Recommended order: 01 → 02 → 03 (Python ramp), then 04 (C++), then 05
(new toolchain). 03 is independent if you want to jump around.

## How grading works

- Tests load your code from `exercises/` by file path; setting
  `HFT_EXERCISE_TARGET=solutions` points the same tests at the reference
  implementations instead.
- Python stubs raise `NotImplementedError` → reported as a skip, so the
  repo-wide `uv run pytest tests/` stays green while you work. The skip
  count is your progress bar.
- C++ placeholders throw (`exit 42` from the harness) and the VHDL stubs
  hit a `severity failure` sentinel — both map to the same skip.
- Exercises and solutions are never imported by production code and are
  not part of the installed package.
