943	## Added in Lesson 0011 (Low-Latency vs Ultra-Low-Latency)
944	
945	### Adverse selection (in latency context) — `intro`
946	Losing money systematically because faster participants see the same signal
947	microseconds before you and pick off the favorable side. The structural risk
948	of running at a lower tier than your venue's median competitor.
949	
950	### App-to-app latency — `intro`
951	Latency measured between two points inside your application code only
952	(e.g. signal extracted → decision made). Excludes wire and kernel. Useful
953	for internal optimization, not for competitive comparison.
954	
955	### ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) — `intro`
956	Custom silicon fabricated for one purpose. Faster than FPGAs but multi-
957	million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen logic. Tier 6 of the latency ladder;
958	only the largest desks justify it.
959	
960	### Hardware timestamp — `intro`
961	A nanosecond-resolution timestamp attached to a packet by the NIC or FPGA at
962	ingress/egress. The only trustworthy clock at ULL scales — immune to OS
963	scheduling and clock skew.
964	
965	### Inside-FPGA latency — `intro`
966	Latency measured between registers on a single FPGA, i.e. a fixed number of
967	clock cycles. At 250 MHz, 1 cycle = 4 ns. Fundamentally different unit than
968	wire-to-wire latency.
969	
970	### Jitter (latency variability) — `intro`
971	The variability of latency across events, often quoted as `p99.99 − p50` or
972	as the standard deviation. ULL systems are judged on jitter as much as on
973	median latency.
974	
975	### Latency ladder / tier — `intro`
976	The 6-rung industry mental model of trading-system latency, from Tier 0
977	(web app, ms) through Tier 6 (ASIC + microwave, ns + cross-market RF). Each
978	rung is ~10× more expensive than the one above.
979	
980	### Latency tail — `intro`
981	The high-percentile portion of the latency distribution (p99, p99.9,
982	p99.99). At HFT message rates, tail events happen multiple times per
983	second; the tail is what loses money, not the mean.
984	
985	### Low-latency (LL) — `intro`
986	Industry term for systems with microsecond-scale tick-to-trade (~1–100 µs).
987	Tuned C++, lock-free queues, kernel TCP. Tier 2 of the ladder.
988	
989	### Microwave / RF link — `intro`
990	Line-of-sight wireless link used for cross-market arbitrage. Light through
991	air ≈ 1.0c vs ~0.67c through glass — a few ms edge over a thousand km. The
992	basis of the Chicago↔NJ trading corridor.
993	
994	### One-way latency — `intro`
995	Time from event ingress to action emission, measured in one direction
996	(e.g. tick arrival → order on wire). Distinct from round-trip; both are
997	quoted in HFT and must be specified.
998	
999	### p50 / p99 / p99.99 — `intro`
1000	Quantiles of the latency distribution: 50%, 99%, 99.99% of events come in
1001	under this latency. HFT systems are evaluated on the higher percentiles.
1002	
1003	### Real-time (OS sense) — `intro`
1004	Bounded worst-case latency. Distinct from "fast" — a 10 ms deterministic
1005	system is real-time; a 100 ns average with a 10 ms tail is not. ULL systems
1006	aim to be real-time first.
1007	
1008	### Round-trip latency — `intro`
1009	Time from event ingress to action egress through the full pipeline, including
1010	the order leaving your NIC. The headline tick-to-trade number in most
1011	benchmarks is wire-to-wire round-trip.
1012	
1013	### Strategy cadence — `intro`
1014	The natural decision rate of a strategy (per day, per second, per tick).
1015	The single most useful input to deciding what tier of latency the strategy
1016	needs.
1017	
1018	### TSC (Time-Stamp Counter) — `intro`
1019	x86 CPU register incremented every cycle. Read with `rdtsc` in ~10 ns;
1020	nanosecond resolution but needs `tsc_reliable` and per-core synchronization
1021	on multi-socket systems.
1022	
1023	### Ultra-low-latency (ULL) — `intro`
1024	Industry term for systems with nanosecond-scale tick-to-trade (~10 ns – 1
1025	µs). FPGA, kernel-bypass NIC, hardware timestamps, microwave links. Tiers
1026	3–6 of the ladder.
1027	
1028	### Wire-to-wire latency — `intro`
1029	Time from the last bit of an inbound packet arriving at the NIC to the
1030	first bit of an outbound order leaving the NIC. The most defensible
1031	endpoint pair for competitive benchmarking.
1032

1035	## Added in Lesson 0012 (RF Engineering in HFT)
1036	
1037	### Anova Financial Networks — `intro`
1038	Major common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT firms. Competitor
1039	to McKay Brothers on the main US/EU corridors.
1040	
1041	### Aurora (Aurora, IL) — `intro`
1042	CME Group's data center, the futures venue side of the famous CME↔NJ
1043	arbitrage corridor. Pairs with Carteret/Secaucus for the equity venues.
1044	
1045	### Carteret (Carteret, NJ) — `intro`
1046	The equities-side endpoint of the CME↔NJ corridor — Nasdaq's primary
1047	data center. The NYSE-side anchor in Mahwah and Secaucus play the same
1048	role.
1049	
1050	### Common-carrier (microwave) — `intro`
1051	Operating model where one company runs the towers, licenses, and antennas
1052	and sells tiered access to multiple HFT firms. McKay Brothers and Anova
1053	are the dominant examples on US/EU routes.
1054	
1055	### E-band (millimeter-wave) — `intro`
1056	71–86 GHz licensed band. Carries gigabits but only over 5–10 km hops due
1057	to atmospheric absorption and rain fade. Used for last-mile in/out of
1058	exchange data centers; not for long-haul.
1059	
1060	### FCC licensing (microwave) — `intro`
1061	Each individual microwave hop in the US requires an FCC frequency
1062	authorization. The lower bands (6, 11 GHz) are heavily licensed and
1063	incumbents have priority, which is one of the structural reasons HFT
1064	firms rent rather than build.
1065	
1066	### Fresnel zone — `intro`
1067	The ellipsoidal volume around the line-of-sight between two microwave
1068	antennas. Must be roughly 60% obstruction-free for the link to work.
1069	Buildings, trees, terrain, and seasonal crops all matter for route planning.
1070	
1071	### Great-circle distance — `intro`
1072	Shortest path between two points on Earth's surface, ignoring terrain. The
1073	floor against which any real route — fiber or microwave — is compared.
1074	
1075	### Hollow-core fiber — `intro`
1076	Optical fiber where light travels through an air-filled channel inside
1077	photonic-crystal walls, at ~99% c instead of ~68% c through silica. Wider
1078	bandwidth than microwave, weather-immune; ~1 ms slower than microwave one-way
1079	on CME↔NJ. Many HFT firms now run both in parallel.
1080	
1081	### Line-of-sight (LOS) — `intro`
1082	Direct visual path between transmitter and receiver. Earth's curvature
1083	limits hop length to 40–70 km on typical towers. HFT microwave links are
1084	always LOS; tropospheric scatter is not used.
1085	
1086	### McKay Brothers — `intro`
1087	Dominant common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT corridors,
1088	including a CME↔NJ route with published target of <8 ms round-trip.
1089	Also offers hollow-core fiber and integrated packages.
1090	
1091	### Microwave link — `intro`
1092	Wireless point-to-point communication link in the 3–30 GHz range used for
1093	long-haul HFT routes between exchanges. Travels through air at ~99.97% c,
1094	narrow bandwidth (~100 Mbps), weather-sensitive, line-of-sight.
1095	
1096	### Modulation (in HFT RF context) — `intro`
1097	The scheme that maps bits onto a radio carrier (QPSK, 16-QAM, 256-QAM,
1098	1024-QAM). Higher orders carry more bits per symbol but need higher SNR
1099	and add encoding latency. HFT uses lower orders to minimize per-hop latency.
1100	
1101	### Rain fade — `intro`
1102	Signal attenuation due to rainfall absorbing radio energy. Sharply worse
1103	at higher frequencies (severe at 80 GHz, negligible at 6 GHz). One of the
1104	reasons HFT long-haul stays in lower bands.
1105	
1106	### Refractive index — `intro`
1107	Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to speed in a medium. Higher index =
1108	slower light. Air ~1.0003 (~0.997c), hollow-core fiber ~1.005 (~0.995c),
1109	silica fiber ~1.47 (~0.68c). The dominant physics behind the microwave
1110	vs fiber gap.
1111	
1112	### Sponsored access / Common carrier vs Private link — `intro`
1113	**Common-carrier**: shared infrastructure rented by multiple HFT desks
1114	(McKay, Anova). **Private link**: a single firm owns the towers and
1115	licenses. Largest desks may build private; everyone else rents.
1116	
1117	### Tier (microwave subscription) — `intro`
1118	A pricing/priority level for a common-carrier microwave link. Premium tier
1119	gets the lowest latency and dedicated slots; standard tier pays a slightly
1120	higher serialization delay. Annual cost: undisclosed but in the seven
1121	figures per route at premium.
1122	
1123	### Tower spacing / Hop length — `intro`
1124	Practical distance between consecutive microwave repeater towers, typically
1125	40–70 km on long-haul HFT links. Limited by Earth's curvature and tower
1126	height. Each hop adds ~10s of ns of equipment latency.

1135	### From Lesson 0013 (DMA)
1136	
1137	- **Direct Market Access (Trading DMA)** — Buy-side firm submits orders directly to the exchange matching engine through a broker's infrastructure, no human in between.
1138	- **Sponsored Access** — Lowest-latency form of DMA where the buy-side uses the broker's MPID and connectivity but skips most of the broker's order-management stack.
1139	- **Naked access** — Pre-2011 sponsored access with no pre-trade risk filter. Prohibited by Rule 15c3-5.
1140	- **MPID** — Market Participant Identifier, the 4-character code identifying a broker on a venue. Sponsored customers trade under their sponsor's MPID.
1141	- **FIX protocol** — The dominant exchange messaging protocol for orders. NewOrderSingle = 35=D.
1142	- **SEC Rule 15c3-5** — US Market Access Rule (2011). Requires brokers to maintain undisableable pre-trade risk controls on customer order flow.
1143	- **Direct Memory Access (Hardware DMA)** — Peripheral (NIC, FPGA, GPU) reads/writes host RAM via PCIe without CPU executing every transfer.
1144	- **Descriptor ring** — Pre-allocated array in host memory; entries describe DMA transfers. The mailbox between CPU and device.
1145	- **Doorbell register** — Memory-mapped register on device; CPU writes to it as a single PCIe write to signal "new work in the ring."
1146	- **Zero-copy** — Design property where data is read/written from its final location, no intermediate buffers. Requires DMA but isn't synonymous with it.
1147	- **RDMA** — Remote DMA. Device accesses another machine's host memory over the network (InfiniBand, RoCE).
1148	- **PIO** — Programmed I/O. CPU executes load/store instructions to copy every byte. The pre-DMA way.
1149	
1150	### From Lesson 0014 (Hardware Acceleration)
1151	
1152	- **DPU** — Data Processing Unit. SmartNIC with full ARM CPU complex and OS. NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando.
1153	- **SmartNIC** — NIC with programmable packet engines and embedded compute. DPU is the marketing term.
1154	- **NPU** — Neural Processing Unit. ASIC specialized for matmul + activation patterns of neural nets.
1155	- **TPU** — Tensor Processing Unit. Google's NPU for training and inference.
1156	- **Acceleration vs Offload** — Acceleration: same work, faster. Offload: same work, elsewhere so the original CPU is freed.

1255	## Added in Lessons 0025–0028 (regression suite + alpha/beta, 2026-06-11)
1256	
1257	- **OLS (Ordinary Least Squares)** — Fit β to minimize Σ(y − Xβ)². Closed form via the normal equations β = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy; computed stably via `np.linalg.lstsq` in `solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py:_ols`.
1258	- **Normal equations** — XᵀXβ = Xᵀy, the first-order conditions of OLS. Conceptual form only; inverting XᵀX in code amplifies rounding error when features are collinear.
1259	- **R² (coefficient of determination)** — 1 − SSR/TSS, fraction of target variance explained. In-sample R² only grows with added features; out-of-sample R² is the honest number and can be negative. A few percent is good on daily returns.
1260	- **Standard error (coefficient)** — Uncertainty of an OLS coefficient, from σ̂²(XᵀX)⁻¹. β̂/SE is the t-statistic; powers the Dickey-Fuller test and the "is the alpha real?" question.
1261	- **Shrinkage (learning rate ν, boosting)** — Scaling each boosted tree's contribution by ν before adding (sklearn default 0.1). Lower ν + more trees generalizes better. Distinct from covariance shrinkage (Lesson 0006).
1262	- **Stochastic gradient boosting (subsample)** — Fitting each boosting round on a random row sample (`subsample < 1`), trading a little bias for variance reduction.
1263	- **Function-space gradient descent** — Boosting's framing: each round adds a tree approximating the negative loss-gradient at every training point — a gradient step where the step is a function.
1264	- **Sigmoid (logistic function)** — σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), maps a linear score to (0,1). σ(0)=0.5, σ(±2)≈0.88/0.12. The link function of logistic regression and a classic NN activation.
1265	- **Log-loss (cross-entropy)** — −[y·ln p̂ + (1−y)·ln(1−p̂)]. Unbounded penalty for confident wrongness; forces calibrated probabilities. The loss logistic regression minimizes.
1266	- **Logistic regression** — Linear score + sigmoid, fit by log-loss; a *classifier* despite the name. Not used in this repo by design — binarizing `fwd_ret_1d` would destroy the magnitudes the top-N ranking needs.
1267	- **Linear probability model** — OLS fit directly to a 0/1 label. Works crudely; predictions escape [0,1]. The "why logistic regression exists" foil.
1268	- **Calibration (probability)** — Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies ("0.9 events happen 90% of the time"). Distinct from ranking quality (AUC).
1269	- **CAPM** — r_s = α + β·r_m + ε. Single-factor model decomposing strategy returns into market exposure and skill. Estimated with the same OLS as everything else.
1270	- **Beta (β, market)** — cov(r_s, r_m)/var(r_m): the OLS slope of strategy returns on market returns. β≈0 = market-neutral. Same formula as `hedge_ratio` in exercise 03 — different x.
1271	- **Alpha (α, Jensen's)** — The CAPM regression intercept: average return left after subtracting β×market. The scarce, paid-for part of performance; leverage replicates β but never α.
1272	- **Market-neutral (measured)** — Portfolio whose *measured* β ≈ 0, re-estimated on a rolling basis. A maintained property, not a one-time label.
1273	- **Factor model (multi-beta)** — CAPM generalized to several regressors (size, value, momentum — Fama-French). Multi-feature OLS; factor neutrality = driving all those betas to zero.
1274

# Glossary — HFT_practice

Terms the learner has been introduced to. A term is promoted from *introduced* to
*understood* only after they've answered a question about it correctly or used it
correctly themselves.

Status legend: `intro` = covered in a lesson · `solid` = demonstrably grasped.

---

### Algorithmic trading — `intro`
Any trading where decisions are made by code rather than a human. A superset of HFT.

### Ask (offer) — `intro`
The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.

### Adverse selection — `intro`
The risk that the counterparty who hit your quote knew more than you did about
where the price was about to go. The reason market makers cancel orders aggressively.

### Bid — `intro`
The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.

### Colocation — `intro`
Renting rack space inside the exchange's data center so your trading server is
physically next to the matching engine, minimizing wire latency.

### FPGA — `intro`
Field-Programmable Gate Array. Reconfigurable hardware wired into a fixed
pipeline at synthesis time. Used in HFT for deterministic nanosecond-scale latency.
Example in this repo: `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### HFT (High-Frequency Trading) — `intro`
Automated trading defined by microsecond-to-nanosecond latency, very high order
rates, and short (often sub-second) holding periods.

### Limit order — `intro`
"Buy/sell at price X or better." Rests passively in the book until matched or
cancelled. The order type market makers post.

### Limit Order Book (LOB) — `intro`
The full list of resting buy and sell orders at every price level on a venue.
The core data structure of modern electronic markets.

### Market maker — `intro`
A strategy that simultaneously posts both a bid and an ask, earning the spread
when both sides fill. `fpga/market_maker.vhd` is a hardware example.

### Market order — `intro`
"Fill me now at the best available price." Crosses the spread and pays for
immediacy. The order type takers send.

### Mid-price — `intro`
`(bid + ask) / 2`. A common reference for "fair value" between the two sides of
the book. Computed explicitly in `fpga/market_maker.vhd`.

### Q16.16 fixed-point — `intro`
A 32-bit signed integer encoding where the lower 16 bits represent the
fractional part: `real_value = integer_signal / 65536`. Used in
`fpga/market_maker.vhd` so all arithmetic stays in one-cycle integer ops.

### Spread — `intro`
`ask − bid`. The cost of crossing the book; the prize a market maker tries to
capture on round-trips.

### Tick — `intro`
A single market data update — a trade, a quote change, a cancel. The unit of
input to an HFT pipeline.

### Tick-to-trade latency — `intro`
The time between receiving a market data tick and your responding order leaving
your NIC. The headline latency number in HFT (top firms: ~100–500 ns on FPGA).

---

## Added in Lesson 0002 (FPGAs in HFT)

### ASIC — `intro`
Application-Specific Integrated Circuit. Silicon manufactured for one design.
Fastest possible, but multi-million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen forever —
which is why HFT firms use FPGAs (reconfigurable) instead.

### Bitstream — `intro`
The binary file produced by synthesis + place-and-route. Loading it onto the
FPGA configures every LUT, flip-flop, and routing switch to realize your
design. Reloading is a seconds-long operation, not a recompile of a chip.

### Combinational logic — `intro`
Logic whose outputs depend only on current inputs — no clock involved. Inside
each pipeline stage in `fpga/*.vhd`, arithmetic between clock edges is
combinational.

### Determinism (FPGA sense) — `intro`
The property that the same input takes the same number of cycles every time.
The opposite of CPU jitter from OS scheduling, cache misses, branch prediction.
The single biggest reason HFT firms tolerate the pain of FPGA development.

### DSP slice — `intro`
A dedicated multiply-accumulate block inside the FPGA fabric. Each `*` in
VHDL (e.g. `W_F0 * feature_0` in `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`) typically
maps to one DSP slice.

### HDL — `intro`
Hardware Description Language. VHDL or Verilog. Describes hardware
register-by-register, not as an executing program.

### HLS — `intro`
High-Level Synthesis. Toolchain that takes annotated C/C++ and generates HDL
for you. Faster to write than hand-VHDL; sometimes worse timing or area.
`fpga/hls_synthesis.tcl` drives the HLS flow in this repo.

### Jitter — `intro`
Variability in latency from one event to the next. HFT cares about jitter as
much as average latency, because strategies are sized against the worst-case
not the median.

### Kernel bypass — `intro`
Networking techniques (DPDK, Solarflare OpenOnload, XDP) that route packets
from the NIC directly to userspace, skipping the Linux kernel network stack.
A 20–30% latency win for CPU-based HFT; obsolete on FPGA NICs where parsing
is on-chip already.

### LUT (Look-Up Table) — `intro`
The basic configurable unit of FPGA fabric. A small truth table that can be
programmed to compute any function of N inputs (typically N=6). LUT count is
the headline capacity metric of an FPGA part.

### Pipeline stage — `intro`
A combinational chunk of logic terminated by a register (flip-flop). More
stages = higher clock frequency but more cycles of latency. `linear_regression_predictor.vhd`
has 2 stages; `market_maker.vhd` has 1.

### Place-and-Route (PAR) — `intro`
The step after synthesis that assigns each gate in your netlist to a physical
LUT on the chip and routes the wires between them. Where timing closure is
won or lost.

### Sequential logic — `intro`
Logic that uses flip-flops driven by a clock to hold state between cycles.
Each pipeline stage boundary in the repo's VHDL is sequential.

### Synthesis — `intro`
The step that turns HDL source into a netlist of generic gates. Distinct from
Place-and-Route, which maps those gates onto the physical chip.

### Timing closure — `intro`
The act of making your design meet the target clock period at every register-
to-register path. The real bottleneck of FPGA HFT development — not the
arithmetic, not the algorithm, but proving the silicon can run that fast.

### Valid handshake — `intro`
The convention of carrying a `valid` bit alongside every datum through a
pipeline, so each stage knows which cycles contain real data. Used uniformly
in all three `fpga/*.vhd` modules.

### VHDL vs Verilog — `intro`
Two HDLs that compile to the same gates. VHDL: verbose, strongly typed, used
in this repo. Verilog/SystemVerilog: terser, more common at web-scale silicon
firms. The choice is cultural, not technical.

---

## Added in Lesson 0003 (ML Algorithms in Trading)

### Boosting — `intro`
Sequentially combine many weak learners (typically shallow trees), each trained
to correct the errors of the previous ensemble. Contrast with bagging
(independent learners averaged together).

### Classification vs Regression — `intro`
**Classification** predicts a discrete label (up/down). **Regression** predicts
a continuous number. This repo uses regression because the downstream step
ranks tickers by predicted-return magnitude, which requires the number itself.

### Cross-sectional ranking — `intro`
At each date, rank all tickers by their predicted return and act on the top-N.
The model's predicted *magnitude* matters less than its *order*. The whole
selection step in `paper_trading_sim.py` (`sort_values("pred")`) depends on this.

### Ensemble — `intro`
A model made of many sub-models combined to produce one prediction.
`GradientBoostingRegressor`'s default is 100 trees combined additively with a
0.1 learning rate.

### Feature engineering — `intro`
Turning raw data into model inputs. In this repo: returns, moving averages,
MA gap, rolling vol, RSI — all computed in `build_features` from raw Close prices.

### Gradient Boosting — `intro`
A boosting method where each new weak learner is fit to the gradient of the
loss with respect to the current ensemble's predictions. For squared error,
the gradient is just the residual `y − F(x)`, so each tree learns the current
error pattern.

### GradientBoostingRegressor — `intro`
scikit-learn's class for gradient-boosted decision trees on a continuous target.
The flagship model in `paper_trading_sim.py:train_model`.

### Inference — `intro`
Applying a trained model to make predictions (`model.predict(X)`). The
latency-sensitive half of ML — what HFT cares about almost exclusively.

### Learning rate (ν) — `intro`
The scalar that scales each new tree's contribution before adding it to the
ensemble. Smaller = more conservative updates, more trees needed, better
generalization. Default 0.1 in sklearn.

### Linear Regression — `intro`
`ŷ = w₀ + Σ wᵢ xᵢ`. Closed-form least-squares fit. Parametric, additive, fast.
Used in `fpga/linear_regression_predictor.vhd` because four constants fit in
silicon trivially.

### Look-ahead bias — `intro`
The bug where a feature secretly contains information from the future relative
to the target. Backtests look great; live trading loses money. The
`.shift(-1)` discipline in `build_features` is what prevents this when done
correctly.

### Mean-variance optimization — `intro`
Markowitz's portfolio framework: choose weights `w` to balance expected return
`μᵀw` against risk `wᵀΣw`. Closed-form long-only solution `w ∝ Σ⁻¹μ` is
implemented in `predict_next.py:meanvar_long_only`. Not ML — it's optimization
on top of the ML output.

### Non-parametric model — `intro`
A model whose effective parameter count grows with the data. Gradient-boosted
trees are non-parametric in this sense. Contrast: linear regression's
parameter count is fixed at N+1 regardless of dataset size.

### Overfitting — `intro`
When a model fits noise in the training data and fails to generalize to new
data. In `GradientBoostingRegressor` it appears as training R² climbing while
test R² drops. Fixes: lower learning rate, shallower trees, more
regularization, early stopping.

### Parametric model — `intro`
A model with a fixed number of parameters regardless of dataset size. Linear
regression: N feature weights plus an intercept, done. Parametric models are
much easier to fit on an FPGA.

### Residual — `intro`
`y − F(x)` — what the current ensemble got wrong on a given row. Gradient
boosting fits each new tree to predict the residuals of the previous step.

### RSI (Relative Strength Index) — `intro`
A 0–100 momentum oscillator that rises when up-days dominate down-days within
the lookback window. Computed in `paper_trading_sim._rsi` with window=14 and
normalized to 0–1 in `build_features`.

### Supervised learning — `intro`
Learning a mapping from inputs `x` to known outputs `y`, using a dataset of
labeled examples. All three "ML" elements in this repo (linear regression and
gradient boosting) are supervised. The MA rule in VHDL is *not* supervised —
it isn't learned at all.

### Target — `intro`
The value the model is trained to predict. In this repo: `fwd_ret_1d`, the
next-day return, computed via `out["ret_1d"].shift(-1)`.

### Training vs Inference — `intro`
**Training** is the expensive offline step that produces parameters (`fit`).
**Inference** is the cheap online step that uses them (`predict`). HFT cares
about inference latency; training latency essentially doesn't matter.

---

## Added in Lesson 0004 (Linux Internal Networking)

### 0.0.0.0 (wildcard bind) — `intro`
A wildcard address meaning "listen on every interface in this network
namespace." Used in this repo's `Dockerfile`. Distinct from `127.0.0.1`,
which means "loopback only."

### Bridge (Linux bridge) — `intro`
A software L2 switch in the kernel. Docker creates one (`docker0` by default,
or a per-project bridge for `docker-compose`) and plugs every container's
veth into it so they can talk to each other and to the outside.

### Busy polling — `intro`
Kernel networking option (`SO_BUSY_POLL`) that spins a CPU on the NIC's RX
queue instead of sleeping for an interrupt. Trades a CPU core for ~100 µs
of latency reduction. Useful for HFT-adjacent workloads, wasteful for web apps.

### DNAT (Destination NAT) — `intro`
iptables rule that rewrites the destination IP/port of inbound packets. Docker
installs DNAT rules to implement `ports: "HOST:CONTAINER"` mappings.

### DPDK — `intro`
Data Plane Development Kit. Userspace networking framework that maps the NIC's
DMA rings directly into application memory, bypassing the kernel stack. Common
in HFT and high-perf network appliances.

### eth0 (container) — `intro`
The conventional name of a container's primary virtual ethernet interface.
One end of a veth pair; the other end sits on the host bridge.

### iptables / Netfilter — `intro`
The Linux kernel's packet-filtering and NAT framework. Docker programs it to
implement port forwarding (DNAT) and outbound source rewriting (MASQUERADE).

### Kernel bypass — `solid` (promoted from intro in Lesson 0002)
Skipping the kernel network stack to cut tick-to-trade latency. DPDK,
OpenOnload, XDP are CPU-side; FPGA NICs go further by doing parsing in
hardware.

### Loopback (`lo`, 127.0.0.1) — `intro`
A virtual interface inside the kernel where packets never reach any NIC.
Every network namespace has its own private loopback — the container's
`127.0.0.1` is not the host's `127.0.0.1`.

### MASQUERADE / SNAT — `intro`
iptables rule that rewrites the source IP of outbound packets. Used by Docker
so that traffic from a container's private bridge IP appears to come from the
host's outbound IP, so replies can route back correctly.

### Namespace (network namespace) — `intro`
A kernel object that gives a group of processes their own copy of the network
stack: their own interfaces, routing table, iptables rules, loopback. The
isolation primitive containers are built on.

### Network stack (Linux) — `intro`
The kernel's layered TCP/IP implementation: socket layer → TCP/UDP → IP →
netfilter → qdisc → driver. Each layer adds latency; total is typically
~50–120 µs round-trip on a busy host.

### Port — `intro`
A 16-bit number that distinguishes endpoints on a host. Part of the socket
5-tuple `(proto, src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port)`.

### Port forwarding — `intro`
Common name for DNAT-based "expose container port X on host port Y." What
`ports: "8000:8000"` in `docker-compose.yml` actually does.

### Qdisc (Queueing discipline) — `intro`
The kernel's packet-scheduling layer between the IP layer and the NIC driver.
Decides which packet goes out next when the wire is busy.

### Socket — `intro`
The kernel object representing one endpoint of a connection, identified by
the 5-tuple. A listening socket can spawn many connected sockets, all sharing
one port.

### TCP/UDP — `intro`
The two main L4 transports. TCP is reliable, ordered, connection-oriented.
UDP is unreliable, unordered, connectionless. Exchange market data is almost
always UDP (multicast); orders are usually TCP-based protocols like FIX.

### veth pair — `intro`
A pair of virtual ethernet interfaces in the kernel, connected back-to-back.
Packets out one end appear at the other. Docker uses veth pairs to bridge a
container's network namespace to the host bridge.

---

## Added in Lesson 0005 (Prediction Models in Trading)

### Adaptivity (model) — `intro`
Whether a model is trained once (`paper_trading_sim.py`) or refit periodically
on rolling windows (`walkforward_sim.py --rolling_retrain`). One of the five
axes that define a trading prediction model.

### Cross-sectional model — `intro`
A model that ranks N assets against each other at the same point in time.
This repo's GBM is cross-sectional: every day it scores all tickers and picks
the top-N. Contrast with time-series, which forecasts one asset's future from
its own past.

### Cross-sectional pooling — `intro`
Training one model on rows from many assets stacked together, assuming the
feature→target relationship is roughly universal. The repo does this; sector
or market-cap bucketing is the production refinement.

### CUSUM (cumulative sum) — `intro`
A change-point detection statistic. Triggers when the cumulative deviation of
a series from its mean exceeds a threshold. Used in `walkforward_sim.py` as
one of four stress detectors that gate exposure.

### Distributional forecast — `intro`
A prediction that includes uncertainty — quantiles, mean+variance, or a full
distribution. Lets downstream sizing be risk-aware. This repo currently
emits only point estimates.

### Filtering (vs forecasting) — `intro`
Estimating a *present* hidden state from past observations (HMM/GMM regime
detection). Distinct from forecasting, which estimates a *future* value. The
repo's `GaussianMixture` overlay is filtering, not forecasting.

### Foundation model (time-series) — `intro`
Large pretrained model (TimesFM, Chronos, Kronos, Moirai) trained on billions
of time-series points, used for zero-/few-shot forecasting. On tabular daily
equity features, GBM still beats them for cross-sectional ranking — for now.

### Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) — `intro`
A probabilistic clustering model that fits K Gaussian components to a dataset.
Used in `walkforward_sim.py` to estimate the probability that today's returns
belong to a "high-vol" regime, then to scale exposure down accordingly.

### Hidden Markov Model (HMM) — `intro`
A state-space model where an unobserved discrete state evolves over time and
emits observations. Common as a regime model in finance. The repo's GMM is a
simpler cousin (no transition matrix — just clustering).

### Horizon (forecast horizon) — `intro`
The future window over which the target is measured. This repo: 1 trading
day. Choose tick-level and you need a completely different infrastructure.

### Output shape — `intro`
The form of a model's prediction: point estimate, distribution, or action.
One of the five axes; the repo emits point estimates only.

### Per-asset model — `intro`
One model per ticker, trained on that ticker's data only. Opposite of
cross-sectional pooling. Captures asset-specific quirks but starves on
data and fails for new tickers.

### Pooling (model pooling) — `intro`
The choice between training one shared model across assets vs one per asset.
One of the five axes; this repo pools across all tickers.

### Regime model — `intro`
Any model whose primary output is the identification of a hidden market state
(calm/stress, bull/bear). Used to switch strategies or scale exposure, not to
predict returns directly. `walkforward_sim.py:GaussianMixture` is the
project's regime model.

### Reinforcement learning (in trading) — `intro`
Learning an action policy directly from a reward signal (P&L). Promising for
execution and market-making but notoriously hard to train on financial data.
Not used in this repo.

### Rolling retrain — `intro`
Periodically refitting a model on a fixed-length window of the most recent
past data only. `walkforward_sim.py --rolling_retrain --retrain_freq monthly
--train_window_days 756` is the repo's default flavor.

### Stationarity — `intro`
A property of a time series whose statistical moments don't drift over time.
Returns are roughly stationary; prices are not. Pooling across tickers
requires features and targets that are at least approximately stationary —
this is why the repo predicts returns, not prices.

### Target axis — `intro`
The choice of what the model predicts: direction (binary), magnitude
(regression), volatility, jump probability, regime, or action (RL). The
single most consequential design decision in a trading model.

### TimesFM / Chronos / Kronos — `intro`
Time-series foundation models from the 2024–2025 wave (Google, Amazon,
Tsinghua respectively). Pretrained transformers for general forecasting.
Strong zero-shot on benchmarks; not yet a slam-dunk on tabular cross-sectional
equity alpha.

---

## Added in Lesson 0006 (Statistics Math in Trading)

### Annualization factor — `intro`
Convention for converting per-period statistics to per-year. For US equities,
252 trading days. Means scale by ×252; standard deviations scale by ×√252
(because variances add across independent periods).

### Bessel's correction (ddof=1) — `intro`
Dividing by (n−1) instead of n when computing sample variance/std, to get an
unbiased estimator. pandas defaults to `ddof=1`; NumPy defaults to `ddof=0`.
Cross-library default mismatches are a real bug source.

### CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate) — `intro`
Geometric annual return: `(final / initial)^(252/N) − 1`. The actual
compounded growth rate. Always ≤ arithmetic APR; gap is volatility drag.
Computed in `analyze_equity.py:compute_metrics`.

### Correlation — `intro`
Standardized covariance: `cov(i,j) / (σᵢ σⱼ)`. Unit-free, bounded in [−1, 1].
Use for comparing relationships across assets; covariance for portfolio
variance formulas.

### Covariance matrix (Σ) — `intro`
Symmetric matrix whose entry (i,j) is the covariance of asset i and asset j
returns. Diagonal entries are variances. The repo estimates Σ from the recent
`--cov_lookback` days in `predict_next.py:compute_returns`.

### CUSUM (cumulative sum) test — `intro`
Change-point statistic that tracks deviations from the mean. Two running sums
(positive and negative drift) update each period with a slack term k. The
repo uses `k = cusum_threshold * σ` (default 3σ) as one of four stress
detectors in `walkforward_sim.py`.

### Drawdown — `intro`
Percentage drop from the running peak so far:
`DD_t = equity_t / max_{s≤t}(equity_s) − 1`. Always ≤ 0.

### Log return — `intro`
`ln(P_t / P_{t-1})`. Sums across time linearly; symmetric around zero. Used in
academic risk math. Numerically ≈ simple return for small moves.

### Maximum drawdown (MaxDD) — `intro`
The minimum of the drawdown series over the full period — the worst
peak-to-trough loss the equity curve ever felt. Investors emotionally trade on
this number more than on Sharpe.

### Sharpe ratio — `intro`
Risk-adjusted return: `(mean_return × 252) / (std_return × √252)`. Unit-free.
This repo's version assumes risk-free rate = 0. >1 solid, >2 excellent, >3
raises eyebrows.

### Shrinkage (covariance) — `intro`
Mixing the sample covariance matrix with a more stable target (typically the
diagonal): `Σ_shrunk = (1−λ) Σ_sample + λ diag(Σ_sample)`. Trades a little
bias for much less estimation noise; vital when Σ is going to be inverted.
Lives in `predict_next.py` via `--shrink`.

### Simple return — `intro`
`(P_t − P_{t-1}) / P_{t-1}`. Computed by pandas `.pct_change()`. Aggregates
linearly across *assets* in a portfolio: `r_p = Σ wᵢ rᵢ`. This repo's
default everywhere.

### Sortino ratio — `intro`
Like Sharpe but divides by downside standard deviation only (negative returns
counted, positive ignored). Kinder to positively skewed strategies. Not
computed in this repo.

### Standard deviation (σ) — `intro`
Square root of variance. Same units as the underlying. In finance: "volatility."

### Variance — `intro`
`E[(r − μ)²]`. Units: returns². Adds linearly across independent periods,
which is why annual std = daily std × √252.

### Volatility drag — `intro`
The gap between arithmetic and geometric mean return, approximately σ²/2 in
log terms. A high-vol strategy with the same mean as a low-vol one will
compound *more slowly*. The reason `analyze_equity.py` returns both
`APR_simple` and `CAGR`.

---

## Added in Lesson 0007 (Neural Networks in Quant)

### Activation function — `intro`
The elementwise nonlinearity inside each NN layer (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU).
Without it, a stack of linear layers collapses to one linear layer.

### Attention / self-attention — `intro`
The mechanism at the heart of transformers: each output position is a weighted
combination of all input positions, with weights computed from the inputs
themselves. Replaces the sequential recurrence of an LSTM.

### Backpropagation — `intro`
The chain-rule algorithm that computes gradients of a loss with respect to
every weight in a network. Combined with an optimizer (Adam, SGD) it's how
neural nets train.

### BERT / FinBERT — `intro`
BERT is a 2018 transformer pretrained on text via masked-language-modeling.
FinBERT is BERT fine-tuned on financial corpora (news, filings). Alpha
Vantage's news sentiment is a BERT-family model's output.

### CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) — `intro`
NN that applies learned filters across local windows of its input. Dominant
on images and the 2D price-level grid of LOB snapshots (DeepLOB).

### Deep RL — `intro`
Reinforcement learning where the policy and/or value function is a neural
network. Used in quant for execution and market-making research; production
deployment is rare due to backtesting difficulty.

### DeepLOB / TransLOB / TLOB — `intro`
Neural architectures for limit-order-book modeling. DeepLOB (2018): CNN+LSTM
on LOB snapshots. TransLOB / TLOB (2024–2025): transformer variants with
attention over price levels. The natural NN bridge to this repo's FPGA work.

### Embedding — `intro`
A learned dense vector representation of a discrete input (a word, a ticker,
an article). The intermediate layer outputs of a transformer are embeddings
of the input — much richer than a single scalar like a sentiment score.

### Epoch / Iteration / Batch — `intro`
**Batch**: a chunk of training rows for one gradient step. **Iteration**: one
batch processed. **Epoch**: one full pass through the training set.

### Feedforward / MLP — `intro`
A neural network where every layer is fully connected and information flows
forward only (no recurrence, no attention). The simplest deep NN.

### Fine-tuning — `intro`
Taking a pretrained model and continuing training on a smaller task-specific
dataset. FinBERT is BERT fine-tuned on financial text.

### Gradient descent (in NN context) — `intro`
The optimizer that updates weights `W ← W − η·∇L` to reduce the loss.
Variants (Adam, RMSprop, SGD with momentum) differ in how they adapt the
step size per weight.

### hls4ml — `intro`
Open-source toolchain that compiles trained scikit-learn/Keras/PyTorch models
into HDL for FPGA deployment. Documented in `fpga/README.md` as the bridge
from the Python model side to the silicon side.

### Linear collapse — `intro`
The fact that the composition of linear functions is linear. Stacking N
linear layers without nonlinearities is mathematically equivalent to one
linear layer.

### LSTM / GRU — `intro`
Recurrent NN cells designed to remember information across long sequences
via gating. State-of-the-art for sequence forecasting from ~2016–2022;
now often replaced by transformers.

### Loss function — `intro`
The scalar objective the optimizer minimizes. MSE for regression, cross-entropy
for classification, Huber for robustness. Distinct from the activation function.

### Neural network — `intro`
A stack of (linear transform → nonlinearity) layers, trained by minimizing a
loss with gradient-based optimization. Not used in this repo's Python code
today, but Alpha Vantage's sentiment score is one consumed silently.

### Pretraining — `intro`
Training a large model on a huge generic corpus before any task-specific
training. The base half of "pretrain + fine-tune."

### ReLU — `intro`
Rectified Linear Unit: `max(0, x)`. The default activation function in
modern feedforward networks. Cheap to compute, mostly avoids vanishing
gradients.

### RNN / Recurrent NN — `intro`
NN that processes a sequence step-by-step, carrying hidden state forward.
LSTM and GRU are RNN cells designed to mitigate vanishing gradients.

### Transformer — `intro`
NN architecture built on self-attention; processes all sequence positions in
parallel. Dominant in NLP, increasingly in finance time-series (TLOB,
TimesFM, Chronos, Kronos).

### Universal Approximation Theorem — `intro`
A theoretical guarantee that a NN with one sufficiently wide hidden layer can
approximate any continuous function. Comfort, not a recipe — depth is what
makes networks practically trainable on real data.

## Added in Lesson 0008 (LLM Use-Cases in HFT)

### Agent (LLM agent) — `intro`
LLM that plans → calls a tool → reads result → plans next step, in a loop.
Useful for open-ended research; brittle in production. Failure modes include
infinite loops and confident wrongness.

### Alpha-GPT — `intro`
Class of research systems (2024–2025) that use LLMs with prompt engineering
to propose trading signal code, then backtest the result. Promising as an
exploration loop, not as an autonomous trader.

### Cold path / Warm path / Hot path — `intro`
Three latency regimes for LLM-relevance in a trading firm.
**Hot path** (ns–µs, FPGA/CPU tick-to-trade): LLMs forbidden.
**Warm path** (ms–s, intraday research/alerts): LLMs sometimes.
**Cold path** (seconds+, overnight research/docs): LLMs obvious.

### Completion model — `intro`
LLM endpoint that generates text given a prompt. Distinct from an *embedding*
model, which produces vectors for similarity search.

### Distillation (LLM) — `intro`
Training a small model to mimic input/output pairs of a frontier model.
Get most of the quality at a fraction of cost. Standard for high-volume
feature-extraction jobs (e.g. scoring millions of articles).

### Embedding model — `intro`
LLM endpoint that turns text into a dense vector for similarity search.
The retrieval half of RAG.

### Fine-tuning (LLM) — `intro`
Continuing training of a base LLM on task-specific data. Changes the model's
weights. Slower to update than RAG; usually justified only with abundant
labeled examples and a single repeatable task.

### Function calling / Tool use — `intro`
The protocol whereby an LLM emits a structured request to call a specific
function on the host (e.g. `compute_metrics(equity_csv)`), then incorporates
the result into its final answer. Lets the LLM stay symbolic and accurate.

### Hallucination — `intro`
The model fabricates a fact (a paper, a function, a citation) that doesn't
exist. Distinct from being wrong about a real fact. Both look the same to the
user; both demand verification before acting.

### Hosted vs Self-hosted LLM — `intro`
**Hosted**: API call to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google. Cheap per call, no infra.
**Self-hosted**: run an open-weight model (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek)
on your own GPUs. Mandatory for sensitive data; cheaper at scale.

### LLM (Large Language Model) — `intro`
Transformer-architecture neural network with 10⁹–10¹² parameters, pretrained
on internet-scale text. Larger cousins of BERT/FinBERT from Lesson 0007.
General-purpose; expensive per call; cannot sit on the HFT hot path.

### MCP (Model Context Protocol) — `intro`
2024–2025 open standard for exposing tools, resources, and prompts to LLMs.
The agreed-upon plumbing layer between an LLM client and your codebase.

### Prompt engineering — `intro`
Writing inputs to an LLM that reliably produce useful structured outputs.
Includes system prompts, few-shot examples, format constraints (JSON mode),
chain-of-thought instructions.

### RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) — `intro`
Pattern where relevant chunks of an external corpus are retrieved at query
time and stuffed into the LLM's context. Default architecture for codebase
or document Q&A; cheap, deterministic-ish, no fine-tuning required.

### StockBench — `intro`
2025 benchmark for LLM agents trading real-world stock data. Headline result:
most LLM agents underperform buy-and-hold. Implication: LLMs are tools, not
traders.

### System prompt vs User prompt — `intro`
**System**: the persistent instruction set ("you are a quant assistant").
**User**: the per-query message. Mixing them weakens guardrails.

### Temperature — `intro`
The decoding parameter controlling sampling randomness. `temperature=0` gives
deterministic-ish output (still subject to provider model changes). Always
use 0 for feature pipelines that need to be reproducible.

### Vector store — `intro`
A database (FAISS, sqlite-vss, Pinecone, pgvector) that indexes embeddings
and supports nearest-neighbor retrieval. The R in RAG.

## Added in Lesson 0009 (Low-Latency C++ for Trading)

### Atomic (operation) — `intro`
A single hardware-level read/modify/write instruction (CAS, LOCK XADD) that
is indivisible. ~25 ns. Building block of lock-free queues.

### Branch elimination — `intro`
Rewriting code so a conditional is replaced by arithmetic
(`x = cond*a + (1-cond)*b`). Worth it when the branch is unpredictable.

### Branch prediction — `intro`
The CPU's front-end guesses which side of a conditional will be taken before
the comparison resolves. Mispredict cost ~10–20 ns (pipeline flush).

### Cache line — `intro`
The unit the CPU fetches from main memory: 64 bytes on modern x86. Reading
one byte fetches the whole line; sequential access is cheap, random access
across lines is expensive.

### Cache (L1/L2/L3) — `intro`
On-die SRAM hierarchy. L1 ~1 ns, L2 ~3 ns, L3 ~15 ns. The 100× gap to main
memory (~100 ns) makes "is the working set cache-resident?" the most
important performance question.

### Constexpr — `intro`
C++ keyword guaranteeing a value or function is evaluable at compile time.
Lets the compiler fold the value into the generated machine code as an
immediate instead of a runtime memory load.

### CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern) — `intro`
Static-polymorphism idiom: a base class is templated on the derived type so
all dispatch is resolved at compile time. Replaces virtual functions in
HFT-grade C++.

### False sharing — `intro`
When two threads write different variables that happen to share a cache
line, the line ping-pongs between caches and performance collapses. Fix
with `alignas(64)` padding.

### Hot path / Cold path — `intro`
**Hot path**: the per-tick code that runs millions of times a second. No
allocation, no I/O, no syscalls. **Cold path**: setup, teardown, rare
events. Allocate, log, and call APIs freely.

### Inlining — `intro`
Compiler optimization that replaces a function call with the function body.
Removes call/ret overhead and enables cross-boundary optimization. Templates
inline; non-final `virtual` calls do not.

### `[[likely]]` / `[[unlikely]]` — `intro`
C++20 attributes that hint to the compiler which branch is the common case.
Help with code layout and icache pressure; do not replace the hardware
predictor.

### Lock-free queue / SPSC ring — `intro`
A fixed-size circular buffer where a single producer thread writes and a
single consumer thread reads using only atomic head/tail indices — no
mutex. The HFT-grade alternative to `std::cout` from the hot path.

### `noexcept` — `intro`
Function specifier promising no exceptions will escape. Lets the compiler
skip generating unwinding scaffolding and inline more aggressively. Default
on every leaf hot-path function.

### Pipeline (CPU pipeline) — `intro`
The CPU executes instructions in ~15 overlapping stages. A branch mispredict
or a long-latency memory access stalls the pipeline. Modern HFT C++ is
largely about avoiding pipeline stalls.

### Ring buffer (stack) — `intro`
A fixed-size circular array used as a FIFO. O(1) push/pop, no allocation.
The C++ analog of the VHDL `price_reg` shift register in
`fpga/moving_average_trader.vhd`.

### SoA vs AoS — `intro`
**Struct-of-Arrays**: one array per field (`prices[]`, `volumes[]`). Fast
when iterating one field at a time. **Array-of-Structs**: one record per
row (`struct Tick { p; v; }`). Fast when touching multiple fields together.
HFT often prefers SoA for vectorization.

### Spinlock — `intro`
A lock that busy-waits via CAS instead of sleeping. Uncontended ~25 ns;
contended catastrophically slow. Used only when expected hold time is
shorter than a kernel sleep cycle.

### Stack vs Heap allocation — `intro`
**Stack**: pointer move, fixed size, free. **Heap** (`new`, `malloc`,
`vector::push_back`): unpredictable, allocator-locked, ~30–200 ns. Hot-path
code lives on the stack and on pre-allocated arenas.

### Syscall — `intro`
A user-to-kernel transition (`read`, `write`, `mmap`). Cheapest is ~300 ns;
many are much more. Treated as the boundary of "fast code" — hot loops
never cross it.

### Vtable / Virtual call — `intro`
The dispatch table backing `virtual` methods. Each call requires a pointer
load and an indirect jump (~5–15 ns) and, more importantly, blocks the
compiler from inlining. Replaced by templates/CRTP in HFT code.

## Added in Lesson 0010 (Low-Latency C++ Best Practices)

### alignas(64) — `intro`
C++ keyword that forces a variable onto a 64-byte (cache-line) boundary.
Used on SPSC ring head/tail indices to prevent false sharing between
producer and consumer cores.

### Busy polling (CPU side) — `intro`
Spin in user space calling `_mm_pause()` on the data source (a ring, a NIC
queue) instead of sleeping. Near-zero wakeup latency; burns one core at
100% utilization. Used on the strategy thread; not on the logger.

### Cache coherence / Line ping-pong — `intro`
When two cores repeatedly write to the same cache line, the line bounces
between their L1 caches via the L3 (~30 ns per round-trip). The performance
killer that `alignas(64)` defends against.

### CPU isolation (`isolcpus`) — `intro`
Linux kernel boot parameter that tells the scheduler to leave specific
cores free of general tasks. Combined with `nohz_full` (no timer tick) and
`rcu_nocbs` (no RCU callbacks) for true HFT-grade isolation.

### `_mm_pause()` — `intro`
x86 intrinsic that hints to the CPU that this is a spin-wait loop. Slows
speculative execution, conserves power, friendlier to a sibling
hyperthread. Always used in tight polling loops.

### Lock-free vs Wait-free — `intro`
**Lock-free**: at least one thread always makes progress. **Wait-free**:
every thread completes in bounded steps. A correct SPSC ring with the
above pattern is wait-free; most MPMC queues are only lock-free.

### LTO (Link-Time Optimization) — `intro`
Compiler flag (`-flto`) that runs the optimizer at link time across all
translation units, enabling cross-TU inlining and dead-code elimination.
Stacks with PGO.

### `mlockall` — `intro`
Linux syscall that locks all of a process's pages into RAM, preventing the
kernel from paging them out. Used in HFT setups so a memory page fault
can't introduce ms-scale jitter.

### `memory_order_acquire` — `intro`
Atomic load ordering that pairs with `release` on the other side. Ensures
all reads after the acquire-load see writes done before the matching
release-store. Used by the SPSC consumer reading `head_`.

### `memory_order_relaxed` — `intro`
Atomic operation with no synchronization — only atomicity. Cheapest. Used
when the thread owns the variable (e.g. the producer reading its own
`head_`).

### `memory_order_release` — `intro`
Atomic store ordering. Guarantees all writes done before the store are
visible to a thread that acquire-loads the same atomic. The "publish" in
SPSC.

### `memory_order_seq_cst` — `intro`
Atomic ordering that gives a total global order over all seq_cst
operations. Default in `std::atomic`. ~5–10 ns overhead on x86
(MFENCE). Avoid unless you actually need it.

### `nohz_full` — `intro`
Linux boot parameter that disables the 1 kHz scheduling timer on isolated
cores when only one task is runnable. Removes ~1000 interrupts/sec of
jitter from the HFT hot path.

### MPSC / MPMC queue — `intro`
**MPSC**: multi-producer, single-consumer (e.g. many threads feeding one
logger). **MPMC**: multi-producer, multi-consumer. Both are more expensive
than SPSC; design the system to need SPSC wherever possible.

### PGO (Profile-Guided Optimization) — `intro`
Build twice: first with `-fprofile-generate` to instrument, run a
representative workload, then rebuild with `-fprofile-use` so the compiler
knows which branches are hot. 5–15% latency wins on the hot path.

### `pthread_setaffinity_np` — `intro`
POSIX call that pins a thread to a specific CPU core via a `cpu_set_t`
mask. The C++-side mechanism for the per-thread pinning that pairs with
`isolcpus`.

### `rcu_nocbs` — `intro`
Linux boot parameter that offloads RCU (read-copy-update) callbacks off
the specified cores. Removes a class of kernel work from the HFT cores.

### `SCHED_FIFO` — `intro`
Linux real-time scheduling class. A `SCHED_FIFO` thread runs until it
voluntarily blocks; preempts lower-priority work. Used for the strategy
thread.

### SPSC ring buffer — `intro`
Single-producer / single-consumer lock-free queue using a power-of-two
circular array and atomic head/tail indices with release/acquire ordering.
The HFT-grade inter-thread communication primitive.

### Synchronizes-with relationship — `intro`
The C++ memory-model term for the formal guarantee that a release-store on
one thread "synchronizes with" an acquire-load that reads its value on
another thread. The reason SPSC rings need release/acquire to be correct.

### Thread pinning — `intro`
Binding a thread to a specific CPU core so the scheduler can't migrate it.
Eliminates cache invalidation from migration and is the in-program half of
`isolcpus`-based isolation.

## Added in Lesson 0011 (Low-Latency vs Ultra-Low-Latency)

### Adverse selection (in latency context) — `intro`
Losing money systematically because faster participants see the same signal
microseconds before you and pick off the favorable side. The structural risk
of running at a lower tier than your venue's median competitor.

### App-to-app latency — `intro`
Latency measured between two points inside your application code only
(e.g. signal extracted → decision made). Excludes wire and kernel. Useful
for internal optimization, not for competitive comparison.

### ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) — `intro`
Custom silicon fabricated for one purpose. Faster than FPGAs but multi-
million-dollar tape-out cost and frozen logic. Tier 6 of the latency ladder;
only the largest desks justify it.

### Hardware timestamp — `intro`
A nanosecond-resolution timestamp attached to a packet by the NIC or FPGA at
ingress/egress. The only trustworthy clock at ULL scales — immune to OS
scheduling and clock skew.

### Inside-FPGA latency — `intro`
Latency measured between registers on a single FPGA, i.e. a fixed number of
clock cycles. At 250 MHz, 1 cycle = 4 ns. Fundamentally different unit than
wire-to-wire latency.

### Jitter (latency variability) — `intro`
The variability of latency across events, often quoted as `p99.99 − p50` or
as the standard deviation. ULL systems are judged on jitter as much as on
median latency.

### Latency ladder / tier — `intro`
The 6-rung industry mental model of trading-system latency, from Tier 0
(web app, ms) through Tier 6 (ASIC + microwave, ns + cross-market RF). Each
rung is ~10× more expensive than the one above.

### Latency tail — `intro`
The high-percentile portion of the latency distribution (p99, p99.9,
p99.99). At HFT message rates, tail events happen multiple times per
second; the tail is what loses money, not the mean.

### Low-latency (LL) — `intro`
Industry term for systems with microsecond-scale tick-to-trade (~1–100 µs).
Tuned C++, lock-free queues, kernel TCP. Tier 2 of the ladder.

### Microwave / RF link — `intro`
Line-of-sight wireless link used for cross-market arbitrage. Light through
air ≈ 1.0c vs ~0.67c through glass — a few ms edge over a thousand km. The
basis of the Chicago↔NJ trading corridor.

### One-way latency — `intro`
Time from event ingress to action emission, measured in one direction
(e.g. tick arrival → order on wire). Distinct from round-trip; both are
quoted in HFT and must be specified.

### p50 / p99 / p99.99 — `intro`
Quantiles of the latency distribution: 50%, 99%, 99.99% of events come in
under this latency. HFT systems are evaluated on the higher percentiles.

### Real-time (OS sense) — `intro`
Bounded worst-case latency. Distinct from "fast" — a 10 ms deterministic
system is real-time; a 100 ns average with a 10 ms tail is not. ULL systems
aim to be real-time first.

### Round-trip latency — `intro`
Time from event ingress to action egress through the full pipeline, including
the order leaving your NIC. The headline tick-to-trade number in most
benchmarks is wire-to-wire round-trip.

### Strategy cadence — `intro`
The natural decision rate of a strategy (per day, per second, per tick).
The single most useful input to deciding what tier of latency the strategy
needs.

### TSC (Time-Stamp Counter) — `intro`
x86 CPU register incremented every cycle. Read with `rdtsc` in ~10 ns;
nanosecond resolution but needs `tsc_reliable` and per-core synchronization
on multi-socket systems.

### Ultra-low-latency (ULL) — `intro`
Industry term for systems with nanosecond-scale tick-to-trade (~10 ns – 1
µs). FPGA, kernel-bypass NIC, hardware timestamps, microwave links. Tiers
3–6 of the ladder.

### Wire-to-wire latency — `intro`
Time from the last bit of an inbound packet arriving at the NIC to the
first bit of an outbound order leaving the NIC. The most defensible
endpoint pair for competitive benchmarking.

## Added in Lesson 0012 (RF Engineering in HFT)

### Anova Financial Networks — `intro`
Major common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT firms. Competitor
to McKay Brothers on the main US/EU corridors.

### Aurora (Aurora, IL) — `intro`
CME Group's data center, the futures venue side of the famous CME↔NJ
arbitrage corridor. Pairs with Carteret/Secaucus for the equity venues.

### Carteret (Carteret, NJ) — `intro`
The equities-side endpoint of the CME↔NJ corridor — Nasdaq's primary
data center. The NYSE-side anchor in Mahwah and Secaucus play the same
role.

### Common-carrier (microwave) — `intro`
Operating model where one company runs the towers, licenses, and antennas
and sells tiered access to multiple HFT firms. McKay Brothers and Anova
are the dominant examples on US/EU routes.

### E-band (millimeter-wave) — `intro`
71–86 GHz licensed band. Carries gigabits but only over 5–10 km hops due
to atmospheric absorption and rain fade. Used for last-mile in/out of
exchange data centers; not for long-haul.

### FCC licensing (microwave) — `intro`
Each individual microwave hop in the US requires an FCC frequency
authorization. The lower bands (6, 11 GHz) are heavily licensed and
incumbents have priority, which is one of the structural reasons HFT
firms rent rather than build.

### Fresnel zone — `intro`
The ellipsoidal volume around the line-of-sight between two microwave
antennas. Must be roughly 60% obstruction-free for the link to work.
Buildings, trees, terrain, and seasonal crops all matter for route planning.

### Great-circle distance — `intro`
Shortest path between two points on Earth's surface, ignoring terrain. The
floor against which any real route — fiber or microwave — is compared.

### Hollow-core fiber — `intro`
Optical fiber where light travels through an air-filled channel inside
photonic-crystal walls, at ~99% c instead of ~68% c through silica. Wider
bandwidth than microwave, weather-immune; ~1 ms slower than microwave one-way
on CME↔NJ. Many HFT firms now run both in parallel.

### Line-of-sight (LOS) — `intro`
Direct visual path between transmitter and receiver. Earth's curvature
limits hop length to 40–70 km on typical towers. HFT microwave links are
always LOS; tropospheric scatter is not used.

### McKay Brothers — `intro`
Dominant common-carrier microwave network operator for HFT corridors,
including a CME↔NJ route with published target of <8 ms round-trip.
Also offers hollow-core fiber and integrated packages.

### Microwave link — `intro`
Wireless point-to-point communication link in the 3–30 GHz range used for
long-haul HFT routes between exchanges. Travels through air at ~99.97% c,
narrow bandwidth (~100 Mbps), weather-sensitive, line-of-sight.

### Modulation (in HFT RF context) — `intro`
The scheme that maps bits onto a radio carrier (QPSK, 16-QAM, 256-QAM,
1024-QAM). Higher orders carry more bits per symbol but need higher SNR
and add encoding latency. HFT uses lower orders to minimize per-hop latency.

### Rain fade — `intro`
Signal attenuation due to rainfall absorbing radio energy. Sharply worse
at higher frequencies (severe at 80 GHz, negligible at 6 GHz). One of the
reasons HFT long-haul stays in lower bands.

### Refractive index — `intro`
Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to speed in a medium. Higher index =
slower light. Air ~1.0003 (~0.997c), hollow-core fiber ~1.005 (~0.995c),
silica fiber ~1.47 (~0.68c). The dominant physics behind the microwave
vs fiber gap.

### Sponsored access / Common carrier vs Private link — `intro`
**Common-carrier**: shared infrastructure rented by multiple HFT desks
(McKay, Anova). **Private link**: a single firm owns the towers and
licenses. Largest desks may build private; everyone else rents.

### Tier (microwave subscription) — `intro`
A pricing/priority level for a common-carrier microwave link. Premium tier
gets the lowest latency and dedicated slots; standard tier pays a slightly
higher serialization delay. Annual cost: undisclosed but in the seven
figures per route at premium.

### Tower spacing / Hop length — `intro`
Practical distance between consecutive microwave repeater towers, typically
40–70 km on long-haul HFT links. Limited by Earth's curvature and tower
height. Each hop adds ~10s of ns of equipment latency.

## Added in Lessons 0013–0024 (batch update, 2026-06-10)

Compact form: one-line definitions grouped by source lesson. Promote to fuller
entries as terms get used in conversation.

### From Lesson 0013 (DMA)

- **Direct Market Access (Trading DMA)** — Buy-side firm submits orders directly to the exchange matching engine through a broker's infrastructure, no human in between.
- **Sponsored Access** — Lowest-latency form of DMA where the buy-side uses the broker's MPID and connectivity but skips most of the broker's order-management stack.
- **Naked access** — Pre-2011 sponsored access with no pre-trade risk filter. Prohibited by Rule 15c3-5.
- **MPID** — Market Participant Identifier, the 4-character code identifying a broker on a venue. Sponsored customers trade under their sponsor's MPID.
- **FIX protocol** — The dominant exchange messaging protocol for orders. NewOrderSingle = 35=D.
- **SEC Rule 15c3-5** — US Market Access Rule (2011). Requires brokers to maintain undisableable pre-trade risk controls on customer order flow.
- **Direct Memory Access (Hardware DMA)** — Peripheral (NIC, FPGA, GPU) reads/writes host RAM via PCIe without CPU executing every transfer.
- **Descriptor ring** — Pre-allocated array in host memory; entries describe DMA transfers. The mailbox between CPU and device.
- **Doorbell register** — Memory-mapped register on device; CPU writes to it as a single PCIe write to signal "new work in the ring."
- **Zero-copy** — Design property where data is read/written from its final location, no intermediate buffers. Requires DMA but isn't synonymous with it.
- **RDMA** — Remote DMA. Device accesses another machine's host memory over the network (InfiniBand, RoCE).
- **PIO** — Programmed I/O. CPU executes load/store instructions to copy every byte. The pre-DMA way.

### From Lesson 0014 (Hardware Acceleration)

- **DPU** — Data Processing Unit. SmartNIC with full ARM CPU complex and OS. NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando.
- **SmartNIC** — NIC with programmable packet engines and embedded compute. DPU is the marketing term.
- **NPU** — Neural Processing Unit. ASIC specialized for matmul + activation patterns of neural nets.
- **TPU** — Tensor Processing Unit. Google's NPU for training and inference.
- **Acceleration vs Offload** — Acceleration: same work, faster. Offload: same work, elsewhere so the original CPU is freed.

### From Lesson 0015 + 0020 (Alternative Data)

- **Alternative data (alt-data)** — Any non-traditional data source that hints at economic reality before official numbers. Must lead the official metric, be hard to replicate, and map to a tradable.
- **SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar)** — Satellite imaging technique that sees through clouds and at night. Used by Ursa Space for oil tanks and by ship trackers.
- **Ursa Space Systems** — NY firm tracking ~11,000 oil tanks worldwide via SAR.
- **Foursquare** — Geolocation provider; famous 2016 Chipotle revenue prediction from check-in foot-traffic.
- **NDVI** — Normalized Difference Vegetation Index: (NIR − RED) / (NIR + RED). Crop-health signal from satellite multispectral imagery.
- **AIS (Automatic Identification System)** — Mandatory ship position broadcast (ships >300 GT). Combined with SAR to catch dark-fleet behavior.
- **Alpha decay** — The phenomenon where alt-data signals lose value as more funds subscribe. The frontier always moves to harder data.
- **SafeGraph / Placer.ai / Veraset** — Major commercial geolocation data vendors for foot-traffic analytics.
- **RS Metrics / Orbital Insight / SpaceKnow / Planet Labs** — Major satellite alt-data providers.

### From Lesson 0016 (Order-Book Dynamics)

- **Limit Order Book (LOB)** — Continuously updated structure tracking all resting buy/sell orders, sorted by price-time priority.
- **Price-time priority** — Match incoming marketable orders first by price, then by FIFO arrival time within each price level.
- **Order-book imbalance** — `(bid_size − ask_size) / (bid_size + ask_size)`. Microstructure signal predicting short-term mid drift.
- **Top of book** — Best bid + best ask only. L1 data.
- **Queue position** — Where your order sits in the FIFO at its price level. Determines fill priority.
- **LOB events** — ADD, CANCEL, MODIFY, TRADE, NEW LEVEL.

### From Lesson 0017 (Market Making)

- **Reservation price** — In Avellaneda-Stoikov: the inventory-skewed "fair" price the MM uses as the center of its quotes. Not the mid when inventory ≠ 0.
- **Avellaneda-Stoikov framework** — Canonical mathematical treatment of optimal MM quoting under inventory risk and adverse selection.
- **Maker rebate** — Per-fill rebate paid by venues to liquidity-providing orders. Significant secondary income for MMs.
- **Designated Market Maker (DMM)** — MM with formal quoting obligations on a venue in exchange for benefits (relaxed OTR, rebates, sometimes flat fees).
- **Spread capture** — MM revenue mechanism: earn the bid-ask spread on round-trip fills.

### From Lesson 0018 (Statistical Arbitrage)

- **Statistical arbitrage** — Strategy family exploiting statistical patterns across many bets, profitable on average even if individual trades can lose. Not true arbitrage.
- **Pairs trading** — Long one asset, short a related one, trade the spread on mean reversion.
- **Cointegration** — Two non-stationary series whose linear combination is stationary. The math behind pairs trading.
- **Engle-Granger procedure** — Two-step test for cointegration: regress + ADF on residuals.
- **ADF (Augmented Dickey-Fuller) test** — Statistical test for unit root / non-stationarity.
- **Market-neutral** — Portfolio with zero net market beta exposure. Achieved by hedging out the index.
- **Factor neutrality** — Portfolio neutral to specific risk factors (sector, size, value, momentum). Tighter than market-neutral.

### From Lesson 0019 (Order-to-Trade Ratio)

- **Order-to-Trade Ratio (OTR)** — (orders + modifications + cancellations) / executions, per participant per instrument per day. Venue-enforced regulatory metric.
- **MiFID II RTS 9** — EU regulation operationalizing OTR limits at trading venues.
- **Article 51(3) MiFID II** — Requires venues to have systems limiting OTR to prevent disorderly trading.
- **ESU fee** — Excessive System Usage fee. Eurex's mechanism for charging participants who exceed OTR limits.
- **Quote stuffing** — Flooding venue with messages to slow competitors. Targeted by OTR caps.
- **Spoofing** — Posting orders with no intent to fill, to manipulate the book. Illegal; OTR is a noisy proxy.

### From Lesson 0021 (AI Preprocessing)

- **StandardScaler** — Z-score: (x − mean)/std. Default normalization for NNs.
- **RobustScaler** — (x − median)/IQR. Outlier-resistant.
- **Min-max scaling** — (x − min)/(max − min). Bounded to [0,1] but outlier-sensitive.
- **One-hot encoding** — Categorical → sparse binary vector. Simple, dimensionality-expanding.
- **Target encoding** — Categorical → mean target for that category. Powerful but leakage-prone.
- **Embedding (categorical)** — Learned dense vector per category. Standard NN approach.
- **Data augmentation** — Synthetic perturbations of training examples. Geometric, photometric, cutout, mixup. Mostly CV.
- **Walkforward split** — Chronological train/test split that respects time-series causality. Opposite of k-fold.
- **Leakage** — Future information accidentally present in training. Cardinal preprocessing sin.

### From Lesson 0022 (Object Detection)

- **YOLO** — "You Only Look Once" detector family. Production default for object detection.
- **DETR** — DEtection TRansformer. Set-prediction approach without anchors or NMS.
- **Grounding DINO** — Open-vocabulary detector: detects any class described by a text prompt.
- **NMS (Non-Maximum Suppression)** — Post-processing that collapses overlapping high-IoU detections to one.
- **IoU (Intersection over Union)** — Area of overlap / area of union. Box overlap metric in [0,1].
- **mAP** — Mean Average Precision. Standard detection benchmark. mAP@[0.5:0.95] is the strictest variant.
- **COCO** — Common Objects in Context. Reference dataset and metric standard.

### From Lesson 0023 (Segmentation)

- **Semantic segmentation** — Per-pixel class label. Doesn't distinguish individual instances.
- **Instance segmentation** — Per-pixel class + instance ID. Required for counting touching objects.
- **Panoptic segmentation** — Semantic + instance. "Things" get IDs; "stuff" (background) only gets class.
- **U-Net** — Encoder-decoder with skip connections. Foundational semantic-segmentation architecture.
- **Mask R-CNN** — Detection + per-instance mask head. Two-stage, accurate, slow.
- **SAM (Segment Anything Model)** — Meta 2023 foundation model for segmentation. Prompt-driven, zero-shot.
- **mIoU** — Mean IoU averaged across classes. Standard semantic-segmentation metric.
- **Dice coefficient** — 2·|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|). Boundary-friendly mask metric.

### From Lesson 0024 (Geometric Deep Learning)

- **Geometric Deep Learning (GDL)** — ML on non-Euclidean data (graphs, manifolds, Lie groups). Bronstein et al's framing.
- **Equivariance** — `f(g·x) = g·f(x)`. Output transforms predictably with input.
- **Invariance** — `f(g·x) = f(x)`. Output ignores transformation.
- **GNN (Graph Neural Network)** — Permutation-equivariant network on graphs. Message-passing over nodes/edges.
- **Lie group** — Continuous symmetry group (rotations SO(3), rigid motions SE(3), translations).
- **Group-equivariant network** — NN respecting a specified symmetry group's transformations.
- **Manifold network** — NN operating on data lying on a curved manifold (sphere, hyperbolic, SPD).
- **SPD manifold** — Symmetric Positive-Definite matrix cone. Where covariance matrices live.
- **Riemannian optimizer** — SGD/Adam variants that respect manifold structure of constrained parameter spaces.
- **PyTorch Geometric** — Standard PyTorch library for GNNs.
- **Geomstats** — Standard Python library for Riemannian computations and manifold-aware ML.

---

## Added in Lessons 0025–0028 (regression suite + alpha/beta, 2026-06-11)

- **OLS (Ordinary Least Squares)** — Fit β to minimize Σ(y − Xβ)². Closed form via the normal equations β = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy; computed stably via `np.linalg.lstsq` in `solutions/03_stat_arb_risk/pairs.py:_ols`.
- **Normal equations** — XᵀXβ = Xᵀy, the first-order conditions of OLS. Conceptual form only; inverting XᵀX in code amplifies rounding error when features are collinear.
- **R² (coefficient of determination)** — 1 − SSR/TSS, fraction of target variance explained. In-sample R² only grows with added features; out-of-sample R² is the honest number and can be negative. A few percent is good on daily returns.
- **Standard error (coefficient)** — Uncertainty of an OLS coefficient, from σ̂²(XᵀX)⁻¹. β̂/SE is the t-statistic; powers the Dickey-Fuller test and the "is the alpha real?" question.
- **Shrinkage (learning rate ν, boosting)** — Scaling each boosted tree's contribution by ν before adding (sklearn default 0.1). Lower ν + more trees generalizes better. Distinct from covariance shrinkage (Lesson 0006).
- **Stochastic gradient boosting (subsample)** — Fitting each boosting round on a random row sample (`subsample < 1`), trading a little bias for variance reduction.
- **Function-space gradient descent** — Boosting's framing: each round adds a tree approximating the negative loss-gradient at every training point — a gradient step where the step is a function.
- **Sigmoid (logistic function)** — σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), maps a linear score to (0,1). σ(0)=0.5, σ(±2)≈0.88/0.12. The link function of logistic regression and a classic NN activation.
- **Log-loss (cross-entropy)** — −[y·ln p̂ + (1−y)·ln(1−p̂)]. Unbounded penalty for confident wrongness; forces calibrated probabilities. The loss logistic regression minimizes.
- **Logistic regression** — Linear score + sigmoid, fit by log-loss; a *classifier* despite the name. Not used in this repo by design — binarizing `fwd_ret_1d` would destroy the magnitudes the top-N ranking needs.
- **Linear probability model** — OLS fit directly to a 0/1 label. Works crudely; predictions escape [0,1]. The "why logistic regression exists" foil.
- **Calibration (probability)** — Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies ("0.9 events happen 90% of the time"). Distinct from ranking quality (AUC).
- **CAPM** — r_s = α + β·r_m + ε. Single-factor model decomposing strategy returns into market exposure and skill. Estimated with the same OLS as everything else.
- **Beta (β, market)** — cov(r_s, r_m)/var(r_m): the OLS slope of strategy returns on market returns. β≈0 = market-neutral. Same formula as `hedge_ratio` in exercise 03 — different x.
- **Alpha (α, Jensen's)** — The CAPM regression intercept: average return left after subtracting β×market. The scarce, paid-for part of performance; leverage replicates β but never α.
- **Market-neutral (measured)** — Portfolio whose *measured* β ≈ 0, re-estimated on a rolling basis. A maintained property, not a one-time label.
- **Factor model (multi-beta)** — CAPM generalized to several regressors (size, value, momentum — Fama-French). Multi-feature OLS; factor neutrality = driving all those betas to zero.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import math
import pandas as pd


def compute_metrics(eq: pd.Series) -> dict:
    eq = eq.dropna()
    if len(eq) < 2:
        return {"error": "Not enough data"}

    initial, final = float(eq.iloc[0]), float(eq.iloc[-1])
    total_return = final / initial - 1.0

    ret = eq.pct_change().dropna()
    n = len(ret)
    ann = 252.0

    cagr = (final / initial) ** (ann / max(1.0, n)) - 1.0
    vol = float(ret.std()) * math.sqrt(ann) if n else 0.0
    apr_simple = float(ret.mean()) * ann if n else 0.0
    sharpe = (float(ret.mean()) * ann) / vol if vol > 0 else 0.0

    cum = (1.0 + ret).cumprod()
    roll_max = cum.cummax()
    maxdd = float((cum / roll_max - 1.0).min()) if len(cum) else 0.0

    years = n / ann

    return {
        "Initial": initial,
        "Final": final,
        "TotalReturn": total_return,
        "Years(approx)": years,
        "CAGR": cagr,
        "APR_simple": apr_simple,
        "Vol": vol,
        "Sharpe": sharpe,
        "MaxDD": maxdd,
    }


def main() -> None:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Compute portfolio performance metrics from an equity CSV")
    p.add_argument("--equity_csv", type=str, default="walkforward_equity.csv", help="Path to equity CSV (date index, column 'equity')")
    args = p.parse_args()

    df = pd.read_csv(args.equity_csv, index_col=0, parse_dates=True)
    if "equity" not in df.columns:
        raise SystemExit("CSV must contain an 'equity' column")

    m = compute_metrics(df["equity"])        
    for k, v in m.items():
        if isinstance(v, float):
            if k in ("TotalReturn", "CAGR", "APR_simple", "Vol", "Sharpe", "MaxDD"):
                # Print returns/vol as percents except Sharpe
                if k == "Sharpe":
                    print(f"{k}: {v:.2f}")
                else:
                    print(f"{k}: {v:.2%}")
            else:
                print(f"{k}: {v:.4f}")
        else:
            print(f"{k}: {v}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
